events.title: Noni Madueke salvages draw for Arsenal at Newcastle United as Raya injured
events.summary: League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday. Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-half fightback from Newcastle held the defending champions to a 2-2 draw . The Gunners led on Saturday through Eberechi Eze’s strike after a dominant first 45 minutes. But Mikel Arteta’s men were suddenly headed for defeat when goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw provided a much-needed boost for under-fire Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle. Noni Madueke salvaged a point for Arsenal and stretched their lead at the top over surprise package Brighton to six points. However, the loss of influential goalkeeper David Raya to injury could provide a twist in the title race that many believed Arsenal would cruise. Newcastle remain in the bottom half of the table with just one win in six games in all competitions. Yet, Jaissle can point to his side’s second half performance as a potential turning point after a difficult start to his reign at St. James’ Park. Arsenal move back six points clear of third-placed Manchester City, but missed the chance to put their foot down in the defence of their title. Madueke continued his impressive form in the injury absence of Bukayo Saka and hit the post early on. Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes was roundly booed on his first return to Tyneside since making a £75 million ($98m) move to the Emirates Stadium In August. The Brazilian nearly silenced his former faithful when he prodded just wide from a Madueke cross as Arsenal pressed for the opener. It duly arrived 10 minutes before the break when Kai Havertz pounced on a poor touch by Lewis Hall and brilliantly played in Eze to blast high past Lukas Hornicek. Jaissle got the response he needed from his half-time team talk as Newcastle came out a completely different proposition after the break. Arsenal also played a part in letting the home side back into the game and lifting the 50,000 crowd in doing so. Martin Odegaard shanked his attempt at a long ball forward to allow William Osula to play in Barnes to level. Suddenly an Arsenal side that had kept seven clean sheets in their opening 10 league games was on the rocks. Thiaw bundled home a second for Newcastle just 13 minutes later after Dan Burn was left completely unmarked from a corner and his header was only parried by Raya. That proved to be one of Raya’s final interventions as the Spaniard had to be replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga. Raya would be a massive miss if the Spaniard is sidelined for a significant spell. But Arsenal regained their composure in time to salvage a point that keeps them well in the driving seat to retain the title. Odegaard made amends for his earlier error by freeing Madueke down the right and he cut inside before his tame deflected shot found a way past Hornicek. Madueke told Sky Sports that he thought 2-2 was a “fair” result. “Game of two halves is fair. First half we were outstanding. Should have got three goals to be honest. Missed a couple of chances myself. Everything else was there,” he said. “The second half, the first 20 minutes, was not good by our standard. When you give this team and crowd belief at home, it is difficult. We showed character to get back in the game, but 2-2 is a fair result.”

events.title: Iran strikes 3 tankers as it shows off missile launchers, and other Mideast news
events.summary: Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States and Israel accelerates once more. Meanwhile, in the Gaza Strip , an Israeli airstrike hit a truck carrying food, killing three men, the head of Shifa Hospital said. The Israeli military said that it struck Islamic Jihad militants. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here . Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher that it said was capable of firing two liquid-fueled missiles. The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory. The location of the missile site wasn't revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter statements from Washington that the U.S. has destroyed the missile program, amid fears that the war could intensify once again. During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, said that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly." “We have integrated ‘surprises’ and highly effective assets into our combat structure," he said. Separately, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday that Tehran remained in contact with mediators from Qatar who visited Iran on Friday to explore “whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy.” At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint. The U.K. military’s maritime security center said in online postings that two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait. One was hit in the stern, the other in the engine room, and there were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported. Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled There was no immediate comment from Iran on the center’s report. The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait before noon and caught fire. State media also said that the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels, aimed at foiling the U.S. military’s efforts to escort shipping through the narrows. Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports. An Israeli strike hit a truck carrying food in Gaza City’s Tel al-Hawa district on Saturday, said Mohamed Abu Selmiya, the director of Shifa Hospital, where the casualties were taken. Three men in the truck were killed, Abu Selmiya told The Associated Press. Videos circulating online showed a pickup truck reduced to twisted metal with boxes of cooked rice torn open in the back. It wasn't immediately known where the food was being taken or whether it was connected to an aid organization. Most of Gaza's more than 2 million people are homeless and dependent on food distributions by the United Nations and other aid groups. The Israeli military said later Saturday that it had struck Islamic Jihad militants who were traveling in a vehicle used to transport food and logistical supplies to fellow militants. The vehicle wasn't visibly marked as belonging to a humanitarian aid organization, the military said. One of the men had been fired from such an organization after Israel's military notified it of his militant role, a military official said on condition of anonymity in line with military regulations. The men were targeted because they had “advanced attacks” against Israel's military and civilians in recent weeks, the military added. Israel has continued airstrikes almost daily even after a ceasefire deal with Hamas came into effect in October 2025. The Israeli fire has killed more than 1,650 people during that time, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn't distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll, but says women and children make up around half the dead. Sally Abou AlJoud reported from Beirut, and Wafaa Shurafa from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip.

events.title: Even FEMA officials are worried about the string of outages and withdrew extra cash — ‘This is scary, and there is no leadership’
events.summary: The Trump administration has insisted that the recent surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure. Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence. One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency. “There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post . “This is scary, and there is no leadership.” FEMA didn’t respond to a request for comment. Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already on edge after the Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS , which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains. Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” The Nvidia spy scandal also didn’t help sentiment. Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable. Days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo , United Airlines , and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves. U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch newly uncovered vulnerabilities were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Despite the administration’s denials that cybersecurity was an issue, the White House removed U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday. CNN also reported Friday that said the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database—the second such breach in recent months. The steady drumbeat of alarming news has pushed many Americans into panic mode. Costco and Walmart have seen more shoppers stocking up on emergency supplies. “Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco,” Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a recent note. Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption. And for good measure, the stock market has been pummeled with some of the worst declines since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic as investors fear the end of the AI boom could take the U.S. economy down with it. The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has caused Americans to fear the worst. Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press last week “there’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack. “We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.” But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino , Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages. “This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The county at the heart of America's data center boom hits pause on new projects
events.summary: Virginia's Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. Nathan Howard/Bloomberg via Getty Images Virginia's Loudoun County paused legislative data center applications for a year. Loudoun officials say the pause will give the county time to review its data center regulations. Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers worldwide. The Virginia county at the heart of America's data center boom has paused applications for a year. Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors voted for a break on data center and electrical substation applications during a meeting earlier this week. Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, which earned it the nickname "Data Center Alley." Google and many other tech companies have facilities there. The board said the pause will end once it decides on amendments to Loudoun County's comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance. The board initiated a review of its data center and electrical substation policies in February 2024. "The Board's reason for considering pausing action on legislative applications is to allow time for the county to complete the ongoing review of current data center policies and regulations," a press release from Loudoun County said. The county said developers can continue to submit applications during the pause, and Loudoun County staff will continue to review them and schedule hearings with the planning commission. However, the board says there will be no public hearings or votes until the review is complete. The decision could affect 33 active applications, according to the county. Many US towns and cities have paused or outright banned large data center projects as residents debate their impact on communities. Supporters say new data center developments will create jobs and boost local economies. Critics are concerned about how they could affect the environment, utility costs, and their quality of life. Despite support from the Trump administration and influential tech leaders, data centers proved deeply unpopular during the US midterm elections earlier this month, playing a major role in ushering in a so-called "blue wave" of Democratic candidates. events.title: I grew up with 5 siblings and raised 4 kids. The biggest lesson I learned is that fair doesn't always mean equal.
events.summary: The author grew up with five siblings and learned a lot about parenting before having her four kids. Patty Schmidt I grew up with five siblings and learned about fairness and conflict long before becoming a mom. I became a stepmom at 25 and used lessons from my childhood to help raise my four kids. I've learned that every child needs something different and not every problem needs fixing. My two sisters, three brothers , and I were raised by parents who married just out of high school. They were young and figuring out adulthood while raising babies , yet they stayed together through all the peaks and valleys that came with it. By the time I became a stepmom at 25, I already knew a few things about raising children . I knew fairness didn't always mean giving everyone the same thing. I knew some arguments required an adult and others disappeared faster without one. I had learned all of this before reading a single parenting book because of growing up with so many other children around. A large family can be daunting, beautiful and gritty, sometimes all in the same afternoon. There was less individual attention to go around, but there was more love coming from more directions. We learned to share space, read moods, recover from arguments, and recognize when one of us really needed time to ourselves. We helped raise each other If one sibling was in trouble, the news would eventually make its way through the house. Secrets were difficult to keep, and privacy was a luxury. You knew not to get too attached to your older sister's motorcycle-riding new boyfriend because he probably would not be around forever. My parents were in charge , but the six of us helped raise one another. Older siblings became second parents, whether they volunteered for the role or not. Younger siblings learned to keep up with the pack. We watched each other make mistakes and recover from heartbreak. It was my first education in human nature. Years later, those lessons followed me into a family of my own. Today, our four children range in age from 16 to 32. I have parented through the late 1990s and every decade since, into a world that my 25-year-old self could never have imagined. Parenting has changed over those years, but so have I. Less attention can teach children to pay attention Children in large families don't receive the same amount of individual attention. There is simply too much happening at once. The middle-schooler needs a ride. The toddler is crying again. Someone can't find a shoe. The grumpy teenager is attempting to slip unnoticed out the door. As a child, I learned to observe the people around me. I could tell when one sibling wanted advice and when everyone would be better off if I stayed out of it. That awareness later helped me as a parent. With four children, it wasn't always the loudest child who needed me most. Sometimes it was the one who had become unusually quiet. Parenting required me to look beyond what my children said and notice what had changed. Growing up with five siblings taught me to read a room way before I knew that was a skill. Fair does not always mean equal My four children needed different things from me. One might respond to a long conversation at midnight while another needs space before being willing to open up. One required a firm boundary. A rule that motivated one child could make another shut down completely. When I was younger, I thought good parenting meant consistency. Experience taught me that consistency matters, but rigidity does not. Being a sibling prepared me for that reality. The six of us shared parents and a home, but we did not share the same childhood. Birth order, personalities, and family circumstances gave each of us a different experience. My children would also experience our family differently. Accepting that made me a more empathetic parent. Not every problem requires intervention The number of times I have said to myself, "They have no idea what they're talking about," comes from a place of peace. I promise. After raising four children , I sometimes hear newer parents discuss an issue as though the decision they make will determine the entire course of their child's life. I understand the feeling because I once had it, too. With the first child, every stage feels permanent. A bad grade becomes an academic crisis. A friendship ending feels like something that must be immediately fixed. By the fourth child, you know how quickly life changes. You also know that when a teenager promises he will never sneak out, it may be time to "trust, but verify." Experience taught me how to decide where my concern (or worry) would be useful. Large-family life had introduced me to that skill. With five siblings, there was always a new disagreement, questionable decision or romantic drama developing. Some situations called for help, but many worked themselves out before the rest of us fully understood what had happened. As a parent, I learned that stepping back could sometimes be as important as stepping in. My husband and I grew up, too We raised four children while also learning how to be a stronger couple. We had many opportunities to get things wrong, and we were forced to admit when we overreacted or when a strategy that once worked had stopped working. We learned to support each other through difficult stages, even when we disagreed. The mother I was at 25 is not the mother I am at 52. The younger version of me wanted to prevent every mistake. The older version knows that mistakes are often where the most important lessons begin. At 52, I am still rolling with it. Sometimes good parenting simply means admitting that the answer you used five years ago, or with a different child, no longer works. I learned that long before I had children of my own. In a family of six siblings, no one gets to remain exactly who they were. We pivot, forgive, compete, protect, and try again. Raising four children has required those same things. My siblings were my first lessons in human nature. My children have been the next four. They grew up under my care, but they helped raise me, too. I was a super sibling before I became a superparent, and I am still becoming both. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A French billionaire hunter is taking his fight global after California tax defeat
events.summary: French economist Gabriel Zucman speaks to the press after participating in a debate on taxing the super-rich at the National Assembly in Paris on October 1, 2025. STEPHANE DE SAKUTIN/AFP via Getty Images A 40-year-old French economist wants to put the world's billionaires on notice. Gabriel Zucman backed the California wealth tax before it was defeated at the polls. Now he's in Paris, rallying politicians to tax the super-rich, POLITICO reported . Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world's billionaires on notice. The 40-year-old French economist, who has spent more than a decade designing ways to tax the ultra-rich, hosts a summit against "international oligarchy" in Paris on Saturday. It comes less than three weeks after California voters rejected a billionaire tax he backed, in a campaign where Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other opponents spent more than $300 million to thwart the initiative. "Everywhere, we see very, very strong popular support for taxing billionaires," Zucman told POLITICO this week, arguing that his loss in California was only a minor setback. "That's true even in the United States." Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the US midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races. "Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?" said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. "The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world," he told POLITICO. Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) are due to speak at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue off the Champs-Élysées loaned for the occasion by Emmanuel Grégoire, the socialist mayor of Paris. Left-wing leaders from Italy, Brazil, Spain and the UK are also expected to attend. A "Paris Manifesto" published Friday calls for a minimum tax on the largest fortunes, protections for independent media and rules for artificial intelligence. The question is whether anyone outside the theater will buy into Zucman's ideas. His signature proposal, a minimum annual tax of 2% on the largest fortunes, was rejected by the French Senate last year. "It's a real program to save our democracy," said Eva Joly, a former French investigating judge who jailed the boss of oil giant Elf in the 1990s and later served as a European lawmaker for the Greens. Zucman "carries it brilliantly," she told POLITICO. The fight goes on Global talks on taxing the super-rich have stalled this year under the US presidency of the G20, according to Zucman, who expects the impasse to persist as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. Still, he hopes to revive the debate when Britain takes over the G20 presidency next year. In Brussels, meanwhile, tax legislation generally requires the unanimous agreement of all 27 EU governments, making a bloc-wide solution difficult. Rather than wait for international agreement, Zucman expects individual governments to take the lead, just as France did with value-added tax in the 1950s and several EU countries have done more recently with digital services taxes. Bills to tax the wealthy are in the works in the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, he said, while the British government has begun looking at the idea. Joly is less ready to write off Brussels, calling the EU "a field of possibilities." She argued that low taxes on multinationals distort competition with domestic firms and said it was the responsibility of the European Commission and Parliament to address the problem. There are also signs of movement on corporate taxation. European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on US tech giants to help fund the EU's next seven-year budget, POLITICO reported Thursday, after Trump's poor showing in the midterms eased fears of retaliation by Washington. "Europe cannot afford to calibrate its tax policy to America's mood swings," said Paul Monaghan, chief executive of the UK-based Fair Tax Foundation, which campaigns on corporate tax conduct. At the United Nations, negotiators will meet in Nairobi from November 30 to December 10 for the next round of talks on a global tax convention, with a final text due in 2027. Beyond the left In California, Zucman said, billionaires flooded voters with "disinformation" that the tax would bankrupt the health system, even though 90% of the revenue raised would have gone toward health care. But money was only part of the story. Unions split over the measure, POLITICO reported, and Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned against it . A state-only wealth tax "creates economic incentives for money and jobs to leave the state," his chief of staff, Nathan Barankin, said. Zucman rejects the notion that Saturday's gathering is a rally of the left. He said he had invited former EU competition chief Margrethe Vestager and former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi, but both declined. A spokesperson for Vestager declined to comment. Yet in France, the far-left France Unbowed party and the Greens were the only ones to fully embrace Zucman's proposed 2% annual wealth tax ahead of next spring's presidential election. MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, who is running for a left-wing coalition that includes the Socialists, has instead proposed to raise the tax rate for inheritances above €1.8 million, and a one-off 5% levy on fortunes over €100 million. François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po's OFCE, has challenged Zucman's arguments. In a paper updated last month , he argued that Zucman had exaggerated the extent to which billionaires are undertaxed and proposed a remedy that could do more harm than good. Geerolf acknowledged that the ultra-rich can use holding companies to shield income from taxation, but argued for closing the loophole instead of imposing an annual tax on fortunes. He also questioned estimates that the tax would raise €20 billion a year in France, putting the likely proceeds at just €2 billion to €6 billion. His verdict: "A real problem, a false diagnosis, a bad remedy." Other critics have also been mobilizing. Trop c'est trop ("Enough is enough"), a campaign group backed by business executive Eric Maumy, presented a study Wednesday characterizing Zucman's tax proposal as confiscatory and unconstitutional. But Zucman believes it is the status quo that is untenable. "Do you think it's normal that billionaires can pay zero personal tax?" he said. "It's the current situation that is radical." events.title: Is the Australian Dream easier overseas? Three stories from Berlin
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts These Australians are rewriting the Australian Dream – in Berlin These three millennials struggled to achieve the Australian Dream. This is what happened when they moved to Berlin. In the buzzing, pub-lined streets of Berlin's Neukölln, Toby Knyvett is rarely able to walk far without stopping. The Australian lighting designer, recognisable by his rock-star hair and broad Sydney accent, has just finished a library reading session with his two-year-old son Adam. Groceries are tucked beneath the child's stroller. But before heading home to cook dinner, Toby is taking Adam to a nearby playground to catch the last of the afternoon sunshine. During the 15-minute walk he stops every few steps to greet someone: a tattoo artist, the owner of a record shop, a customer emerging from a Späti, one of Berlin's ubiquitous corner shops. Friends crouch down to play with Adam while Toby exchanges neighbourhood news. These small encounters are among his favourite parts of the day. At the playground, Adam clambers over the equipment with a cheerful grin. Toby recognises several parents through his son. There are around 11 playgrounds within walking distance of the family's tiny apartment, along with Adam's daycare, shops, a library, music venues and several major public-transport lines. It is a compact life that Toby struggled to imagine achieving in Sydney. Adam was born in Berlin to Australian parents. His mother also works in the city's creative sector. Toby grew up on the outskirts of Sydney. In 2016, as he approached 30, Toby began looking closely at his future in Australia. His profile as a freelance lighting designer was rising. He was securing work at the Sydney Opera House and designing large installations, but the economics still did not add up. Even if he became one of Australia's 10 leading lighting designers, Toby calculated, he would be "lucky to ever get a mortgage on a house less than a 90-minute drive from the city". "I grew up on the fringes of Sydney, and I was sick of book-ending every long day with more hours of driving," he said. Toby had always wanted to live overseas and was approaching the age limit for several working-holiday visas. Following his partner to Berlin, Toby initially planned to spend three months in Germany before trying Canada and the United Kingdom. "But I never left," he said. "Berlin just clicked straight away." As the cost of living climbs in Australia, for many taking with it the dream of home ownership, some like Toby are exploring what it might be like to live and work in a different country. But how significant are the potential savings or career boost? And how does a cheaper way of life or greater work opportunities stack up against leaving behind family and homeland? What initially attracted Toby was Berlin's less commercial and more collective cultural scene. "In Sydney, you have to be a multimillionaire to have a pub and put on some bands, while in Berlin it's often done by collectives of volunteers," he said, exaggerating a little to make his point. Berlin was not free from bureaucracy, he cautioned, but it offered relatively affordable housing, a lower cost of living and public transport that made living without a car possible. Establishing himself professionally still took time. It was around 10 months before Toby secured his first locally paid job. Limited German language prevented him from working in text-heavy theatre, pushing him instead towards music, software and clients elsewhere in Europe. Then, in 2018, an unexpected opportunity transformed his career. Volkswagen offered Toby a full-time position using the same interactive software he had employed in his lighting installations to help develop prototype vehicles. He initially planned to stay for a year or two, but remained for six. "When Volkswagen came along, that was something I could never have done in Australia," he said. "We just don't make much stuff like that in Australia anymore, let alone design it." Today, Germany's contracting automotive industry has made employment less secure. Toby is combining his manufacturing experience with his creative skills to develop his own software and electronic products. Berlin did not eliminate career uncertainty. It gave him a different range of possibilities. After six years of full-time work at Volkswagen, Toby secured permanent residency in Germany, having previously lived and worked there on an EU Blue Card. A secure contract with Volkswagen also allowed Toby to do something he believed might never be possible in Sydney: buy a home. In 2019, he purchased a 50-square-metre apartment in Berlin.

events.summary: One of sport’s biggest rivalries takes centre stage as Liverpool host a Man United side in the EPL relegation zone. Who: Liverpool vs Manchester United What: English Premier League When: Sunday, November 22 , at 4:30pm (16:30 GMT) Where: Anfield in Liverpool, United Kingdom How to follow: Al Jazeera will have full text commentary coverage of the game with build-up from 13:30 GMT The latest rebuild of Manchester United begins at Liverpool on Sunday with Mauricio Pochettino in the hot seat – a position that some see as the impossible job. list 1 of 4 Usman Khawaja and David Warner taken off air over Australia’s Sandpapergate list 2 of 4 Cavaliers’ Harden passes Bryant, closes on Jordan in NBA 50-point game list list 3 of 4 Harry Kane to miss ‘a few months’ after injury as Bayern Munich draw list 4 of 4 Why is Pochettino the favourite to replace Carrick at Manchester United? The match at Anfield comes four days after the arrival of the Argentinian , who only oversaw his final game as United States coach on Wednesday. The 54-year-old is tasked with ending a 13-year wait for a 21st Premier League title – only Liverpool have won the competition as many times as the Red Devils. United sacked Michael Carrick last week with the team third from bottom in the league and suffering their worst league start for 40 years. Pochettino is the ninth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired with the club’s last league title in 2014 and he is the fourth in the last three years. United’s recent pain is made worse by Liverpool’s revival in the last decade, with the Reds sitting fourth in the table and hoping to mount a challenge this season to move clear as the team with the most English top-flight titles. What were the key takeaways from Pochettino’s Man United media conference? Given the swift turnaround from his previous role to his new one, Pochettino’s unveiling as United manager was combined with the pre-game media briefing ahead of the Anfield trip. Understandably, most of the questions centred on how United’s form can be reversed in the short and long-term. “It is about building our own way here,” Pochettino said when asked what he can do differently to the other managers who have taken on the role since Ferguson’s farewell. “The past is not going to help, to think about yesterday.” “We feel the support and we are going to work really hard to help the players to perform. That is the priority. “It is normal when you don’t win games that the confidence starts to go down,” he said. “I think the players need to feel from us that we believe and trust in them. “With the schedule we have ahead we have to settle on our principles. The players are intelligent, they have quality. Sometimes it is unlocking some things that didn’t appear for different reasons.” A key figure ⁠⁠⁠⁠in any rebuilding effort will be captain Bruno Fernandes, whose future has been the subject of speculation as he has ⁠⁠⁠⁠yet to agree a new deal. Pochettino revealed he had already held extensive talks with the Portugal midfielder and indicated he remained central to his plans. “Bruno is our captain and a very important player but other players have to feel they are important from the bottom to the top,” he said. “We spoke, I spent three hours chatting with all the players individually. It was ⁠⁠⁠⁠very nice contact.” Questions about the squad’s fitness levels have swirled around Old Trafford, but Pochettino refused to criticise what he had inherited. “It is about proposing that idea to be brave and take it to the field,” he said. “We ⁠⁠⁠⁠cannot talk about data without context. It is easy to manipulate data but we need to ⁠⁠⁠⁠be honest, sometimes they don’t show something that you can see on the field. “We are here not to denounce things. We are here to build something with our players.” What have Liverpool said ahead of Manchester United’s visit? Liverpool had lost consecutive games before their 3-1 win against bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace in their last match. The run summed up the mixed start to life at Anfield for Andoni Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer – the former Bournemouth manager admits an epic encounter awaits. “You don’t find bigger games than this, honestly. I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be part of these games,” Iraola said. “We have to acknowledge the importance of the game, and also a lot of ingredients, such as their new manager. “It is important for us in lots of different ways because we want to improve our form at home and the first chance we have to do that is on Sunday.” Iraola also admitted he fears Pochettino, whose Premier League experience was gained at Tottenham and Chelsea, will have an advantage because he does not know the Argentinian’s preferred tactics with his new club. “We’ve faced each other. Obviously he has a lot of Premier League games that we can look at and we can look at games in the US, but they still have this small advantage,” Iraola said.

events.title: ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says
events.summary: Meta employees have raised concerns about the company’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters . In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal. “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted. A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported. Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.” In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters. “These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.” The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations. A Meta spokesperson said employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback in order to implement privacy safeguards, adding that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public does and that some functions aren’t available elsewhere. As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android users have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse. “With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained. Since Muse was launched in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social-media giant’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI. But other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf. Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents. The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages . In recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo , United Airlines , Apple , and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out. Because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times . In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino , Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages. “This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Russian strike kills two, wounds 60, in Zelenskyy’s hometown
events.summary: Attack on Kryvyi Rih comes as Russian missiles land in NATO member Poland and US-led peace efforts face uncertainty. A Russian attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih has killed two people and wounded 60 others, according to local officials. The strikes hit the central Ukrainian city on Friday night, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while six children were among the injured. list 1 of 2 Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond? list 2 of 2 Russian crew evacuating ship hit by drones off coast of Finland About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were damaged, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s city administration. Vilkul said on Saturday that Russian forces launched further missiles after emergency workers arrived, hitting rescuers, medical personnel and utility crews. Footage released by Ukraine’s emergency services appeared to show additional strikes during the rescue operation. Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine killed two people in the southern Zaporizhia region, according to its governor. Russian authorities also reported six deaths, including a child, from a Ukrainian attack on a residential area in Russian-controlled Luhansk, an eastern Ukrainian region. The violence followed a separate incident on Friday in which two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a member of NATO, the military alliance linking the United States, Canada and European countries. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident on Friday as a deliberate provocation, questioning its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries preparing for a possible post-war security mission in Ukraine. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory. The incidents have unfolded as US President Donald Trump seeks progress in negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv. Trump said on Friday, following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, that the Russian leader wanted to end the war diplomatically. Zelenskyy, however, told reporters in Kyiv on Saturday that he remained less convinced than Washington that Putin was prepared to compromise. Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian withdrawal from the entire eastern Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses to surrender. Zelenskyy also reaffirmed Ukraine’s ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering Kyiv security guarantees resembling the alliance’s collective-defence commitments. Such guarantees remain under discussion as negotiations continue over how to end the war and protect Ukraine from future attacks.

events.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
events.summary: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

events.title: Trump says there could be a 'positive spin' from the latest FBI database hack
events.summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday that a reported hack into the FBI criminal records system could be positive. "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he said. President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database. The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information. The hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified and it is unclear what data was extracted. CNN had first reported on the suspected hack, citing sources familiar with the issue. In a wide-ranging interview on Fox, Trump said there could be upside from the news. "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he said. "I always like to put things on a positive spin." This would be the second recent intrusion into the FBI system; the previous one came in September, when a group known as "ShinyHunters" broke into an FBI jobs website. The result compromised data on current and former FBI employees and shut down part of the agency's operations until the issue was resolved. Trump said it's possible there could be information gleaned from the latest hack. "I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?" he said. "People should hear about it, because it actually put our country in danger, and so maybe we'll learn things that we wouldn't have learned otherwise." The FBI did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

events.title: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
events.summary: President Trump said Saturday he'd gladly work with Democrats to cap interest and fees on credit cards , arguing that card companies simply make too much money now. Why it matters: Though some argue capping rates would save consumers billions of dollars a year, the banking industry is equally adamant that it would deny credit to millions of Americans by making lending too risky. Driving the news: Trump, in a Fox News interview Saturday morning, was asked whether a rate cap on cards was something on which he could find common ground with Democrats. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), poised to be the new chair of the Senate Banking Committee, is an outspoken advocate for such caps and has recently said she's ready to work with Trump to pass a bill. What they're saying: " I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot — and the credit card fees that they charge. I'm all into it," Trump said . "I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise. But what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said 'let's charge a fee that's too high.' So I'm all for that," Trump said. "The credit card companies, they're getting too much. The fees are too high and the interests are too high." Context: The credit card industry argues that capping interest rates would reduce the revenue needed to cover losses when borrowers default, prompting lenders to reject more applicants. Reality check: This isn't the first time Trump has said he'd cap card rates. In January, he said on Truth Social he'd set a 10% cap for one year and any lender that didn't comply would face legal consequences. Nothing came of the threat, which credit unions claimed could deprive more than 47 million people of access to cards. Nonetheless, the mere idea was enough to send shares in major card issuers lower, and prompt a full-throated response from the industry. What to watch: As much as both Warren and Trump support the idea, it's not clear how much Democrats will want to prioritize it once they take control of Congress in January.

events.title: Some of my friendships faded after I became a mom. The ones that lasted got stronger.
events.summary: The author said some of her friendships have changed a lot since she had a child. Courtesy of Virginia Isaad. When I was pregnant, a lot of people reached out to offer their love and support. Once the baby arrived, things were very different. I'm learning to surround my family with people who actively support us regularly in meaningful ways. Pregnancy has an impressive way of getting even total strangers to squeal excitedly when they notice your bump. It's a happiness that grows with each month, seemingly from everyone around you. The joy of preparing for a baby can be downright infectious. So when the confetti has settled, and the baby arrives, it can feel a little lonely when that very excitement wanes and many people's attention goes away with it. For moms especially, this is a time of transition and adjustment, so the people who actually make an effort to be present and help are the ones who stand out. I've noticed there is now a very stark contrast between the relationships I have with the people who passively "like" an Instagram post with my baby and those who actually checked in on us months later. Those who ask how I'm doing, not just how the baby is. Those who offer to come spend time with us and cook a meal or clean instead of saying they'll take the baby while I do that — if they offer help at all. After talking to my mom friends , I've learned that I'm not alone in my experience. Yes, it's true that parenting takes a village, but it's not always made up of the people you expect. Relationships slowly shifted Since this was my first baby, I remember appreciating the friends, even the ones I only talked to on social media, who reached out, offering advice or items they were ready to pass along. I was so touched by the kindness and camaraderie. Now, as a mom to an 18-month-old, I make an effort to do the same for the new moms in my life. The dynamics have shifted with many of my friends, though. There are those who can't seem to comprehend how much my life has changed because of my son. At times, it feels like some are judging me and the choices I make, from choosing to stick to his schedule versus going out, to what products we're using, what food we're giving him, or what his sleep schedule is. It seems there's always someone with an opinion, whether I've asked for it or not. It can be quite a lot to take in. The ones that get to me the most are those who have been close to me in the past, both friends and family, but now seem to be present only on social media rather than calling to check in or making time for our family regularly. With time comes clarity Having a baby makes it crystal clear who wants to be in your life, and by extension, your baby's, and who is fine just being a witness to it. Realizing this has led me to shrink the circle of people I trust, which feels isolating at times. But it's also shown me something important. It's given me the clarity I needed to filter out the people who were only surface-level connections. I would rather surround my baby with people who make an effort with us, not those who passively click a heart on a picture. Sometimes that means downgrading relationships. Looking at that from another angle, it also means I'm upgrading the connections that matter. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Anthropic held its historic Nasdaq debut on Thursday, raising $93.5 billion and becoming one of the most valuable companies on the planet. A day after the Claude creator started trading, Nvidia's stock closed out its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. Anthropic opened at $111.50 on Thursday and closed on Friday at $88.91. Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar. "This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem. It was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge , which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020. Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a company that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence. That question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple , Microsoft , Alphabet , Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX . With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits. After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025. When going public was 'not worth it' Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar. "There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," said Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said. Anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus. For a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said. Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to." "At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy said. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that." Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation." That's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic missed its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money." Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The company looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to use alternatives from Amazon and Google as well.

events.title: India’s opposition stages protests against Meta over account removals
events.summary: Youth wing of Congress party issues a seven-day ‘ultimatum’ to the US technology giant, urging it to lift all restrictions. The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party has staged protests outside Meta offices in three cities, demanding that the United States technology company restore the Instagram accounts of its leaders. The protests took place in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram, near New Delhi, on Friday and led to clashes with police and security guards, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress on Saturday. list 1 of 4 ‘Manipulated’: Kenya to US midterms, Indian bots help campaigns sway votes list 2 of 4 The Global South’s digital future must not belong to Bezos and Musk list 3 of 4 Will India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement force Modi’s BJP to rethink its politics? list 4 of 4 How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building that houses Meta’s offices and clashed with police. In Mumbai, protesters spray-painted slogans on the walls outside, and in Gurugram they held banners reading “restore Youth Congress accounts”. The party has alleged that on November 19, Meta illegally withheld the Instagram accounts of the youth wing’s president and the party official overseeing the wing on orders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). In a statement accompanied by videos of the protests, the Congress youth wing said, “If Meta wants to do business in India, it must respect the Indian Constitution, not surrender to arbitrary BJP government orders.” It had also warned Meta on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the accounts were restored. Manu Jain, who runs the group’s social media, told the Reuters news agency on Saturday that two accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of other accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government are still restricted. The youth wing issued a seven-day “ultimatum” to the technology giant, urging it to lift all “restrictions on opposition voices, journalists and creators”. It asked how many Indian accounts were withheld on government orders in the past six months, and how many remain blocked. It also asked Meta to explain what it called the automated blocking of posts that mention Congress leader Rahul Gandhi or criticise Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP. On Saturday, the protesters also posted a video of workers putting up a banner in central Delhi that mocked Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, as “Mark BJPberg” – suggesting that Meta favours Modi’s party. Meta has yet to issue a statement on the matter. Police registered a complaint against four Youth Congress leaders in Mumbai and detained some protesters, Dainik Jagran English reported. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the ruling BJP, accused the protesters of vandalising Meta’s Hyderabad office and “flaunting it on social media”. India is Meta’s biggest market by users. In February, the government ordered platforms to remove unlawful content within three hours of notice, down from 36 hours. The government issued nearly 195,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July, the Indian Express reported. Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025, according to its disclosures. It said most were cases in which it was “obligated to proactively restrict content” under local law.

events.title: Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
events.summary: Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges. Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said. Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. list 1 of 4 Ecuador’s president denies existence of US military base list 2 of 4 Mexico captures FBI-wanted cartel boss in military raid list 3 of 4 What we know about Mexican drug cartel leaders still at large list 4 of 4 Is the US arming Mexican cartels? The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.” “I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.” Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of? Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel. Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States. US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge. The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction. “Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list. He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder. Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army. Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said. It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors. Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave. The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads. Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported. Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents. “These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

events.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
events.summary: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.
