events.title: I tried Ina Garten's overnight mac and cheese. It's super easy, and one of the best dishes I've made for Thanksgiving.
events.summary: Ina Garten's overnight mac and cheese was everyone's favorite dish at Friendsgiving. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I made Ina Garten's overnight mac and cheese recipe for Friendsgiving. The dish includes Gruyère and white cheddar, and the simple recipe barely requires any prep. It was the dish everyone couldn't stop talking about. From a comforting five-cheese penne to her easy weeknight Bolognese , an Ina Garten pasta dish has never led me astray. So why should I stop just because it's the holidays? The "Barefoot Contessa" star calls her overnight mac and cheese the "perfect make-ahead dish," which sounded great for the hectic season. Plus, Garten says it's the "creamiest, crustiest, most delicious mac and cheese" she's ever made. Obviously, I had to try it. Ina Garten's overnight mac and cheese only needs a few ingredients. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To make Garten's dish for four, you'll need:  8 ounces of cavatappi or elbow macaroni  3 cups of heavy cream  2 cups of grated Gruyère cheese 1 cup of grated sharp white cheddar  2 tablespoons of unsalted butter, melted ¼ teaspoon of ground nutmeg 1 ½ cups of fine fresh white breadcrumbs I doubled this recipe to make enough pasta for six people, and I should note that I didn't make my own breadcrumbs. I was cooking multiple Ina Garten dishes for Friendsgiving and, as Garten herself says, sometimes store-bought is fine! If you do want to make your own breadcrumbs, Garten's instructions are as follows: Remove the crusts from five slices of white bread and dice them. Put the bread into the bowl of a food processor fitted with the steel blade and process until you have fine crumbs. My prep needed to start the day before serving, and the first step was to (briefly) cook the pasta. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I brought a large pot of water to a boil and added 2 tablespoons of salt.  I let the pasta cook for four minutes, then drained the pot and set it aside. While the pasta was cooking, I grated both the Gruyère and sharp white cheddar cheeses. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider If you're making this dish for four, you'll want to grate 1 cup of the Gruyère and ½ cup of the cheddar.  Then I got to work on the sauce. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Unlike most mac-and-cheese pastas, you don't need to make a roux for Garten's overnight version.  After adding the grated cheeses to a mixing bowl, I threw in the heavy cream and seasonings. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Six cups of heavy cream sounded like too much, so I added a full 32-ounce bottle (equivalent to 4 cups) to the sauce. The result was still wonderfully creamy — trust me. Then I added the nutmeg, along with salt and pepper. You'll want to add 2 teaspoons of salt and 1 teaspoon of pepper if you're making this for four. Once the sauce was ready, I threw in the cavatappi pasta. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I stirred the hot pasta into the creamy mixture, then covered the bowl with plastic wrap and threw it in the fridge for 24 hours, per Garten's instructions.  The next day, I took my pasta out of the fridge and buttered my baking dish. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten recommends letting your creamy mixture sit at room temperature for about an hour before baking it. If you don't have that kind of time, she says you can microwave it for four minutes. I added the pasta mixture to my baking dish, along with the leftover cheeses. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider If you're making this for four, combine 1 cup of Gruyère with ½ cup of cheddar. I topped everything off with the breadcrumbs. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider If you made your own breadcrumbs, Garten recommends combining them with 2 tablespoons of melted butter before sprinkling them on top. I cooked my mac and cheese for 25 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit, rotating the dish halfway through. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Since you can prepare it a day or two ahead, this is a great pasta for a dinner party where you'll be juggling quite a few things — or a quick but easy dish to delight everyone at a potluck. Garten's overnight mac and cheese was the star of my Friendsgiving. I know I'll be making it long after the holidays have passed. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Among a delicious spread that included Garten's cornbread and mashed potatoes , as well as brisket, roast chicken, and the wildest Thanksgiving cake you've ever seen, this mac and cheese was still the clear favorite. We loved the dish so much that we even nibbled on it the next day without bothering to warm it up — it's that delicious. The breadcrumb crust gave each bite a nice crunch, and the sauce was decadent without overpowering the dish. My fiancé, who was my sous-chef for the night, said the pasta was "exceptionally creamy" and the "perfect mix of salt and breadcrumbs." "I love how all the pasta just hugs the cheese and breadcrumbs," our friend Jeff added. "It's like a hug in your mouth." Whether you're looking to impress at the next holiday party or just want a soothing bowl of ooey-gooey pasta , this overnight mac and cheese has got you covered. events.title: Trump says FBI hack might expose Russia "hoax"
events.summary: President Trump on Saturday said the reported hack of a crucial FBI database might have a silver lining — it could, he claimed, expose more details of what he called the " Russia Russia Russia hoax ." Why it matters: The president remains laser-focused on many of his past grievances about the FBI , even as the public grows increasingly alarmed about the vulnerability of government infrastructure. Driving the news: CNN and NBC reported Friday night that the FBI was looking into an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, which connects local and national law enforcement for information sharing. That follows breaches and outages that struck the FAA, NSA and USDA, just in the last week. What they're saying: Trump was asked about the FBI reports in a Fox News interview Saturday morning. "Well we just heard about it and I will say that it's not good, I don't like that," Trump said. "But maybe we'll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise. You had the Russia Russia Russia hoax, you had all these other hoaxes," he added, referring to Ukraine in particular. "Maybe we'll learn about them. Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place." "I always like to put things in a positive spin," Trump added. "Wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia Russia Russia," he said. The intrigue: The president's comments come just days after a summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia, after which he described Putin as a " friend ." What to watch: It's not clear who breached the FBI database, or what they might do with the data obtained.

events.title: US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
events.summary: What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress? The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not take power until January. Election officials are still certifying results, while the newly elected lawmakers are preparing to take office, and the outgoing Congress is continuing its legislative work. list 1 of 3 Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House list 2 of 3 Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia list 3 of 3 How is US Senate majority leader chosen? So what happens between now and January, and what will change as the 120th Congress takes office? After the elections, officials have been finalising the results and completing the certification process, which varies by state. On November 9, the existing Congress returned to Washington for what is known as the “lame-duck” session. A lame-duck session occurs when Congress meets after an election but before the new Congress takes office. This means the Republicans still have the majority in both chambers of Congress and can continue passing legislation until the new Congress takes office in January. November-December: New lawmakers prepare to take office During this time, newly elected members start preparing to take office in January. They attend orientation sessions in Washington, hire staff, and learn more about how Congress operates day-to-day. Political parties also choose their leaders in the House of Representatives and the Senate. The party controlling each chamber selects the majority leader, while the other party selects the minority leader. The House will also vote on a speaker, who leads the House leadership. The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as its Senate leader, entering the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight . Among Democrats, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator and current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York to be Senate majority leader, with a vote scheduled for December 1. Speaking on Al Jazeera’s This Is America , Democratic strategist Roger Fisk suggested that the differences between the two candidates may be more about their methods than their political goals. “I think the difference would probably come in the how rather than the what,” Fisk said. Republican strategist Doug Heye said the leadership debate reflects wider questions facing both parties after the midterms. “Both parties have somewhat of an identity crisis,” he said, referring to the Republicans’ losses and the future of the party but also the divisions in the Democratic Party between moderate Democrats and more progressive ones. December 11: A government funding deadline One of the biggest challenges of the current Congress is a December 11 deadline to approve government funding. Congress passed a temporary spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to keep the federal agencies functioning without approving a full-year budget. But before the measure expires, Congress must approve another bill to keep the government funded. If lawmakers do not reach a deal, part of the federal government could face a shutdown. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Heye suggested a temporary funding extension could push negotiations into February, by which time Democrats will control both chambers. “So that would probably go through February,” he said, referring to a possible continuing resolution. Heye also said the federal debt ceiling is another challenge for the new Congress. “These are two things that never come up on the campaign trail, but it can be very important to tell us about the next two years,” he added. The current Congress is expected to finalise its legislative work before the Christmas holidays. The House’s final sitting day is planned for December 17 and the Senate’s for December 18. But lawmakers could remain in Washington longer if major issues remain unresolved. Even if lawmakers finish their work earlier, the 119th Congress’s term does not officially end until January 3. January 3, 2027: The new Congress takes power The 120th Congress starts its term at noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, 2027. But January 3 falls on a Sunday, and Congress could pass a law setting a different date for the first meeting. When the new House convenes, lawmakers must elect a Speaker before being sworn in. Newly elected senators will also take their oaths. With Democrats controlling both chambers, they will gain authority over congressional committees, legislative priorities and investigations into the administration of President Donald Trump. “You’re going to have in the House and the Senate something called committee chairs, and they’re all going to be Democrats, and they’re all going to have subpoena power,” Heye told Al Jazeera.

events.title: An entrepreneur is transforming a Cold War-era nuclear silo into an underground data center. Take a look.
events.summary: Halik's decommissioned nuclear silo is 165 feet deep. Nuclear Bunker Living/YouTube Entrepreneur Nik Halik bought a defunct nuclear missile silo in Colorado for over $10 million. The US government once used the facility to power, house, and potentially fire nuclear missiles. Halik plans to turn the 200,000-square-foot facility into a data center to power AI. A decommissioned nuclear silo near Denver that could once launch three 4.5-megaton nuclear missiles at a moment's notice is now an entrepreneur's pet project. Nik Halik, an Australian venture capitalist, purchased the decommissioned Cold War-era nuclear missile silo from the US government in 2021 for more than $10 million. For the past five years, Halik has been overseeing its transformation into a modern, renovated facility, where he plans to house an AI data center . After recent tech outages have prompted some people to stock up on generators and emergency kits , the underground facility in Colorado offers a closer look at Cold War-era infrastructure built to operate off the grid, as well as efforts to protect servers in ultra-secure facilities. The project is on brand for Halik, a self-described "thrillionaire" whose past endeavors have included skydiving over Mount Everest , training in Russia as a civilian cosmonaut, and diving 5 miles deep to the deck of the Titanic . He said his interest in these types of structures pairs with his vision for what they could become. "I'm immersed in the world of castles and underground bunkers," Halik told Business Insider. "I'm a value-facturer. I like things that I can add value to." Halik took Business Insider on a tour of the facility . See what it looks like inside the roughly 75-year-old nuclear silo. The facility was built in Colorado in 1959 for $47 million, or $350 million in today's dollars. Other Titan I silos like Halik's were built in Colorado. Carl Iwasaki/Getty Images At the beginning of the Cold War, the US began developing intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) at a rapid pace. Following the US' first operational ICBM , the SM-65 Atlas, the Titan I went under development in the mid-1950s. According to the National Park Service , the Titan I missiles were 98 feet tall and could deliver a nuclear warhead over 6,000 miles. Eighteen silos, like Halik's and the one pictured, were built across the US to house these missiles during the Cold War. Four large diesel engines powered the facility. Another Titan I silo near Denver. Thanks to diesel power, the facilities could be powered without the grid. Carl Iwasaki/Getty Images Thanks to the silo's use of diesel fuel, it had the ability to stay running without being connected to the electrical grid. The amount of fuel in the silo was enough to fuel around 2,000 houses for roughly 2 weeks. Just one of the silo's three diesel tanks has the capacity to hold about 50,000 gallons of fuel, Halik told Business Insider. The missiles were removed from the silo less than a decade later. All Titan I missiles were decommissioned in 1965. Carl Iwasaki/Getty Images In all, 54 Titan I missiles were operational between April 1962 and January 1965, according to the National Park Service. Despite the impressive stature of the Titan I silos, they proved to be short-lived. All were removed by early 1965, becoming obsolete due to rapid technological developments that led to the Titan II and Minuteman I ICBMs. In the years that followed, the US government removed valuable materials from the silos and sold off most of the facilities to public and private owners. Halik said after his bunker was decommissioned, it was used by government defense contractors and The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. Halik is now renovating the silo at an estimated cost of $30 million. Halik's facility is in an isolated area near Denver, Colorado. Business Insider Halik, with help from others, has been renovating the facility, located in a top-secret location in Colorado, for over four years. Aside from the facility's rusty metal scraps and loose wires, other hidden dangers lurk throughout the complex. The basement level, Halik said, is riddled with cyanide, lead paint, mercury, and asbestos. The entrepreneur has taken a hands-on role in exploring and renovating the facility. Halik has taken a large role in the renovation process despite safety risks. Tyler Merkel He's documented every step of his journey in the facility on the YouTube channel Nuclear Bunker Living. The first episode, uploaded in September 2021, shows him exploring the bunker by himself for the first time. As Halik's videos show, he often jumps into the exploration and renovation headfirst, despite the safety risk. On one occasion, he crawled through a rusty pipe, only to realize later that it had a live wire running through it that he said could've electrocuted him instantly. "There are so many variables of danger here," Halik said in a video. "This place is unforgiving, and it always reciprocates with interest." The bunker totals 200,000 square feet. The bunker needed to be deep enough to house the 98-feet-tall Titan I missiles. Tyler Merkel The silo descends 165 feet below the surface, deep enough to house the missiles and the equipment necessary to launch them. Seventeen distinct chambers make up the facility, connected by a network of tunnels spanning 4,500 feet. A network of tunnels connects the complex's rooms. Tyler Merkel Different launcher rooms, control domes, a power dome, and other areas make the facility a sprawling complex. The most secure part of the complex can withstand a nuclear blast. One part of the facility has strong concrete walls reinforced with steel. Tyler Merkel One portion of the facility was built by what Halik called "Hoover Dam-type engineering." Featuring multiple layers of steel-reinforced concrete, each square inch of the wall could withstand roughly 15,000 pounds of pressure. In this room, operators would stand ready to launch the missiles at a moment's notice. Operators for the missiles would stand ready for a call from the Pentagon. Nuclear Bunker Living/YouTube The control room was where the missile operators would have pressed the fateful buttons to launch missiles that were 300 times more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima . "The fate of the Western world was in the hands of these 21- to 22-year-olds who had the keys to the missiles, ready to employ them on the instructions of the Pentagon from the president," Halik said. Halik wants to turn one part of the facility into a museum. Halik and his team found papers pertaining to the missile's launch in the bunker. Nuclear Bunker Living/YouTube Many relics still remain in the control room and other areas, including pieces of the desk where a launch would've been programmed. events.title: The 9 biggest differences between the 'Sunrise on the Reaping' book and movie
events.summary: Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is based on the novel by Suzanne Collins. The film stays true to the book, with a few noticeable exceptions. Maysilee's actions in the arena changed, and Plutarch Heavensbee played a larger role. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" was released on Friday, bringing Haymitch Abernathy's Hunger Games to the big screen. Directed by Francis Lawrence , the film was a largely faithful adaptation of Suzanne Collins' 2025 "Hunger Games" prequel , "Sunrise on the Reaping." It was no small feat to make the movie book-accurate, as the story features twice as many tributes sent into the Hunger Games arena and a slew of heartbreaking deaths that Haymitch, played by Joseph Zada, witnesses firsthand. However, Lawrence and his crew did make a few notable deviations from the original book in the movie, some of which had lasting implications for the larger "Hunger Games" universe. Check out nine of the biggest changes between the "Sunrise on the Reaping" book and movie. Spoilers ahead. The mockingjay pin only makes a blink-and-you'll-miss-it appearance. A Mockingjay pin from "The Hunger Games." MediaNews Group/Bay Area News via Getty Images Any "Hunger Games" fan knows the mockingjay pin is a significant symbol in the series. In the books, Madge Undersee gives Katniss the pin to wear as her token in the arena, and as a result, Katniss comes to be synonymous with the mockingjay as a beacon for the rebellion. In "Catching Fire," Katniss learns the pin originally belonged to Madge's aunt Maysilee Donner, who competed alongside Haymitch in the 50th Hunger Games. And in "Sunrise on the Reaping," readers get even more context about the pin. According to the novel, Tam Amber, Lenore Dove's uncle, designed the pin as part of a set for Maysilee and her twin Merrilee for their 13th birthdays. Merrilee lost her hummingbird pin, while Maysilee refused to wear hers because she thinks there is "something unnatural about a bird that's half-mutt," as she tells Haymitch. She says she will wear the pin if she makes it home from the Hunger Games after learning they're viewed as a symbol of resistance, though she's never given the chance. The pin's origin in the films has been different since "The Hunger Games" was released in 2012. Madge doesn't exist in the movie; instead, an older woman gives Katniss the pin at the Hob. The differentiation continues in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Tam Amber doesn't appear in the film at all, and there is no mention of him making the pins for the Donner sisters or of Lenore Dove's feelings about it. However, the sisters wear their pins to the reaping, and Maysilee quickly hands hers to Asterid, Katniss' mother, after her name is called. Haymitch and Maysilee never speak about the pin, and the film doesn't explain how it went from Asterid to the woman at the Hob. It's a plot hole the film leaves open. A pivotal showdown between Maysilee and the gamemakers didn't make the film. Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace as Haymitch Abernathy and Maysilee Donner in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Murray Close/Lionsgate Maysilee is crucial to Haymitch's experience in the Capitol and the arena in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." But the movie omits a scene from the book that leads to Maysilee's death. Toward the end of the games, Maysilee and Haymitch are fleeing from the career tributes Maritte and Silka and run into three gamemakers trying to fix an error Haymitch caused when he attacked the arena. The gamemakers try to run, but all three die. Maysilee shoots one with her poison blowdart, Maritte spears another with a trident, and the final gamemaker falls down the tube that leads to the Sub-A floor beneath the arena. It's an important scene in the book because it shows Haymitch that people don't have to submit to the rules the Capitol imposes on them. To punish her for her act of rebellion, the gamemakers later kill Maysilee with a mutt attack, programming large pink birds to attack only her. The showdown with the gamemakers doesn't happen in the movie, though Maysilee does die by a bird attack. Without the gamemakers, though, the mutt's attack seems to be a punishment for Haymitch rather than Maysilee herself. The film also changed Haymitch's relationship with Wellie and Silka. Courtesy of Lionsgate In the "Sunrise on the Reaping" novel, the final three tributes in the arena are Haymitch, Silka, and Wellie, a younger tribute. Haymitch sets off to find Wellie after Maysilee and Maritte die, calling for her until she responds by ringing the bike bell she brought into the arena as her token. Wellie is starving to death in a tree, and Haymitch tries to nurse her back to health during the night, giving her water and some of the rations sponsors gift him, including chocolate. As he feeds her, Silka comes to the bottom of the tree. She doesn't attack them. Instead, Haymitch hears her crying, and in a moment of District solidarity, he drops a few chocolates for her to eat. Though Silka later kills Wellie, it's one of the most bittersweet moments in the book , but it didn't make it into the film. In the movie, Haymitch hears Wellie's bell ringing after Maysilee dies, and he runs toward the sound to discover that Silka has already killed Wellie and taken the bell. Haymitch then defeats Silka with the help of the force field surrounding the arena, becoming the Victor, as he does in the book. The broad strokes of the scene are the same, but fans who only watch the movie won't see the moment of connection between Haymitch and Silka, nor Haymitch's kindness to Wellie. Lou Lou has a more in-depth backstory in the book. Murray Close/Lionsgate After Haymitch's district partner, Louella McCoy, dies in the chariot parade ahead of the Games, Snow replaces her with a body double. Haymitch and the other District 12 tributes decide to call her Lou Lou. While Lou Lou appears in the film, the movie omits some of the information the tributes learn about her in the book. In the book, Mags discovers Lou Lou has a device implanted in her chest that can sedate her. She also appears to have a speaker in her ear that can listen to her conversations, instruct her on what to say, and hurt her, with her ears bleeding throughout the book. Lou Lou also unintentionally reveals that she is from District 11, becoming emotional when she sees a roll from her home before the Games begin. None of that information is included in the film, and her appearance in the arena also differs slightly. Inside the arena, Lou Lou intentionally searches for Haymitch, saying, "Find Haymitch," as they cross paths. In the film, she stumbles upon him. He takes her under his wing in both, though. events.title: What Jensen Huang’s allies say they've told him since his resignation: 'Let's fight'
events.summary: Jensen Huang is fielding calls and emails from tech CEOs as he games out a possible return to Nvidia. Jens Kalaene/picture alliance via Getty Images Jensen Huang is working the phones as he games out a return to Nvidia as CEO. A slew of tech CEOs say they've recently spoken to the 63-year-old chip mogul. Nvidia's board said it has no plans to reinstate Huang as CEO. As Jensen Huang games out a possible return to Nvidia as CEO, the 63-year-old chip mogul is turning to a pocket-sized lifeline: his phone. On the other end of the line are a series of tech CEOs, Nvidia employees, and President Donald Trump, who are offering kind words and positing avenues by which he could return to the helm . "I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," venture capitalist Gavin Baker said recently in an interview on CNBC. "I think he has more to contribute to America, to AI, and technology." Huang resigned on November 12 in the wake of accusations that he had at least two affairs, one with a Chinese executive that US intelligence says is spying for Beijing and another with a direct report at Nvidia. Huang has since indicated an interest in returning as CEO. In a lengthy X post five days after he resigned, Huang said he's seen an "outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO." "Many continue to reach out to me directly," he added. Nvidia's board, however, has said that it has no plans to reinstate the founder, who wrote in a note to staff that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife, Lori Huang. Here's what some influential people say they told Huang. President Donald Trump President Trump said he called Huang to ask how he's doing. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images Trump says he called Jensen Huang at least twice since news of his affairs broke. In a White House press conference three days before Huang resigned, Trump said he'd called Huang that day "just to see if he's feeling all right." Trump said he asked Huang whether he knew that Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of Megaspeed and his alleged paramour, was a spy for China. Trump said Huang said he didn't know. Then, in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, Trump said Huang called him at a separate time, telling the president that he feels bad for what he's done to his family. The New York Times reported that in one of those calls, Trump urged Huang to fight to keep his job. Travis Kalanick, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick said he wrote to Huang advocating an Nvidia employee walkout. Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber who now heads an AI robotics firm called Atoms, said he wrote Huang with an auspicious promise. "I will show up to Nvidia HQ with a wafer-encrusted megaphone, with tons of Nvidia employees who want to walk out, tons of CEOs, founders," he said recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin. Kalanick resigned from Uber in 2017 under pressure following an investigation into its workplace culture. He said he told Huang that a petition for a CEO's return was good, but a walkout was better. "Let's fight for what's right," Kalanick said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman YUICHI YAMAZAKI/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he's spoken with Jensen Huang since the scandal. "It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen," Altman said at The New York Times DealBook summit. OpenAI President Greg Brockman, sitting beside Altman, said he and his wife are friends with Huang's family. He said he reached out "just to be there for him." Asked whether Huang thinks he can return as CEO, Altman said: "Greg and I have like a little more empathy toward the situation than the average person." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Satya Nadella said he has sympathy for Huang. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he texted Huang to let the Nvidia founder know he is thinking of him. "I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said at a media roundtable on November 17. At the DealBook summit, Nadella called the situation "pretty tragic." Venture capitalist Gavin Baker Gavin Baker said he told Jensen Huang to work out and watch the sunrise. Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said his "most consistent message" to Huang has been to work out and maintain healthy habits. "I have been telling Jensen that he needs to work out, watch the sunrise, and get eight hours of sleep," Baker said on CNBC. "Because to be a sound mind, he needs to be a sound body." Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at the hedge fund Atreides Management, said he considers Huang a friend and added that Huang has more to contribute to AI. events.title: Redwood Materials found a very practical use for AI: Sorting old batteries
events.summary: A Redwood Materials battery-sorting system. Redwood Materials A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Recycling batteries sounds like a great idea. Until you realize someone has to sort through mountains of them first. It's a tricky job. Batteries come in all shapes and sizes, with different chemical ingredients . Mixing up the wrong ones can make recycling less efficient and more expensive. Enter AI . Redwood Materials , the battery recycling startup founded by Tesla cofounder JB Straubel, has built an automated sorting system that can identify batteries with more than 98% accuracy, according to the company. Here's how it works. Old batteries arrive in a jumble of boxes and bins. Machines separate them into a single-file line. Each battery then passes through a tunnel equipped with cameras and sensors that examine its label, shape, and weight. AI figures out what kind of battery it is and sends it to the right place for recycling. Redwood developed an AI model for this, trained on the company's voluminous battery data, and it runs on a cluster of GPUs on site. The system was built in just a few months and can handle several tons of batteries an hour. Why does this matter? Redwood wants to recover valuable materials such as lithium, nickel, and cobalt, rather than relying so heavily on mining and imports. This is a neat example of AI tackling a messy, unglamorous industrial problem. And potentially making American manufacturing more competitive. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: The $120,500 cost of being ‘Sister’: SNL sketch puts a face on America’s caregiving crisis
events.summary: On the Nov. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live , host John Mulaney starred in a parody drug ad for “Sister,” “a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.” The sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it. Its jokes land on real pressure points in American caregiving: who does the work, what it costs them, and how much more of it is coming. 63 million Americans now provide ongoing care A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability. That is 45% more caregivers than a decade earlier. The work has also gotten harder. More than 40% of caregivers provide high-intensity care, and more than half perform medical and nursing tasks such as giving injections and managing catheters. Only 22% have been trained to do them. An aging population is the main driver, says Geoff Gross, founder and CEO of Medical Guardian, a Philadelphia-based medical alert and connected-care company. But strains on the broader care system are pushing more Americans into the role. “What we’re also seeing is pressures on in-home care and labor overall,” Gross said. “There’s a burden on caregivers right now that is not scalable.” Paid help is scarce and expensive. As gerontologists Jane Tavares and Marc Cohen wrote for Fortune , a home health aide runs a median of about $6,688 a month, while the direct care workforce remains underpaid and short-staffed. The bill comes due in lost wages and retirement savings The sketch opens with Mulaney’s character weighing a nursing home against a private aide who “could cost thousands a week.” For real families, the costs keep compounding long after the caregiving ends. A report published Nov. 4 by the AARP Public Policy Institute modeled the lifetime income losses of working caregivers born between 1981 and 1985. The typical caregiver in that group stands to lose about $120,500 in earnings, workplace retirement income, and Social Security, including roughly $15,400 in retirement and Social Security income alone. Across that single five-year birth cohort, the losses add up to an estimated $2.3 trillion. Only 3.4% of working caregivers in the model lost no work hours to care. Chandra Bozelko, who cares full-time for her parents, ran those numbers on her own family in a recent Fortune commentary. For some, the strain reaches the basics. In the 2025 AARP survey, 1 in 5 caregivers said they couldn’t afford necessities such as food. Women give three more years of care than men, and the gap is growing The sketch’s sharpest line comes from a doctor, played by Mikey Day, who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours.” Research from the University of Michigan published in October suggests the gap behind the joke is widening. If current rates hold, U.S. women can expect to spend seven years of their lives caring for older family members or friends, up from six in 2011. Men’s lifetime total held steady at four. The difference isn’t in caring for spouses, where men and women spend about the same time. It shows up in care for parents and grandparents. Edward Jones managing partner Penny Pennington has called it “the elder daughter phenomenon,” arguing that eldest daughters are quietly propping up family finances. “Women still bear disproportionate financial burden, time burden, and energy burden,” Gross said, adding that any progress on the issue “isn’t happening fast enough.” Demand for care will only grow. The U.S. Census Bureau projects that in 2029, Americans 65 and older will outnumber those under 18. “Caregiving is really a societal crisis, but it isn’t designated in that way as much as it should be compared to other things we read about each and every day,” Gross said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Diallo present as Africa’s Motsepe reiterates support for FIFA’s Infantino
events.summary: Africa’s CAF join South America’s CONMEBOL in giving unanimous support of FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election. African football supremo Patrice Motsepe has said that all 54 members of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) support Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president. Motsepe made the declaration on Saturday in Abuja, where CAF is holding its ordinary general assembly and at which one of Infantino’s two rivals, French football chief Philippe Diallo, is present. list 1 of 3 Usman Khawaja and David Warner taken off air over Australia’s Sandpapergate list 2 of 3 Can Mauricio Pochettino save Manchester United? list 3 of 3 ‘Total error of judgement’: Drone operator removes United training footage Former Japan Football Association president Kozo Tashima is the other candidate . The trio will learn whether they have been successful on March 18 next year in Rabat – the winning candidate must obtain a majority of the 211 associations. CAF’s support for Infantino comes hours after another of his steadfast supporters, South American football’s governing body CONMEBOL, gave him their “ unanimous ” backing. CAF has been consistently behind Infantino – who is seeking a fourth and final term – even after the furore he stirred up in July with his short-lived FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Morocco is cohosting the 2030 World Cup. “Gianni, you have our support on behalf of the 54 nations in Africa to be our candidate,” Motsepe said. “I have a report from all 54 member associations in Africa to say that we are unanimously supporting Gianni.” Infantino has faced multiple calls to step down and lost the backing of European football’s governing body UEFA, while CONCACAF has also been strident in its criticism of the 56-year-old Swiss lawyer. Motsepe, though, has been a vocal supporter, and Infantino said such loyalty was reciprocal. “You will always find, in me and in FIFA, a trusted partner,” Infantino told the assembly, announcing cash inflow of $25m to each member of CAF, starting January 2027 for development projects. On Wednesday, UEFA Vice President Laura McAllister told the AFP news agency that Diallo, a 63-year-old lawyer whose Senegalese-born father boxed for France at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, should not be seen as solely a European candidate. “He is a Francophone, which is an important asset in lots of CAF countries,” she said. McAllister, who in 2023 became the first woman to be elected a vice president of UEFA, noted that confederations do not vote as a bloc. “There is a soft space which Philippe can exploit and convince some federations within each confederation to support a reform agenda,” the 61-year-old said. “There is a lot of discomfort around the behaviour of Gianni Infantino and a desire to challenge the concentration of power in his hands. “This applies everywhere in world football. This is not about Europe; the same rules apply globally.”

events.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
events.summary: We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception. Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor. On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains. Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his. “The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied. Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped. So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account. So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. events.title: ‘An extraordinary and extreme backstop’: Earthjustice warns Army off bypassing paused Iowa permit
events.summary: A federal appeals court has paused the emergency permit authorizing the U.S. Army to blow up nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. But the Justice Department told the court Friday that the Army may be able to proceed without it. In a notice filed on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency, government lawyers said they would oppose a motion by two environmental groups to keep the permit on hold. The notice added that “in qualifying emergency situations,” EPA regulations authorize the Army, which is not a party to the case, “to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit” when there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.” The notice did not say whether the Army plans to go ahead with the detonation, now set for Monday, Nov. 23. An Army Sustainment Command spokesperson did not respond Friday when asked whether the Army would proceed while the stay is in place, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported . On Friday evening, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state, federal, and local agencies ahead of the planned blast. Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the groups, called the emergency provision “an extraordinary and extreme backstop” and said the groups “strongly urge” the Army not to rely on it. The standoff leaves residents of southeastern Iowa and western Illinois facing a weekend of uncertainty over whether a plume of lead-laden dust will drift across their towns and farmland on Monday. A one-sentence order The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued its order late Thursday, pausing the permit the EPA issued to the Army on Nov. 13 after finding the material posed an “imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment.” The pause lasts until the court rules on the groups’ emergency motion, which asks it to keep the permit on hold while it decides the case. The government said it would file its full response by Sunday. Cody Smith, director of climate initiatives at the Iowa Environmental Council, one of the groups that filed the lawsuit, said detonating without the court’s approval would be unlawful. The council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter argue that the permit lacks adequate protections for health and the environment, that the EPA did not fully consider alternatives, and that it was issued without the public notice and comment they say the rules require. Hours before the court acted, the Army postponed the detonation from Friday to Monday. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Monday was the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.” The 68 drums of lead azide, an explosive used to set off munitions, were stored on site for more than 20 years in a bath of ethanol and water. The Army says the material degraded and recrystallized, leaving it highly sensitive to friction and shock. Who knew, and when The blast is expected to release a plume of dust containing lead. Army maps modeled for a Friday detonation projected the dust settling across a roughly 25-mile stretch north of the plant, with low levels of airborne lead traveling farther. The Army asked some residents of Middletown , a town of about 360, to leave their homes during the blast because it could shatter windows. The permit required the Army to model the plume using conservative assumptions so as not to “under-predict” potential impacts, and it states that EPA and Army experts agree the modeling is “not necessarily representative of actual conditions.” The Army held a public open house about the planned detonation in mid-October. On Nov. 15 , five days before the original blast date, it released the detonation date and plume maps, meeting the permit’s requirement to publish a preliminary forecast at least five days in advance. Smith said the council began receiving calls from concerned residents on Monday, Nov. 16, and when it contacted state and local officials, “We were telling them for the first time.” Reynolds’ office has said neither the governor nor any state agency was told of the plans before the Army’s Nov. 15 announcement, Little Village reported . “This lawsuit is largely the outcome of a last resort,” Smith said. A letter from the EPA paints a different picture. Writing to Reynolds on Friday, Jim Macy, who heads the EPA’s Region 7 office, said the agency issued three emergency permits for the lead azide between April and September and notified Iowa’s congressional delegation, state lawmakers, and local officials each time, and again on Nov. 13 when it approved the detonation. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Illinois Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth, and Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek were among a bipartisan group of officials who wrote to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin urging a delay. “We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives,” they wrote, according to CBS News . Why the Army chose to blow it up The Army’s environmental assessment considered chemical neutralization, which would avoid a blast plume, but rejected it. The assessment concluded that the 7 to 22 days of handling it would require created an unacceptable risk of a fatal accidental detonation, with no guarantee that neutralization would work. Macy’s letter said the Army also weighed building a structure over the material, moving it to the plant’s open detonation unit, and leaving the drums in place, and found each posed “an unacceptable safety risk” because of “advanced crystallization.” The Army, he wrote, “concluded the only viable option was a controlled detonation in place with extensive mitigation measures.” The environmental groups say the Army chose detonation “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead.” “It’s not our role to recommend to the Army or the EPA how to deal with explosives most effectively,” Smith said. “As far as we can tell, it’s been stored on site for at least 20 years, and they’ve known about this for at least the last several months. And they decided to wait until the very last minute to issue that permit and make it publicly known.” In September 2025, the Army posted a federal contracting notice saying it planned to have American Ordnance LLC, which operates the plant, perform “lead azide neutralization.” The notice did not describe the method. The Army’s environmental assessment says the material’s degradation was discovered in March 2026

events.title: Amazon’s first digital photo frame is up to 50 percent off for Black Friday
events.summary: Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos. If you prefer the walnut trim over the birch or standard black models, it’s also on sale at Best Buy for $134.99 ($95 off) — which, like with the others, is the first discount we’ve seen. Amazon Alexa Photo Frame Where to Buy: $229.99 $114.99 at Amazon (birch) $199.99 $114.99 at Best Buy (black) $229.99 $134.99 at Best Buy (walnut) The Alexa Photo Frame features a 10-inch, semi-matte touchscreen that’s designed to make digital photos look more natural, with built-in light sensors that automatically adjust brightness throughout the day. It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud. You can choose which people or albums to display, or let Alexa Plus do the work, which often results in photos based on your facial expression, the season, and even the lighting. You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself. If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app. For example, you can add a recording of your kid explaining their Halloween costume to a trick-or-treating photo. Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up. We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member. A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads. That said, you don’t need a subscription to use it, and new users can always access a limited-time trial of Alexa Plus.

events.title: I've stayed at dozens of all-inclusives. My new favorite was surprisingly affordable and unlike any resort I've visited.
events.summary: I loved staying at Bahia Principe Escape Tequila, an all-inclusive resort with Texas-style barbecue, drag shows, and tons of bars and restaurants. Simone Paget I've stayed at many all-inclusive resorts. Bahia Principe Escape Tequila especially impressed me. Throughout my stay, I had a lot of tasty food, including poolside tacos and Texas-style barbecue . The resort blew me away with its value and nightlife, even if parts of the trip weren't perfect. As someone who travels to all-inclusive resorts frequently, I find many of them start to blend together, with similar food options and predictable entertainment. If I never eat at another bland buffet restaurant or hear a requisite cover band sing slightly off-key 80s hits, I'll be OK. However, one of my most recent trips to an all-inclusive resort left me genuinely surprised. In April, my best friend and I stayed at Bahia Principe Escape Tequila, an adults-only all-inclusive resort about an hour and a half south of Cancún. We went in with zero expectations, only hoping to have some long-overdue R&R on the beach and catch up over margaritas by the pool. By the time we left, we'd gotten so much more. Our stay felt like a great value for an all-inclusive resort. Tequila lobby Simone Paget When planning our stay, we saw double-occupancy rooms for as little as $289 a night, which felt like a great value for an all-inclusive resort that includes unlimited food and drinks, plus activities. We settled on four nights in a junior suite, which came to about $1,400. The nightly room rate was based on double occupancy, so my friend and I each had access to all-inclusive amenities at Bahia Principe Escape Tequila. Split between the two of us, we spent about $700 a person — or, broken down further, about $175 a person per night. Tequila has a lot of bars and restaurants, but we also paid to access sister resorts. Pool and DJ booth. Simone Paget Bahia Principe Escape Tequila has almost a dozen restaurants and bars within its property. However, it's also part of a mega-resort complex, which includes five Bahia Principe resorts: Tequila, Coba, Akumal, Tulum, and Sian Ka'an — each with its own restaurants, bars, and pools. When we checked in, we learned that for an additional fee (about CA$30) per person per day, we could upgrade our wristbands and get access to 50-plus restaurants in this resort complex. So, we did. The property was bright and colorful with lots of playful touches. Tequila signage Simone Paget A lot of other all-inclusive resorts I've visited were covered in beige and gray and lacking in personality. Meanwhile, one of my favorite aspects of Bahia Principe Escape Tequila was how fun the decor was. Throughout the resort, I found kitschy neon signs encouraging people to drink more tequila, along with tons of colorful patterns and lights. I even found nods to Mexican culture, like the colorful papel picado (traditional Mexican paper decorations) in common areas. The breakfast buffet was above average, with plenty of authentic Mexican options like tamales. Breakfast buffet offerings. Simone Paget I'm a self-proclaimed breakfast-buffet connoisseur, and the one at Bahian Principe Tequila didn't disappoint. I loved the balance of tasty American-style foods, like fluffy pancakes, and Mexican-style dishes , like empanadas and tamales. The buffet also had lots of fresh-tasting fruit. We were also able to get all-you-can-eat Texas-style barbecue. The Smoked Simone Paget One of our favorite dining experiences was at The Smoked, one of Tequila's restaurants, which serves all-you-can-eat Texas-style barbecue. Once again, the food was delicious. Texas BBQ dinner Simone Paget I had the smoked brisket , which was excellent, and it came with mac and cheese, grilled corn, and some of the creamiest mashed potatoes I've ever had. The main pool area was super nice and never felt too crowded. Tequila pool. Simone Paget At Tequila, the pool area was fairly large and complete with a DJ booth, though it didn't seem to get used during our stay. The decor felt super new and modern, with plenty of large day beds for lounging, available to use at no extra charge. The pool often felt very quiet, probably because we were visiting at a less busy time of year. We wanted to relax, so this suited us perfectly. The poolside snacks were top-tier. Casita Simone Paget We were able to order street tacos via a touchscreen kiosk from Casita, a Mexican snack bar right next to the pool area, whenever we got hungry. During our trip, a food cart would also appear on the pool deck mid-afternoon. From it, a vendor would serve tostilocos — street snacks made by cutting open a bag of corn chips, like Fritos or Doritos, and topping them with various salsas and condiments. They were delicious. I was also blown away by the evening entertainment options. Entertainment schedule. Simone Paget At night, Casita transforms into Tequila's nightlife hub. The nightly entertainment was unlike anything I've seen at another resort. As a huge "RuPaul's Drag Race" fan, I loved that we could catch a drag show while on vacation. Another entertainment highlight was the fake Mexican wedding party we attended, which included traditional Mexican dances, music, and a faux bride and groom. It was as silly and over-the-top as it sounds, and so much fun. I'm pretty sure the top-notch entertainment at Bahia Principe Tequila has ruined all other resorts for me. It also didn't take long to realize that the resort-hopping access was worth it. Ku_uk Simone Paget Although there's certainly enough to do and eat at Tequila, hopping around the resorts in the complex added a sense of adventure to every day. We checked out the various pools, sampled the drinks, and had dinner at a different resort every night. I had one of my favorite meals at Ku'uk, a Mexican fine-dining restaurant included with our upgraded wristband access. I'm still thinking about their pumpkin-seed hummus. I'm confident we'd still have had fun if we just stayed at Tequila, though. I found the various resorts could kind of bleed into one another and appear quite similar — especially at night or after a margarita or two. Everything we needed was within walking distance, or a short golf-cart ride away. Golf cart pick up in the lobby. Simone Paget All the resorts in the mega complex were within walking distance, except for Sian Ka'an, which was on the other side of the highway and required a golf cart to reach. Although it was easy to walk around Tequila, we often took complimentary golf-cart rides to and from the other resorts. Typically, drivers would stop golf carts in front of each resort's lobby every few minutes. We never had to wait long. The beach was a short walk from our room. View from our room. Simone Paget The resort complex where Tequila is located is huge, so most rooms aren't right on the beach. Our room had a lovely garden view and was only about a seven-minute walk from the beach. It felt crowded at times, though. Vie

events.title: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor says using AI is riskier for them
events.summary: The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers. For younger workers, using AI could come with a different set of professional risks than it does for their more experienced colleagues. “Because younger workers haven’t had the same amount of time in their career fields to build up their standing as experts, using a technology that blurs their own contribution to their work can feel especially risky,” Jessica Reif, an assistant professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, told Fortune . The survey of more than 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers, conducted in June through NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel, found that 58% of Gen Z employees use AI in their current roles, compared with 60% of baby boomers, 63% of millennials, and 67% of Gen Xers. Seramount defined Gen Z as workers 29 and younger. That leaves a puzzle. Gen Z workers, often cast as digital natives, use AI at nearly the same rate as baby boomers but show far less interest in getting better at it. Younger workers worry AI makes them look less capable Younger workers are considerably more concerned about what using AI might say about their own abilities. Some 22% of Gen Z employees surveyed by Seramount worry that using AI could lead others to question their skills, compared with 10% of millennials and Gen Xers and just 8% of baby boomers. Only 27% of Gen Z employees feel comfortable acknowledging their use of AI for a work task, compared with between 47% and 53% of their older colleagues. Those concerns are not entirely unfounded. In four experiments involving more than 4,400 participants, Reif, then at Duke University, and her co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll found in a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that employees described as receiving help from AI were perceived as less competent, less diligent, and lazier than those described as receiving other forms of help or whose use of help wasn’t specified. The stigma could also influence hiring decisions. In one experiment, managers who used AI less frequently themselves favored candidates who did not use AI, while managers who were more frequent AI users favored candidates who used it daily. The penalty in those experiments held regardless of the age of the employee being evaluated. But Reif said its consequences could be more substantial for workers who are still trying to establish themselves professionally. “A senior employee who uses AI has a more substantial record of results that can offset doubts about their effort or ability, but an early-career employee doesn’t have that record yet so others might weight their AI use more heavily when evaluating them,” Reif said. The pressure can work in the opposite direction, too. A survey of 3,001 professionals worldwide released Tuesday by the London School of Economics’ Inclusion Initiative and consulting firm Protiviti found that 48% of employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough at work, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. For workers at the beginning of their careers, that presents a dilemma: They need to demonstrate their ability to work with AI while also proving what they are capable of doing themselves. Gen Z is less convinced AI improves its work Beyond concerns about their professional reputation, younger workers appear less convinced of the benefits of using AI in the first place. Only 30% of Gen Z employees in Seramount’s survey believe AI helps them work more efficiently, compared with roughly half of their older colleagues. And 41% believe it improves the quality of their work, compared with 56% of Gen Xers. Young people are also questioning whether the immediate benefits of AI could come at the expense of their long-term development. A survey by Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29, released in April, found that 80% believe using AI tools is very or somewhat likely to make learning more difficult for them in the future. Among employed Gen Z respondents, 48% believe the risks of AI in the workforce outweigh its benefits, compared with 15% who believe the opposite. Some 69% place greater trust in work completed without AI than in AI-assisted work. That skepticism, as Fortune has reported, partly reflects how poorly schools, employers, and government have prepared young people for an AI economy . Gen Z feels less supported by employers Younger employees’ attitudes toward AI may also reflect the environments in which they are being asked to use it. Only 27% of Gen Z respondents in Seramount’s survey said their organization provides support to help them integrate AI into their work, compared with 38% of millennials and 43% of Gen Xers. Younger employees were also the least comfortable seeking help from colleagues on how to use AI tools, with only 18% saying they felt comfortable doing so, compared with 34% of baby boomers. Seramount suggested that junior employees may also have less need for AI in their current roles or more limited access to enterprise AI tools. The LSE and Protiviti research points to the importance of training in AI adoption across generations: 93% of employees who had received AI training used the technology at work, compared with 50% of those who had not. Not all research suggests young workers are being left behind on training, though. The LSE and Protiviti study found that 66% of Gen Z employees had received AI training in the past year, compared with 40% of baby boomers. That study polled professionals worldwide, while Seramount surveyed only U.S. workers. For employers, failing to engage their youngest employees in AI adoption could create a longer-term talent development problem, echoing warnings that automating entry-level roles could cost companies their future workforce . “If Gen Z falls behind on AI, employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline,” Diana Forster, senior director of research at Seramount, said in a press release . She called on employers to provide clearer guidelines, training, and opportunities for young employees to practice using the technology. Sam Altman sees an opening for young workers Despite the challenges young workers face in embracing AI, the technological disruption could also work in their favor. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes that periods of rapid technological change give people at the beginning of their careers a chance to gain a competitive advantage. events.title: Tech outages are fueling a new doomsday economy
events.summary: Recent technology outages have left some worried about AI cyberattacks and the U.S. electricity grid. Consumers have increased spending on emergency preparedness products as a result, according to exclusive data from Consumer Edge. Wall Street analysts have followed what the push toward doomsday prep has meant for retailers like Costco. Americans are shopping like there's no tomorrow. A spate of high-profile technology outages that grounded planes , halted email access and slowed bank transactions have left many people worried about artificial intelligence -driven cyberattacks and the state of the U.S. energy grid. Government officials have dismissed rumors and speculation circulating online that there could be a nefarious culprit for the series of malfunctions. Despite those assurances, consumers like Sabrina Cepeda are readying for a larger-scale technology blackout or other emergency event. In recent days, the Houston resident has purchased propane and lighter fluid for cooking and heating equipment that can be used without electricity. The mother of three also replenished her backup stockpiles of non-perishable foods, hygiene products and allergy medicine in the event that her family is homebound for several days. "I have a way to keep my family fed, clean, hydrated, warm and safe," said Cepeda, 39. "You want to have these things and not need them, rather than need them and not have them." The doomsday economy is catching a bid. Wall Street and retailers are taking note. At least half a dozen major technology outages took place in the U.S. between Nov. 12 and Nov. 17. In that time frame, spending at brands specializing in emergency products spiked about 400% compared with the same period a year prior, according to card data analyzed exclusively for CNBC by Consumer Edge. At Ready America, which sells products like emergency survival kits, prepackaged water and high-calorie food bars, sales through e-commerce platforms have seen a roughly five-fold increase in recent days. In addition, corporate customers who keep the Vista, California-based company's supplies in their offices in case of emergency have called in to order more. The company has rarely seen this much demand since the Covid pandemic sent Americans into lockdown more than six years ago, said Ready America President Trevyn Reese. As a result, Ready America asked its suppliers to scale up production. The family-owned business has faced a shortage of water purification tablets, and redirected shoppers to alternative offerings like prepackaged water pouches. "With everything going on in the news right now, we've seen a large spike of people wanting to get prepared," said Reese. While the string of outages brought power-related concerns to a boiling point, data shows that worries had been bubbling under the surface for weeks. Shoppers began significantly ramping up buying from emergency preparedness brands late last month, according to Consumer Edge. Around that time, Fox News reported that the Pentagon was preparing U.S. military bases to operate for at least 90 days without external support. Exacerbating those fears was the ongoing war with Iran that President Donald Trump signaled could ramp back up . Firearm trade group NSSF said that gun sales rose about 8% in October from the same month a year prior. Retailers and gun manufacturers have anecdotally reported that demand has remained elevated into November, which NSSF said can be attributed to a combination of uncertainty tied to the midterm election and the recent outages. "If people are investing in firearms and ammunition, they're telling you very directly, with their wallet, what their priority is," said Mark Oliva, NSSF's managing director of public affairs. "You're literally investing in a product that's going to be able to protect your life and protect the lives of your family." Now, the doomsday talk has begun making its way to Wall Street. Mizuho told clients on Monday that consumer worries about the outages — coupled with what the bank called "apocalyptic concerns" swirling on social media — drove shoppers to stock up on emergency supplies at Costco . As a result, Mizuho said it expects a key measure of non-fuel sales growth for Costco in November to rise above 10% for the first time since 2022. And RBC said so-called doomsday prepping has had a "real impact" on buying behavior around the globe over recent weeks. Still, the Canadian bank reported that the trend has so far boosted sales for only a small basket of items, such as shelf-stable proteins, water purification products and dry-pantry foods. Clients of Richard McWhorter, a private wealth advisor at SRM, have been rushing to Costco to buy goods in bulk and splurging for power generators. McWhorter said he's also fielded questions about how to prepare for a situation in which the financial system goes down. "I've never seen anything like this in my life," McWhorter said.

events.title: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
events.summary: British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine. British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway. The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February. list 1 of 3 Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit list 2 of 3 Swimmer braves tanker attacks to expose Hormuz contamination list 3 of 3 Iran says it downed US drones over Hormuz as bid to end war remains stalled Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast. Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said. No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels. Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait. In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off. The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO. Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week. Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”. “This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.” If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added. Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either. He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes. The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway. The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

events.title: I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad
events.summary: Life American in Denmark: The No. 1 lesson the Danes taught me about slowing down Work Getting laid off can be a lonely experience—I found an unexpected way to cope Unlocked We left the U.S. for Spain and bought a house for $72,000 Millennial Money I quit my $250K/year tech job–now I make $33K/year selling matcha Unlocked She bought an abandoned church for $45K and is turning it into her dream home I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas. My manager was only a few years older than me, and while my coworkers seemed motivated by the idea of working their way up to his position, I felt no desire to follow that path. It all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb. I wanted to work, but I couldn't wrap my head around building my whole identity around a job. I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve. For a long time, I wondered if something was wrong with me. It wasn't until I finally made a long-term move abroad about a decade ago that I realized it was okay to want something different. I never dreamed about traditional milestones After college, I got a job in travel sales. I was good at it. Talking about travel all day suited the wanderlust I'd carried since my first trip abroad in my teens. I continued working in sales, marketing and the odd temp role for years. But they were always just jobs. I didn't feel like they defined me or feel a calling to an industry or title the way people around me seemed to. Of course, I wanted financial stability, but I was unwilling to sacrifice my time and well-being to get it. I just didn't connect with the version of ambition that meant grinding toward a corner office. What I wanted the most wasn't status; it was freedom, growth and new experiences. The wanderlust eventually caught up to me, and at 26 I moved to Spain to teach English. Even though I was working, people saw it as taking a year off from my career and warned me it could damage my resume. I simply didn't care. Living for my resume had never made sense to me. Looking back, I think being abroad offered an escape from the pressure to chase the traditional path of the American Dream. There, I felt free to enjoy life and figure out who I was without worrying about what box I needed to tick next. I wanted to stay in Spain, but I couldn't find a visa that would let me live there long-term, so I returned to the U.S. I became a serial job hopper for almost 10 years, quitting a job every year to spend summers visiting friends in the Netherlands, the U.K. and Switzerland or solo traveling in Spain on the money I'd saved up. On the personal side, I wasn't in a rush to get married or have kids . In my 30s, single and childfree, I felt like I was failing at adulthood, even though deep down, I didn't actually want the things I was supposedly behind on. Settling down just because everyone else was doing it never felt right to me. And I couldn't shake the dream of living in Europe. In my 20s, people mostly assumed my desire to travel was a phase. By my 30s, the conversations had shifted and I was getting pulled aside. Friends, family and colleagues all had some version of the same message: It was time to get serious and build a life in Texas. But my gut said to try one more time. So I did. Moving abroad helped me redefine success In 2015, on my fourth attempt, I finally made it to Spain for good . It was scary to shake things up when everyone around me was settling down, but deep down I knew at 35, this was my chance to stop trying to conform and start building a life that felt right for me. In my new home, the pace was slower. I quickly noticed that people actually took their vacations. Strangers at a dinner party didn't immediately ask me what I did for work. Adults in their 30s, 40s and beyond were out living full social lives. Single, childfree women my age didn't feel like an anomaly. Living abroad didn't solve everything overnight. I still had to figure out how to support myself. But having the space to define myself professionally without constant judgment changed what felt possible. In 2017, I launched She Hit Refresh , where I help women over 30 figure out how to move to Europe and build new lives for themselves. It's not something I could have created from anywhere else, with any other experience than my own. In the process, I've met so many others who left corporate America behind to create something different for themselves. I've seen more women asking the same questions I spent years asking myself. Burnt out, disillusioned with hustle culture, realizing that checking all the boxes of the American Dream they grew up on didn't deliver the feeling they were promised. We're all figuring it out together; each of us writing a version of a life that didn't fit a standard template.
