events.title: Goldman Sachs admits the ‘AI unwind’ has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it’s watching for 3 signs of bottom
events.summary: The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year . Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom. Snider’s note said the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days. Goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged. The three conditions Goldman said any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning. Condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40 times trailing sales for Anthropic. A US Bank Asset Management executive said the valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” Goldman’s own outlook says the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond “is highly uncertain.” Condition 2: the Fed. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, and the Fed meets Dec. 9. Goldman’s economists expect hikes in December and March, sending the federal funds rate to a peak of 4.25% to 4.5%. A dovish signal looks unlikely soon. Treasuries did rally sharply Friday as investors looked for safety, which is not the same as a Fed pivot. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%. Condition 3: A big drop in investor positioning. This has often marked the end of past drawdowns. The first condition is unsettled, to say the least. Anthropic’s historic IPO turned into a sort of referendum on the entire AI trade, an unfair weight to put on a single, albeit remarkably important, company. The company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, passing SpaceX’s $85.7 billion as the biggest IPO on record. The shares jumped 17% on Thursday, then gave most of it back Friday to close at $88.91 , not far above the $83 IPO price. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly,” said Dakota Wealth’s Robert Pavlik. “I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company… I think they’re just skeptical of this market.” Morgan Stanley , the underwriter tasked with stabilizing the shares, closed its support position , removing a potential pillar of support. UBS said the debate had shifted from whether AI investment will continue to whether it can generate enough revenue and returns for shareholders. A Capital Economics economist wrote that the IPO’s success while other AI stocks fell shows the parts of the AI ecosystem “no longer move as one,” as chipmakers Nvidia , Broadcom , Micron and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14% . Nvidia’s 14% fall on Friday was its worst day in almost two years. It lost 22.9% on the week and is down 47.5% since Oct. 6, a loss of $2.7 trillion in market value. Reuters reported the SEC is probing its accounting practices . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 , and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The VIX, Wall Street’s “Fear Gauge,” closed at 35.89, its highest in 19 months . “It’s a meltdown right now,” said Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research. JPMorgan Asset Management’s David Kelly took the other view: “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu.” Positioning hasn’t washed out On the third condition, Goldman’s note says hedge funds have already cut back. Their net leverage is the lowest since April 2025. A companion report, Snider’s Hedge Fund Trend Monitor, says the most popular hedge fund longs were crowded into the AI trade and have lagged the S&P 500 by 14 percentage points over six months. That is among the worst stretches in the basket’s 20-year history. The note described the situation for hedge funds as “bruised and broadening.” But Goldman’s broader Sentiment Indicator is still above average. U.S. equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in nearly $170 billion in the fourth quarter so far. Asset managers’ net equity futures positions are in the 82nd percentile of the past 10 years. Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. Goldman Research says AI capital spending produced “about half” of this year’s earnings growth. The Street is split on whether this is the top. Capital Economics expects further declines. Goldman’s Nov. 17 outlook , written before the drop, forecast 8,700 by the end of 2027. In the Nov. 20 note, its range runs from about 5,800 to 8,100 depending on whether investors regain confidence in earnings. From Friday’s close, that is roughly 16% downside and 17% upside. Those percentages are my math, not Goldman’s. After the 22 S&P 500 corrections since 1980, the index averaged a 4% return over the next three months. It rose in 17 of them. E*Trade’s research is less reassuring. Of the 14 times since 1983, the index first closed 10% or more below a record, five became bear markets. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Retirees face a looming deadline for required withdrawals — missing it could trigger a tax penalty
events.summary: Most retirees must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, from pretax accounts at age 73. The first annual RMD is due by April 1 of the year after turning 73, and Dec. 31 is the deadline for subsequent withdrawals. If you miss your RMD due date, the IRS penalty is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn. Every year, millions of Americans must take required withdrawals from retirement accounts by Dec. 31. Amid the busy holiday season, it's easy to miss the year-end deadline for required minimum distributions — a mistake that can trigger a hefty IRS penalty , experts said. "One of the most common RMD mistakes is waiting until the last minute," said certified financial planner Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth at Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon. How to get Anthropic stock — without buying the IPO There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Most retirees must start RMDs from pretax accounts at age 73. The withdrawal is based on the previous year's account balances on Dec. 31, your age and an IRS " life expectancy factor ." The first annual RMD deadline is April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and future withdrawals are due by Dec. 31. If you wait until April 1 for the first one, you'll need two RMDs that year. RMDs also apply to certain inherited IRAs if the original IRA owner reached RMD age before their death. In 2023, more than 14.8 million taxpayers age 70 or older had a traditional individual retirement account, according to the latest IRS data. The average year-end market value of the accounts was about $330,000. Deferring RMDs until the last minute raises the likelihood of mistakes, such as overlooking certain retirement accounts or making withdrawal calculation errors, Canellopoulos said. Some 7% of Vanguard investors at RMD age missed their yearly withdrawal in 2025, up slightly from 6.7% in 2024 , according to a Vanguard analysis of about 400,000 RMD-age retirees with IRA balances published in December 2025. Among those investors, the average missed RMD was $10,500 in 2025, Vanguard told CNBC. Investors who don't take RMDs by the annual deadline may owe an excise tax to the IRS, worth up to 25% of the amount they should have withdrawn. For example, the excise tax could be up to $2,625 for a $10,500 missed RMD. How to reduce the IRS penalty for missed RMDs If investors miss a required withdrawal, they could reduce the penalty to 10% if they "timely corrected" the RMD within two years and file Form 5329 , according to the IRS. In some cases, the IRS could waive the penalty entirely due to "reasonable error" if investors take "reasonable steps" to fix the shortfall, according to the agency. Investors can file Form 5329 with a letter of explanation to request the waiver. "If you don't ask, you're not going to get it," said certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird. "I've never heard of anybody being denied the waiver." Charitable transfers could cover RMDs Investors who give to charity may be skipping a specific donation strategy that can reduce or eliminate their annual RMDs, according to Lawrence Pon, a CFP and CPA based in Redwood City, California. They can use a so-called qualified charitable distribution , or QCD, Pon said. A QCD has a dual tax benefit: It doesn't count as taxable income and may also satisfy at least part of an investor's yearly RMD, Pon said. The move requires a direct transfer from an investor's pretax IRA to an eligible nonprofit organization . They can donate up to $111,000 in 2026. While QCD eligibility begins at age 70½, transfers won't start counting toward RMDs until an investor reaches their RMD age. Generally, taxpayers only get a tax break for large charitable donations if they itemize deductions on their tax returns. But QCDs still provide a tax benefit for charitable gifts when investors use the standard deduction. QCDs "provide a real benefit if you are not itemizing [tax deductions]," said Pon. While there's no tax deduction for QCDs, the transfer won't increase a taxpayer's adjusted gross income, or AGI. Raising AGI can cause other tax consequences, such as higher premiums for Medicare Part B and Part D.

events.title: Goodwill CEO says hiring managers are going behind their bosses’ backs and looking for workers with college degrees, not skills
events.summary: More bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers. Just because an employer claims it’s ditching degree requirements to recruit more diverse talent, that doesn’t mean its hiring managers are actually doing it. When major employers like Google , Microsoft , IBM , and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs , other firms rushed to follow their example. But that promise may be limited to their job ads. Goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer. And so the promise of skills-first hiring may not be reaching the millions of jobless Gen Zers who need it. “Right now, employers are consistently saying they want to hire for skills, not necessarily degrees,” Preston said. “But the proof is in the pudding. Not everybody does it.”  He added: “What I hear from a lot of people is, ‘Yeah, the top says we need to do this,’ but when it gets to the hiring professionals, it doesn’t always trickle down.” The charity has more than 650 job centers and saw nearly 2 million people use its employment services last year, and Preston said he’s preparing for an influx of jobless Gen Zers thanks to automation . Gen Zers without degrees are struggling most with unemployment While the opportunities for young people without degrees are certainly growing, Preston says they’re ultimately still more likely to face unemployment than Gen Zers with a degree.  “What I’m seeing is, of the overall unemployment, people without college degrees have no jobs,” the 66-year-old CEO, who formerly served as the 14th United States secretary of housing and urban development, revealed. Research has shown that the issue is even more acute for young men.  “It’s much harder to find a job,” Preston added. “It’s really hitting college students right now in the marketplace. It’s really hitting young adults without college degrees.” So why are hiring managers still shutting the door on people who didn’t go down the higher education path, despite such a clear push to do the opposite?  “I think when somebody comes out with a four-year degree from college, there’s a certain sense that that person has a foundation that will be valuable in the workplace, and there’s a suspicion that if somebody hasn’t done that, they may be lacking some core skills,” Preston said, while pointing to critical thinking, team building, and communications as potential skills built from school projects and essays. “So somebody with a strong collegiate background provides a high degree of comfort that these other capabilities are in place,” he added. “It’s also just easy to interview people who are like you, if you went to college, if you’ve gone down a particular pathway, you speak the same language, you have many of the same experiences. It’s much easier to connect with somebody who’s like you.” For young people without degrees, Preston argued the key is proving you’ve built those prized skills elsewhere—whether that’s through upskilling, volunteering, or work experience. Even joining a sports team can help open doors because it teaches you confidence, teamwork, discipline, and more. “Employers have to be able to see that many of those capabilities are acquired in different ways,” he said. For closed-minded employers, Preston stressed the research is clear: Inclusive hiring isn’t just the right thing to do, it’s also good for business. “Organizations that have a much broader aperture in looking for talent are more likely to have the roles in their organizations filled; they’re much less likely to say that they’ve got deficiencies in their team; they’re more likely to say they’ve got a healthy workplace; and they often find higher engagement scores among their teams because of the culture that they’ve created,” he added. “Honestly, I think that’s important for society as well, on many levels.” A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on September 26, 2025 . events.title: Tech investor Bill Gurley says workers who went through the ‘college conveyor belt’ and chased safe jobs are at high risk of AI automation
events.summary: Professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career. But within a matter of years, AI has disrupted the world of work , and it’s quickly taking over the office roles humans were once promised. Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint. “This is new and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley said during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year. “It’s creating a lot of anxiety, but I don’t know that we can put it back in the bottle.” The prolific tech financier, famous for his early investments in Uber and Zillow , is skeptical the government could pass AI regulation or pull off a massive reskilling effort. So as the technology continues to automate traditionally stable and lucrative roles, like lawyers and software engineers, it’s imperative workers actually be invested in their profession—or risk facing the chopping block. “The people that are most at risk are the ones that are sitting idly in the job and don’t really have a why or a purpose for it,” Gurley said. “A lot of the people that go through that college conveyor belt, that are chasing a safe job, that end up working as a widget or a cog in an industry they may not love—I think they are ripe for disruption.” The Benchmark Capital general partner acknowledges it’s easier said than done, but the best plan is to “craft your own career path” and tailor it to an individual’s distinct skills. For those who can’t switch sectors or become self-employed, AI can act as career “jet fuel” that can make them even better at their jobs and indispensable to their employers.  “If it’s out of your control, I just would say understand what it’s capable of in your industry and be the most AI-aware person in your job,” Gurley advised. “You’re going to then be the last person that they want to get rid of.” The tech investor says college has turned into a ‘pressure cooker’  Gurley explores the idea that chasing a career of passion is a strategic edge, and not fluffy advice, in his newest book Runnin’ Down a Dream . He’s also one of several business leaders questioning the efficacy of how young professionals are trained to approach college.  The investor has noticed a few worrying trends that may inhibit young professionals from following their true aspirations, hurting their career success. Gurley explained that kids today are “programmed from a time perspective” more than other generations. The budding talent start worrying about having a stacked résumé from a young age, and now some colleges require students to apply with a major in mind.  These restraints don’t allow them to freely explore what jobs they’d enjoy, instead funneling them into a professional path very quickly. He believes that’s part of the reason why so many people are checked out at work—a group that’s most susceptible to disruption.  “There seems to me to be somewhat of a problem out there in that people aren’t landing where they’re passionate about what they’re doing,” Gurley said. “I don’t think it’s anyone’s fault, but I think we’ve turned the college matriculation process into this pressure cooker.” Business leaders agree that AI-savvy, passionate workers will succeed  Former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky echoes some of Gurley’s philosophy about career success in the AI era. Workers won’t be able to simply coast on a glitzy Ivy League degree: They need to have passion for their professions and the necessary tech skills to succeed in their careers. “My guess is that the future of work belongs not anymore to the people that have the fanciest degrees or went to the best colleges,” Roslansky said during a fireside chat at the platform’s San Francisco office last year.  Instead, he predicted talent most likely to land a job and succeed are “the people who are adaptable, forward thinking, ready to learn, and ready to embrace these tools…It really kind of opens up the playing field in a way that I think we’ve never seen before.” Fei-Fei Li , a Stanford professor and CEO of AI startup World Labs, dubbed the “Godmother of AI,” says being tech-savvy on the job matters more than anything else. Now it’s essential for professionals to “superpower” themselves quickly with the tools, she advised. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 3, 2026. events.title: Microsoft’s CFO admits she joined the tech giant without even knowing her salary—and then missed her first day of work
events.summary: As an economics undergraduate at Duke University in the 1990s, Amy Hood had no master plan that would one day land her the top finance job at one of the world’s biggest tech companies.  In fact, now Microsoft’s chief financial officer, Hood, said her career has looked more like a roller coaster than a ladder—and the lesson she told the class of 2026 still resonates today. “As you start out, many successful careers are rarely—if ever—a straight line,” she said at Duke’s commencement ceremony in May. “Your next step doesn’t have to be a perfect one. It just has to be an opportunity.” Hood learned that the hard way. After graduating from Duke in 1994, she built her early career at Goldman Sachs and later earned her MBA from Harvard . But over time, she realized corporate banking wasn’t how she wanted to spend the rest of her life. So she quit—without much of a plan of what would come next. She considered going back to school for a third degree, but eventually stumbled upon what seemed like a perfect reset: an internship with the National Park Service. “I thought, this is perfect. It’s a sign—I’ll get assigned to Yosemite or Yellowstone, someplace iconic,” Hood recalled. “I’ll work outdoors, I’ll live somewhere beautiful, and feel the space and energy that nature provides.” Instead, the then-30-year-old was assigned to a less glamorous spot: Alcatraz Island, or as she called it, “a prison on a rock.” Not the manifestation she had imagined, she quit after a single day. Months later, after an extended job search, a friend called and asked whether she wanted to interview at Microsoft—even though she had already faced two rejections from the company. This time, she landed a role in investor relations and accepted the offer without even asking about the salary. “It was a job, a step forward, and truthfully, I needed a paycheck,” she said. Even then, her start at Microsoft in 2002 was rocky. Hood admitted she missed her first day after miscalculating how long it would take to drive her silver Volvo from California to Seattle. Still, the gamble paid off. Over the next decade, Hood steadily rose through the company’s ranks before being named CFO in 2013. Microsoft’s business has thrived under her leadership, and it ranks highly on Fortune ’s lists of World’s Most Admired and America’s Most Innovative Companies . In 2025 alone, she earned $29.5 million in total compensation. Microsoft CFO’s advice for Gen Z: ‘Lower your bar’ For today’s college graduates, Hood’s winding path to the top may feel increasingly out of reach as many young workers struggle to land even their first full-time job. Companies across the tech industry— including Microsoft —have cut thousands of roles in recent years as businesses restructure and ramp up investments in artificial intelligence. The uncertainty has weighed heavily on young workers. More than 60% of the class of 2026 are pessimistic about their career prospects, according to a report from Handshake . At the same time, many graduates are entering the workforce with expectations that are not aligned with today’s labor market. College seniors surveyed by real estate platform Clever said they expect to earn roughly $80,000 within a year of graduating. But the average starting salary for recent graduates is closer to $56,000—a gap of nearly $24,000. Hood acknowledged the uncertainty facing Gen Z , but argued that many young workers are more prepared than they think. The bigger challenge, she said, is letting go of the expectation that they need to have everything figured out immediately. “I can’t believe I’m saying this to some of the most accomplished young people on the planet, but maybe lower your bar a little,” she said. “Be open that something may not be exactly right, but could turn out to be a perfect place to learn about yourself—what you like, what you don’t. All the steps matter, and it took me decades to figure that out.” She also urged graduates to stay adaptable and curious in a world that is changing faster than any previous generation has experienced.  “You will figure out who you are by stepping in and letting people push back, by doing things that scare you just a little, by raising your hand when you’re pretty sure you don’t have the right answer, and by taking a job that doesn’t make sense on paper but makes sense to you,” she told graduates.  And when setbacks inevitably happen, Hood said resilience matters more than perfection. “Remember, there aren’t that many one-way doors—so go through a few of those things. And if you get a no, just try a new door,” she said. “Every step builds confidence, even the ones that feel like mistakes at the time—especially those. After all, the best stories always come from those moments.” A version of this story was published on  Fortune.com  on May 11, 2026. events.title: A 10% drop for the stock market is unnerving, but it's not that unusual
events.summary: The U.S. stock market has dropped 10% from its high set last month amid concerns about the growing hurdles faced by the high-flying artificial intelligence industry The U.S. stock market has dropped 10% from its high set last month amid concerns about the growing hurdles faced by the high-flying artificial intelligence industry. The fall for the S & P 500 is steep enough that Wall Street has a name for it: a “correction.” Such drops have happened regularly for more than a century, and market pros often view them as potentially healthy wipeouts of overdone euphoria, which could send stock prices too high if unchecked. But corrections are unnerving in the moment. And the larger fear always accompanying a correction is that it could be a warning sign of a coming “bear market,” which is what Wall Street calls a drop of at least 20%. Here’s a look at what history shows about past corrections, and what market watchers are expecting going forward. Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence boom drove the markets to all-time highs in October. But a confluence of events caused investors to question whether the enthusiasm is overblown and if the AI industry can deliver on the lofty expectations. For one, investors are worried that stock prices in AI companies shot too high and that the strong demand for memory, processors and other building blocks of data centers could fizzle out if AI proves less profitable than promised. The large sums needed to invest in technology and data centers are another concern. The industry is racing to develop more capable models and infrastructure, which requires billions of dollars, but increasingly companies are having to raise money by selling bonds to investors. Now, the Federal Reserve is expected to hike its short-term interest rate next month. That could drive up borrowing costs for AI companies, among others. More recently, investors have grown anxious about the regulatory environment under a new Congress. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction. Then there’s Nvidia. The company's chips power the AI industry and it also provides the cash that’s helped companies across the industry to grow. The sudden downfall of Jensen Huang , its former CEO and co-founder, has punished the company's stock and been a big factor in the broader sell-off. “Jensen Huang’s departure may have been the catalyst for this sell-off, but the underlying concerns in the technology sector have been building for some time,” said Karan Ramchandani, managing partner at Post Oak Group. “Investors have poured enormous amounts of capital into AI based on expectations of transformational growth, and we’re now entering a period where those expectations need to translate into measurable earnings and returns.” Not even the blockbuster market debut of AI lab Anthropic this week could stem the selling. Given their lofty valuations, Wall Street has been anticipating a correction in AI stocks for a while. Some who've referred to the run-up in the stocks a bubble think it hasn't popped completely. “The bubble is popping and it has much further to go,” said David Trainer, head of investment research firm New Constructs. “We’re in the early innings of reconciliation with economic reality of egregious over-investment in AI. Like all other booms, this one is having its bust.” Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Others see the sell-off as another instance of the fear and anxiety that periodically grips the markets. Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., likened the current downturn to market corrections in March 2020 around the pandemic and in April 2025 following the Trump administration’s escalation of its global trade war. But he sees the selling as panic-driven, and not a “red flag moment indicating darker times ahead for tech and the market.” “This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years,” Ives wrote. “And that is the wrong move in our view.” Ramchandani sees the sell-off as more of a reevaluation of the AI sector than the bursting of a bubble. “AI isn’t going away,” she said, “but the market may be entering a phase where investors become far more selective about which companies can actually deliver on the promises.” Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide, says the washout being led by AI stocks could ultimately prove constructive for the broader market.

events.title: Defense tech VC hit a record $37.9 billion last quarter. Two investors say it looks like 2021
events.summary: When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector said onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. “I’m a long-term optimist and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” said Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners. “There are a lot of new entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he said. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.” The money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum . Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer . Even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.” Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly. “There is a pretty big YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis said. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme… [and] maybe they’re most excited about who invested in the last round and the signal that that gives, versus a hardcore underwriting of a real set of capabilities that can truly pierce into a market.” An Nvidia-sized jolt to private markets That froth now meets a broader shock. Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, under pressure from the chipmaker’s board, has left the startup ecosystem primed for change and possible disruption. AI startups are most exposed, but private capital markets more broadly are in flux, including the deep-tech bets now crowding into defense. For startups, the harder test is selling to the government. It has long been a difficult market to crack, and the Pentagon, which has used the name Department of War as a secondary title since a 2025 executive order , is among the hardest. Part of the trouble is that government isn’t a monolithic customer, even if it looks like one. “There’s a misconception that the Pentagon is this all-or-nothing type of customer,” said Faltas. “It’s actually not. The building itself is… called the Pentagon. It’s got five corners, and each of those five corners needs to be engaged with, and educated with, and listened to… That requires a very focused ground game.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
events.summary: Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine. Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with the United States. list 1 of 3 Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know list 2 of 3 US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces list 3 of 3 Trump claims Iran is developing bioweapons: Is there any evidence? The future of Iran’s nuclear programme has become a major sticking point in efforts to end the war, with Washington insisting that it must have guarantees that Iran will never develop a nuclear weapon before it will agree to a full ceasefire. So, is Iran’s nuclear policy changing, and what could that mean for the conflict? What is Iran’s official nuclear policy? Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes only, such as for electricity generation, medical research and agriculture. This policy has been underlined by a decades-old religious decree, or fatwa, issued by the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, banning the development of nuclear weapons. However, Iran has also insisted it has the right to enrich uranium for these purposes under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), which it joined in 1970. It has called this right “non-negotiable”. What have Araghchi and other officials said? In an interview with Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency on Saturday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran’s stockpile of enriched material would remain inside the country . The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated in 2025 – before Israel launched strikes on Iran in June that year – that Iran had about 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched to about 60 percent. This is short of the 90 percent required for making nuclear weapons, but is the level at which it becomes much quicker to reach 90 percent. It is also far beyond the roughly 3 percent needed for power generation. This material, Araghchi said during his interview, would “be used according to our needs however those needs are defined”. Araghchi also made reference to an ongoing debate among lawmakers and officials in Iran about altering its nuclear doctrine, and said people on both sides of that debate have “strong arguments”. “This is a major strategic debate, and there is nothing wrong with examining it seriously because it directly concerns national interests and security,” Araghchi said, adding that those in favour of reform argue Iran’s current approach of no nuclear weapons has “failed to protect” the country’s nuclear facilities, which have come under attack from US and Israeli forces both last year and this year. However, Araghchi acknowledged that any official change to the policy would have “far-reaching consequences”. “For now, our doctrine has not changed, and our official position remains the same,” he said. Other Iranian officials have also spoken about a potential review of the country’s nuclear doctrine. Earlier this month, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said “there is a discussion on whether we want to continue to follow the previous nuclear doctrine in the event of a new war breaking out”, though he also stressed that Tehran has not yet made any change. On November 12, Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body that appoints the supreme leader, said reviewing “the country’s defence doctrine and establishing the necessary deterrence have become unavoidable necessities”. Ali Fathollah-Nejad, a German-Iranian political scientist who directs the Center for Middle East and Global Order (CMEG), told Al Jazeera the move by the Assembly of Experts “appears to mark the first time a governing institution has endorsed this position”. Why do the US and Israel think Iran is developing nuclear weapons? Besides being a signatory to the NPT in 1970, Iran also initially complied with a nuclear agreement it struck with the US and other global powers in 2015 – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which required it to limit uranium enrichment to very low levels and undergo inspections. But after Washington pulled out of the deal in 2018 under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Tehran eventually went back to intensifying its nuclear programme and abandoned restrictions imposed by the deal. In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was no longer complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards.

events.title: Why Anthropic's blockbuster IPO couldn't escape the stock market correction
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO was a success for the company, but achieving success with stock market investors for more than a day is the harder part in this market. The selloff on Friday in "ANT" shares amid the AI-led stock market correction shows that demand for a hot-name deal is a fleeting moment in valuation, which is not atypical for new publicly traded tech companies. SpaceX is still below its first-day closing price, and it took Facebook over a year after its 2012 IPO to regain its first-day valuation. It may not be any different for AI, or any easier for OpenAI, say IPO and investing experts. No one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a success for the company. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for " ANT " shares. But what came within a day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead. The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF ( IPO ). "The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday. And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock. It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street adding downside risks to research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatement (or most subtle equities research joke) in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18. "It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added. The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF ( LAZR ) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge." "You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said. Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin , and repositioning for 2027 based on their new outlooks . "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said. "From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based on Fed policy , geopolitics , the midterm elections results, or the AI trade . "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added. Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taken by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLK ), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.

events.title: I'm a real estate developer selling a $30 million mansion, and here’s why I’d accept Anthropic shares instead of cash
events.summary: Phillip Braunstein, a developer in LA, is willing to trade his $29,995,000 mansion for shares of OpenAI or Anthropic. Courtesy of Carolwood Estates Phillip Braunstein is willing to trade his $29,995,000 mansion for shares of OpenAI or Anthropic. The LA developer says a sluggish LA luxury market and his AI optimism prompted the offer. Braunstein says he believes that AI shares could multiply in value over time. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phillip Braunstein, president of Colossal Properties and owner of the home at 1210 Chickory Lane in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. The property is listed for $29,995,000 and accepts shares from OpenAI and Anthropic as payment. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I've been in construction and real estate development for almost 15 years, and I've also become increasingly involved in tech investing . I started building this house in Brentwood in 2021. When you walk through the front door onto the main floor, there's a 110-foot wall of motorized glass. You press a button, and the entire wall opens up. It creates this indoor-outdoor experience with 270-degree views. What's also special is that even though the architecture is very modern, with all the glass and concrete, the house feels warm. events.title: I've bought Amtrak's USA Rail Pass 4 times. There are huge perks to using the $499 pass, and a few frustrations.
events.summary: I've bought the Amtrak USA Rail Pass four times. Malia Yoshioka Over the past year and a half, I've purchased Amtrak's $499 USA Rail Pass four times. The pass, which allows me to book 10 train tickets in 30 days, is a great way to see the country. However, delays can throw off my entire itinerary, and I can't book a roomette using the pass. Over the past year and a half, I've traveled through most of the continental US by train. One way I've kept costs down is by taking advantage of Amtrak's $499 USA Rail Pass , which allows 10 train segments — or tickets — within a 30-day period. I've now purchased the pass four times, often combining trips to visit friends, attend conferences, and explore destinations I might otherwise overlook. Although there are definite frustrations with planning and managing a Rail Pass trip, the perks still outweigh the downsides, in my opinion. The pass makes it easy to explore the country. zrfphoto/Getty Images One of my favorite ways to use the pass is to add stops to existing trips. For example, I needed to travel from Chicago to Florida to see my mother for Mother's Day, which already would've cost more than $200 round-trip if I purchased individual train tickets. Flights were similarly priced as well, so I opted to use a Rail Pass and tack on a few extra stops along the way. During the trip, I traveled to Holland, Michigan, for the annual Tulip Time festival, rerouted through Washington, DC, just in time to make the peak blooms of cherry blossom season , and spent 24 hours in Savannah visiting with a friend. The stops really added to the experience and were things I wouldn't have experienced had I flown or bought a single Amtrak ticket. When my train has a Sightseer Lounge, I take full advantage of the views. Malia Yoshioka It's not available on every train, but when it is, I love spending time in the Sightseer Lounge , a spacious public car with panoramic windows to take in the views. There's nothing better than starting my mornings there with a cup of coffee and the sunrise. I've seen passengers writing postcards, knitting, drawing, reading, or (like me) just sitting and taking in the changing scenery out the window. It's the perfect place to slow down. However, when I'm using the pass, delays can throw off my entire itinerary. Malia Yoshioka For me, the biggest downside of the USA Rail Pass is managing unexpected delays and cancellations. Although many of my trains have arrived promptly (occasionally even early), I've also experienced significant delays and last-minute cancellations. When I'm trying to fit in 10 segments of travel during a 30-day window, sometimes delays can require me to adjust the rest of my trip. Once, aboard a Chicago-bound train from Washington, DC, I was delayed for nearly eight hours. So many of us missed our connections that Amtrak arranged hotels for two busloads of passengers from our train. This meant rearranging my remaining pass segments and missing the first night of a hotel reservation that I had booked for my next destination. Although I was grateful for the accomodations, the experience definitely threw off the rest of my itinerary. Sometimes, sleeping in coach gets old. Malia Yoshioka One of the most common questions I get from others is whether I sleep in a roomette on long-distance routes. However, when I'm traveling with the USA Rail Pass, I'm only able to book a seat in coach. Thankfully, I've found the seats spacious enough, especially when the train isn't crowded and I can stretch across two seats. Still, I won't pretend that sleeping in a seat is ever comfortable, even with extra space. For me, the savings are worth the trade-off, but I've learned not to schedule too many consecutive nights on board. At the end of the day, I've found the perks outweigh any frustrations. Malia Yoshioka Even with the occasional delay or cancellation that forces me to adjust my plans, train travel remains one of my favorite ways to explore the US . With four Rail Passes under my belt, I still have plenty of ideas for my next itinerary. So, I'm sure a fifth pass is in my near future. Business Insider reached out to Amtrak for comment. events.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
events.summary: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell. I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work? They have a long way to go

events.title: I’m house-hacking by living in a shed in my backyard. Here are 4 things I learned from building a tiny home and downsizing.
events.summary: Lauren Patton downsized from her main home into a tiny home she built in her backyard. Courtesy of Lauren Patton. After Lauren Patton was laid off, she could no longer afford her $4,000 mortgage. To make ends meet, she moved into a tiny home in her backyard and rents out her main home on Airbnb. Downsizing has helped her pay down her mortgage, but there are trade-offs. In 2022, Lauren Patton bought a 1,000-square-foot bungalow in Central Texas for about $400,000. At the time, she had a steady, well-paying job in tech, and felt ready to buy her first home as a single woman. She didn't expect she'd be laid off a year later, or that she'd eventually struggle to afford her $4,000 monthly mortgage. "I wasn't super worried at first. I thought, 'Hey, I was a data science manager. I'll be able to find something.' But after interviewing at numerous places, nothing was happening," Patton told Business Insider. "By then, money was tight. I had very little savings and was still paying off a lot of credit card debt." After filing for unemployment, Patton began staying at friends' homes while renting out the two bedrooms in her house on Airbnb to help cover her mortgage. But it was a short-term solution to a long-term problem. "I was 35 and thought, 'I can't keep doing this.' I knew I needed to do something," she said. "That's when I came up with the idea to build a little structure in my backyard to live in." In 2025, Patton bought a 100-square-foot shed kit for about $8,500 and built it herself. She lives in the backyard tiny home and rents out her main house on Airbnb. The income doesn't cover her entire mortgage, but it has helped her make payments and tackle other debt. For Patton, it has been an imperfect but necessary solution. "It was tough at first, downsizing to a tiny home ," she said. "Emotionally, it felt like I was regressing in life, and physically, it felt really claustrophobic. But I don't mind it as much now. I'm doing better mentally." Here are four things Patton has learned about building and living in a tiny home . Building a tiny home can be a lonely experience. Patton's shed kit did not come with a roof. Courtesy of Lauren Patton Patton bought a cabin-style shed kit that came with stackable wood slats, beams, and large windows. The kit did not include a foundation, roof, or floor, all of which she had to build herself, along with an outhouse and outdoor shower. Patton had no formal construction training, so she relied on YouTube and ChatGPT to guide her through the project, which required a lot of time, money, and energy. She said she became so obsessed with the undertaking that it took over her life for a while. "I don't think people in my life necessarily understood what was going on," she said. "I was dating a guy at the time, and I told him I was going to build a tiny home, and he immediately broke up with me. I lost a few friends over it." Figuring out the utilities is challenging. Patton built her tiny home on her own without formal training. Courtesy of Lauren Patton There were a lot of things for Patton to consider when building the tiny home , like how she'd get water or electricity flowing to the unit. "I actually didn't have a plan for that," she said. "I thought there must be a way to get full plumbing without actually having to install it and get it permitted." Ultimately, she installed a dry-flush toilet. In the summer, she uses a solar-heated outdoor shower; in the winter, she relies on propane heat. Electricity has been more difficult to manage. "Find out how much power you'll need before you start building, because it's been kind of challenging," Patton said. "There have been plenty of mornings where I've had to choose between having heat, making coffee, or blow-drying my hair." There never seems to be enough storage space. A mini fridge. Reni Purnama Sari/Getty Images Moving from a 1,000-square-foot home into a 100-square-foot tiny home means Patton has had to go without a lot. She still has many of the basics she had in her main home, including a TV, desk, and bed, but she does not have a kitchen. "I have a tiny, itty-bitty fridge, and I don't have ice or running water, so I have to stock up on jugs of water," she said. Patton said the hardest part of living in such a small space with limited storage is making sure she has everything she needs on hand. "There's always one thing missing," she said. "I'll go to grill chicken and realize I'm out of salt, or that it's back in the main house," she added. "I'm constantly running out to buy little things, and sometimes I wonder whether it's really financially worth it." It's weird having people in your house while you're nearby. A pool. Viola Lopes/picture alliance via Getty Images Patton has rented her main home out on Airbnb for the past couple of years. On a typical weekend night, she charges about $200, and weekday rates during the school year are closer to $125. October is an especially lucrative month for her because of the Austin City Limits Music Festival. In October, the home had about 96% occupancy, bringing in about $6,517. While the extra cash has been helpful, Patton said it still feels strange to have guests staying in her home while she lives on the property. "I've lived outside of my house longer than I've lived in it," said Patton, who bought the home in early 2022 but officially lived there for only about eight months. "It's interesting watching people enjoy my pool." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Saudi Arabia announces new tax to begin on January 1, 2027
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority announced a new tax applicable to companies that function as part of multinational groups or corporations. The domestic minimum top-up tax (DMTT) is applicable on companies with recorded revenue of €750 million, or its equivalent in Saudi currency (3.08 billion riyals), in at least two of the four fiscal years preceding the fiscal year in which the tax applies. The tax is not applicable to purely domestic companies that do not have branches outside the kingdom or do not belong to a covered multinational business group. Minimum 15 per cent threshold The DMTT applies when the effective tax rate falls below the established global minimum threshold of 15 per cent. This threshold is in accordance with the two-pillar reform programme agreed by member states in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in 2021. The organisation set up a global minimum corporate tax to ensure large multinational enterprises pay a minimum 15 per cent tax on profits in each country where they operate. The UAE has a similar top-up tax that has been in effect since 2025. This percentage refers to the minimum effective tax rate on profit, and is not levied on the total revenue of the companies.

events.title: Warren Buffett quadruples Thanksgiving gifts: A breakdown of how much wealth he's giving away
events.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.) Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as his Thanksgiving gifts soar Warren Buffett, 96, more than quadrupled his Thanksgiving donations to four family foundations this year to $5.5 billion . The gifts consist of Berkshire Class B shares that have been converted from his roughly $160 billion of Class A shares. The increase is in line with his new goal, announced last July , to give away all of his Berkshire Hathaway shares "within about eight years," with no additional annual donations going to the Gates Foundation . Around $2.2 billion of shares goes to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation , named for his late first wife, with the three foundations run by his children, Susie Buffett's Sherwood Foundation , the Howard G. Buffett Foundation , and Peter Buffett's NoVo Foundation each getting $1.1 billion each. In July of last year, Buffett gave shares worth $4.6 billion to the Gates Foundation with another $1.4 billion going to the family foundations. This July, the family foundations received $5.9 billion in stock, bringing the year's total to $11.4 billion, an increase of almost 55% from last year, even as the Gates Foundation received nothing. In comments included in the Berkshire news release this week announcing the new gifts, Buffett reaffirmed his confidence in his children's ability to disburse his fortune over time, saying they "have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity." He also said his confidence in Berkshire is "as strong as ever." Recalling that in last year's lengthier Thanksgiving message he had said, "Kindness is costless but also priceless," Buffett wrote, " A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie [Munger] and I ever bought." "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham , Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy . Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received. "Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I'm grateful to every one of them. "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else." Berkshire rally stalls but it's not as bad as S&P's AI selloff Berkshire Hathaway's fourth quarter rally that had produced a string of record highs cooled this week as both classes of its stock posted five straight daily declines. That sent them down 3.9% for the week. Last Friday, Berkshire was up 19.1% since October 1. Now that gain has been cut to 14.5% The S&P's decline of 8.6% this week, however, was even bigger than Berkshire's 5-day drop, as investors sold to lock in profits from AI-related stocks. The benchmark index, along with the Dow Industrials , are in a correction after falling 10% from their recent highs , and the Nasdaq Composite has erased all of its year-to-date gains. Berkshire's smaller decline increased its year-to-date outperformance of the S&P to 12.5 percentage points. One Wall Street firm, however, thinks Berkshire's run-up has run its course. Argus Research downgraded the B shares to hold from buy Friday, saying the stock is "fully valued" at about 25 times next year's estimate for operating earnings per share. Berkshire buys Delta, sells BofA in quiet quarter As foreshadowed by its 10-Q financial report released almost two weeks ago, Berkshire Hathaway's Q3 13F portfolio snapshot filed with the SEC on Monday showed it wasn't doing much buying and selling of equities this summer. And the two largest additions, Lennar and Bending Spoons , had been previously disclosed , along with additional purchases at the start of the fourth quarter. The most notable change we didn't expect was a 12% increase in Berkshire's Delta Air Lines position, bringing it just short of a 10% stake, now valued at $5.2 billion . Exceeding 10% triggers a number of regulatory burdens, including the requirement to promptly disclose new buying or selling, so we may not see additional purchases going forward. Delta's return to the portfolio after Warren Buffett sold all of Berkshire's airline stocks in 2020 has been something of a surprise given his bumpy ride with the industry over the years. As expected, Berkshire continued to trim its Bank of America stake. After nine consecutive quarters of sales, it's been cut by 56% but remains the fifth largest portfolio holding at $21.4 billion. Berkshire also cut another financial, Capital One , by almost 62%, although it was already a relatively small position, now worth $207 million. Also notable are two positions that didn't change.

events.title: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom
events.summary: ‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout T he Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence. Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich. This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else. Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble. The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland. Many of these are under construction; some are little more than announcements. CoreWeave is building them by taking on staggering quantities of debt. The company now owes $47bn (£36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn of this figure due next year. It bled $709m last quarter, on revenues of $3.6bn. CoreWeave already looked dangerously exposed this autumn, when creditors put its risk of default – being unable to pay its debts – at over 60% at some point over the next five years. Its earnings, released earlier in November, provided a brief respite from some of their fears – its margins and revenues “knocked it out of the park”, said Jordan Chaflin, head of technology at CreditSights, a financial research firm. That was before scandal hit Nvidia, the most valuable business in AI and the company that makes CoreWeave’s entire business model possible. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . He’s now out. This will have consequences, and no one knows what they are yet. Huang ran his business on close relationships and, as Nvidia grew, these relationships became the scaffolding of the AI economy. Few companies will be more affected by his removal than CoreWeave. Its vulnerabilities – and they are many – are a blueprint for the wobbly structure of the AI bubble itself, on which the fortunes of the world’s stock market and the global economy now depend. A repository for other companies’ risk CoreWeave is what is called a “neocloud”. Its basic business model is this: the world’s biggest AI companies, like OpenAI, want billions of people to start using their products but don’t want to sink a fortune into building the large datacentres it takes to run them. Nvidia, its primary backer, wants to sell lots of computer chips to the world’s biggest AI companies. So Nvidia provided the finance for CoreWeave and its peers to buy its chips, stuff them into datacentres, and rent that computational power to the world’s biggest AI companies. Nvidia owns approximately 11% of CoreWeave. There are other arrangements, too, including a $6.3bn deal in which Nvidia agreed to buy “compute” that CoreWeave cannot sell – a sort of guarantee. That’s not the only side of the equation Nvidia is propping up. It also has invested in CoreWeave’s clients – companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and nearly a dozen others that rent these chips. A dollar that Nvidia invests in one of these can end up as income on CoreWeave’s balance sheet, and then revenue for Nvidia as CoreWeave purchases chips. Circular arrangements like this are the scaffolding of the AI economy. CoreWeave – and companies like it – are the vehicle through which Nvidia can make its balance sheet look spectacular, and OpenAI and Anthropic can provide ever-more-powerful models to their customers without paying workmen to break earth in Texas. Think of it as a sandwich where neither slice of bread – Nvidia or a frontier AI company using its chips – wants to finance or build, say, $1tn worth of sheds stuffed with semiconductors, so the peanut butter in the middle takes on the risk. Analysts expect CoreWeave to be a capital-intensive – meaning big-spending – business. Someone has to be. Most appear to have accepted its considerable risk. “Their business model is essentially … you’re doing this massive buildout of infrastructure,” said Chaflin. “It is really quite painful from a free cashflow perspective, during the buildout.” That infrastructure “needs to get funded with debt” Chaflin said. He emphasises that CoreWeave is not the only company doing this: it is the business model of “hyperscalers” and “neoclouds” – the companies building AI datacentres to support a future, still-theoretical AI economy. In a US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing this summer, CoreWeave listed 18 different varieties of debt it is now paying back, amounting to roughly $35bn. In its most recent earnings, which do not break down this debt, that number is up by nearly $12bn, to $47bn.

events.title: An early breakdown in the polar vortex is threatening already depleted gas stocks
events.summary: A record-early polar vortex breakdown is coinciding with a powerful El Niño, leaving forecasters without a historical comparison. Colder weather and low wind speeds could strain Europe’s gas market, where storage started winter at its lowest level in more than a decade. The rare weather combination adds a new source of volatility to energy markets already exposed to geopolitical risks. An unprecedented early breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex and a record-breaking El Niño event has put energy traders on alert this winter, with analysts warning the weather and climate phenomena could have an outsized impact on Europe. Meteorologists are currently observing a record early breakdown of the polar vortex, a large-scale circulation of strong winds that typically keeps extremely cold air over the North Pole. Changes in the strength and shape of the polar vortex can influence weather patterns much lower down in the atmosphere, potentially bringing in colder weather to parts of Europe and North America. This year, however, the collapse of the stratospheric polar vortex, or SPV, is taking place at the same time as an unusually powerful El Niño, a climate event that can boost global temperatures and disrupt rainfall. The collision of these two events raises the risk of a prolonged cold spell that could lift heating demand and force European countries to draw down already-low reserves faster. That would leave the continent more reliant on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) at a time when supplies from the Middle East are disrupted. To be sure, Europe's natural gas storage levels started the winter at their lowest level in more than a decade. The International Energy Agency warned earlier this month that low European storage levels and limited storage options in several LNG-importing countries in Asia and South America could intensify the competition for cargoes and put upward pressure on prices during periods of high demand. Simon Lee, a lecturer in atmospheric science at the U.K.'s University of St Andrews, said the combination of a sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) with an El Niño event is not necessarily unusual, but meteorologists had been expecting a polar vortex breakdown in February — not as early as November. The early SPV disruption is an "extremely rare" event that could influence winter weather in northwest Europe and the eastern U.S., Lee said, increasing the chance of colder conditions although likely not to the extent that a polar vortex event caused parts of Niagara Falls to partially freeze in January 2014. "Geopolitics and weather are the two key volatility drives for energy and now they seem to be happening at the same time — and that's always the biggest risk for markets," Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank, told CNBC. For months, meteorologists expected an El Niño event would result in a milder winter in Europe and relatively muted heating demand, Schmit said, which was broadly seen as welcome news given ongoing concerns over the continent's tight regional supplies for gas and crude oil. The prospect of a colder-than-expected winter due to an early breakdown of the polar vortex could be "incredibly difficult" for Europe to navigate, Schmit warned. She noted that the region's gas storages have seen "very, very strong withdrawals" over the last two weeks, "which is quite unusual for this time of year." "If you continue to see the same storage withdrawals over the next couple of months, that means energy prices will spike again — and they won't spike because of geopolitics. This time it will be the weather driving that spike and that volatility," Schmit said. European gas prices have soared to levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis in recent weeks, notching 103.9 euros ($113.99) per megawatt hour in late October. European benchmark Dutch TTF futures for December delivery stood at around 87.28 euros on Friday afternoon. "We have never seen an early breakdown of the polar vortex and a super el Nino in the same winter so we have no historical precedent on how this will impact global gas demand," David Lewis, principal research analyst of gas and liquified natural gas at Wood Mackenzie, told CNBC by email. El Niño is commonly associated with milder winters, while a SSW event typically leads to colder temperatures and higher snowfall, Lewis said, noting this could materialize in December and January within Europe. "So far, the start of the European winter heating season has been quite cold but more importantly has seen low wind speeds across Northern Europe," Lewis said. "The drawdown in stocks in the first half of November has been amongst the highest on record. With inventories starting the winter at their lowest level on record, any further deterioration in temperatures or wind speeds will have an outsized impact on European balances and lead to higher prices across Europe," he added.
