events.title: I worried my son would have a hard time making friends after we moved. I was the one who struggled.
events.summary: The author's son made friends in Kentucky before she did. Courtesy of Tonilyn Hornung My family moved from LA to Kentucky about eight years ago, before my son started kindergarten. I worried about him making friends in a new school. However, it turned out I was the one who had trouble. Standing alone next to my car, I watched the group of moms huddle up at the front of the parking lot. It wouldn't take much for me to walk up and join them, but I'd make it awkward. The group knew each other super well, and I didn't know anyone. When my family and I moved from Los Angeles back to Louisville eight years ago, I expected my son might feel like the new kid in kindergarten, but it turns out I was the new mom in the carpool. I had no mom friends here. I didn't realize it would be this tough to make friends after our move Moving from California to Kentucky was a big deal. But once we decided, my husband and son were ready for the adventure. We looked forward to living closer to family and having seasons in our seasons — especially those mythical snow days my kiddo had heard about. After years of discussion, my husband and I decided to move the summer our son turned 5. This way, he could start school fresh in the fall, joining the kindergarten class. As I prepared to pack up our lives, I wondered if our kiddo would have a hard time making friends in a new school , but I never unpacked the idea that I'd be the one without besties. Before we left LA, I let my husband in on my clever plan: I would attend all the parent-led events at my son's school — having kids in common would be a great way to connect! I'd have instant friends immediately following the first Back-to-School Ice Cream Social! So, I went to the open houses, volunteered to help with classroom parties, and showed up for PTO meetings. And guess what happened? Nothing. I brought out my biggest smiles and most engaging small talk — asking questions about our new school and explaining our family's recent move back to my hometown . The other parents were polite and friendly, but after a few months, I understood they didn't need me like I needed them. Their friendships were long established, and I was stuck in the acquaintance zone and couldn't get out. Short of holding up a sign that read "Please Be My Friend" in big, bold bubble letters, I was running out of ideas, and PTA meetings . "How did pick-up go today?" my husband asked. This was a consistent question, but now that we were moving into the holiday season, I was beginning to panic about having no local friends . Each time I saw the moms laughing it up in the carpool line, my stomach sank, and I felt isolated. I worried I was missing out on playdates and pizza parties — activities that would help my son adjust, too. My son made friends first, and eventually, I found a way in In LA, my friend group was small but mighty. Spending time together served a dual purpose: my son learned life skills like how to take turns on the playground slide, and I got in some much-needed adult conversation. When you find friendships that click, the validation and support they offer is everything. Yeah, I still went to the playground, but it was just the two of us. Ugh. Was my lack of social life negatively affecting him? I felt like a terrible, friendless mom. "Who'd you play with during recess today?" I asked my son most days. But one afternoon before Thanksgiving break, I got this response, "My best friend and I played tag." Oh. That was new. Apparently, my son was better at this friend thing than his mom. I was so proud of my kid moving to a different city and finding good friends. I hoped I would, too. Finally, in the spring, at one of the many kindergarten class birthday parties, I ran into a mom I'd seen often at carpool. We'd never actually talked, but I decided to introduce myself. We connected immediately, and that conversation was all we needed to move forward. It gave me confidence to put myself out there over and over, and now, I've found mom friendships that last. And we're going to need each other since high school is only a year away. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: P-8 Poseidon sub-hunting missions are hard enough. Bad weather can make these flights harder.
events.summary: For RAF P-8 pilots, the hardest part of an hourslong flight may come at the very end. Paul Christian Gordon/UK MoD Crown Copyright Business Insider joined an RAF P-8 crew hunting a submarine during a NATO exercise. The aircraft uses sensors and sonobuoys to find submarines hiding beneath the sea. Bad weather can complicate the hunt — and the landing after a long mission. SOMEWHERE ABOVE THE BALTIC SEA — Anti-submarine warfare is widely considered to be among the most demanding and complex maritime operations. Business Insider joined a Royal Air Force P-8 Poseidon flight during NATO's Dynamic Merlin exercise, which saw allied aircraft and warships hunt a submarine role-playing an enemy. For P-8 crews, the hunt for a submarine can mean long hours, multiple flights a week, and low-level runs just a few hundred feet off the water. Bad weather can make those missions — and the return to base — more difficult. At RAF Lossiemouth in northern Scotland, where Britain's P-8 fleet is based, and in the Baltic Sea area, rough flying conditions are not uncommon, especially in the winter months. A militarized version of Boeing's 737-800 airliner , the Poseidon is a maritime patrol aircraft fitted with radar, cameras, electronic support equipment, and acoustic sensors. It can also carry anti-ship missiles and torpedoes, making it one of NATO's key submarine-hunting assets . It is more than capable of handling bad weather, but conditions can still take their toll on the crew, especially at the end of a long mission. The flight deck of a P-8 during a recent NATO exercise. Sgt Beth Roberts/UK MoD Crown Copyright Britain's P-8 fleet is based at RAF Lossiemouth in Scotland. Sgt Beth Roberts/UK MoD Crown Copyright The Poseidon's ability to find and track submarines relies heavily on disposable sonobuoys , which the aircraft can drop into the sea. Once in the water, they passively listen for noise or emit sound waves and record any echoes that bounce back. The aircraft can carry up to 129 of these devices. Releasing the buoys and picking up their signals require flying at low altitudes, sometimes only a few hundred feet above the surface. That work can become even more demanding in rough weather , when turbulence, wind, and rough seas complicate an already challenging mission to find a submarine designed to be hidden, lurking beneath the waves. P-8 crew members described the Dynamic Merlin flight as one of the busiest sorties they've flown, with one of the most complex weather forecasts they had seen in years, involving wind, storms, and high sea states. The forecast required extra planning before departure. The crew had to take off from Lossiemouth via a shorter runway, which meant the aircraft had to carry less fuel and ultimately stop in Sweden to refuel en route to the exercise. P-8 flights are physically and mentally demanding on crew members. Sgt Beth Roberts/UK MoD Crown Copyright Sometimes, the most challenging part of the day for P-8 pilots may be landing back at base. Sgt Beth Roberts/UK MoD Crown Copyright The total flight time was 10 hours, which is taxing on the crew. The days are long. "It's a marathon, not a sprint," said a P-8 pilot, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details. The crew can't lose focus at any point. For the pilots, for instance, the final approach on the return to base can be just as demanding as the hours spent on station, hunting a submarine. The P-8 pilot said that the last five minutes of the flight can be just as important as the hunt. While searching for a submarine is challenging, on some flights, the most difficult part might come at the very end of the day, said Group Capt. Kevin Latchman, the deputy assistant chief of staff in No. 11 Group, which oversees RAF global air operations, in an early November interview. "From a pilot perspective," Latchman explained, "after a really long mission where you've been down at low level for a long period of time, you then have to go and do potentially the hardest thing you're going to do all day, which is land in really bad weather in RAF Lossiemouth." "So they are very challenging missions," he added. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Sessions offer advice on rising energy costs
events.summary: A charity is offering free advice on how to save on energy bills as winter approaches A charity is offering free advice on energy bills with prices expected to climb further from January . Devon Communities Together said it was hosting drop-in sessions across the county, which include help with energy bills, smart meters and switching suppliers. Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to rise by £443 a year from January. Heating oil prices have also risen drastically since the start of this year , from about 60p to £1.11 a litre, according to the Action with Communities in Rural England network. Devon County Council said many households in rural parts relied on heating oil because they were not connected to mains gas. Listen to the latest news for Devon Nora Corkery, chief executive of Devon Communities Together, said: "Behind every statistic is a household making difficult choices: rationing the heating, putting off filling up a tank, or cutting back on journeys they can't really do without." The charity said people could access confidential one-to-one support to find financial help, with a limited number of free winter warm packs available for those who attend. Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, from Devon County Council, said: "I'd urge anyone who is struggling, or worried about the winter ahead, to seek advice and find out what help may be available." events.title: Mark Carney is so popular he can get away with a lot. Will it last if the Trump spell breaks?
events.summary: Canadians have put a lot of trust in their prime minister but some question if it can last if the trade wars were to end In the hours after polls in the US midterm elections closed and it became clear that Donald Trump had been rebuked in historic fashion, Canadian politicians were elated. “I was doing cartwheels down the street, and have you ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels?” said Ontario premier Doug Ford, a prominent critic of American tariffs. For more than a year, Canada has stared down crippling levies on key industries, threats of annexation and petty feuds on social media launched by the president of the United States. Now, finally, there was a sense within Canada that it could be entering the next stage in its “war” with its ally. But while Ford was doing metaphorical cartwheels, the response from Mark Carney was more measured – perhaps not surprising for a prime minister whose political capital stems in many ways from his decision to position himself as Canada’s bulwark against Trump. Unlike other leaders who negotiated trade deals with Trump only to find them largely worthless months later, it was Carney who walked away from talks with the Americans, saying the current US administration couldn’t be trusted to uphold any agreement and its signature was “written in pencil”. Carney has pledged to rebuild Canadian manufacturing and industrial capacity, to transform Canada into a global energy super power and to lessen its reliance on the US. The result has been an extraordinary reserve of goodwill from voters. Just months after entering politics, Carney has built an unlikely coalition of support. He is simultaneously the most popular politician in francophone Quebec and in historically conservative Alberta, two provinces that have often found themselves on opposite sides of the political divide. In April, he became the first prime minister to turn a minority government into a majority, wooing floor-crossers from rival parties and winning key byelections. Carney is equally feted abroad – heralded as the torchbearer of an ascendant “middle powers” movement, holding summits with like-minded world leaders. According to pollsters, if an election were called soon, Carney’s Liberals would win one of the largest raw seat counts in Canadian parliamentary history. “Newly elected political leaders soar high in polls. They enjoy honeymoons. But Carney’s popularity is wholly different,” said Scott Reid, a political adviser and former director of communications to the former Liberal prime minister Paul Martin. “He is poaching from both the left and the right. This popularity is of a character that we’ve not witnessed before.” But as the political circumstances that propelled him to power begin to shift, it is unclear how much of that latitude is his to keep. Political analyst Philippe Fournier says current seat projections , if an election were to be held now, are “insane” in their scope. “I don’t even believe them.” Since he entered politics in 2025, Carney has styled himself as someone uninterested in horse-race politics – more concerned with macroeconomics, trade strategy and economic development than partisan manoeuvring. Calling a federal election could shatter the carefully constructed image. “The Liberals would be perceived as opportunists if they called an election now, and I’m pretty sure they would face blowback from voters. Trying to convert his immense popularity into seats could backfire,” said Fournier. For now, the extraordinary reserve of political capital that has flowed to the prime minister has given him the freedom to pursue an ambitious and sometimes controversial domestic agenda with relatively little resistance. The prime minister’s decision to approve an oil pipeline to the Pacific, for example, might once have provoked more ire. Former prime minister Stephen Harper’s push to increase oil and gas production triggered fierce opposition from environmentalists and Indigenous communities. But while Harper framed it as an ideological and economic imperative, Carney has presented the pipeline as a matter of national sovereignty and economic security. Carney has also shown an appetite for deficits that Reid says are “vastly larger than anything that the most lefty political leader in Canadian history has ever contemplated”. In early November, the government’s budget announced C$140bn (£74bn) in new spending – pledging to use windfalls from high oil prices to eradicate homelessness, invest in homes, roads, bridges, schools and health facilities, and water systems, all in First Nations communities. Carney and his finance minister have also touted a huge tax credit for businesses – at a cost of C$36bn (£19bn) in forgone revenue over five years. Under Justin Trudeau, large deficits were justified as a means of improving people’s lives.

events.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
events.summary: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human. Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform. We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course. We may double down in stubbornness, insisting on our rightness. We express ourselves, connect with others, reproduce, indulge, purge; we strive toward a goal, transform in an encounter, make vows, renege them, encounter the void, try to fill it, fail, drown out the dread, and go about the humdrum tasks of everyday life as honestly as we can. From a young age, we are nurtured and protected by our caregivers. We experience beauty and sit with mysteries. We do not exist merely for utility. Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark. Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside. Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange. Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings. Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine. And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live. If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world. So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity? Well, I have a radical suggestion for all of us, but especially the tech billionaires searching for answers in Christianity. Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones. If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul. In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible. When you leave church, carry those teachings back to your offices and boardrooms. Ask how the decisions you make affect the poor, the workers whose livelihoods are being transformed, and the neighbors who will never share in your wealth. The mystery of the Christian faith is inseparable from its demands upon how we live.

events.title: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
events.summary: American Airlines' last flight with international, long-haul first class lands this week. The airline was the last major U.S. carrier to offer an international, long-haul first class. Airlines have instead moved to offering giant business-class cabins, like American's new 70-suites section on its largest plane. The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers. U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes. Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites , bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding. It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits. The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china. A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now. "When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive. The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said. "People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites." There was still a hefty price gap between first and business. A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat. American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles. Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.) Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class. American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s. "You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats." Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details. On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class. First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered. And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access. "It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer." Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites , respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

events.title: I'm a first-generation college graduate working in tech. I owe it all to my full-ride scholarship.
events.summary: The author graduated from college debt-free and now works in tech. Courtesy of Denia Rosiclair I earned a full-ride scholarship to college and graduated debt-free. I didn't have to worry about my finances, so I challenged myself at an internship at McDonald's. I was then offered a full-time job in tech, and I feel thankful as a first-generation college grad. Months after my cybersecurity internship at McDonald's Corporation ended, the company offered me a full-time role in its global technology rotational program, a two-year track that rotates early-career hires through various tech areas, including cybersecurity. For a lot of new grads, that might sound like a natural next step. For me, it was a step I never knew I could reach. No one in my family had studied computer science. As a first-generation college student , I had to figure out how to choose classes, land internships, and picture what a tech career looked like on my own. I learned by asking questions, seeking out mentors, making mistakes, and putting in the hours. The offer reflected the work I put in. But it also reminded me of all the people and experiences that helped me get there. I first earned a full-ride scholarship When I enrolled at Florida Atlantic University, I was selected for the Kelly/Strul Emerging Scholars Program, which gives first-generation students the opportunity to graduate debt-free . Its financial support gave me stability and allowed me to focus on my education and the opportunities in front of me. The program also gave me access to mentors who helped me navigate college, prepare for my career, and think about my future in technology. I wanted to start my internship at McDonald's overprepared After a lengthy application process and several rounds of interviews, I landed an internship on McDonald's data security team. I was excited, to say the least. I also knew I wanted to make the most of it. Before my first day, I spent time strengthening my cybersecurity knowledge , working on projects, and learning as much as I could. I wanted to walk in overprepared and ready to contribute. Once I started, I saw how what I had learned in class applied to real situations. Topics that had once existed only in lectures, assignments, and labs became part of my work: identifying vulnerabilities, assessing risk, and protecting data and applications at scale. Getting to attend college for free helped me better prepare for the real-world workplace. The uncomfortable moments taught me the most at my internship I asked questions constantly and learned from the people around me. I also volunteered for tasks that made me uncomfortable because I knew they would help me grow. One of those tasks was leading Agile meetings, which I had never done before. I had to guide conversations in rooms where I was still learning and finding my footing. At first, it was intimidating. Over time, I became more comfortable trusting myself. I realized I didn't need to know everything to contribute. I needed to be prepared, willing to learn, and open to feedback. Those moments were often the ones that helped me grow the most. Each time I asked a question, accepted a new responsibility, or spoke up when I felt unsure, I became more confident in my abilities. Throughout the internship, I received recognition for my work ethic and willingness to learn. I took pride in that feedback because those qualities had carried me through college. Months later, that feedback turned into a full-time offer to join the McDonald's Global Technology Rotational Program. Over the next two years, I'll rotate through different areas of the company's tech teams. What becomes possible with the right support Looking back, I can see how much of this the Kelly/Strul program made possible. Its financial support gave me stability. Without the weight of financial stress, I could focus on my education and the opportunities in front of me. But the program helped me in ways beyond financial support. It put me in rooms with people who were motivated and doing big things, which pushed me to think bigger for myself too. Having people who believed in me gave me the space to pursue opportunities I might otherwise have passed up, including the one that led me to McDonald's. As I begin my career, I hope my story shows other first-generation students and women in technology how far support, community, and access to meaningful opportunities can take them. There will be moments when you enter rooms where not many people look like you. There may also be times when everyone else seems to understand what's happening while you're still trying to catch up. That doesn't mean you don't belong there. I didn't get here because I had all the answers from the beginning. I got here because I kept asking questions, learning from the people around me, and figuring things out one step at a time. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people
events.summary: All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’ The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said. The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday. Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK. Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy. Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election. However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities. Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.” Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement. Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime. The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit. Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”. “Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.” He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed. Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees. The foreign secretary said: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.” On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people. “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.” The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

events.title: I quit my career at 63 because I was burned out. Now, I'm focusing on my soft retirement.
events.summary: The author is in soft retirement after two decades in her career. Courtesy of Ava Brenengen After over two decades as a VP of comms, I was burned out and decided to quit at 63. But I wasn't ready to fully retire, so I started my own consulting business, which hasn't been easy. I'm calling this my soft retirement, and I'm unearthing a lot about myself for the first time. My plan for an exit strategy from a demanding career with a national healthcare trade association was hatched during a January snowstorm, while I was digging my car out of an icy airport hotel parking lot. I was rushing to make a flight to New Orleans for a professional retreat, the kind where one holes up in a hotel ballroom with hundreds of others to brainstorm ideas on a flip chart about expanding affordable healthcare. I made it to the retreat, but the only idea that consumed me was stepping down from my role as vice president of communications and public relations of an organization where I had spent the past 24 years. I knew it was time to leave, but I wasn't ready for full retirement . I was burned out The mental machinery of tasks once second nature — deadlines, project management , and juggling back-to-back Zoom meetings — was draining. Business travel and moving through unfamiliar conference hotels became challenging. I once shampooed my hair with body lotion because I could not read the small print on the bottle labels. My feet ached from wearing heels. To counter ageism, I spent a fortune each month coloring the gray out of my hair. Burnout was a convenient term that drove my decision: I also sensed something deeper. Chronic stress left me emotionally dysregulated to the point that the chime sound from a Teams message triggered a jolt of panic. Ending full time work has been a long process I always stumbled into career transitions on the blind faith that everything would work out: as a news producer, a Capitol Hill aide, and then a C-suite nonprofit executive. Ending full time work was a life transition that demanded more than just winging it. I looked at my timetable and finances, and prioritized my health and personal growth. I met with a financial advisor who advised that starting a consulting business could generate enough monthly income to cover COBRA payments until Medicare kicked in, and to defer Social Security until age 65. The moment felt right after my daughter began her last semester in college. I paid the final tuition installment, then let my employer know I was ready to hand over my role to someone else. Preparing for the next chapter was easy; executing was hard My aim for soft retirement as a consultant was to focus on distilling the tasks I enjoyed — media relations, editorial writing, and speeches— while culling unwanted tasks. After a few months of rest, I registered as an LLC and launched a low-budget website. The planning was easy; the execution was more complicated. I found steady, gratifying work for an organization led by a CEO whose leadership and advocacy I admired. Though I needed more clients to boost my income, my motivation to drum up new business was low. Naming and promoting my value as a consultant was hard, even to colleagues who knew my track record. Being a sole operator, without an executive title and large organization behind me, has been humbling. I spent years cultivating relationships with the media who sought me out as a source. Now it's a struggle to pitch reporters from a personal email address. I've lost the "street cred." The once familiar ecosystem around me was rapidly changing, and so was I. Imposter syndrome doesn't quite capture my unmoored feeling; I was fiercely protective of a newer, excavated self I had just unearthed. Soft retirement helped reclaim a self I lost Soft retirement has granted ample time to reckon with traumas that festered on the edge of awareness while I buried myself in work. In the mornings, I now leave my smartphone in another room and start journaling. I recently finally had the courage to write about surviving a brutal divorce after 20 years of marriage that forced my daughter and me to move from our family horse farm to a small apartment over a barn. That emotional work, which the New York Times columnist David Brooks has called "re-storying" or taking a "fragmented life and slowly cohering it into a new narrative," helped move me toward recovery and repair. I may not be drawing a big paycheck, but I don't need to be tethered to a title anymore to understand who I am becoming. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: We did a Trader Joe's Thanksgiving grocery haul in NYC and a smaller Northwest city. The cheaper one might surprise you.
events.summary: Business Insider reporters Gabbi Shaw and Tristin Hoffman shopped for a Thanksgiving dinner at Trader Joe's, one in New York City and the other in a small Northwest college town. Hoffman/Insider Thanksgiving is approaching, and Trader Joe's newsletter, Fearless Flyer, has a suggested menu. We compared the prices for a full Thanksgiving meal at TJ's locations in New York and Oregon. The prices were similar, but the Manhattan one was slightly cheaper. Grocery stores across the US this weekend will likely be packed with Thanksgiving shoppers. Affordability is top of mind for many Americans right now, and retailers are leaning into those concerns ahead of the big turkey dinner. Walmart has its $35 Thanksgiving basket that feeds 10 people; Aldi advertised a dinner for 10 for less than $39 . Trader Joe's has gone a different direction to give people more flexibility, instead creating a Thanksgiving shopping guide in its Fearless Flyer — its free seasonal newsletter found online and in stores. In it, shoppers are guided on which meats to choose, the best stuffing options , different cheeses to assort, and so much more, from wines to desserts. It also pitches some of its holiday items as budget-friendly through playful price callouts — from $2.49 mushroom soup meant to "expand your sense of Trader Joe's value" to $3.79 fried onions intended to avoid "frying your budget." We wanted to test out what a Thanksgiving dinner grocery receipt looks like at Trader Joe's locations in very different places. Our New York City-based reporter, Gabbi Shaw, went to one in Manhattan, and our Oregon-based fellow, Tristin Hoffman, went to the only Trader Joe's in her Northwest college town, Eugene. Oregon has no sales tax, while most groceries in NYC are tax-exempt. Here's what we found, and which shopping trip was cheaper. Gabbi went to her local Trader Joe's on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Gabbi went on a Tuesday in the mid-morning, and it was still packed. There's really no time to avoid crowds at Trader Joe's. It's a refurbished New York City Department of Transportation warehouse. It opened in 2021. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider Gabbi said it's easily the most architecturally pleasing Trader Joe's she'd been in — but the lack of easy parking isn't exactly an equal trade-off. But that's typical of all the Trader Joe's locations in New York City. There were tons of decorations around the store for fall and Thanksgiving. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider In the aisles, there were also tons of holiday-season products, like advent calendars, peppermint-scented candles, and gingerbread cookies. The first component of Fearless Flyer's menu Gabbi looked for is also the centerpiece of Thanksgiving: the turkey. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The organic turkey was slightly pricier than the pre-brined turkey. The turkey she selected was $33.42 at $2.49 per pound. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider She selected a turkey that weighed about 13.42 pounds. The turkey was brined in water, sea salt, sugar, natural turkey broth powder, and other natural flavors. Next up was the other meat, ham. Gabbi chose spiral-sliced uncured ham. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The Frick's uncured ham wasn't available at this store, but per the Trader Joe's website, it's the same price. This ham was $52.44 at $6.49 per pound. That's an 8-pound ham. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider It also came with a glaze packet. A display combined gravy and stuffing. The turkey gravy was $1.69. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The box contains about 17 ounces of turkey gravy. A box of cornbread stuffing mix was $4.99. Gabbi Shaw/Business Insider The stuffing mix is made with toasted white bread, cornbread croutons, and spices like oregano, sage, onion, and garlic, along with chicken broth and celery. events.title: Fair-weather Silicon Valley pivots away from the right after blue wave: ‘I’m not Maga’
events.summary: From Elon Musk to Palantir’s Alex Karp, CEOs are softening hardline stances in expectation of an influx of Democrats A short two years ago, Elon Musk stood before an audience of tens of thousands of people in New York City and proudly told them: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.” On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”. Silicon Valley’s tycoons made a hard-right pivot during Donald Trump’s second term, courting the president both on X and in private meetings, donating millions to his inauguration and, later, to his pet project, the White House ballroom. Musk himself spent more than $200m through his political action committee, America Pac, to help elect Trump in 2024. The attempts to cozy up to the president appeared to work. Trump took office in January 2025 flanked by some of the very executives who once banned him from their platforms in 2021. Musk, for his part, was installed as the head of the so-called “department of government efficiency”, a newly conceived and temporary federal initiative. After Democrats’ decisive triumph in the US midterm elections, though, many of the tech barons are retreating. The CEO of Palantir, Alex Karp, was among the first to attempt a pivot, softening his previously hardline stance on immigration a week before Musk in an interview with Politico. The animated leader of the tech firm that has powered Trump’s deportation apparatus said that the president mishandled immigration enforcement. “I was really happy to hear the president be honest that – you know, his words, I believe, were something like: ‘Yeah, we kinda went too far,’” Karp told Politico. “And I’m glad he’s saying in public now what I’ve been saying in private.” Karp, who once described the company as “anti-woke”, broadened his retreat from immigration to right-leaning politics in general. “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive,” he said. Karp’s latest comments stand in stark contrast with Palantir’s work with the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), functioning, according to Lesley Nash, a staff attorney at immigration defense organization Just Futures Law, as the “corporate and data analytics backbone of ICE”. “Look, we power ICE,” Karp said in an earnings call in November 2025. “We power efforts to defend America and Ukraine. And with allies. We’re on the frontline of all adversaries, including vis-a-vis China. And we support ICE, and we’ve supported Israel. I don’t know why this is all controversial, but many people find that controversial.” “Our ability to win while sticking by what we believe is important for the world,” he added in the call. Other Silicon Valley leaders had also changed their tones in the immediate aftermath of the midterms. Mark Zuckerberg, the CEO of Meta, is reportedly showing signs of shifting left. After the company bid farewell to Joel Kaplan, its president of global affairs and former adviser to George Bush, Meta recruited and promoted a more bipartisan slate of executives, according to Axios . Kaplan, who has been at Meta for 15 years, was promoted at the start of the Trump administration and was known for his ties to the the Republican party. Many Silicon Valley CEOs have helmed their companies for years, and it’s not their first time maneuvering the changing tides of American politics . Though a self-described moderate, Musk previously donated to the Democratic national committee as well as Barack Obama’s re-election campaign in 2012. In 2018, he celebrated Tesla achieving a perfect score on an index of LGBTQ+ equality in the workplace for a fourth year in a row. “Don’t buy our car if that’s a problem. People should be free to live their lives where their heart takes them ❤️🧡💛💚💙💜🖤💖🌈,” he wrote . Eight years later, having moved from California to Texas and donated hundreds of millions of dollars to Republican candidates, Musk struck the opposite tone. He fear-mongered about the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, by tweeting that James Talarico “will trans your kids”. After a blue wave swept over the US, though, he seems to again be shifting his stance. Responding to a question Wednesday about Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, Musk said, “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor, and based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think everything will be fine in Texas with Gina [Hinojosa] as governor.

events.title: After historic Southern wins, Black organizers prepare a push for governing power
events.summary: After years of being overlooked by national Democrats, Black organizers are using stunning Southern election upsets in the pursuit of something more lasting: a new generation of candidates who can win and govern. Why it matters: Activists say the 2026 midterms proved Southern races long dismissed as unwinnable could flip with grassroots organizing and investment. Now they're building a multiracial, working-class political bench — from school boards to statehouses. Organizers want to turn Black political gains into a durable Southern coalition united by economic interests, not just opposition to Republicans. By the numbers: The midterm election results gave organizers fresh ammunition. Roughly nine in 10 Black voters backed Democratic House candidates nationally, according to the AP Voter Poll . Democrats flipped 10 South Carolina House seats, seven won by Black candidates, ending the GOP supermajority, the South Carolina Daily Gazette reports. State of play: The Working Families Party plans candidate recruitment events in Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina and Mississippi in early 2027, targeting community organizers, teachers, young activists and other political outsiders. It plans training, digital outreach and spending to support dozens of Southern candidates. Its Southern Made initiative aims to recruit and train 1,000 working-class candidates by 2030. Zoom in: South Carolina illustrates the opportunity. WFP-backed Jumelle Brooks , a home health care provider, lost a 2024 House race by roughly 700 votes before winning this year by nearly 10 percentage points. Another WFP-backed Democrat, Sonja Ogletree Satani , won a Charleston-area rematch. What they're saying: "We are building concentrated governing power," Britney Whaley, WFP's Southeast regional director, tells Axios. Whaley wants clusters of allies in elected bodies who can pass legislation, not isolated progressives powerless to advance an agenda. "Black people across the country voted for historic change, and now it's time for systemic policy change," Kristin Powell of Black to the Future Action Fund said in a statement to Axios. Zoom out: The Southern breakthroughs extended well beyond statehouses. Mississippi: Scott Colom became the state's first Black senator elected since Reconstruction. South Carolina: Annie Andrews won a long-shot Senate race. Georgia: Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation's first Black woman elected governor; Democrats flipped the state House . Texas: James Talarico became the first Democratic U.S. senator elected since 1988. Yes, but: The South remains deeply Republican, and organizers say Democrats left winnable races on the table. WFP-backed Angie Nixon lost in Florida by roughly three points; Justin J. Pearson lost Tennessee's 9th District by 2,539 votes . The WFP spent about $200,000 on each race and argues more national investment could have tipped them. That's unproven. The intrigue: Pre-election findings from the 2026 Black Census , a nationwide voluntary survey by the advocacy group Black Futures Lab, found 95% of respondents planned to vote — yet just 3% trusted Washington and 22% trusted Black elected officials. Economic anxiety runs deep, with 44% hoping to escape debt, 35% to earn more and 25% to find affordable housing. Southern organizers now face a test of turning votes into economic relief, though the survey isn't representative of all Black voters.

events.title: How much Taylor Swift owes in pied-à-terre tax
events.summary: Taylor Swift on the steps of a Tribeca building in 2018. TheStewartofNY/Getty Images New York City has instituted a new tax on wealthy property owners with second homes in the city. The pied-à-terre tax will hit some notable property owners — including superstar Taylor Swift. According to Department of Finance records, Swift will likely owe just over $133,000. Welcome to New York! Your tax bill's waiting for you — and music superstar Taylor Swift no longer has a blank space on what she owes the city. Newly updated Department of Finance documents show how much wealthy second-home owners in the city are being asked to pay come January 1. Based on those documents, Swift's new pied-à-terre tax bill for her part-time homes in New York will add up to just over $133,000. The bulk of that, or just shy of $71,000, will come from the Tribeca penthouses she purchased for $19.95 million in 2014. The remaining roughly $62,000 will come from her townhouse next door; she bought the townhouse and an adjoining unit in the building where she owns the penthouse in 2017 for a combined $27.75 million. The new levy more than doubles what the city's records show she would pay in property taxes for those homes, bringing the total bill to $205,750 for the year. "It sure looks like she's getting a good deal relative to what it could be in a couple of years," real estate appraiser Jonathan Miller said. Representatives for Swift and the Department of Finance did not return requests for comment from Business Insider. New York City's pied-à-terre tax, which is estimated to raise more than $500 million, got a green light from state lawmakers in May after years of proposals. It is supposed to apply to one, two, and three-family homes worth over $5 million and condos worth over $1 million that are not primary residences, rental properties, or in use by relatives, and its rollout has moved forward despite legal challenges from deep-pocketed opponents. The tax overwhelmingly applies to properties in Manhattan, according to an analysis done by Tom Flaschen , a former trader at Jane Street who writes a newsletter about New York City law and policy. He wrote that an analysis of public bills showed that $563 million in taxes have been levied on 7,489 homes, most of which are condos. The amount raised by the tax could fund some of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's priorities . In the grand scheme of the $129 billion city budget, however, it's rather small. Even so, it's already received pushback from wealthy New Yorkers who don't live in the city full-time; Business Insider's James Rodriguez previously reported that those part-time New Yorkers had been furiously calling up tax advisors and lawyers to figure out what it means for their properties. Homeowners have sued the city in hopes of stopping the tax, but so far, none of those lawsuits have blocked the rollout. Earlier this month, an Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court ruled in favor of the tax in a suit challenging the initial publication of potential tax rolls and letters to homeowners saying they may have to pay it. Another lawsuit more directly challenging the underlying constitutionality of the tax, filed by billionaire Steve Wynn and former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, is ongoing, with arguments scheduled for December. For now, unless any of them either move in full time or sign an immediate family member to a legitimate lease, it's looking like they'll have to pay up. That shouldn't be a problem for Swift. Her total tax expense of $200,000 is just 0.01% of her $2 billion net worth. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A six-figure middle manager job — no desk or suit required
events.summary: Ramsess Salazar, who oversees about two dozen employees at a Sweetgreen in Chicago. Mustafa Hussain for BI Early in her Target career, Brooke Pratt wondered whether shoppers mistook her for an hourly worker as she helped restock shelves. She was actually a department manager, earning substantially more than she had in her previous job, an entry-level desk position at a public-relations firm. "I was thinking, this isn't too bad," Pratt told Business Insider. "I'm putting cereal on the shelf, and I'm making this kind of money. It's pretty cool." Pratt, 34, is now a store director overseeing 350 team members and 10 department managers at one of Target's largest locations, in Chaska, Minnesota. Though a Target spokesperson said employees aren't permitted to disclose their salary, the retailer recently advertised a role in Minnesota with the same title, offering $106,000 to $212,000 in annual base pay. The spokesperson said store directors are also eligible to receive an annual bonus and stock equity. A premium for frontline managers The six-figure salaries that some managers in retail, hospitality, and other service industries now command suggest that leadership sees them as on par with their white-collar managerial counterparts. The higher pay comes at a time, though, when some tech leaders are questioning whether they need so many middle layers in the first place. Companies including Meta and Block have been cutting their managerial ranks in recent years, arguing that layers of bosses slow decision-making. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong has said org chart layers impose a "coordination tax. " Meanwhile, Walmart increased pay, annual stock grants, and potential bonuses last year for about 440 of its market managers, who oversee around a dozen stores. Top earners can now make as much as $620,000 in total compensation , up from about $569,000 previously. Sweetgreen has said that some managers at top-performing locations could earn more than $200,000 a year starting in 2027. Mustafa Hussain for BI Salad chain Sweetgreen has said it plans to introduce a 2027 total compensation plan that could pay some managers of its top-performing locations more than $200,000 a year , part of a broader retention effort. Similar pay ranges are on offer across other labor-intensive industries. Examples include $200,000 to $300,000 for a general manager at a car dealership in Illinois and about $117,000 to $195,000 for an Apple store leader in California. Managing the unexpected The cost of getting management wrong can be especially high in big-box retail, where managers are expected to run increasingly sophisticated operations across physical stores and online orders, said Scott Benedict, a retail consultant who worked in merchandising and e-commerce at Walmart and Sam's Club. "There's a difference between finding a warm body and finding a leader of the caliber that you need to run what in some cases can be a $100 million or more business," he said, referring to annual sales at a single big-box location. The pressure can also be intense at a single restaurant. On a recent Friday morning, two online orders for 50 salads apiece came in back-to-back at a Sweetgreen in Chicago, where Ramsess Salazar, 48, oversees 26 employees who serve several hundred customers a day. With fewer people on the floor than usual, the general manager said he split his team between the digital rush and in-store guests. He then told everyone to stay calm and keep pushing. "I have stress as well, but I cannot show it to them," Salazar said, adding that about 90 minutes later they were laughing about how many salads they had made. Another time, a walk-in cooler broke down before lunch at a Sweetgreen in Boston, leaving Salazar with a 100-plus-salad corporate order to fill. He said he rerouted that day's delivery to a nearby sister location's cooler while a technician repaired the broken one. Close to the frontline The value that managers provide in consumer-facing businesses goes beyond solving crises. They often see problems and opportunities as they unfold — from a menu item that isn't selling to a staffing or service issue — and have to respond before headquarters can. Joe de la Torre, 25, is the general manager of Crush Yard's Nashville location, a 34,000-square-foot entertainment venue offering pickleball, golf simulators, food and drinks, and other games and activities. He oversees six direct reports and 33 hourly employees, helping to run an operation that attracts between 500 and 2,000 visitors a day. De la Torre said he keeps close tabs on the facility, walking around to ensure it meets the company's standards for cleanliness, customer service, and the overall guest experience. He also sometimes helps resolve customer disputes, including disagreements among pickleball players. He then shares his observations with Crush Yard's vice president of operations. "You get to see all fronts of the business," said de la Torre. He said he makes $84,000 a year in base salary, plus a bonus, which he estimated could bring his annual compensation to as much as $150,000. Proximity to day-to-day operations can give service-industry managers local knowledge and influence over workers that headquarters can't easily replicate, said Raffaella Sadun, a Harvard Business School professor. In many tech companies, by contrast, leaders believe digital tools and AI can move information without a human in the middle. Managers in service industries often have local knowledge, as well as influence over workers that headquarters can't easily replicate. Mustafa Hussain for BI That offers a lesson for white-collar managers , Sadun said: Stay close to clients and the work — and raise insights that headquarters can't see on a dashboard. Doing what it takes The work of a frontline manager can be decidedly unglamorous. It often means spending nearly all day on one's feet, pitching in when staffers call out, wearing a uniform, and working nights and weekends. Pratt, the Target store director, wears tops in the retailer's signature red while on the job, and carries a walkie-talkie throughout her shift to stay in constant contact with her staff. She's also certified to use the store's powered equipment, including a forklift, and fills in for junior colleagues when needed. "It doesn't matter really what level you are," said Pratt, who added that she learned about leadership while serving as a cheerleading team captain in college. "We all work together as a team to get something done." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘National scandal’: residents in England rally against surge in mega-warehouse developments
events.summary: Campaigners call out ‘greed’ of developers after 95% of ‘megashed’ planning applications approved in last 10 years When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen. He had just moved into the property in Bingham, Nottinghamshire , with his wife and toddler in June. Now, he said he was being told: “‘By the way, there’s going to be 21.5-metre-high warehouses right next to you, and there’s going to be eight of them, and you’re going to have 400 HGVs and it’s going to be a 24-hour operation’.” He added: “I’ll be honest with you, I cried. I was so upset.” That planning application would add to the more than 8,500 warehouses or large distribution units that have been approved across England in the past decade, fuelled by the growth of online shopping. Analysis of official figures by the Guardian showed that almost all (95%) of the 9,009 planning applications for “megasheds” were given the go-ahead in the 10 years up to June 2026. Of the 4,300 approved in the last five years, nearly half (1,922) were in the east, south-east and north-west of England, and 17 were in national parks, despite them having stricter rules on major developments. Six industrial developments were approved in the South Downs national park since 2021, alongside five in the North York Moors and one in the Lake District. England’s “golden logistics triangle” – historically the Midlands area, which is within a four-hour drive of 90% of industrial developments – has expanded significantly, with the data showing that many planned developments are in newly-held Reform councils or constituencies. Robert Jenrick, Reform MP for Newark, which Bingham falls under, met with the developer and the local council to discuss residents’ fears about the developments. Davis closely followed events in Astley, a village in Wigan, where a public inquiry was held over towering mega-warehouses licensed to operate 24/7 being built metres from people’s homes. The powerful fightback of Astley villagers against what they described as “torture” from increased noise, light, and traffic made them figureheads in a nationwide battle against superstructures. Davis considers them “the canary in the coal mine”. “They’ve been so inspirational,” he added. “Seeing their videos, I was like, ‘Well, if they can do it, I think we can and I think we should.’” Astley’s villagers had help from the Community Planning Alliance, an umbrella organisation for around 700 community groups nationwide. Other local groups have highlighted instances where planning proposals were subtly changed or where councils cited un-evidenced demand for warehouse space. There were also suggestions that the government was not helping, after the National Planning Policy Framework, which was published in August, made it more difficult for the public to challenge planning decisions. “The planning system is 100% biased against communities,” said Marj Powner, who runs the CPA. “We have so little power, it’s unbelievable.” She said developers had six months to appeal a planning rejection, whereas communities had “zero, no right of appeal, none whatsoever” if an application was approved, leaving a judicial review as their only option. “The community have six weeks to find and instruct a legal team and put together the grounds that they may have for their judicial review, and it will cost them around £60,000, which that community has to raise from donations,” she added. Ten minutes away from Astley, residents near a 70 hectare (173 acre) site in Gibfield began their own campaign against a development that they said would tower over their homes and take away their only green space. The development was initially backed by the Reform-led Wigan council and is managed by the Peel Group, one of Britain’s biggest landowners, which is privately run by the billionaire John Whittaker. Although the developer outlined warehouses 12.5m tall, the elevated ground level put the true height closer to 15.5m, relative to their homes, residents said. “I think there’s just this view that we’re all kind of middle-class nimbies. We’re not. We’re normal working-class people,” said Amanda Coleman, who lives in a house immediately adjacent to the site. “It’s heartbreaking.” The site is one of a number of green belt areas controversially designated as “grey belt”. While intended for previously developed land when it was introduced in 2024, a CPRE report found that 88% of grey belt approvals upon appeal were on land that had never been built on. Protecting nature was at the heart of many of the battles different groups were embroiled in across the UK. In Northamptonshire, campaigners spent six years fighting two mega-warehouses on a 60 hectare (150 acre) site that is adjacent to the Upper Nene Valley Gravel Pits, a legally-protected nature reserve for golden plover and lapwing birds.

events.title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
events.summary: Supporters of the climate movement Fridays for Future protest in Berlin on Nov. 13. Ralf Hirschberger/AFP/Getty Images You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away. Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise , particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage . CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.  At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.  Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades. Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually. Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?  Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work. I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.  One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window: Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections. Note: The modeled pathways, what we call projections, for deployment of carbon capture and storage are from text and tables in the International Energy Agency’s Energy Technology Perspectives and World Energy Outlook reports, and from correspondence with the IEA. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.  So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:  Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not. Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase. They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice. In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.  They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill. Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.” They assume that stored CO2 will stay put. Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”  The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-world costs have steadily climbed. When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal. In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance

events.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
events.summary: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said. Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.” China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant. At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 . Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal. But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31 , released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.” Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry. While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans. But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power. Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels , meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts. Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said. China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy. One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023 , but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday , but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners . The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.” China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU , which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field. Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt. Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said.
