events.title: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
events.summary: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming ANTALYA, Turkey -- Work crews were boxing up the venue of this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will result in concrete plans to drastically slash the use of fossil fuels. The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, called COP31 , which was supposed to end Friday, drew strong condemnation from activists and some countries for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The final document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which is contributing to devastating heat waves, floods and other disasters. To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas. In the lead up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. “No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be,” said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International. Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the “pavilions,” where countries showcased their climate policies and hosted panel discussions, workers were packing up electronics and other belongings Saturday morning. The hallways, normally bustling with participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos in front of the deserted pavilions. “COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier,” said Rachel Cleetus from the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya. Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year’s heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly. Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world. The United States, a major polluter and the world’s largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks. Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027. Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid intensify ahead of winter UN climate talks in Turkey risk being ‘worst COP ever’ as fossil fuels go unmentioned On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan “you are killing the future” interrupted official COP proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting “You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait.” The Global South is a term that isn’t geographical, but a reference to developing countries in general. “You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now,” the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the room by security. The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said “let’s try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks. “Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it’s nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here watching the negotiations and waiting for the next iteration of the text,” said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits. “We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on,” he said. Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. events.title: Telegraph departures signal concerns over direction under Axel Springer’s ownership
events.summary: Insiders say they only see cuts, with no discernible long-term strategy, since title’s purchase by German media firm A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times. Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week. Speculation swirled about the future of both its editor, Chris Evans, and his loyal deputy, Rob Winnett. It was accompanied by days of long, hushed meetings between senior figures at the title, now under the ownership of the German media company Axel Springer . The intrigue was heightened by Evans’s apparent early return from a trip to the US. Suggestions did the rounds that both editor and deputy could be leaving – a rumour dampened by Evans’s continued presence in the newsroom. In the event, it emerged that only Winnett was departing. Winnett, who led the Telegraph’s coverage of the MPs’ expenses scandal, is heading to the title’s bitter rightwing rival, the Daily Mail. He has been installed as its chief content editor, instantly elevating him as a likely successor to the Mail’s editor, Ted Verity. However, at the Telegraph, Winnett’s departure is being seen in the light of widespread concerns about the title’s direction under its new owners. Axel Springer and its all-powerful chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, swept in to buy the titles for an eye-watering £575m earlier this year, with promises of investment and expansion. However, five months into Axel Springer’s tenure, insiders say they are only seeing cuts – and no discernible long-term strategy. “I don’t think they have a particular plan – they clearly want money saved,” said one staffer. “They’ve clearly given Evans a target of savings to make. In terms of a plan, it’s all very vague.” Winnett’s departure, one insider said, was “a huge loss”. Winnett had been part of a team who headed to Florida to scope a base for an expanded US operation . So far, solid plans have not emerged. It follows a recent town hall meeting between journalists and the Telegraph’s new chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol, at which reporters asked a series of questions that they felt went unanswered, and cuts in which large numbers of employees were told they were being made redundant , including senior figures in the newsroom. Hulshoff Pol said the strategy was to reinvent the reader experience, build new revenue streams and grow internationally. Reporters asked for more details about the wider plans behind the cuts and what the company meant in its repeated insistence that the Telegraph would become a “global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”. Staff remain unclear what the use of AI will entail. There is also confusion about who is making the cuts. Evans is credited with keeping the Telegraph operation going during three years in which it was without an owner and unable to take major, strategic decisions. He now also appears to have been tasked with making cuts for Axel Springer. Some believe Evans is being used by the company to carry out “the bulk of the current bloodletting”. A source said the company was having to take “difficult proposals that we believe are necessary for the future of the business”. Some staff had initially detected a change in the Telegraph’s politics in the months after Axel Springer’s purchase. They presumed the loosening of ties with Reform’s Nigel Farage and the departures of some of its most rightwing writers, such as Allison Pearson and Sherelle Jacobs, were part of a shift towards a global centre-right audience. However, many now believe the changes so far have been more about costs than politics. Elsewhere, there has been no such turn to the centre. The Telegraph’s new US podcast, The Right Track with Poppy Coburn, most recently featured the rightwing media host Steve Bannon, an ally of Donald Trump. It has left Telegraph staff scratching their heads about the takeover. Many had expected Axel Springer to arrive with money to spend. Insiders said executives seemed to be focused on boosting advertising. The cuts are being made despite the Telegraph making underlying profits. “This is a business that generates healthy margins, healthy profits,” said Alex DeGroote, a media analyst. “So at face value, the restructuring – all these redundancies – is not because of financial pressures. “Even allowing for the fact that the advertising market this year has probably been a bit soft, both print and digital, the scale of the restructuring would suggest that this is quite a deep strategic rethink. Basically, I’m afraid it points to AI.” It has all focused attention on the intentions of Döpfner, a billionaire who has made numerous attempts to buy media assets in an attempt to establish himself as a modern media mogul.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Eyre Peninsula residents worried about further blackouts as ElectraNet works on fix Transmission tower and powerlines down at Wharminda. ( Supplied: Chris Prime ) Eyre Peninsula residents say they are counting on temporary fixes to the power grid to carry them through the next few weeks. About 24,000 properties were without power on Thursday during a mass blackout. The region is now temporarily being serviced by the mothballed Port Lincoln power station and reconfigured power lines. An intense storm damaged three transmission towers, which operator ElectraNet said crippled the "radial line" powering much of the peninsula, including Port Lincoln. Storm clouds above grain fields on the Eyre Peninsula where wild weather lashed the region on Thursday afternoon ( Supplied: Benjamin Wandel ) The company is investigating whether any structural defects were to blame but said that it is unlikely. Port Lincoln mayor Diana Mislov acknowledged the severe weather was "an unexpected event" but wanted assurances that the construction requirements were met. "I think the whole line needs to be looked at and more work undertaken to ensure that this doesn't happen again," Ms Mislov said. Port Lincoln's Mayor Diana Mislov said she was putting her faith in the people operating the regional city's mothballed power station. ( Robert Lang ) "I understand the cost-benefit analysis that needs to happen with some of this decision-making, but we can't afford to allow our communities to be without power." The nearby power plant, which is privately owned and will shut down permanently in 2028, will be used for several days, according to ElectraNet. Ms Mislov wanted to see the plant maintained long-term as a back-up option. "The fact we were able to fire up the power station … and get it back into action for our communities is incredibly important," she said. She also urged people who had lost power to switch off their solar panels, in line with SA Police's instructions, to avoid overloading the grid. Multi-day blackout 'wouldn't be good' On Friday, Premier Peter Malinauskas also warned that predicted storm events and hot weather on Sunday could further strain the grid. The Bureau of Meteorology is predicting early thunderstorms and temperatures to reach around 30 on the Lower Eyre Peninsula. Restaurant owner Craig McCathie, of the Fresh Fish Place, said he was concerned about more blackouts over the next few weeks while repairs are underway. The venue's back-up generator kicked in, but Mr McCathie said a blackout running into several days – such as in 2016 – "wouldn't be a good scenario" if the town's reserves run out. "It does cause a bit of a stress because of what's happened in the past," he said. Fresh Fish Place owner Craig McCathie said businesses and industry in the region are dependent on reliable power. ( ABC News: Duncan Bailey ) "We keep enough [fuel] for about 20 hours, but when the town is down, the diesel pumps are down too, so we haven't got a back-up plan for when we run out of our storage." There is still no timeline for when the damaged towers will be permanently replaced, but temporary structures are expected to go up within days, which will bolster energy reliability. Speaking to 891 Adelaide, ElectraNet's Alex Trento said the company was confident its designs were structurally sound. "Depending on the investigation, that'll determine whether we go down the path of looking at a different design," Mr Trento said. "But at this point in time we're of the strong view that the design is adequate, tested to the requirements of the Australian standards ... and constructed by very competent contractors, with ElectraNet personnel overseeing [them]". events.title: ‘Like an invisible stealth tax’: ways to shield your cash from UK inflation
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . With living costs set to rise higher in 2027, here’s how you can help your savings and pension keep up with soaring prices F or many of us, it is when we go to the supermarket that we really notice the impact of inflation. The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has broken the £100 barrier , and some of the packets look smaller than they were. But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded. UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October and the Bank of England expects it to rise even further, to about 5% by mid-2027 , as higher energy prices continue to push up costs and bills. If your savings account interest rate is lower than the inflation rate, you are losing money in real terms, even if the balance in your account is growing. It is much easier to beat inflation if you do not pay tax on the savings interest you earn. So if you are a non-taxpayer, or the money is in an Isa, any interest rate over 3.6% is inflation-beating. If you do pay tax on the interest, you will need to earn a rate of interest that is a fair bit higher than inflation for your returns to outpace the rising cost of living. Just to match 3.6% inflation, a basic-rate taxpayer would currently need to earn 4.5%, while a higher-rate taxpayer would need to earn 6%. This is not about a few pence or even a couple of pounds. Based on current inflation and a £10,000 savings balance, choosing a one-year fixed-rate savings bond paying 5.21% (one of the top rates available this week) compared with an account paying 2% could leave a saver £321 better off over one year. Lots of people will remember index-linked savings certificates, which were offered by National Savings and Investments (NS&I). They guaranteed that your investment would “grow in spending power each year, whatever happens to the cost of living”, but they are no longer available, though people can renew maturing certificates. No other provider offers anything similar, so you need to get the best rate on savings that you can. The good news is that the financial data firm Moneyfacts says there are 1,649 available savings accounts that pay more than the 3.6% you need to match inflation if there is no tax to pay. That includes 879 fixed-rate savings bonds, which typically involve you having to tie up your money for between six months and five years. At the time of writing, best-buy rates on these ranged from 4.67% on a six-month bond from GB Bank to 5.37% on a five-year bond from StreamBank. That total also includes 130 easy access accounts. Top-paying providers include Chase and Cahoot, which were this week paying 4.75% (which includes an interest bonus for 12 months) and 4.52% respectively. Meanwhile, more than 400 fixed-rate cash Isas pay more than 3.6%. This week, top payers included UBL UK offering 5.3% and Shawbrook Bank with 5.27%, though to get those rates you would need to tie your cash up for five years. Best-buy easy access cash Isas include those offered by the Chip and Moneybox apps, which pay an initial 4.87% and 4.86% respectively. In the example above, based on inflation at 3.6% and £10,000 saved for one year, a one-year fixed-rate savings bond paying 5.21% would return a £521 interest payment at the end of the term. However, the real return after inflation would be £161, says Moneyfacts. If the same sum was in an account paying 2%, while the saver would get £200 interest after a year, their real return after inflation would be negative. They would be £160 worse off in real terms. Caitlyn Eastell at Moneyfacts says that with inflation forecast to continue going up, “it’s crucial that savers secure the most competitive rates to ensure their money isn’t losing its spending power”. There are now more than 250 accounts that pay interest of 5% or more, which is “a real win for savers”, though it is increasingly important to make use of tax-efficient options such as cash Isas, she adds.. A retirement income that increases every year Although falling out of favour among retirees, an annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular guaranteed income for the rest of their life, or for a fixed term . You pay a life insurer a lump sum, and in exchange it guarantees you a regular payout. There are various types. Level annuities are the most popular – these pay the same income each year. But if you want to avoid inflation taking a bite out of your spending power over time, escalating annuities provide an income that goes up every year. You can choose between an annual increase at a set rate, such as 3% or 5%, or one that is index-linked, which means it rises in line with inflation.

events.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
events.summary: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism W hat child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.” Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy. One in eight young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are classed as not in education, employment or training (Neet). Until I finally secured an office job this September I was one of them, going down to the jobcentre every week hoping there’d finally be a good work opportunity. Here is what life was like: for a long year after graduating in 2025, things that I had taken for granted while working student jobs at university – routine, colleagues, a purpose in life – felt far away. Yet there remained hope. Hope that one employer would say yes, and you could finally stop spending weekdays at your local library, with its view of a graveyard. Perhaps some people can rationalise long-term unemployment after university as an opportunity to take a sabbatical from life or become a lady of leisure. But try being a lady of universal credit (UC). The glamour of doing nothing all day – with no money – isn’t so glamorous after all. You have all the free time in the world, but you can barely afford to do anything – the £338 a month is just enough to cover the occasional coffee as a treat. Or maybe you won’t get any UCpayment at all. I was sanctioned by the job centre for three months for not applying for a restaurant vacancy that I hadn’t been told was mandatory. That was despite having applied to hundreds of jobs – from a surf camp in Spain to a year-round Christmas shop in Edinburgh. Throughout this time, with no money, I was still expected to attend weekly meetings at the job centre in my home town. UC is a far cry from life at university. While I was on it, the Department for Work and Pensions asked for all my bank statements. Every supermarket basket, train ticket, coffee shop trip all under their watchful eye. It made me feel guilty for every purchase I made. I was interrogated during a particularly brutal phone call about my transactions; even an innocent payment from my grandfather was treated as suspicious. Now, you may think that finally finding a job has brought about a sense of relief. Yet getting the job is just the first hurdle. Like many young jobseekers, I was offered a fixed-term contract. Sure, I have a job for 12 months, but what next? A friend of mine was unemployed for six months after his fixed-term contract ended. Eleven other people were hired by my employer at the same time as me – what will we all do once this period ends? You feel, in a sense, trapped, bouncing between benefits and fixed-term contracts. Having looked at the Milburn review, there are many aspects that I think look very promising. For a start, the aim of doubling apprenticeships over the next decade is laudably ambitious. For too long a degree has been privileged as the best route towards prosperity, and it is encouraging to see an embrace of alternative pathways. Incentives for employers to hire young people, including cuts to national insurance and a previously announced Youth Jobs Grant of £3,000 for hiring those who have been Neet for six months, could make all the difference too. I was also pleased to see that employers will be encouraged to hire those who are disabled or have been in care through an additional £2,000 payment. As someone who knows how it feels to be on UC all too well, I think the introduction of a new “youth allowance” could be a good opportunity to reform how young people are treated by the welfare system. But if it is just as dehumanising as UC – with its sanctions and intrusiveness – what difference is this making for young people? Is it the same thing with a different name? One of my biggest concerns with the report is that its help is focused on those under the age of 25. That is, of course, the working definition of a Neet. But it suggests that there is no plan for those who age out of Neet-hoodand are still facing the same issues in the job market. The graduate employment crisis is not new, and there are many people who have been Neet and are now approaching 30. They still need all the help they can get, otherwise they will truly become a lost generation.

events.title: Anthropic's post-IPO slide shows hype not enough to ease AI investor fears
events.summary: The glitz of Anthropic's stock market debut faded quickly on Friday after a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence shares sent a signal that even history's biggest IPO could not temper investor concerns about the sector. San Francisco-based Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $83 per share, jumping to about $100 before settling at $97, placing its value at about $1.76 trillion. However, the stock stumbled on Friday, retreating 8.5 per cent to $88.19. Anthropic's IPO comes at a volatile moment for the sector, including the downfall of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after revelations of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The broad AI sell-off dragged the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average to technical correction territory – a scenario in which an index falls more than 10 per cent from recent highs. The tech-rich Nasdaq Composite, meanwhile, dropped 5.28 per cent to erase its gains in 2026. "The trouble in the tech sector – particularly areas linked to AI, such as semiconductors and memory – has been brewing for a while now," said Neil Wilson, an investor content strategist at Denmark's Saxo Bank. "[Anthropic's] success or failure will have huge ramifications for the wider AI ecosystem and in particular the timing for OpenAI's own delayed public listing ... the question we ask is simple: is it worth it? Can Anthropic justify at $1.5 trillion valuation, or $2 trillion for that matter?" The Nasdaq 100, which tracks the index's 100 biggest companies by weight, fell to its lowest level since the 2020 pandemic year, pushing it near bear market territory. That is when an index retreats 20 per cent or more after a recent high. Nvidia, the Nasdaq's 100's third biggest component that this week forecast a strong outlook amid Mr Huang's scandal, sank more than 14 per cent after reports US authorities were investigating the company over its accounting practices. The Nvidia results and Anthropic’s IPO failed to provide the relief investors had hoped for, as enthusiasm around the listing gave way to renewed selling across AI stocks and the broader market, said Mathieu Racheter, head of equity strategy research at Swiss bank Julius Baer. "The moves are further amplified by a liquidity squeeze that strong company results alone cannot resolve. Resilient nominal growth, elevated energy costs and rising public and private investment needs are absorbing capital, while a more hawkish [US Federal Reserve] is keeping financing expensive," he said. "This limits the multiples that investors are willing to pay, even when earnings remain strong, and intensifies scrutiny of the returns on AI infrastructure spending." Bitcoin and gold plummet Bitcoin, on the other hand, fell to its lowest level in more than two years as the worries over AI stocks spilt over into other riskier assets. The world's biggest cryptocurrency slumped to an intraday low of about $55,659 on Saturday, matching levels last seen in September 2024, data from CoinMarketCap shows. Bitcoin, after trending upwards in mid-August, is back on a downward slope, consistently declining after sentiment was hit in the aftermath of the $6.3 billion breach of Binance in late October. Gold, meanwhile, slid to its lowest level in more than a year amid the AI sell-off and as investors digested signals that the Fed might raise interest rates again in December. The precious metal, widely considered a safe haven asset, fell 4.33 per cent to $3,524.80 an ounce, after nearly falling below $3,500 earlier in the session. Silver fared worse, shedding nearly 8 per cent to $40.99 an ounce.

events.title: Bitcoin falls to more than 2-year low as global markets sink
events.summary: Bitcoin slumped to its weakest since September 2024. Bitcoin fell to a more than two-year low, dropping 6% in the US and 5.7% in Asia to US$55,533. It has lost over half its value since October 2025. The sell-off was driven by a Binance hack, US election worries and money leaving Bitcoin ETFs. Investors are also cutting risk as the AI trade weakens. A stronger dollar and fears of more Federal Reserve rate rises have added pressure. About US$2 billion in long crypto bets were liquidated, showing heavy leverage and weak confidence. NEW YORK/SINGAPORE – Bitcoin fell to the lowest level in over two years, extending its reversal from market darling after the re-election of Donald Trump to a casualty of a broader retreat from speculative bets. The original cryptocurrency slumped 6% in the US on Nov 20 and another 5.7% in Asia on Nov 21 to US$55,533, its weakest since September 2024. It has lost more than half its value since reaching a peak above US$126,000 in October 2025 and is now worth less than it was when crypto-friendly Trump retook the White House. Bitcoin has been caught in a confluence of pressures in recent weeks. A hack of Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, at the end of October rattled digital assets, while sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections the following week fuelled concerns that the crypto industry’s push for friendlier rules has lost momentum. “The broader market has shifted into a sharp lack of confidence, and investors are de-risking,” said Andy Baehr, managing director of asset management at GSR. “Bitcoin is along for the ride here, typically weak in deleveraging environments.” The latest leg lower has been fuelled by investors pulling money from Bitcoin exchange-traded funds amid an unravelling of the artificial-intelligence trade. Bitcoin ETFs have seen year-to-date outflows of more than US$3 billion (S$3.9 billion). The broader backdrop is becoming less favourable as well. For much of the past decade, cryptocurrencies occupied a privileged place in the risk-taking economy. Now, a stronger dollar and rising expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase are adding to the pressure. The market is pricing a more aggressive Fed rate hike and a slowdown in the AI buildout, prompting “an excessively negative market interpretation right now”, said Fabian Dori, chief investment officer at Sygnum Bank. On Nov 20, Bitcoin’s slide triggered the liquidation of roughly US$2 billion in long crypto bets over 24 hours, with Bitcoin positions accounting for the majority of that sum, according to Coinglass data. “What made the move so fast was leverage,” said Andrew Yang, research analyst at Kaiko. “As Nasdaq losses deepened again in late-morning New York trading, Bitcoin broke below US$60,000, triggering US$94.6 million in BTC liquidations on Binance, Bybit and OKX in a single hour.” The downturn is unfolding at what should have been a triumphant moment for the industry. With Trump as US President, crypto has secured many of the victories it spent the better part of a decade pursuing: a sympathetic White House, friendlier regulators, institutional acceptance and a legislative framework that increasingly treats digital assets as a permanent part of the financial system. Yet, rather than unleashing a new wave of demand, those milestones have coincided with one of Bitcoin’s deepest retreats in years. Earlier crypto crashes were punctuated by spectacular failures or waves of forced selling. This downturn has been marked by a steadier erosion in demand. Bitcoin fell even as inflation worries mounted, doing little to bolster its case as a hedge. And when geopolitical turmoil sent investors looking for safety, they turned to traditional havens. Institutional acceptance has not gone away, but the early enthusiasm has cooled. The question now is whether the biggest buyers will keep adding to their holdings at the pace the industry once expected. BLOOMBERG

events.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
events.summary: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that J ust outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. “You will see robots and humans working in harmony,” she declares as we move between different stations of the warehouse. Everything is designed to maximise what humans are good at, she continues, and what robots are good at – “working without getting tired”. Almost every judgment call here seems to be made by a computer – not just where to stow items when they arrive at the warehouse (the system shines a light on to the spot on the specific shelf where the worker should place each item) but also which size box to pack something in once it’s been ordered, and even precisely how much tape to use to seal that box. The human beings are here to provide the hands, not the brains. So far, at least, there is no hardware or software to rival a human hand. Humanoid robots – often called “embodied AI” – have made great strides over the past decade (literally, as evidenced in China’s recent five-day robot Olympics ). But producing a robot that can pack a shelf, tighten a bolt and also pick a raspberry – actions that would make them useful rather than simply entertaining, actions most of us perform without any conscious effort – has proved surprisingly difficult. Replicating the breadth of function of the human hand is one of the biggest remaining challenges in robotics. Until robots are dexterous, human workers will always be necessary. But investors are now gambling on humanoid robots soon becoming as much a part of everyday life as AI-powered large language models are for many of us today. The Chinese government has pledged to invest more than £100bn in robotics and high-tech industries over the next two decades. Earlier this year, Tesla halted production of its Model X and Model S cars so that factories could focus instead on producing Optimus humanoid robots. “Human hands have evolved to be this incredibly sophisticated machine. Your hand is actually a remarkable thing,” Tesla chief executive Elon Musk told a conference last year. “In order to create a robot that can be a generalised humanoid, you must solve the hands problem.” Amazon employs more than 1.5 million people worldwide today. But from what I can see on the warehouse floor, it seems that if a task could be done more efficiently by a machine, Amazon would rather leave it to a robot. What will happen to these workers when the “hands problem” is solved? And what will happen to the rest of us? Artificial dexterity combined with artificial intelligence will be hugely consequential for humanity. Forget retraining as a plumber in the age of AI – if engineers manage to replicate human hands, then potentially no job will be future-proof. Dexterous robots that can rival a human hand are not here yet, but they are coming. What makes hands so difficult to reproduce in hardware and software? How close are robotics engineers to getting it right? And what will happen to the world of work when they do? “T he hand is our conduit between the brain and the world,” says Alistair Hunter, a hand and wrist surgeon at University College London hospitals. “The hand is our way of turning thought into action.” Hunter has spent most of his professional life seeking to understand how hands work, and how to return them to normal function when they don’t. “Hands are special because they are very complicated anatomically,” he tells me over coffee in north London. “There are 27 bones in the hand; there are nerves and muscles that control it. But behind all that is the brain, which is interacting millisecond by millisecond to understand what the hand is sensing, adjusting to that, and then providing action.” We might assume that we owe our evolutionary advantage to our intelligence, but Hunter argues it’s actually the combination of our cognitive power and our dexterity that has given us the edge.

events.title: How China is using summits to expand its global influence
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump had a rare trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. A year earlier, Beijing helped bring about a globally influential photo-op with Putin, Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. "China hopes to play a more constructive role in this conflict-[ridden], unstable world," a research fellow said. SHENZHEN, China — For a second year in a row, Chinese President Xi Jinping has brought Russian President Vladimir Putin together with another major world leader on mainland Chinese shores. U.S. President Donald Trump had a trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin on Thursday, after the three met the prior evening during a welcome banquet for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen. It marked the first time they had met together in person. In September 2025, Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly laughed together for a friendly photo-op alongside an annual meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in Tianjin, China. The gathering followed easing tensions between Beijing and New Delhi. China's "ability to engage directly with the world major powers" reflects the country's influence across the Global South and Eurasia, said Jodie Wen, postdoctoral fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University. "China hopes to play a more constructive role in this conflict-[ridden], unstable world." In the future, "China will hope to provide more platforms" within its borders for countries to discuss issues, she said. Trump, Xi, Putin said they plan to boost oil production, revamp UN after trilateral talks I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways Trump holds talks separately with Putin and Xi ahead of their historic trilateral meeting Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019 Why the Middle East is watching the Trump-Xi-Putin summit Trump arrives in China for historic meeting with Xi, Putin China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China China has increasingly played the role of broker, for instance, providing the forum for restoring diplomatic ties between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023. By participating in and hosting different multilateral organizations, China has stayed in the Western orbit while cultivating relations with non-Western countries. The two photo-ops last year and this year reflect only a portion of Xi's large number of meetings with different world leaders. Xi has hosted more than 40 heads of state so far this year, including at least eight around the APEC meetings in Shenzhen this week. That's on top of receiving over 60 state visits in 2025, according to CNBC analysis of official Chinese readouts. Domestic Chinese media have highlighted how Xi has met with many foreign leaders around the China-hosted events. "Beijing sees these multilateral platforms as opportunities to expand its international influence and demonstrate its commitment to multilateralism, while bilateral diplomacy remains equally important," said Yue Su, principal economist for China at EIU. But she noted that different countries increasingly pursue different geopolitical and economic priorities, making it challenging to reach consensus even through multilateral organizations. "Against this backdrop, China's diplomatic priorities are increasingly focused on delivering tangible economic benefits through trade, investment, financial connectivity and technology cooperation," she said. On Thursday, Xi announced at the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting that China would provide $20 million in support for the Asia Pacific region. He also advocated for the development of an "Asia-Pacific community with a shared future," an iteration of his commonly used slogan on a "shared future" for humanity more broadly. The Shenzhen summit can create meaningful outcomes for crisis management, as well as diplomatic space for future negotiations, Tsinghua University's Wen said. She added that it's important for leaders to come together in person in order to avoid misunderstandings and further tensions. Trump said Thursday at the trilateral that the U.S., China and Russia are " uniquely positioned" to discuss reducing nuclear weapons at their historic meeting. A Chinese readout subsequently said the three leaders discussed Ukraine, the Middle East and the Korean Peninsula. —CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

events.title: Europe's cyber weak spot is the everyday businesses nobody thought to protect
events.summary: Recent cyberattacks highlight how seemingly mundane equipment used by everyday businesses can be left exposed to cyber sabotage Experts told CNBC that these threats will only get worse as AI enables cybercriminals to become faster and more sophisticated. While typical national security risks such as power infrastructure tend to be well protected, civil infrastructure such as food supplies and gas stations remain vulnerable, said Guy Segal, CEO of cybersecurity firm Sygnia. Cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act. But it wasn't fast enough. Attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November. The affected stores had been scheduled for security upgrades just two days later, a company spokesperson told CNBC. Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks. Experts are warning that a combination of known vulnerabilities, basic security failures and ambiguity over whether suppliers or their clients are responsible are making things worse, as AI makes cyber threats faster and more sophisticated. Guy Segal, CEO of cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNBC that his company handled 285% more incidents in October than a year earlier, with demand forcing it to turn away some businesses seeking emergency assistance. "It's going to get worse before it's going to get better," Segal said. The recent cyberattacks targeted refrigeration systems across hundreds of European supermarkets, remotely altering temperature settings and forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. France has since accused a cyber unit with links to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps of the attacks, an allegation Tehran denies. Fredrik Blix, a cybersecurity researcher at Stockholm University, told CNBC that thousands of industrial control systems remain accessible over the public internet, sometimes despite manufacturers' warnings. Segal said that basic cyber protection measures such as multi-factor authentication and basic network segmentation are more important than ever. He said risks to major civic infrastructure like the electrical grid were front of mind and so "usually pretty well protected." "There are always those civil supply chain components that are way, way less protected. Could be supermarkets, could be gas stations, could be… the screens on the Tube," Segal said, referring to London's underground rail system. The supermarket attacks showed "this is the new normal, and definitely it's a wake-up call for every company out there," Segal added. Segal said that inexpensive AI tools mean technical expertise and resources are no longer needed to launch attacks. He described one recent incident in which clients suffered breaches within six hours of a vulnerability becoming known, as perpetrators used AI to act faster — a process that might have taken weeks a year earlier. Segal, whose firm helps companies respond to breaches and strengthen their defenses, warned that businesses without prearranged incident-response support could struggle to secure emergency assistance, as overwhelmed cybersecurity firms prioritize existing clients. In one case, he said, Sygnia had to turn down a company because no response teams were available. Segal added that the company in question had already been turned down by ten other providers. Jacob Silverman, CEO of risk advisory firm Kroll, told CNBC earlier this month that the company was operating at full capacity in its incident-response business amid what he described as "the most rapid uptick in threat activity that we've ever seen." Segal argued that retailers should treat cybersecurity risks with the same seriousness as fire safety and food hygiene, including when outsourcing maintenance. When Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were attacked on Nov. 2, it exposed how different independent store operators had responded to the warnings following the earlier attacks in France. Retailers had been warned about the vulnerabilities following earlier attacks in France, and those that implemented the recommended protections were spared, CEO Frans Muller told investors in an earnings call earlier this month, but smaller operators with fewer technical resources had struggled to make the necessary changes. Coop, whose stores are owned by regional consumer cooperatives or operated by franchises, told CNBC that public attention on the recent attacks was the main driver of security improvements. It said the vulnerability at the affected stores had since been addressed. The financial consequences of cyberattacks can be substantial. Ahold Delhaize told investors in November that a separate October cyberattack on its online operations and supply chain would reduce fourth-quarter sales by 200 million euros ($219 million).

events.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
events.summary: Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark. He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true. But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64). The fee, in place since February , has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025. “The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero . The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects. Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket. The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections. Eric and Patty, a young couple from New York, said they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies. Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”. “I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” said Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.” A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson said the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception. The initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year. A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He said people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.” The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

events.title: Spirit IV ferry docks late again after 'technical issue'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Spirit IV ferry docks in Geelong four hours late after another 'technical issue' The Spirit of Tasmania IV has suffered multiple technical issues within its first month of operations on Bass Strait. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) Spirit of Tasmania IV docked four hours late in Geelong on Saturday morning due to a "technical issue". The ABC understands it is related to the same steering fault that caused a similar delay three weeks ago. TT-Line says the incident has been reported to the relevant authorities. One of the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries has once again docked hours behind schedule because of a "technical issue" with its primary navigational system. Spirit IV was heading towards Geelong when the issue occurred early on Saturday morning, resulting in a tugboat being called to escort the vessel and passengers being dropped off four hours late. A track map shows the ferry started to perform a series of loops within Port Phillip Bay from about 4.40am, with the vessel only resuming its course towards Geelong about 8am. The Spirit of Tasmania IV spent more than three hours performing a series of loops early on Saturday morning. ( Supplied: MarineTraffic ) TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone apologised for the inconvenience to passengers but said "safety is a more important consideration than meeting schedule". "We experienced a minor technical issue with the primary navigational system, but at no point was Spirit of Tasmania IV at risk," Mr Carbone said. "The secondary system performed as designed and the Master acted in accordance with his training." The ABC understands the issue was related to the same steering fault that previously caused the Spirit IV to arrive four hours late into Geelong on November 5. This is the second time the Spirit of Tasmania IV has been escorted into Geelong by a tugboat, following a similar incident in early November. ( ABC News: Harrison Tippet ) One passenger posted on social media that the vessel was roughly on time before they were advised it "requires assistance from a tugboat", while another said it was "another day, another technical hitch" for Spirit IV. Mr Carbone said the incident was "reported to the relevant authorities" and there was not expected to be any delay to the departure time for the Spirit IV's journey from Geelong to Devonport on Saturday night. As a result of the incident in early November, TT-Line announced it had suspended the use of autopilot on the new vessels within Port Phillip Bay while it probed the steering faults. That incident is being investigated by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, which is also looking into a separate steering fault which affected the Spirit V on a trial voyage in October. The two vessels started ferrying passengers between Devonport and Geelong last month when they replaced the Spirit of Tasmania I and II. events.title: Honda, Toyota recall 1.6 million US vehicles over airbag rupture risk
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Honda and Toyota recall 1.6 million vehicles in US over Takata airbag rupture risk At least 28 deaths in the US have been linked to faulty Takata airbag inflators. ( ABC News ) 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs have been recalled by Honda and Toyota in the US after fears their Takata airbag inflators could rupture. At least 28 US deaths have stemmed from the inflators since 2009. Honda and Toyota say they will replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles. Car makers Honda and Toyota have announced they are recalling about 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs in the US over a risk that their Takata airbag inflators could rupture. Honda and Toyota both said there were no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no airbag inflator ruptures. But the companies added that they would replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles. There have been at least 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009, an issue prompting the largest recall in US motoring history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a drying agent, with at least 20 of those fatalities occurring in Honda vehicles. More than 20 car companies have recalled around 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators over the past decade. ( Reuters: Rick Wilking ) The vehicles in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks. "Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA said. It added that other car makers continued to conduct inflator analysis and testing. The Honda recall includes certain years of its popular Accord and Civic models. ( Reuters ) The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the US. The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 IS250, 2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles. The Honda recall applies to vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 US states or territories. Over the past decade, two dozen major car companies have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators worldwide, including about 67 million vehicles in the US. Metal shrapnel was reportedly unleashed when the airbags exploded. ( Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon ) Hundreds of injuries in vehicles since 2009 have been reported from Takata airbag inflators that can explode, unleashing metal shrapnel inside cars and trucks. In some cases, it has killed or injured drivers or other vehicle occupants. Car company denies liability over airbag incident Toyota Australia says it should not be held liable for traumatic injuries linked to an airbag incident in Darwin. Honda said long-term monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions. Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries. In Australia, Lexus has recalled more than 7,000 vehicles over concerns about Takata airbag inflators that could deteriorate over time. The recall, announced earlier this month , covers certain Lexus IS250, IS250C, IS350 and IS-F vehicles manufactured between 2005 and 2012. It remains unclear whether other Australian vehicles are affected by the latest global recalls. Australian motorists can check whether their vehicle is affected through the federal government's Vehicle Recalls website or by contacting their manufacturer. Owners of recalled vehicles should arrange repairs through an authorised dealer, with replacement of defective airbags carried out free of charge. events.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
events.summary: Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology. GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch , an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch. Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims. In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024. Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1. “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing. In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale. Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android . Apple did not respond to a request for comment. India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China . The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth. events.title: Anthropic pulls off mega IPO amid AI slump, gold tumbles: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, raised more than US$81 billion on Nov 19 in the biggest initial public offering in history. SINGAPORE – Artificial intelligence company Anthropic pulled off a blockbuster stock market debut even as a sell-off in technology shares weighed on broader markets, while gold prices slumped as investors assessed the outlook for US interest rates. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, raised more than US$81 billion (S$105 billion) on Nov 19 in the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history, topping SpaceX’s US$75 billion base deal. Its shares closed at US$97.17, more than 17% above its offer price. Still, the historic debut did little to lift sentiment in the broader AI sector, with technology stocks continuing to face selling pressure over concerns about valuations and the significant sums being poured into AI development. Zavier Wong, market analyst at eToro, said the broader market was grappling with several developments at once, including expectations of further US interest rate hikes, scrutiny over chip exports and a short-selling report targeting chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices. He noted that Nvidia had also given up the gains it made following its latest earnings announcement, while the departure of its former chief executive Jensen Huang added to market uncertainty. The chipmaker had reported a 103% year-on-year jump in revenue to US$115.8 billion for its third quarter ended Oct 25, beating analysts’ expectations. Its net profit more than doubled to US$65.3 billion, while revenue from its data centre business rose 110% to US$107.6 billion. “The different factors are why the sell-off has been so hard to quell,” said Wong, noting that the S&P 500 had fallen for six consecutive sessions and was down about 8% from its record high in October. “An interest rate hike in December is more or less priced in, which makes the Fed’s upcoming meeting the next key date the market is watching.” Meanwhile, gold saw its worst weekly decline since March , tumbling about 7% to hover just above US$3,500 as expectations of further rate hikes and selling by investors seeking to cover losses in equities weighed on the precious metal. Gold is down 8.5% in 2026 and is 37% below January’s intraday peak of US$5,602. CMC Markets sales trader Alex Ho noted that the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note had risen above 5%, while real yields, which are adjusted for inflation, had climbed from 2.66% to 2.88% since Nov 9. This has made gold, which does not pay interest, less attractive to investors. The AI stock sell-off also added to the pressure on the precious metal. “When portfolios are hurting, investors sell what they can, not what they want... So gold is being sold to raise cash, but that is not the same as it failing as a hedge,” said Ho. “A quick bounce is possible, but a lasting recovery needs gold back above US$3,850 to US$3,900, and that won’t happen unless real yields and the dollar ease “The next tests are the Fed’s meeting on Dec 8 and 9 and US inflation data on Dec 10,” he added. Alvin Lee, premium client manager at IG Singapore, said the stronger US dollar had added to selling pressure on gold by increasing the opportunity cost of holding the precious metal. “The general risk off sentiment now is driving investors to hold on to cash and the safe haven status for gold has been called into question recently but for reasons stated above, it seems like the market has a preference for holding cash now,” he said. The decline in gold prices also weighed on Singapore-listed gold-related stocks. Pawnbroking firms ValueMax Group and MoneyMax Financial Services have also come under pressure in recent months, with their shares falling 25% and nearly 36.6%, respectively, over the past six months. ValueMax shares fell 8.7% over the week to close at 74 cents on Nov 20, while MoneyMax declined 6.25% to close at 45 cents. STI dips below 5,000 points, S’pore banks decline The broader Singapore market also came under pressure on Nov 20, with the benchmark Straits Times Index falling to a six-month low of 4,980.81 before paring some losses to close at 4,972.23 points. The three local banks were among the decliners , with DBS falling 5.26% over the week to close at $66.11 on Nov 20. OCBC declined 7.3% to $26.54, while UOB lost 6.17% to close at $35.42. James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers, said hawkish signals from the latest US Federal Reserve meeting minutes and concerns over US restrictions on AI chip exports continued to weigh on investor appetite. He noted that Singapore’s index heavyweights had benefited from a significant rise in valuations earlier this year, but said the market’s direction would increasingly depend on whether earnings growth could catch up with valuations.

events.title: Why life insurance matters long after you buy it
events.summary: For many, the primary purpose of life insurance is family protection. “If people understood what life insurance does – then we wouldn’t need salespeople to sell it.” This is a now famous quote from Ben Feldman, who set a Guinness world record in the 1970s for the most insurance products sold in a year and is widely considered the greatest insurance salesman of all time. Did Mr Feldman have a point? Perhaps. He is also quoted as saying “I don’t sell insurance, I solve problems,” which is an interesting take on how life insurance is positioned in the market. So, what problems does life insurance solve? In its simplest form, it is a policy that pays a lump sum to persons of your choice if you die. Most commonly, protecting loved ones financially is the reason most of us buy a policy, and this is certainly an important purpose; however, life insurance can play a much broader role within a well-structured financial plan. Depending on an individual’s circumstances, life insurance can be used to replace income, repay debt, cover a future tax liability, provide liquidity for an estate, and help ensure wealth passes to the next generation in an orderly way. The starting point When considering life insurance , the starting point should therefore not simply be “Do I need life insurance?” but instead “What financial problem would arise for my family or business if I were no longer here?” For many, the primary focus is family . Consider a family where one or both parents are working and their combined incomes support everyday living expenses, from rent payments to school fees and grocery bills. If one partner dies unexpectedly, the emotional impact is accompanied by an immediate financial question: how does the family maintain its standard of living without that source of income? A life insurance policy can help to replace that lost source of income. It also means the surviving spouse does not have to rely solely on savings or investments to pay household expenses. A metaphor I regularly hear is to consider yourself as an ATM which pays out your salary every month. Would you pay to insure that ATM if it were to break down or be stolen? Very likely, yes. This can be especially important for younger families with financially dependent children. Someone in their 30s or 40s may have relatively small amounts in savings but has decades of future earnings ahead of them. In this scenario, the value being protected is not necessarily today's wealth and earnings, but the income that person would otherwise have generated over the remainder of their working life. This idea highlights an important aspect of calculating the appropriate amount and time frame of cover. Looking only at current income and outgoings may underestimate the family's actual requirement. Parents should also consider important future requirements, such as school and university costs for their children. A comprehensive assessment should include both existing liabilities and future expenditure that the individual or family would reasonably have expected to fund. Debt protection Debt protection is another very common use of life insurance. A mortgage is likely to be one of the largest financial commitments an individual or family has. A life insurance policy can be created so that the liability is repaid in full should the owner die. These types of policies can also be structured to reduce the amount of cover required as the debt is paid back. The same principle can apply to other significant liabilities, including personal borrowing or certain business debts. Some banks will even mandate an insurance policy before taking on the debt to guarantee it can be repaid. Life insurance can also be an important component of business planning and ownership. For owner-managed businesses, the death of a founder, shareholder, or key employee can create financial difficulties. The business may lose someone responsible for generating significant revenue, managing important client relationships, or having key knowledge that is difficult to replace, all of which can impact the business in a financially negative way. Key person insurance can provide the business with capital following the death of an insured employee or owner, helping it absorb the financial impact and fund the transition or recruitment of a replacement. As personal wealth grows, the purpose of life insurance can change from protecting income to protecting and transferring capital within or outside an estate. An individual’s estate may contain considerable wealth in the form of property , private businesses, and long-term illiquid investments; however, it may not contain large amounts of liquid cash, which in turn can create a liquidity problem following death. Taxes, liabilities, and other expenses may become payable, but beneficiaries of the estate may not be able to sell assets quickly enough to meet them. An insurance policy can provide cash to meet liabilities at the point it is required, while allowing the underlying assets to remain invested or pass to the intended beneficiaries. An individual may have considerable wealth within their estate, and therefore a substantial inheritance tax liability when they die and the estate passes to their beneficiaries. As the tax cannot be paid in advance, an insurance policy can instead be purchased to cover the future liability only arising on death. Depending on the country that will receive the proceeds of the inheritance tax, differing policies can be used to mitigate effectively. Insurance can also help to equalise inheritances. If one child is expected to inherit a family business or property, for example, an insurance policy may provide an equal capital value for the other beneficiaries, reducing the need to divide or sell the underlying asset. Estate transfers and inheritance tax mitigation strategies require careful planning. Life insurance should complement other protection methods, such as wills, succession arrangements, and the broader estate plan, rather than being considered as the only option. Alongside life insurance, there are many additional coverage options that can be equally as valuable, such as critical illness protection and disability cover. An individual may survive a life changing illness or accident; however, they may not necessarily be able to work again. If we consider the ATM metaphor once more, this situation can cause the ATM to stop paying the regular income, however the rent, bills, and kids education fees continue to come. Taking additional cover for this instance gives added protection and peace of mind. How much cover is enough? A question that is asked regularly, although difficult to answer, is how much cover is enough? This depends on the individual, their financial position, and what they consider to be the most important current and future financial debts and commitments to cover – there is no one size fits all answer. events.title: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
events.summary: The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day , publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history. The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement. The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.” The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013 . It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar. The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time. The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain. Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic. Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever. Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs. Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved. While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities . With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets. There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world. The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post. “GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.” With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse
