events.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
events.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge. The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further. The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge. In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit. “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.” The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf. “I

events.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
events.summary: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year NEW YORK -- A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S & P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark S & P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S & P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.2%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 14% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang , its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5% to $88.91, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Florida father kills wife and 3 children in apparent murder-suicide: Sheriff Administration tries to intervene after Kalshi is threatened with restraining order Players reject MLB international draft proposal; ask for higher bonus pools and more Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S & P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

events.title: Petition against AI cameras at junior basketball attracts 13,000 signatures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Concerns raised over Basketball Australia's use of AI cameras at junior games Pixellot smart cameras will soon be used to film basketball games around Australia. ( Source: Pixellot ) New AI-powered filming technology that will allow basketball players to watch games and view stats online is being rolled out by three basketball associations. A cyber-safety expert and activist groups have raised privacy and monetisation concerns. Basketball Australia plans to roll out the technology in more stadiums in coming months. Basketball Australia has defended the use of new AI-powered recording software set to be introduced at stadiums around Australia, after criticism from activist groups and a prominent cybersecurity expert. The software, called Hoops TV, was developed from a partnership between Basketball Australia and Israel-based sports footage company Pixellot. It uses "smart cameras" installed in stadiums to record games, including amateur and junior matches. The footage and game statistics, which are gathered using AI, are then made available for players and their guardians to access online through their Basketball Australia log-ons. Basketball Australia says the technology is an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball". ( ABC News: Mackenzie Heard ) The cameras have been trialled with three basketball associations this week — in Darwin, the Illawarra region in NSW, and Brisbane's northern suburbs — and are set to be rolled out more widely in coming months. Basketball Australia spokesman Tim Brenton said Hoops TV presented an "exciting opportunity for Australian community basketball". "Video recording and capturing kids on video isn't new in Australian basketball. It's quite uncontrolled and you can go into any stadium around Australia at any night of the week and find people videotaping," he said. Tim Brenton says any revenue generated via Basketball Australia-led programs and products is reinvested back into basketball. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) However, cyber-safety expert and former member of the federal government's Online Safety Working Group, Susan McLean, said the software's privacy implications were "particularly concerning". "I'm not sure why Basketball Australia and all the states and territories are hell-bent on putting filming before child safeguarding concerns," she said. "We have seen almost on a weekly basis [that] things are getting hacked. Coles has been hacked, Medicare has been hacked, Optus has been hacked. Activist groups GetUp! and Not All Clubs launched a petition last month urging Basketball Australia to "stop filming kids with Israeli AI Cameras", which has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures. The petition cites concerns Pixellot's co-founders previously worked for an Israeli weapons company and an "IDF [Israel Defence Forces] intelligence unit". It also alleges a woman protected by a family violence intervention was "contacted by the man in it" after her game was live-streamed during an earlier trial in Victoria. A petition opposing the rollout has so far collected more than 13,000 signatures. ( ABC News: Sam Bradbrook ) "The association had been warned a week before, and said only Pixellot could block the stream," the petition reads. Pixellot did not respond to a request for comment. GetUp! media and campaigns lead David Sharaz said the group was concerned children's sport may be being monetised by Basketball Australia. "These aren't professional athletes who are being critiqued at half-time on ESPN, these are kids. And the overall question is why are we filming kids?" he said. "Are we going to be watching kids' sport and seeing an advert for Woolworths? Are your children being monetised?" David Sharaz says GetUp! is concerned about the potential monetisation of children's sport. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) Asked about concerns around monetisation, Mr Brenton did not answer a question from the ABC during an interview, but he later responded in a statement. "As a non-profit governing body, any revenue generated via BA-led programs and products are reinvested back into basketball nationally," he said in the statement. "Our aim is to create a model that benefits participants and contributes to the long-term growth of the sport." The Hoops TV trial is operating on a opt-out model, which means games will be recorded using the technology unless parents or players object. Ms McLean said an opt-out model was "not a legally sound process for filming permissions".

events.title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
events.summary: German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade. Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”. He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more. The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid. Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job. The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US. “The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement. Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto , which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018. The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims. Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer. The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Get the most important news as it breaks In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits. Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court. “We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement. Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

events.title: Anthropic’s post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
events.summary: Anthropic’s stock closed at US$88.91, 8.5% below the Nov 19 close and not far from its US$83 IPO price. Anthropic’s Wall Street debut disappointed, with shares closing at US$88.91, 8.5% lower, showing the AI trade is still under pressure. Investors worry AI spending may top US$1 trillion in 2026 without quick returns, while Nvidia, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell. Analysts expect more volatility, with OpenAI’s planned listing, index buying and Morgan Stanley’s ended support all likely to test demand for AI stocks. Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Nov 20 as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. As the first large machine-learning model maker to go public, Anthropic is widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, and its listing had been viewed as a potential boost for a sector struggling to regain its footing. But the stock closed at US$88.91, 8.5% below the Nov 19 close and not far from its US$83 IPO price, while declines in other technology heavyweights suggested the listing had done little to stem the broader selloff. “Anthropic faded relatively quickly. I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company, management or business. I think they’re just skeptical of this market,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. The AI boom has come under pressure over the past month as concerns mount that spending on the technology, expected by some estimates to top US$1 trillion in 2026, is not generating returns quickly enough. Fears of political hurdles to data centre construction and the leadership turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia have also added to those worries. “Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds. Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia fell about 14% and Meta Platforms dropped nearly 6%, Amazon lost about 4% and Microsoft ended3% lower. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Marvell Technology down about 13% and 12%, respectively, and Intel losing roughly 8%. The focus now shifts to a potential listing by another AI leader, OpenAI, which could provide another test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year. Despite a strong IPO pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027. Anthropic’s stock could find support in the coming weeks. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30% of Anthropic’s shares by year-end. Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained. But Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing Anthropic’s shares after its market debut, closed a position meant to do that, the company said, removing a potential pillar of support for shares. Anthropic had a fully diluted valuation of about $1.6 trillion at the latest price, and a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. “We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results,” said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street’s main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Nov 20. Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , whose June listing was the second-biggest on record. Anthropic raised US$93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX’s US$85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record. While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing. “There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co. Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012. The stock’s sharp swings have left investors weighing the prospects of a rebound against further losses. Options trading, set to begin next week, could add to the volatility. “It’s not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment,” said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg. REUTERS

events.title: Nvidia stock plunges 14%, wraps up longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
events.summary: Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday and headed for their seventh straight weekly drop. The stock is down 46% over the period, shedding about $2.6 trillion in market cap. Once the most valuable company, Nvidia is now fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet. The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis. Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008. On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further. Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple , Microsoft and Alphabet . Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD. Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere. On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December. For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT. Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. WATCH: Walter Isaacson on Nvidia export control scrutiny

events.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
events.summary: GTA 6 central characters Lucia and Jason Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release , hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history. Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game. To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas . Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access . In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast. In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany. The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (£1.2bn) in just five days. The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history . At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state. The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason. GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history. BBC News Mundo’s Rafael Rojas visits the real-life Miami locations that inspired GTA 6's Vice City. Research firm Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%. The firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available. Around three quarters of the game's sales have been on PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said. Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year. That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind , which has made an estimated $4.5bn (£3.44bn), adjusted for inflation. Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years. The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet. If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks. GTA 6 launched around the world on 19 November Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait. GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece. The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play. The launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles. The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China. Police departments have also reminded Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement reached a fever pitch in the US. events.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
events.summary: Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago. The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development. Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth. "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said. "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability." Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices. Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record. But tech stocks more broadly also fell. Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls. Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit. Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower. Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses. Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990. events.title: Wall St ends sharply lower on AI sell-off, S&P 500, Dow in correction
events.summary: Specialist traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Nov 20. US stocks fell sharply as AI shares sold off, pushing the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory after Anthropic’s weak debut failed to calm fears. The S&P 500 had its seventh straight fall, while the Nasdaq had its worst weekly drop since March 2020. Nvidia, Amazon, Meta and other AI-linked names all slid. Investors now focus on inflation and the Fed, with markets pricing a near-certain December rate hike and next week’s PCE data set to guide policy hopes. NEW YORK – US stocks extended their rout on Nov 20, and the S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally. All three major US equity indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10% below their record closing highs,confirming both indexes have entered a correction. The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020. The S&P 500 and the Dowlogged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “liberation day” tariff package. The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative territory for the year. “This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. “But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.” “Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things. Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) in market cap, failed to catch fire on Nov 19, closing 17.1% above its US$83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session. In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1%. Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8%. The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology. “Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.” The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6% in mid-June. That lustre has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7%. Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%. Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1% and its peer Nebius slid 16.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73. The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025. Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said the central bank’s policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels. Markets are pricing a near-certain likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Next week’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed’s monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week. Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 12.8% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about US$3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much. UnitedHealth rose 2.8% after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a “buy” from a “hold” rating. The AI sell-off also sent Caterpillar 5% lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment. Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3% and 9.6% after bitcoin dropped below the $60,000 level. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 new highs and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.

events.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
events.summary: President Donald Trump said Chinese leader Xi Jinping called Jensen Huang a "brilliant man" when they discussed the former Nvidia CEO. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that Huang was not mentioned in the talks he had while in China. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged. President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating. A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations. Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO. "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important company to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies." Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week. The president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries. Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips. Bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week. "We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said. "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China. The administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO. Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI. They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI. In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department , led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed. Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said in that interview.

events.title: Farmers warned to pay up or potentially lose drivers licences
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers could be put off road for not paying transmission protest fines Colin Fenton (right) says he will not cave to pressure to pay his fine. ( Supplied: Colin Fenton ) Victorian drivers can lose their licence if they do not pay a fine, even if the offence is not driving-related. Many farmers in the path of VNI West have been fined for refusing access to their land. The Coalition says it will scrap VNI West and waive associated fines if it wins the state election. Farmers fined for fighting the controversial VNI West transmission line are being warned they face penalties including no longer being able to drive. If you do not pay a fine in Victoria, the state government can take away your drivers licence, deregister your vehicle, take money from your bank account or sell your land or other assets. These penalties are now confronting farmers in Victoria's north-west who have been fined for denying VNI West developers access to their land and are refusing to pay up. The threat of being put off the road was met with incredulity and outrage among farmers, given the fines they received had no connection to driving offences. Many farmers have locked the gate to VNI West transmission line builders, despite threats of fines and further penalties. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Colin Fenton, who is in his 80s, farms near Kerang. In 2024, he learned the VNI West transmission line would cut through his farm. Since then, he has fought against the project, which he says would disrupt his farming operations and devalue his property. He has refused to grant project planners access to his land, and in August this year was one of 12 farmers fined $814 each for doing so. He said he would not pay the fine, which is now overdue. He now faces losing his drivers licence and having his vehicles deregistered. Farmers have received this information on their infringement notices, describing the penalties they face if they do not pay up. ( Supplied: Trent Carter ) Mr Fenton said that was an inexplicable and unjust penalty. "I was appalled due to the fact they've connected the fine to road traffic offences," he said. Mr Fenton said despite the threat of losing his licence, he would not be paying the fine, and would risk driving while unlicensed. "We live out of town and there is no public transport and we need our drivers licences to run our farms, to get provisions, and in my case I've got a very sick wife and we take regular trips to Bendigo, an hour and a half away," he said. "I find it pretty intolerable — are we living in a communistic country, or where are we living?" Farmers have held numerous rallies against VNI West, which they do not want built across their land. ( ABC News: Tamara Clark ) Mark Woods is a specialist in criminal law and past president of the Law Institute of Victoria. He said driving-related penalties for unpaid fines disproportionately punished rural and regional Victorians. "It's particularly concerning, because whether you have your licence suspended has nothing to do with where you live," he said. "So if you're in a regional area with no access to public transport … you can lose your ability to travel about, notwithstanding that you might be the safest driver in the state. 'It's interesting that it's state election time, and therefore if people are concerned about the law, they ought to find out what candidates are going to do it about it, particularly for people in regional Victoria." Mark Woods says driving-related penalties affect regional Victorians more than their urban counterparts. ( Supplied: Mark Woods ) Mr Woods said the current penalty structure had been in place since 2014. "In 2014 there was a law passed called the Fines Reform Act, and that created an agency called Fines Victoria, and there's a director of Fines Victoria who has a whole lot of powers to do things to you if you don't pay your fines," he said. "Fines Victoria can direct VicRoads to suspend your licence or suspend the registration of the car, direct the sheriff to go out and find property that you own that can be sold to pay the fine, or seize control of your land and have that sold for the purposes of paying the fine." Mr Woods said a term of imprisonment was also possible under the legislation, although there had been a moratorium on that since 2024. Mr Fenton is hinging his hopes on a change of government on November 28. "That'd be an understatement, wouldn't it," he said. While Labor is firmly committed to VNI West, the Coalition and One Nation have vowed to scrap it and waive the fines of those who have resisted it.

events.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
events.summary: President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan. In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war. Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders. At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil. “We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said. He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms. “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said. With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built. The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months. China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China. In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.” He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.” Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”. “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran. “I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.” He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election. “I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said. Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.” And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

events.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
events.summary: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

events.title: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
events.summary: CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, according to a report from Bloomberg. Zscaler shares popped in extended trading after the report. CrowdStrike is currently valued at $235 billion, and Zscaler has a market cap of $32 billion. Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion. Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap. Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion . CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode. events.title: Second judge to block Trump's contested D.C. arch
events.summary: A second federal judge will block construction on President Trump 's embattled arch set to be erected near Arlington National Cemetery , multiple outlets reported Friday. Why it matters: It represents yet another barrier to the multi-year project to build a 250-foot arch that challengers said would obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said she will issue preliminary injunction that will indefinitely block the project, which she reportedly called a "rushed job" from the bench Friday. Zoom out: Brinkema's rebuke comes after D.C.-based District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday extended her separate order blocking construction on the arch for two weeks. Chutkan, who is overseeing consolidated challenges from military veterans and from the District of Columbia and Virginia, issued her initial temporary restraining order earlier this month. That order prohibited construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery reported. What they're saying: "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. State of play: The legal hurdles came after the National Capital Planning Commission , which is stacked with Trump loyalists, gave its final approval for the project. Challengers, however, have argued the project requires congressional approval — and as Chutkan noted , "Congress has not enacted any statute authorizing construction of the Arch." Between the lines: The arch is one prime example of the president's quest to remake the nation's capital as he sees fit, from a sprawling White House ballroom to a community golf course . The NPS has backed Trump's arch, despite noting it "would alter several historic views." The FAA deemed the arch, which would sit near Ronald Reagan National Airport, safe for air travel, but said it should have "a non-standard eternal flame on top" and "floodlight projectors pointed" toward it. What we're watching: A Justice Department spokesperson said they would appeal the decision "immediately." Go deeper: The next two months are pivotal for Trump's D.C. projects

events.title: Abu Dhabi's MGX emerges as major winner in Anthropic IPO
events.summary: Investment firm MGX 's windfall from Anthropic 's historic public debut made it a major winner in the Claude maker's IPO, as Abu Dhabi seeks more opportunities to deepen its ties with US companies. Anthropic closed at $97.17 per share in its Thursday debut, giving MGX's stake an unrealised market-to-market gain of roughly $20 billion and establishing it as one of the Silicon Valley-based company's largest institutional investors, a representative told The National . MGX co-led Anthropic's $30 billion funding round in February, participated in its $65 billion Series H in May and added to its position during the company's public debut. The Abu Dhabi Investment Council was also among the Claude maker's major backers, as was the Qatar Investment Authority. Anthropic fell about 8.5 per cent during Friday's session to about $88.9 per share, slightly higher the $83 per share at which it priced its IPO. The MGX representative said Anthropic's IPO represented a significant validation of the Emirati firm's investment strategy and confidence of its global investor base. The company's portfolio spans the AI stack from frontier AI labs to infrastructure. It raised $49 billion in July from global investors for its AI Fund. Anthropic's public listing on Thursday coincided with the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in New York, as the emirate sought to deepen ties with US companies looking to establish a presence in the Gulf. Tom Hudson, adviser to the director general of the Abu Dhabi Investment Office (Adio), said between 80 and 100 people were expected to have made the trip. "It's basically matchmaking, and the idea is that we're bigger than the sum of our parts," he said of the investment forum. While the forum and the Anthropic IPO were unrelated, it signalled the growing role of the US-UAE AI nexus . Health care and AI were expected to be among two high-priority sector for investment. "AI has genuinely been a part of the discourse in the UAE for 10 years, if not more," Mr Hudson said. "With Adio, we are looking also at how we support AI companies on their regional expansion," Mr Hudson added, pointing to AI for drug discovery and AI with autonomous vehicles. "AI cuts across a lot of the clusters that we are working with and bringing them to Abu Dhabi." Milind Singh, head of technology at Adio, pointed to Anthropic's historic IPO during a panel session at the forum. "We're privileged to have been associated with this story for a long time," he said. MGX plans to invest up to 80 per cent of its total portfolio in US projects. The company also co-led OpenAI's $122 billion raise in March, and participated in xAI's $20 billion funding round in January before it merged with SpaceX. US tech companies Oracle, IBM and Cisco also operate in the UAE's AI infrastructure. Last November, Microsoft announced a $15.2 billion investment in the UAE support its cloud and AI infrastructure, as well as talent. Abu Dhabi is committing $3.5 billion to become the world's first AI-native government by the end of next year. Nvidia, OpenAI, Cisco, Oracle and Japan's SoftBank are working with UAE AI company G42 one a one-gigawatt Stargate cluster in Abu Dhabi. A similar project is being undertaken in Texas.

events.title: Congress gets a historic overhaul from every direction
events.summary: Senate data includes members who served nonconsecutive terms; House data does not. Data: House historian, U.S. Senate ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Americans want change , and they're about to get it: A perfect storm of congressional retirements, primary upsets, gerrymandering, flipped seats and lawmakers who died in office has created the biggest freshman class in decades. Why it matters : Congress had a 14% approval rating (not a typo) when Gallup polled registered voters in October. That's its lowest pre-midterm number since 1974. The big picture: The Senate is on track for its biggest freshman class since 1946. In the House, it's shaping up to be the biggest since 1992. Zoom in: The turnover featured data points that would be stunning on their own, let alone together. 28 House lawmakers chose to run for their next elected office outside the House, Pew noted in September. Six lawmakers died in office this Congress, the most in nearly 20 years. Thirteen House and Senate incumbents lost primary races. The bottom line: Congress is saying goodbye to former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). They've been in Congress since 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987, respectively.

events.title: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
events.summary: The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. events.title: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
events.summary: Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh wants central bankers to talk less about where they expect interest rates to go. Instead, they're talking more. Bank of America says there has been more so-called Fedspeak over the past two weeks than in any similar period going back to the beginning of 2025. The conflicting communications strategies come at a critical time for monetary policy and the economy. In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void. Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake. Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem , entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time. Largely on the sidelines in the debate is Warsh, who has expressed disdain for that sort of forward guidance and argued that it handcuffs policymakers long before they actually have to make a decision. But that hasn't stopped most of the other 18 officials who sit in on Federal Open Market Committee meetings. In fact, according to a Bank of America analysis, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025. "Warsh's refusal to guide markets might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less," Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave said in a note Thursday. "There is always a range of views across the 19 FOMC participants. Typically, the Chair would weigh in, indicating to markets whether the hawks or doves are in ascendence," he added. "Absent this leadership, however, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully." The increasingly vocal debate comes at a critical time for the Fed and has myriad policy implications. Bhave noted "a deepening divide" on the FOMC. The Fed's decision not to increase its benchmark rate at its October meeting "increasingly looks like a mistake," and as a result "the hawks have been very vocal of late," he wrote. Leading the charge is Waller, who has raised the possibility of hiking by half a percentage point when the committee next meets in December. Minutes from the October meeting hint at the tension, particularly when it comes to Warsh's refusal to provide guidance. The summary related that some officials who were looking for a hike in October "could have supported no change in the federal funds rate provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely" — a statement that points toward the forward guidance that Warsh has insisted the Fed avoid. The minutes "revealed that some officials favoring a hike would have accepted a hold if the Fed had clearly communicated further tightening," market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday. "Warsh's communication philosophy may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most." Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point hike, tiptoed around the forward guidance issue during a recent public appearance. Prefacing some observations she made about where she sees policy headed, Hammack noted that, "Those are not promises. Those are not commitments. They're not forward guidance, which is a hot-button topic. But what they are are a conditional set of expectations of where I think the economy can go, based on what I'm seeing." Hammack's comments illustrate a needle that Fed officials have been trying to thread: continuing to be transparent about their thinking without appearing locked into a future policy that changing economic conditions could render obsolete. Speaking Thursday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee framed the argument around credibility. "I am sympathetic to the view that [Warsh] has expressed that let's not be so, in in our language, forward guidance-oriented, saying here is what I think rates are going to be at the next meeting," Goolsbee said, calling such pronouncements "falsely precise." However, he quickly separated forward guidance from transparency. "I think central banks should be careful about doing anything that undermines credibility," Goolsbee said. "That said, I also think that it's pretty important [that] each person who sits around that table explain how they see the world. What do you see in business conditions? You don't want to surprise everybody.
