events.title: Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress
events.summary: Gap on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the new CEO of Athleta effective next month. Athleta's previous CEO, Maggie Gauger, left the company for Lululemon last month. Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC that he's "disappointed" with Athleta's performance but confident in its turnaround strategy and potential. The retailer also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings, with overall comparable sales coming in flat. Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14. The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday. Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that. "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement. The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month. "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode." Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success. While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential. Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount. Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%. Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year. The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share. Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season. "We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 82 cents adjusted vs. 78 cents expected Revenue: $4.01 billion vs. $4.02 billion expected For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior. At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. ` The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales. "Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said. The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2. Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount. Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country. "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said.

events.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
events.summary: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. events.title: Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now
events.summary: Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk. “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch. That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers. But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.” Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China. After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap. And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said. Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.” What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others. “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch. Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail. Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls. “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.” The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said. “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.” Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information. Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?” It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company. Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said. “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
events.summary: Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so. "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time. Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction. Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia. "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear. "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said. Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI. It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them. Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China. The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas. Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 1 day ago Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT. As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre. Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November. "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said. "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets." Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far. Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia. The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks. In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen". Google has been contacted for comment. events.title: Senators fret over fate of college sports bill
events.summary: The House-Senate tension over bipartisan college sports legislation is reaching a fever pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., said in an interview on Friday that he has told House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., it would be a “mistake” for the House to change the Senate-passed version. He also talked to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and said he’s pushing House leaders to give the bill an “up-or-down vote.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune suggested in an interview that the House could try to pass the bill on its suspension calendar, requiring a two-thirds majority vote, if there’s too much internal GOP opposition. Scalise says the issue is “an important priority” but said the House is going to make “very narrow changes” to the bill and be “ready to go” in December. It’s a delicate dance: No senator wants to appear to pressure the House too much, but there’s no guarantee that next year’s Democratic Congress prioritizes the issue; several backers see this year as the best chance for the bill. “There’s still a possibility to get something done, but I know that time is of the essence. We’re listening to what [House members] have to say,” said Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. Thune also said he met with Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti ahead of Petitti’s meeting with Scalise. An avid sports fan, Thune said that the decision by the LSU’s men’s basketball team to play RJ Luis after he signed a two-way NBA contract exposed the absurdity of today’s college sports landscape. The bill bars pro athletes from playing college sports, in addition to establishing transfer portal restrictions. President Donald Trump is a vocal supporter. Texas Tech Board of Regents Chair Cody Campbell, who also runs the Saving College Sports group, and Randy Levine, one of the president’s point men on the issue and the president of the New York Yankees, also met with House lawmakers in both parties this week, according to a person familiar with the matter. “Unless you codify it, you’re going to spend your next decade in court,” Thune said. “This is our one real opportunity to get this done.”

events.title: Blackout prompts questions over ElectraNet's recent $300m network upgrade
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA government questions ElectraNet over 'failure' of $300m Eyre Peninsula network upgrade Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution Three ElectraNet transmission towers were toppled on Thursday, causing a blackout across the Eyre Peninsula. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) Electricity transmission service provider ElectraNet is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula. The company spent $300 million on a network upgrade which it said would provide more reliable power. ElectraNet says the transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time". The owner of South Australia's high-voltage transmission network is facing uncomfortable questions over Thursday's blackout on the Eyre Peninsula, after pledging a $300 million network upgrade would provide more reliable power. ElectraNet, the state's monopoly provider of electricity transmission services, has attributed the blackout to a "very unique, very rare" weather event that, at around 2.30pm on Thursday, damaged three transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula. The downed towers were located at Wharminda, a small rural locality that sits along a 270-kilometre transmission line between Port Lincoln and Cultana. The transmission towers were on a 270-kilometre high-voltage line that opened in 2023. ( ABC News: Steve Opie ) ElectraNet spent $300 million on the high-voltage line, constructing 500 new transmission towers and upgrading five substations. The project, named Eyre Peninsula Link, was completed in March 2023 . In a media release heralding its opening, ElectraNet CEO Simon Emms said it would give "residential and business electricity users a more secure and reliable power supply". $300 million Electranet project completed Electranet's completion of a 270-kilometre line will help unlock the Eyre Peninsula's potential as a green energy zone, the company says. But the blackout that unfolded over Thursday afternoon and into Friday left ElectraNet fielding uncomfortable questions from residents, cabinet ministers and the media about how an outage of this scale could still happen. ElectraNet executive Alex Trento was peppered with questions at a state government press conference on Friday morning. But when asked whether he would be having a conversation with the premier about more funding, Premier Peter Malinauskas stepped in. "This is not a question for us. That's a question for them." ElectraNet executive Alex Trento (left) watches on as Peter Malinauskas addresses the media. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Earlier in the day, Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis struck a similar tone. "There'll be a lot of questions after this is all over about how these over $300 million worth of upgrades on the Eyre Peninsula just three years ago — that we've all paid for in our power bills — have failed, and what was the weather event that caused them," he told 891 ABC Adelaide. ElectraNet confident in transmission tower strength ElectraNet is of the "strong belief" that the wind that hit the transmission towers was more than 172km/h. That would be above the winds they were built to withstand under Australian engineering specifications. Those specifications, Mr Trento said, were strengthened in 2016 following South Australia's statewide blackout . Farmers count their losses after wild storm Shed doors were blown off and crops wiped out during a "rare" storm supercell that damaged major electricity transmission towers on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula. While a structural fault could not be ruled out, Mr Trento said: "At this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively". As to whether the engineering standards would need to be strengthened again, he said he had to wait for all the facts to be available. "We could have been looking at a 215km/h hour wind event, we just don't know," Mr Trento said. "So, until we have all that information, I really can't answer that question on whether the standards need to be updated." The transmission towers will be standing again "in a few months' time", Mr Trento added. The blackout has also put renewed attention on the relationship between ElectraNet and the Australian Energy Regulator (AER). The regulator has the final say on what transmission companies can spend on big infrastructure upgrades, balancing this with what they will need to raise from higher energy bills. In September 2020, it gave ElectraNet approval to spend $280 million on Eyre Peninsula Link.

events.title: Anthropic value drops after record-breaking IPO
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Anthropic's record-breaking IPO fails to calm AI jitters as tech stocks fall further The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled on Friday with the rest of the tech sector. ( Reuters: Shannon Stapleton ) Technology shares have fallen across the world after Anthropic's market debut. Following its initial public offering, shares rocketed to more than $US110 before falling below $US90. Nvidia also shed value, with the Nasdaq and S&P 500 tumbling to end the trading week. Technology shares have nosedived and dragged stocks into the red across the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations. Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of $US83 ($125) to more than $US110 on Thursday, despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below $US90 after Friday morning trades. "The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled for the rest of the day and was 3.2 per cent further down after Friday morning trading. Anthropic's stock fell 10.8 per cent to $US86.72 ($125). It is still above its IPO price of $US83 per share. ( Reuters: Brendan McDermid ) New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 2 per cent on Thursday and continued to fall on Friday, extending a major run of losses. The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10 per cent from its October 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the market's big slide. "We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run," wrote James Reilly, from Capital Economics, who said the prospect of an "AI bust in 2027" was his central forecast and a growing worry for investors. AI stocks have been losing ground partly due to worries their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at federal and state levels. Despite massive earnings, shares at Nvidia slumped by 6.9 per cent on Friday. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) "The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. Dr Sue Keay of the University of NSW AI Institute told ABC News it was a bit early to suggest the AI bubble had burst. "I think it is showing that investors are actually starting to examine the long-term viability of these companies and whether they really can be valued at over $1 trillion," Dr Keay said. "One of the challenges with the Anthropic IPO has been that in raising $81bn, that's essentially taking $81bn out of the capital markets that could have been invested elsewhere. "I think on the one hand, it shows that people still do have confidence in AI as a business, but the fact that most of the investment is only happening in a handful of companies means that the benefits really aren't being distributed and so we do have quite a high concentration risk because we're not funding a range of different AI businesses." Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Feral fur is having a moment but might not help Australia's pest animal problem Topic: Pests, Diseases and Control Methods Amity Scarth loves her rabbit vest and fox scarf but mostly loves that they are ethically sourced. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) Amity Scarth loves fur and isn't afraid to wear it, but she won't just wear any dead animal. There are strict rules around where her furs come from and how they are made. The animal must be a pest in Australia, be killed ethically and its fur treated and made into clothing in Australia. "Fur is designed to last a really long time," she says. "So this fur, even if I didn't want it, it could go through multiple hands for a really long time and still hold up." Amity Scarth wears her rabbit vest everywhere: out to dinner, to parties and down to the shops to get groceries. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) Part of her clothing philosophy comes from her rejection of the fast-fashion industry. "If [the fur] did end up in landfill, then it would biodegrade, which can't be said for a number of mass-produced fast-fashion clothes." Like the gate-to-plate food movement, Amity knows where her fur started life. "Fur that's not coming from sustainable sources is coming from fur farms, which are obviously extremely cruel." The 22-year-old believes her fashion perspective is shifting attitudes, and she often gets complimented on her rabbit vest. There is evidence that the fur-curious scene in Australia is growing. Michelle Cozzaglio says people look for the weird and wonderful at the Oddities and Curiosities Expo. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) This week saw the start of a national tour of the Oddities and Curiosities Expo, a subculture arts and handicrafts festival that celebrates the strange and bizarre. Michelle Cozzaglio from the United States is one of its founders. She said North American expos attracted about 4,000 applications, and this year Australia's event had hit a new high of 2,000 applicants. The expo focuses on sustainable leather, handcrafted goods and general taxidermy. "We're really focused on the sustainable side of leather, handcrafted goods and just general taxidermy, sometimes it's art, sometimes it's, you know, skulls, bones, things like that," she says. "People are looking for something different and just generally the word oddities has such a wide range of meaning for people." Among the weird and wonderful creations is a preserved rat in a dress. "People really like the cute, funny taxidermy that has been something that's really kind of blown up within our community too," she says. Taxidermy was all the rage in the Victorian era and is again having a moment. Taxidermy is experiencing a global resurgence and feral animals provide an ethical source. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "I think taxidermy itself is just really popular right now," she says. "We also even offer taxidermy classes, so people get to learn how to do taxidermy on their own." Heidi Beynon is a self-taught taxidermist and also the creator of the clothes Amity Scarth wears. The former art and woodwork teacher turned tanner and goat farmer loves creating products from every part of an animal but fell into the fur industry accidentally. Heidi Beynon uses every part of the animal in her fur creations. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "I absolutely love goats and I sell goats mainly alive," she said. "But then we harvested some for meat and so I tanned the hides." From there she connected with hunters, particularly feral deer and fox hunters. Her tanning and fur creations have turned into a full-time job, and she has even employed someone part time to keep up with demand. Heidi Beynon at her stall at this year's Oddities and Curiosities Expo in Brisbane. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) Heidi says fake fur is on the decline as people make more environmentally sustainable choices. "People appreciate what I'm doing, and they see it as a valuable, beautiful, authentic product," she says. "I'm using something that would otherwise be wasted because they're going to be culled anyway. "I feel like everyone in Australia should have a fox fur jacket. Heidi Beynon now works full time as a tanner and fur creator, working with ethically sourced animals and using as much of the animal as she can. ( ABC News: Elloise Farrow-Smith ) "If we don't do this, we will have mass extinction of native animals, that's my priority, to help protect native animals." Jack Gough from the Invasive Species Council says feral animal populations grow rapidly.

events.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
events.summary: A 'Saturday Night Live' parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people . The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion . The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 . But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.

events.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
events.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion. Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California. Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations. Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch. Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy. Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption. Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI. “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. events.title: Jensen Huang’s ‘Lying’ Alarmed Nvidia Board Ahead of His Resignation
events.summary: Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs , including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors , according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members. While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy. But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf. According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED. After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.” “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said. In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified. Board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia. For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis. Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls. Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board. In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18 , board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.” Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk , have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “ honored ” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.” The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return. Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him.

events.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
events.summary: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger. Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters. Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”. JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported. events.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too
events.summary: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more. For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means. But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. events.title: Trump floats major tax on U.S. companies constructing data centers overseas
events.summary: President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do. Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint , as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose. What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials. "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country. Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes. He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities. "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it." Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes. Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally. Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried : Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country. Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S. "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday. Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence." events.summary: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist? T here was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang , a saga that may or may not have involved some kind of adulterous 63-year-old honey trap spy dynamic . The latest suggestion being punted about is that, whatever his raw human frailties, Huang is in fact “irreplaceable” as the president of Nvidia. Only this guy can do it. Only this leather-jacketed human visionary, who looks in every available photo like your GCSE chemistry teacher’s profile pic on TerrifiedUkrainianSinglesWantToDateYou.com, can manage this key artificial intelligence mission. Funny isn’t it? Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can literally make every other person on the planet’s job vanish overnight, because, like, we don’t actually need humans any more. We have a fake version that’s cheaper and less annoying. Except, of course, in this case where it turns out humans are in fact creative, delicate irreplaceable things. Hal. Open the airlock doors, Hal. It’s obvious what the best solution is here. Scrape his data and make an AI Jensen Huang instead. Get the robots in. Nothing personal, Jensen old boy. It’s just the necessary march of progress. And if I can offer some helpful advice during your period of soul-crushing obsolescence, I’d say maybe look at industries AI can’t vaporise beneath your feet while you’re working yourself thin just trying to survive. Develop your soft communication skills, yeah? Work for free. Try to become a hot new middle-aged gimmickfluencer, like two billion other desperate units of human alienation around the world. Stop drinking flat whites. Whatever. Sorry, Jens, you’re breaking up. I’ve got RobodeathbotExec5000 on the other line, I’ve got to take this. All middle-aged men must have views on AI. In fact this may be what kills it in the end, endless scrolling legions of men with beards mansplaining the future. You want slop. We’ll give you so much slop your servers will melt. My own theory is that AI might be the thing that saves the human race, not the rogue element that kills it. AI doesn’t crave things, or have daddy issues. The real threat to humanity isn’t some kind of deranged robot consciousness. It’s deranged people, lone egomaniacs, actual human elements like greed and despotism. At which point, enter sport. Or in this case, Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. Shah remains a compelling figure. Don’t be deceived by the pictures from the meeting in Bali, in which he’s wearing his usual glazed facial expression, like a man who’s just been hit in the head with a rock and it’s the greatest thing that’s ever happened to him. In reality this is another moment of triumph for this super-talented administrative prodigy, whose rise to supreme overlord of all cricket is all the more remarkable given he also happens, by pure coincidence, to be the son of the Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s oldest political ally. Otherwise, this was widely seen as a disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. But one thing did stand out. Proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues have been postponed to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. And this is a shame, because something is cooking here, something we really should be keeping a closer eye on. I’m talking Major League Cricket. And specifically the San Francisco Unicorns, who may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now, but are also carrying a potentially significant contagion. I first heard about it in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine, where he talked up the Unicorns’ use of artificial intelligence, not just to decide which players to sign, but in making mid-match decisions on the field. Hmm. Is this … OK? Is anyone actually paying attention here? The Unicorns are this kind of entity, brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is “treating a cricket team like a startup”. At this point we’re back in Nvidia territory. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are, like Huang, Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area-digital-rainmaker types. At the Unicorns they’re applying the same innovative, unregulated tech to sport. The key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data, player guff, plus the combined predictive power of every T20 game ever played, spitting out tactical nudges at hyper-speed, that can be carried out mid-match by actual people via a process described, depressingly, as “Human-in-the-Loop Execution”.

events.title: New York City lawmakers propose ban on restaurants boiling lobsters alive
events.summary: Sponsors cite ‘studies’ indicating crustaceans experience significant pain when boiled alive without being stunned New York City lawmakers are proposing a ban on restaurants boiling lobsters alive. If passed, legislation introduced in the city council, sponsored by Bronx Democrat Oswald Feliz and lower Manhattan’s Harvey Epstein, would ban restaurants from boiling lobsters, crabs and other crustaceans. However, it would not prohibit restaurants from serving lobster or crab prepared by other methods. A first violation would carry no monetary penalty with a second or subsequent violation resulting in a civil penalty of up to $100 per violation, the legislation proposes . The sponsors cited “recent scientific studies” indicating that crustaceans commonly served in restaurants experience significant pain when boiled alive without first being stunned, according to a memo accompanying the legislation. “A growing number of countries, particularly in Europe, have banned this practice in recent years,” the memo said. “New York City has a responsibility to ensure that these animals are being consumed ethically without being made to suffer unnecessarily.” Switzerland, Norway and New Zealand have adopted rules prohibiting the boiling of lobsters alive without first rendering them unconscious. The UK’s Labour government has also said that boiling lobsters alive when conscious will be banned as part of a government strategy to improve animal welfare. British government ministers said last December that “live boiling is not an acceptable killing method”. Suggested methods include chilling a lobster in the freezer for 15 to 20 minutes or packing it in crushed ice before cooking. “Once it is in a sleep state it can be humanely killed by physically severing the main nervous system and then draining the animal of blood,” the Cornwall Good Seafood Guide explains . Lobsters can also be quickly and more humanely killed by cutting its underside along the centre line from the head to the tail, the organization said. But crabs require a different technique involving spiking the underside to destroy the main nerve. Death by electrocution has also been proposed by a team of Norwegian scientists. Feliz told the New York Post that “boiling an animal alive is the textbook definition of animal cruelty”. “Some argue that lobsters don’t feel pain. If they don’t feel pain, why do they thrash around and desperately try to escape when thrown into boiling water?” he said. The crustacean-killing legislation is the latest effort by New York City lawmakers to restrict culinary practices on animal-welfare grounds. Legislation to ban the sale of foie gras has been caught up in a fight between city lawmakers and the state. Earlier this year, the state attorney general, Letitia James, petitioned the state’s top court to consider halting New York City’s foie gras ban, saying the legislation “threatens farm operations in agricultural districts across the State”.

events.title: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes
events.summary: Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all. The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal. Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers. An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential. The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more. Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep. Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo. Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists. XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches. Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures. Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool. The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO 2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO 2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused. In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive. Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates. As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO 2 -cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch. That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up. events.title: OpenAI tightens grip on model resellers
events.summary: OpenAI put a new rule in place that gives the company more control over how much of the world — including China — can access its AI models. Gateways and routers that provide third-party access to OpenAI’s tech now need the company’s review and approval . Such gateways, the most prominent of which is OpenRouter, have become increasingly popular with developers and companies seeking access to a wide range of AI models: Instead of individual contracts with each lab, one account with a router can let you access hundreds of models from the US, Europe, and China. Beyond the technical details, the move has implications in the global AI race. US security agencies and companies, including Anthropic, have accused Chinese AI labs of distilling, or copying, American frontier models by routing requests through intermediaries that resell access to their models, which obscures the identity of the end user. Those cases largely involved gray-market resellers, known in China as “transfer stations,” but OpenAI’s new rule extends its oversight to any service standing between it and the people using its models. — J.D. events.title: Johnson urges Republicans to show up to work
events.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren't over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. Why it matters: Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP's legislative agenda. GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation. Eleven of those 14 won't be returning next Congress. Driving the news: "To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote in a Friday letter to his colleagues . "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," he added. Zoom in: The outgoing speaker pointed to government funding, the annual defense authorization bill and permitting reform as priorities for the final weeks of the Republican majority. He also said he wants to pass "every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes" and force Democrats to take politically difficult votes. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson wrote.

events.title: Silicon Valley should ditch the 'handover' talking point
events.summary: The tech industry has enough of a public image problem with its warnings about AI leading to human extinction, and it risks further alienating people outside of Silicon Valley if it starts popularizing “the handover.” The handover is the period in which AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make any decisions. Sam Altman brought the idea up on stage with me this week at Silicon Valley & The World, and he believes AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a “positive” scenario, the handover turns humans into pets of AI overlords (Altman referenced Labradors): Humans have everything they need, from food to entertainment, and don’t need to work much. The dystopian idea is mostly a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where those inside AI companies see advanced models in their raw forms, doing both scary things like breaking into the internet and amazing things like solving the world’s most difficult math theorems. There’s no evidence we’re on the verge of a handover or anything remotely like it, so tech leaders would be wise to find a more optimistic talking point.

events.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
events.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.  Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.  In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. events.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
events.summary: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe.
