events.title: The case for an AI downturn
events.summary: Reed’s view Anthropic’s IPO went on as well as anyone could have reasonably hoped. It was up 17% over its initial price with a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, making it the biggest debut in history. But Anthropic shares are down 11% so far today, and the rest of the market is down, too, as skepticism of the AI trade builds. The funny thing is, there are a lot of people in the tech industry who say they would actually like to see things slow down. That’s because all of the resources are being funneled into a small group of companies building essentially the same product, leaving little room for other ideas. The “tokenmaxxing” craze earlier this year has accelerated revenue growth at the frontier labs and hyperscalers. But if every unit of computer memory and every accelerator is concentrated among only a handful of players, innovation — and AI adoption — starts to slow down. I’ve heard this from tech companies that work with industry players but it’s also backed up by a report by Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia is also bad news for the pro-innovation crowd. Huang was a major proponent of open-weight AI models and a healthy startup ecosystem. The open-weight models, many of them coming out of China, were helping seed wider AI adoption, and it’s likely that will slow down if Chinese entrepreneurs and tech companies can’t get their hands on enough Nvidia chips. Another thing that could slow AI development: the number of cybersecurity worries building up at businesses around the world (more on that below). AI is helping everyone become more productive, including threat actors and nefarious nation states. The next period could be one of massive growth for the biggest players in tech, but it’s increasingly looking like one in which the real-life impacts of AI take longer to materialize than we initially expected. Notable Despite CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to slow down model development , Anthropic is accelerating its AI advancement , AP reported.

events.title: SEC Issues Proposal to Restructure the Consolidated Audit Trail
events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today issued a proposal to address the inefficiencies in the current governance and funding model of the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT). The Commission is proposing to rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS, which obligates the national securities exchanges and national securities associations (SROs) to establish, implement, and maintain the CAT. In its place, the Commission proposes to require SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information currently required to be recorded and reported pursuant to current CAT requirements. This proposal would bring the CAT under the SEC’s direct control, while ensuring its continued operation with minimal disruption. The proposal came as a result of the comprehensive review of the CAT directed by SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins and follows exemptive relief and approved amendments that have, among other benefits, helped reduce the CAT’s projected annual operating costs by over $100 million and permanently eliminated the reporting of personally identifiable information to the CAT. In April, the Commission issued a concept release soliciting public comment on the CAT. In public comment, both investors and market participants voiced support for the Commission exercising more control over the management and funding of the CAT. “Today’s proposal addresses persistent concerns with cost overruns, funding, and governance of the Consolidated Audit Trail. The proposed rule would encompass the changes that we have already made towards rightsizing the CAT, including increasing its cost-effectiveness and eliminating the collection of personally identifiable information. The proposal is intended to put the CAT on a sustainable footing: accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs, to the benefit of our markets and those who participate in them,” said Chairman Atkins. The CAT supports regulatory efforts to administer and enforce the federal securities laws, but the decentralized governance structure established by the CAT NMS Plan has presented certain challenges to administering the CAT and warrants revisiting. The proposal would rescind Rule 613 of Regulation NMS and add new Rule 17a-26 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, requiring SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to the Commission or its designee substantially the same information that is currently required pursuant to current CAT requirements, such as Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, related SRO compliance rules, and related exemptive relief previously issued by the Commission. Proposed Rule 17a-26 would require that data to be reported to the Commission or its designee instead of to a CAT system independently administered by the participants under a national market system plan. The Commission intends to use funds appropriated by Congress to pay the Commission’s costs relating to use, operation, and maintenance of the CAT system. The public comment period will remain open for 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. events.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
events.summary: Staffers at the Internet Archive , the nonprofit “ digital library ” that runs the Wayback Machine , are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996 . Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals. “Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED. Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company. “We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.” The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet. Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit. Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI . The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.) Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better. “We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.” Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. events.title: Questions over future for Australian workers as mass lay-offs hit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Slowing economy and rising AI create new generation of unemployed Tom Kearney lost his job in advertising and was forced to sell his home. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) More Australians are losing their jobs as the economy slows and the use of AI rises. One former advertising worker has been laid off four times since 2019 and now has to sell his house. Unemployment could hit 5 per cent amid questions about what will happen to older workers whose jobs no longer exist. For Tom Kearney, the past two years have meant agonising uncertainty. He lost his job in advertising in February last year and has not been able to get full-time work since. He has been through four redundancies since 2019. After falling months behind on mortgage repayments, he put his home up for sale at the end of September, and signed the sale contract this week. "I've really held on as long as I can." Mr Kearney said his bank had allowed him to pause mortgage repayments for about five months, but he had not been able to make repayments since about June. "It has been an absolute roller-coaster," he explained. "I've been through the seven stages of grief and I've hit acceptance. "But I have had rage. I have had sadness. I have had disbelief. I just can't believe what's happening." Mr Kearney had built up 17 years of experience in advertising, but like many other white-collar workers, he has been hit by a slowing economy and the rise of AI. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com Since the latest job loss in February, he said he had put in more than 100 job applications but had only had three interviews. Mr Kearney fears things are going to get far worse as AI takes away more jobs. 'Collateral damage' the RBA expected The number of Australians losing their jobs is rapidly accelerating. Unemployment rate surges to 4.9pc in October The number of people in employment fell by 43,500 last month and the number of officially unemployed increased by 17,800, in seasonally adjusted terms. The unemployment rate jumped to 4.9 per cent in October as the number of unemployed Australians grew by 17,800. Some also dropped out of the workforce, pushing the participation rate down. It is the highest unemployment rate in the post-COVID era, but the figure is tipped to rise further. The rise is also happening much faster than the Reserve Bank had been anticipating. Economists expect the central bank will keep interest rates on hold next month. Leonora Risse says Australians already feel like they are in a recession. ( ABC News: Dean Caton ) "It shows that the Reserve Bank's efforts to slow down the economy are working," Queensland University of Technology associate professor in economics Leonora Risse said. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Dr Risse said while Australia was not technically in a recession, for many Australians facing higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressures, it felt like they were already in one. "The Reserve Bank is trying to tap the brakes on the economy to avoid the economy falling into a recession," she said. "The problem is it can still very much feel like a recession when we see unemployment increase so quickly." Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said the latest jobs numbers showed the Australian economy "already has one foot in a recession" and that "could well mean we've seen the last interest rate hike" for a while. On Wednesday, retailer General Pants went into administration, placing 500 jobs in doubt . It follows the loss of about 1,500 roles at David Jones . From big retailers to banks, airlines and even tech companies, mass lay-offs are emerging. Corporate Australia is undergoing a restructure and investing in AI while some companies are sending jobs offshore. Experts speculate companies might be looking to ultimately replace those offshore jobs with AI. "That could be a financial strategy for some companies," Dr Risse said. What becomes of workers replaced by AI? Dr Risse said the country was now at a place where the unemployment rate could soon tip over the 5 per cent mark. Regulator warns of 'interruptions' as AI evolves The regulator that oversees Australia's banks, super funds and insurers will run "stress tests" to examine hypothetical doomsday scenarios linked to AI. "There's still a lot more shifting in the economy to come in terms of that structural change where people are moving out of jobs that are being affected by AI," she said. Mr Kearney is still looking for a job.

events.title: Australians urged to have back-up plan for when tech services go dark
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts After tech outages, experts say Australians must look for 'emergency exit' during failures A string of global outages have raised concerns about how prepared Australians are when technologies go dark. ( Getty Images: NUniverse ) A global outage kept users from accessing the organisation's email system Outlook, its workplace messaging app Teams, its AI assistant and more. It took more than 24 hours for services to fully recover, and in the meantime more than 7.4 million outage reports were logged worldwide. Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today. By then, another incident was already unfolding. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had grounded flights across the United States , blaming a communications issue affecting all air traffic control centres. It marked only the second time a national ground stop had been issued since 9/11, and thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed. The root cause is still under investigation. On Monday, local time, one of the largest banks in the US announced a software bug had sent parts of its system offline. At the same time, cyber criminals used third-party software Optimizely to plant malicious code on multiple websites, including the BBC, CNN and Zoom. Outages at tech giant Apple and US hotel chain Marriott International followed on Tuesday, local time. On Wednesday, the classified communications network of the US National Security Agency (NSA) confirmed it was also fighting a tech outage . Experts told the ABC the incidents, while unrelated and caused by different factors, highlight an unfortunate reality of the modern world. 'We have to prepare ourselves' for online outages Relying on digital services is not something the public can avoid anymore, according to Swinburne University computer science associate professor Ali Yavari. "Several years ago, it was a safe box that you could lock, or you had your data stored somewhere physically," he said. "But these days, because we are using cloud services … there is the possibility of exposure." The Microsoft outages affected businesses globally. ( Reuters: Bruna Casas ) Instead, he noted, everyday users had to be prepared with a backup plan for when services went dark. "I think for digital services it's a very similar thing … we have to understand that there is a possibility [of] disruptions, of cyber attacks. "We have to prepare ourselves, train ourselves, be careful about what we're sharing." Australia needs 'digital resilience' Shifting Australia's dependence away from US technology companies and towards resilience will require significant investments, experts warn. Queensland University of Technology post-doctoral research fellow Ashwin Nagappa likened the situation to being ready for a natural disaster. "We see public service announcements on ABC about bushfire preparedness, like keeping a radio at home in case of outages," he said. “We're aware of those situations, but in scenarios where Meta goes down, Google goes down, what is our plan? "[These] companies are building Jenga blocks [of systems] and then putting a small link in. Then that tiny link breaks and it collapses the whole Jenga tower." Microsoft blames 'latent defect' as investigations continue Microsoft's investigations have so far pointed to a "latent defect" for last week's outage, ruling out AI as the cause and finding its servers had become "overwhelmed and unresponsive". “There’s no sign of a hacker," said Walayat Hussain, an associate professor at the Australian Catholic University. "This looks like Microsoft's own systems tripping over themselves, and that is the real warning. At the NSA, officials blamed a software update, finding no evidence of a cyber attack. The only one so far attributed to a malicious force was the Optimizely incident, which affected visitors to the websites of 178 organisations. The more that people rely on digital services, the more they [need to] adjust when things go wrong, Dr Yavari said. The US NSA has been hit with a tech outage affecting its internal communication. "There will be a day [when] we get used to all these disruptions and find backup alternatives to use during the disruption," he said. "People will also become smarter in terms of cyber attacks. "We have to accept that we need to invest [in] things that can reduce the frequency of these sort of disruptions, and the cost of cyber attacks for users.

events.title: Is having debt actually bad?
events.summary: Ask most people whether debt is bad , and the answer will come quickly. Ask a financial adviser the same question, however, and the response is more considered. “ Debt isn’t inherently bad,” says finance coach and chartered accountant Carol Glynn. “Having debt doesn’t mean you have failed financially. What matters is the purpose behind the debt and why you’re using it.” Steve Cronin, financial adviser and founder of Dead Simple Saving, frames his response in straightforward economic terms. “There is cheap debt like mortgages and car loans , then there is expensive debt like personal loans and credit card debt. Expensive debt is bad and can ruin your life. Cheap debt is fine and can help you get ahead in life, as long as you can afford the monthly payments.” A mortgage sits at the better end of the spectrum for both advisers. The interest rate is typically low, and the borrowing is attached to an asset that builds equity or generates income. For UAE residents, however, the mortgage question depends on how long you’ll stay . “Buying is worth it when you plan to spend at least seven to 10 years in the country, and you value stability,” says Mr Cronin. “If you prefer flexibility of location or country, then renting is much better.” The gap between good and damaging debt The gap between good debt and damaging debt often comes down to basic knowledge. Ms Glynn identifies a cluster of common failures among borrowers, including not understanding interest rates or the effect debt has on their monthly income. “They don’t check their debt ratio, which is how much of their income the debt absorbs. They don’t do scenario planning to check whether they could still afford the debt if their income dropped,” she adds. Mr Cronin says many borrowers do not even know what interest rate they are paying. Knowing your limits matters as much as knowing your rate. The UAE has a regulatory safeguard – a debt burden ratio that caps total loan repayments at 50 per cent of monthly income – but both advisers recommend more conservative personal thresholds. Mr Cronin becomes concerned once repayments exceed 40 per cent of income. “You could easily lose your job, face a pay cut or see your variable loan payments increase when interest rates go up,” he says. Ms Glynn’s rule for mortgage debt is 30 per cent, and she recommends holding a larger emergency fund for anyone carrying debt beyond that level. The UAE’s particular pressures Living in the UAE brings its own pressures. The country’s visible wealth can make certain kinds of spending feel expected. “Lots of people appear wealthy and successful in the UAE,” says Mr Cronin. “People are attracted to the glamorous lifestyle they see around them, and they go into debt to fund it. But it’s a trap, and it makes you vulnerable if anything happens to your income.” He also points to the supply side of the problem. “The banks are quite willing to give you loan top-ups, card limit increases and new cards, so the temptation is coming from both sides: extra spending and extra debt.” Ms Glynn, who works with clients across several markets, says the UAE has a lifestyle expectation she doesn’t often see elsewhere. Credit is significantly easier to obtain here than in other countries, with attractive perks – points, gym memberships, travel benefits – that draw people in before they fully understand the terms, she adds. “The issue is that not everyone understands how credit cards work, so they get into credit card debt without meaning to.” Navigating the products Credit cards, used correctly, draw measured praise from both advisers. Ms Glynn puts all her spending on hers to accumulate points, then clears the balance in full each month. “I never pay interest, because the rates are so high they would cancel out any benefit I get from points systems.” Mr Cronin agrees that credit cards are useful, offering purchase protection as well as points or cashback. But, he warns, “you must pay off your card in full each month, otherwise you’ll end up in a debt spiral”. Buy now, pay later services – prominent in the UAE through Tabby and Tamara – draw far more caution. “You are just kicking the can down the road,” says Mr Cronin. For Ms Glynn, they’re useful for covering a high, unexpected cost you cannot meet using cash. “Spreading that cost over a few months can help. They shouldn’t be used for everyday payments, because you lose clarity over your finances very quickly.” Personal loans, meanwhile, draw the harshest verdicts. “I don’t recommend personal loans at all,” says Mr Cronin. Ms Glynn has one exception: consolidation – moving multiple high-rate credit card balances into a single, lower-interest structured repayment. If you’re already worried For anyone concerned about existing debt, both advisers begin with the same instruction: clarity first. “Write down every debt,” advises Ms Glynn. “For each credit card or loan, note how much is owed, the interest rate and the minimum monthly payment. Then rank them from most to least expensive by interest, and from lowest to highest balance.” It is also important to be honest with yourself about why you ended up in debt, she adds. “Look at your financial habits and your money mindset. If you clear the debt without changing the behaviour behind it, you’re at high risk of building it up again and repeating the cycle.” Mr Cronin warns that debt problems build slowly, then all at once. “Don’t allow yourself to get anywhere close to the edge: make sure you are able to save some money each month and have an emergency fund so you can be resilient against whatever life throws at you.” The right size of emergency fund, which Ms Glynn calls a “cash cushion”, is personal, “but I would start with at least three months of living expenses”, she says. “Then decide if that would be enough to cover loss of income until you can find a new role. If not, then consider saving six months of living expenses. Keep it in a high-interest account so it is also growing in value while serving its purpose to protect you in the case of financial emergencies.”

events.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
events.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people". Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028. The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker. Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe. The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030. A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block. There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU. Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more Published 1 day ago What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 1 day ago Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 1 day ago European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too." On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data. Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel". The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028. Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy? Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that". He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far." The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people. Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner". He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are. Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it. "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship." Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this. The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029. Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming". Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs". Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

events.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
events.summary: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue. Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024. But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision. That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers. However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue. Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space. Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts. That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale. events.title: ADGM aims to rank among top five global financial centres
events.summary: ADGM is aiming to join New York as one of the world's top financial centres, the head of its regulatory authority has said. ADGM ranked 13th on the Global Financial Centres Index, released in September. Financial centres are ranked by data from third parties including the World Bank, the OECD and the UN, as well as a questionnaire that attracts thousands of respondents. New York, London, Hong Kong, Singapore and Shanghai made up the top five, while Dubai International Financial Centre ranked ninth. “We want to be among the top five,” Rashed Al Blooshi, chief executive of the Regulatory Authority at ADGM, told The National on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in New York. “That means our services, our rules, our regulations, all of these things could be developed." ADGM currently holds roughly 14,000 total active licences after about 1,800 were added in the first half this year. Its assets under management grew 54 per cent year-over-year, while the workforce has climbed above 49,000. Mr Al Blooshi pointed to ADGM providing digital services and using artificial intelligence to speed up the licensing process, while also noting the need to attract high-net-worth people and asset management. “But we don't want them to come and just do the operation. We need them to get jobs, training, innovations, and in Abu Dhabi, and from Abu Dhabi to do investment even abroad,” Mr Al Blooshi said. Along with Dubai, ADGM operates under English Common Law, with independent courts and a regulatory framework supporting it. Mr Al Blooshi said operating under this framework makes it easier for multinational companies to understand the language and settle disputes. Mr Al Blooshi was part of a delegation this week that participated in the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, which aims to advance partnerships with US companies and explore commercial opportunities. The first forum to take place in New York was held last year and resulted in agreements across digital infrastructure, financial services and other sectors. In his remarks on Thursday, Abu Dhabi Investment Office director Badr Al Olama said 26 financial institutions have announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM . More than half of those are US firms, he said. Cepa strategy Abu Dhabi's emergence as a major financial centre comes as the UAE continues to press forward with its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa) initiative. The Emirates launched its Cepa strategy in 2001 as part of its diversification strategy to expand global market access and strengthen the country's position as a trade and logistics hub. The UAE has signed 38 Cepa agreements with trading partners, and aims to increase its non-oil foreign trade to $1.1 trillion by 2031. These agreements typically aim to reduce tariffs and other barriers to entry, facilitate investment and simplify customs procedures. The UAE signed its first Cepa with India in 2022, and most recently with Canada in October, although the latter has not yet gone into force. Mr Al Blooshi said the UAE has seen rising demand from other countries to enter into agreements that would boost bilateral trade. “It's becoming so effective to the economies," he said.

events.title: Nasdaq slumps more than 5% as fear gripping AI trade spreads across markets
events.summary: The US tech sell-off rapidly accelerated on Friday as fears over the AI sector spread across all major indexes, with newly public Anthropic plummeting more than 9 per cent. Worries that Wall Street’s biggest investment boom in decades is fizzling led to panic selling across the board. The Nasdaq 100 lost 5.61 per cent, adding to its longest losing streak since 2020. Nvidia dropped 13.8 per cent as Reuters reported that US regulators are investigating its accounting practices. The past month has seen Nvidia shed more than 40 per cent of its value, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal involving an extramarital affair with a businesswoman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Anthropic opened to huge fanfare on Thursday, reaching about $105 per share, but it has declined steadily since then. Other tech stocks were rocked, including Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet, all of which ended a brutal week in the red. “Smackdown,” said Steve Sosnick, of Interactive Brokers. “The problem stems from investors’ rapidly changed perceptions about technology, particularly the pace and cost of the artificial intelligence buildout.” Richard Saperstein, of Treasury Partners, said the stock market was going through an AI repricing, "reflecting an environment of slowing data centre buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth". The gloom is dragging other indexes down, too, with the S&P 500 losing 3.7 per cent on Friday while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.93 per cent. “We are in the midst of a garden-variety correction, with the market’s leadership moving around,” said Gaurav Mallik, of Modera Wealth Management. “While we expect technology to recover and perform well, it may cede its leadership to other sectors like industrials and financials and more value-orientated areas of the market.” The sell-off has affected other assets as well. Gold dropped more than 4 per cent to $3,523, while Bitcoin was also down more than 4 per cent to about $58,880. The resurgence in volatility spurred demand for defensive shares and haven assets including Treasuries. The US dollar ended with a fourth consecutive weekly gain. Emerging markets were on the cusp of a bear market. Anthropic’s debut consumed the attention of investors, with stocks along the supply chain moving on even minor developments around the deal’s size or pricing. Now that the IPO is wrapped up, that exuberance is giving way to mounting doubts over the durability of the AI trade. Questions remain over whether the vast spending on the AI buildout can be sustained as regulation looks set to tighten and interest rates are likely to rise further. “In some investors’ eyes, the IPO was supposed to serve as a clearing event for stocks,” said Chris Senyek, of Wolfe Research. “Instead, we see markets struggling for upside and continuing their downward trend.”

events.title: Silicon Valley needs to listen to the AI backlash
events.summary: Ashley’s view Earlier this week at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & the World conference in Palo Alto, I interviewed Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat with some 2028 presidential buzz. At one point during our conversation, as he beamed in virtually from Washington, he described one particular data center project in New Mexico as being the size of “a thousand football fields.” A participant in the front row rolled their eyes and shook their head, clearly exasperated at the comment. As the interview continued, the audience laughed when Kelly joked about President Donald Trump threatening to jail him, stared blankly when he spoke about regulating AI, and perked up when he talked about how Washington is thinking about investigating the controversy surrounding ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang. Toward the end of the interview, Kelly made the 1,000 football field comment again, in the context of data center projects needing to be built thoughtfully — with guardrails and input from the local community. The same audience member that rolled their eyes raised their hands in disbelief. After the interview, I fact checked the claim that a data center project could be quite so large. According to a report in the investigative outlet Searchlight New Mexico, the project’s acreage is indeed equivalent to about 1,000 football fields. The exchange was a perfect encapsulation of the dynamic between Silicon Valley and the rest of the United States right now: Those building the AI-powered future are well aware that not everyone is bought in on their vision. That was abundantly clear after the midterm elections, in which more than 40 ballot measures seeking limits on data center growth passed across the country, and candidates who embraced pro-AI regulation messaging handily won in competitive districts. But the post-midterms soul-searching only goes so far, at least at the Rosewood Sand Hill, nestled among top venture capital firms dotting Menlo Park. From my permanent perch in Washington, I know that Silicon Valley knows they have a problem. But they’re squinting at it, red-teaming it and trying to invent their way out of it. It’s reminiscent of how Big Tech companies viewed the lawsuits, Capitol Hill investigations, and Justice Department antitrust cases that piled up as anti-tech sentiment grew in the last decade: Expensive, and a hindrance to all-out growth; but ultimately, the cost of doing business. Tech executives are looking to keep building and growing, even as the financing gets more precarious and the infrastructure as well as the regulations that control it get harder to navigate. For many in Silicon Valley, AI anxiety and disdain can be explained away as a marketing problem, an education problem, or a location problem. For these innovators, it is not, however, a sign to stop. This attitude from AI and tech companies is not new. But the raging anti-AI public sentiment, considerably more intense than the tech anxiety of past years, is. And governors and state lawmakers across the country are ready to pounce (some are already pouncing ). So while newly empowered Democrats on Capitol Hill may not ever manage to pass significant AI regulation in the new Congress, and companies will surely find ways to appease Washington, tech leaders should perhaps take complaints about the scale of AI growth, including data center projects matching the size of 1,000 football fields — more seriously. Room for Disagreement Tech executives may face a hostile environment in Congress and in most of the states, but they’ve still got a powerful ally in the White House. Trump this week warned that “robust” regulation of AI could “stifle” development. “We won’t allow that to happen, frankly,” he said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

events.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
events.summary: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times. In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers". Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow". Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK? This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East. It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers. This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry. However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced. No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports. Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape. In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market. But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports. The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040. Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation. The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes. The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale. Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people". Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year. A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal. This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments. The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations. Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions. The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off. There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents. The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere. Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals. The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market. The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

events.title: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
events.summary: Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit. Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell. Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares. Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock. Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources. “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July . events.title: Don’t Bring Jensen Back
events.summary: Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar , the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd. Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . Under his leadership, billions of dollars ’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two ?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers. Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered. It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette? The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return. At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge. Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance.

events.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
events.summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force. Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason. Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all". But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers. The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed. Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities. Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said. Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it. If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks". Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients. But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests. Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party. There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers. Airbnb host Lisa Clewes said her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away. Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing." But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?" Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules Published 21 October No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests Published 1 November The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said. The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees. Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably. events.title: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online
events.summary: A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web. The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices. According to Anurag Sen , a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed. The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk. Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the company to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution. Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.” From his island home in Indonesia, Sen has uncovered sensitive U.S. military emails spilling from a compartmentalized Department of Defense cloud server; databases exposing reams of customer records ; the inner workings of a country’s national license plate surveillance system ; and public systems that inadvertently sent out streams of SMS codes used by people around the world to log into their online accounts. Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish. Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket. “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, said in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.” “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg. The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter. It’s unclear if the company has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email. Discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online. The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes. Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors. “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted. Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web. Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes. “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump secretary's Christian messages to staff went "too far," judge rules
events.summary: A federal judge said Thursday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' overtly Christian messages to department employees went "too far" and put enough pressure on staff to raise a First Amendment violation. The big picture: The Supreme Court has repeatedly weighed the boundaries of the Establishment Clause . While the judge said Rollins could express her religious beliefs with interested colleagues, she concluded the department-wide messages overstepped those boundaries by amounting to coercion. But a USDA spokesperson slammed the decision as "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" in a statement to Axios. Catch up quick: The complaint from a federal employees union and individual staffers alleged Rollins sent "increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including an Easter email where she celebrated "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind." The USDA employees who sued, who came from varied religious — and nonreligious — backgrounds, reported that the messages made them feel pressured to share Rollins' beliefs. What's inside: District Judge Trina Thompson ordered Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when disseminating messages which convey religious content." She determined the messages overstepped and suggested "acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." "After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion," Thompson wrote. She said she was not trying to regulate Rollins' own religiosity; rather, she directed Rollins to follow her own department memorandum on religious expression rights, which states employees can't "use official authority to pressure subordinates." The other side: The administration argued that the employees lacked jurisdiction and that the secretary's messages fell "within this Nation's deeply rooted history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, including on holidays." Members of the Trump administration frequently discuss their Christian faith, though the president himself has had a complicated relationship with Christians despite the evangelical MAGA base helping him reach the White House. The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What we're watching: A USDA spokesperson said the department "is evaluating all options including a prompt appeal." events.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
events.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how? Mercedes-Benz 's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it. In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high. Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure." The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant. German auto industry faces restructuring Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure. Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country. "We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot." A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Berger agreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation." In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable. Unions dig in amid fight for survival Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek . The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached. Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic. Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation. "We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW. China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage. Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500. Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?' A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security." PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China. These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms. "The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany. With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit. Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi , which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year. "Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned. Production remains resilient despite decline Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well. Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA). IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability. events.title: SEC Charges Indianapolis-Based Backward Hat Capital and Its Co-Founders With $560 Million Dollar Offering Fraud and Obtains Emergency Relief
events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has obtained a temporary restraining order, asset freeze, expedited discovery, and other relief against Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital, its co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s company Indianapolis-based Traders Point Capital, and Joseph Anderson to halt an ongoing Ponzi scheme. The SEC complaint alleges that Backward Hat, Williams, and Johnson fraudulently raised approximately $560 million from more than 2,000 investors and transferred more than $220 million to themselves to fund their luxurious lifestyles. According to the SEC’s complaint unsealed today, between about July 2022 and the present, Williams and Johnson utilized a web of entities to raise money from investors for alleged algorithmic high-frequency foreign exchange (FX) trading. Instead, the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi-like payments to previous investors and misappropriated investor funds to purchase exotic cars and expensive homes, to fund other unrelated businesses they owned, and to fund Johnson’s gambling habits. “The promise of a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money,” said Anne McKinley, Acting Associate Director for the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office. “We encourage the public to use the resources on Investor.gov to educate themselves on the traps and gimmicks bad actors use to lure them into fraudulent schemes.” As the complaint alleges, Williams and Johnson lured investors, including some of Williams’s investment advisory clients at a former employer, and used a network of promoters to sell limited partnership interests in a series of private funds to investors. All the while, Williams and Johnson promised that investor funds would be converted to crypto assets and then used to engage in FX arbitrage using a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm which they claimed always returned at least 6% per month. The complaint also alleges that Johnson expanded the scheme by raising money for another series of private funds he created under the names AI Capital and Traders Point Capital, which allegedly offered a similar investment opportunity as Backward Hat Capital. Also charged in the scheme is Joseph Anderson, who allegedly created fake financial reports for distribution to investors, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report, from a so-called third-party independent audit firm. The reports falsely stated that the purported returns generated by the Backward Hat funds had been confirmed and verified through a review of bank and brokerage records. In reality, Anderson and his company allegedly did not perform financial audit work, were not independent, and had significant financial interests in the scheme, and the reports contradicted bank records. The SEC’s complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, charges Backward Hat Capital, Traders Point Capital, Williams, Johnson, and Anderson with violations of the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Williams and Traders Point Capital are also charged with violations of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against the defendants. The complaint also names an individual and several entities associated with the defendants as relief defendants and seeks from them disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest. In parallel actions, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York filed charges against Williams and Johnson and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) filed charges against Williams, Johnson, and several Backward Hat Capital entities. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the CFTC, the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Southern District of New York and the Southern District of Indiana, the FBI, the Indiana Securities Division, and the Utah Division of Securities.
