events.title: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
events.summary: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.” The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets . “Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED. One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face. “Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven. Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One company is pitching its new line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating. The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward. “This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.” Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.” Fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy. The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise. “If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says. To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she says, is “a mind fuck.” Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection company Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status. The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is. “Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients. When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.” That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says.

events.title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
events.summary: Glenn Harvey for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing. His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.  “I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.  It stands to earn much more.  Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year. Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation . The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments. The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said. And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime. “How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked. “Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.  Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future. “I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.  In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.   The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.” Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said. Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.  Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person. “We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond. Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent. KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated. That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.  Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two. The Smith County Sheriff’s Office, based in Tyler, Texas, received nearly $2.2 million in funding through 287(g) from January 2025 through June 2026, more than any other department reviewed by KXAN. Antranik Tavitian for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune “Are You a U.S. Citizen?” Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation. Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.  But task force agreements can also be lucrative. Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.  They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase. The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina . events.title: GTA VI hijacks America
events.summary: The internet's warring tribes converged Thursday for the loud, lawless debut of " Grand Theft Auto VI ," as 13 years of anticipation culminated in one of the great viral spectacles of all time. Why it matters: In a media landscape splintered into dozens of distinct realities, the GTA launch gave Americans a rare common obsession — refracted through vastly different platforms, personalities and worldviews. By Thursday night, GTA VI had generated an estimated $2.36 billion in sales from nearly 25 million copies — almost triple the first-day revenue of its record-breaking predecessor in 2013, according to Sensor Tower . The irony is rich: Amid political rancor and mounting technological anxiety, millions of people sought refuge in a virtual America gone gloriously, spectacularly off the rails. Zoom in: GTA VI drops players into Vice City, a fictionalized Miami that serves as a sprawling digital fever dream of violence, celebrity, corruption and distinctly American absurdity. Players can rob banks, steal planes, wrestle alligators and wreak havoc — or pass the afternoon fishing, shopping, working out and tending to the relationship between the game's central characters. The astonishingly detailed world teems with influencers, conspiracy theorists, criminals and social-media parodies, offering limitless opportunities for the outrageous encounters now flooding the internet. Zoom out: GTA's return has revived decades-old arguments about whether violent video games encourage real-world aggression, while igniting a far stranger debate over masculinity. On Fox News , commentators warned that the game's carjackings and shootouts could desensitize young players to crime. One contributor likened giving children the game to handing them a gun. Meanwhile, corners of the online "manosphere" expressed outrage over missions that reward players for buying flowers, running errands and showing affection toward their girlfriends. Between the lines: GTA VI was an internet phenomenon long before anyone could play it — the most expensive video game ever made, with years of delays that became memes in their own right. A vast economy of streamers, influencers and professional clippers mobilized around its historic debut, churning out viral entertainment for millions who may never touch a controller. At its peak, nearly 8 million people worldwide watched GTA livestreams simultaneously . Gameplay clips have already amassed tens of billions of views across X, TikTok, YouTube and other platforms. The GTA frenzy has spilled into the real world, upending work schedules and drawing corporations, politicians and even the military into the spectacle. A GameSquare survey found that 30% of employed U.S. gamers were considering taking time off to play. At Fort Stewart, Georgia, 43 soldiers committed to another two to six years of Army service after a four-day GTA gaming pass was included as a reenlistment incentive. Prediction market Kalshi received more than 33,000 applications for a job paying up to $135,000 to play GTA and study its virtual economy. Even the White House got in on the act, releasing a GTA-inspired Trump montage dubbed "WELCOME TO MAGA CITY XLVII" — turning a franchise long vilified by politicians into another viral marketing tool. The bottom line: GTA offers a glimpse of what monoculture looks like in 2026. For one extraordinary day, the internet had a common story — and a thousand different ways of telling it.

events.title: America's religious "nones" move from voters to lawmakers
events.summary: America's religious "nones" have gained a visible foothold in Congress: Five lawmakers will claim no religious affiliation in January, up from a single member just two years ago. Why it matters: Washington remains far more religious than the nation it represents. But the last two election cycles have put a series of cracks in that political glass ceiling. By the numbers: Religiously unaffiliated voters made up 27% of the 2026 midterm electorate, up from 23% in 2024, according to preliminary Fox News voter polling . Just three of 532 lawmakers surveyed at the start of the 119th Congress claimed no religious affiliation, according to Pew Research Center . Pew counted one additional humanist. All three lawmakers who claimed no affiliation — Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Abraham Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Emily Randall (D-Wash.) — won reelection in November. State of play: They'll be joined in January by Democratic Reps.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Fred Wellman of Missouri — who publicly acknowledged their nonreligious identities before winning their Nov. 3 elections. Rabb, a five-term state lawmaker representing a majority-Black Philadelphia district, won the seat of retiring Democratic Rep. Dwight Evans. Wellman, a retired Army officer, ousted seven-term Republican Rep. Ann Wagner in suburban St. Louis, flipping a longtime GOP stronghold. Their wins mark a breakthrough for congressional candidates who openly embraced their nonreligious identities before Election Day, according to Secular Coalition for America. Zoom in: Rabb thanked atheists for supporting his campaign after winning his May Democratic primary. Wellman defeated Wagner roughly 51% to 46%, according to Ballotpedia . His pitch? Affordability, corruption and accountability — not his lack of faith. Zoom out: The nonreligious political bench stretches well beyond Capitol Hill. More than 100 openly nonreligious lawmakers are expected to serve in at least 38 state legislatures, up from 81 in 33 states, according to the Center for Freethought Equality . Humanists, atheists or agnostics will serve in the legislatures of Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Ohio and West Virginia for the first time, the Center for Freethought Equality reports. In Texas, Democrat Jon Rosenthal won a statewide race for the Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry. He identifies as agnostic and "multireligious." Yes, but: Don't mistake "none" for a unified political creed. An October Pew survey found 81% of atheist registered voters and 75% of agnostics supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 48% of those claiming "nothing in particular." Nor did Rabb and Wellman break entirely new ground. Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, who left Congress as an independent after being first elected as a Democrat, identified with no religion when first elected to the House in 2012. Nothing in the results proves voters chose either candidate because of his religious identity. "It's not an anti-religious constituency by any stretch," Robert P. Jones, president and founder of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), tells Axios. Jones said many religiously unaffiliated Americans grew up in churches, and some walked away over teachings about gay and lesbian people. Their political opposition, he said, focuses more on white Christian nationalism than on religion itself. Between the lines: The Constitution prohibits religious tests for office, but public expressions of faith have long carried political currency in Washington. The Congressional Freethought Caucus , founded in 2018, now counts 37 members — believers and nonbelievers — promoting church-state separation and science-based policies. Rabb and Wellman's victories suggest candidates can acknowledge a lack of faith without making it their campaign's centerpiece.

events.title: US minerals deal hangs over DR Congo’s power struggle
events.summary: The News The Trump administration’s push to secure access to DR Congo’s critical minerals is fast becoming entangled in a political fight over President Félix Tshisekedi’s controversial efforts to change the constitution and potentially extend his rule beyond 2028 when his second term is due to end. Tshisekedi says implementing the US minerals pact, which gives American investors preferential access, requires constitutional changes, linking the deal to judicial reforms while raising the prospect of a third term. His opponents fear that this is a pitch to claim he is the only guarantor of the agreement and they have also pledged to honor it. Analysts said Washington will be wary of being seen to endorse the president’s political ambitions. The US is seeking access to DR Congo’s vast copper and cobalt reserves, essential for electric vehicle batteries and artificial intelligence, as it tries to challenge China’s dominance of global critical mineral supply chains. The two minerals alone generated $31.5 billion in Congolese export earnings in 2024, according to central bank data. Barred from running again in 2028, Tshisekedi last week signed a law allowing a new constitution to be adopted by referendum. If approved it would reset the count, argued Christian Moleka, a Kinshasa-based political analyst: “We will no longer be talking about a third term, but about a first term under a new constitution.” Days after the law was signed, Frank Garcia, the State Department’s top Africa official, told a congressional hearing that the administration has “had diplomatic discussions” with Tshisekedi on constitutional changes, but despite being asked Garcia did not specifically mention the prospect of a third term. However, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle were more forthright on the risks. Sen. Jim Risch, the outgoing Republican chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told Semafor it would be “ill advised for President Tshisekedi to take actions that would deepen the political and security crisis in his country.” Rep. Gregory Meeks, the Democrat expected to chair the House foreign affairs committee from January, said eliminating term limits would risk “threatening opportunities to partner with the United States.” Joseph Kabila, Tshisekedi’s predecessor, who now leads Rwanda-backed rebels in the east, said in October that the US minerals deal was guaranteed by “the continuity of the state , not by the survival of the regime in power.” Weeks later in Rome, major opposition leaders including Moïse Katumbi and Martin Fayulu pledged that “legitimately elected leaders” would preserve the agreement’s “strategic commitments.” Christian-Géraud Neema, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment’s Africa Program, said the pledges target an unspoken bargain: “There seems to be a quid pro quo coming from Washington that Tshisekedi is our man and as long as he does things regarding our interests, we would not do anything against him.” A quieter Washington The State Department pointed Semafor to the agreement’s text. “We do not engage in hypotheticals,” a spokesperson said, calling peace and security fundamental to the partnership. Rep. Johnny Olszewski, the Democrat who questioned Garcia in the hearing, told Semafor the administration “must do more to make clear to President Tshisekedi that his actions are not acceptable and will have consequences.” Garcia was more critical about the national dialogue Tshisekedi announced in August, The three-month process, meant to cover peace, national unity, and rebuilding the state, has been rejected by the main opposition coalition, and armed groups are excluded. “We haven’t seen it tasked out, we haven’t seen it organized, we haven’t seen an agenda, and these are not indicators that there’s truth behind that,” he said. “There’s no condemnation, but no support either, and that silence can be read as a kind of tacit green light,” analyst Moleka said, referencing the third term. For Kinshasa, he added, Washington’s silence “can be used as a narrative at home to say: Washington is not opposed to this project.” Joshua Walker, an associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank’s Africa program, said the opposition saw the referendum law as “a kind of provocation,” and he fears what comes next. “My concern is that there’s going to be a political escalation and that there’s going to be a military escalation in the east,” he said. “It’s almost becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.” Room for Disagreement Some analysts argue Congolese politicians on all sides are overestimating Washington’s staying power. “Personally I don’t think it’s a good strategy,” Neema said of the Congolese opposition’s pitch, because he doubts the US has a lasting stake in the country. “DRC importance to the US has always been wildly exaggerated,” he said, adding that if Trump leaves power, “I don’t foresee the US having that level of apparent invested interest in the DRC.” Notable An “America first” policy “is likely to favor close relations with Congolese political leaders over democracy and human rights,” an approach that could end up destabilizing the country, DR Congo experts wrote in Foreign Affairs.

events.title: Medicaid expansion isn't a "slam dunk" for new Dem governors
events.summary: Democrats' sweeping electoral wins jump-started prospects for Medicaid expansion in red and purple states that rejected full expansions of the program under the Affordable Care Act. But budget realities could make newly elected Democratic governors pump the brakes. Why it matters: The changing of the guard sets up a test of whether states can expand coverage to more low-income residents right after Republicans in Congress weakened financial incentives for doing so. States that are facing serious budget shortfalls and daunting cost projections already are signaling they may defer until conditions are more favorable. State of play: Incoming Democratic governors in Wisconsin, Georgia, Texas and Kansas who campaigned on Medicaid expansion are now in a position to expand health coverage, and have more Democrats in their legislatures to help. Wisconsin Democrats have arguably the most leverage now that they've captured the state Senate and Assembly in addition to keeping control of the governor's office. Plus, the state already covers adults with incomes up to the federal poverty level. Expansion advocates in Georgia and Texas face a heavier lift, with Republicans still controlling at least one legislative chamber. And in Kansas, the GOP lost its supermajority in the House, a key obstacle in past Medicaid expansion fights, but still controls both chambers. Between the lines: Each state faces unique considerations. But one thing is true for all of the holdouts: The incentives for expanding aren't what they used to be. Though the federal government still would pay for 90% of the expansion cost, last year's GOP reconciliation law made major policy changes and cuts to the program. Expansion states now face stricter limits on provider taxes used to finance Medicaid, as well as on extra payments they make to hospitals and other providers to go beyond standard Medicaid rates. They've also lost an important bonus: A temporary 5% increase in federal assistance for newly expanding states expired at the beginning of this year. What's more, states will have to enforce new work requirements and document whether recipients perform 80 hours per month of work or other qualifying activities, or if they're subject to exemptions. While the Trump administration delayed the requirements for six months, they aren't likely to go away. What they're saying: "You're going to see a lot of [expansion] conversations start, but I don't think they'll be slam dunks. It's complicated and nuanced," said Matt Salo, a health care consultant and former executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors. Incoming Wisconsin Gov. David Crowley already is acknowledging that reality and exploring alternatives for expanding coverage in the near term, including establishing a state-run health insurance exchange with a public option, per the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel . In Texas, some lawmakers are considering a "trigger" bill that would start an expansion only if the incoming Democratic majority in Congress succeeds in rolling back some of the restrictions in the federal law, the Texas Tribune reported. Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms intends to pursue a full expansion next year, but also wants to streamline the state's existing limited expansion program, called Pathways to Coverage, as an interim strategy until full expansion is achievable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Democratic victories in the Texas and Georgia lieutenant governor's races still could boost Medicaid expansion prospects, since the lieutenant governor presides over the state Senate in both states and influences which legislation is considered, Max Reale, an analyst for Gordon Haskett Research Advisors, wrote in a note. He pegged Wisconsin as the likeliest to expand its program and Kansas the long shot, since control of the governor's office alone failed to advance Medicaid expansion in past legislative sessions. But cementing the four as expansion states would diminish the prospects of further Medicaid cuts under a GOP-controlled Congress and free lawmakers to pressure the six remaining holdout states to adopt expansion post-2028, Reale said. What we're watching: New Democratic governors in purple states that already expanded their Medicaid programs could also pursue changes, said Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown's O'Neill Institute. She noted that Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand promised to end the state's contracts with three Medicaid managed care companies due to high rates of improper denials of care, and to have Iowa's Medicaid agency or a nonprofit take over processing and paying claims. Incoming officials in Iowa and Ohio could also go to court for relief from the most burdensome parts of the work rules, Keith wrote in Health Affairs .

events.title: Why AOC’s future could depend on Chuck Schumer
events.summary: The News Chuck Schumer and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are steering clear of each other for now — yet their political futures are increasingly entangled. As the Senate Democratic leader battles an underdog leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., some of his members are hoping for signals about his reelection plans for 2028. If Schumer seeks another six-year term, progressives are agitating for a primary challenge. And if Ocasio-Cortez passes on a White House run, many on the left want her in the Senate. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., said the 37-year-old should challenge Schumer, 75, “if she’s not running for president.” Ocasio-Cortez is keeping fellow Democrats guessing about her plans. While allies like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are backing Van Hollen, she also appears to be staying out of Schumer’s leadership race. Ocasio-Cortez told Semafor in a brief interview that his future as majority leader is “for the other chamber to determine.” Schumer is similarly mum on 2028, even when talking with Democratic senators. He views winning the majority leader job and a future reelection bid as separate choices, with the former having no bearing on the latter, according to a person familiar with his thinking. His decision has an undeniable effect on her options, however. Ocasio-Cortez would likely clear the field in an open primary to succeed Schumer, the only septuagenarian among the top four Hill leaders. Schumer also has good reason, despite Van Hollen’s challenge, to take his time deciding after helping his party flip a historic nine Senate seats this year. Ocasio-Cortez may choose a primary fight for higher office, according to several House Democrats. She made her name eight years ago by dethroning Joe Crowley, a former member of House leadership, and she would be a formidable statewide candidate regardless of Schumer’s decision. “I’m sure she’s thinking about it. I’m not sure she’s thinking about it in the context of what Chuck does,” said Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y. “She’s probably just trying to make a decision on what she thinks she can best contribute.” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., predicted that “there will be” a primary bid, adding that Ocasio-Cortez “has so many options in front of her.” Schumer’s plans Schumer hasn’t tipped his hand to even close allies in the caucus about running for another term. He is the heavy favorite to defeat Van Hollen but taking the battle seriously. Still, sharing his views on 2028 could “obviously” help him more handily defeat the Marylander, one Democratic senator told Semafor. “I don’t think Leader Schumer needs to make some public pronouncement about his future plans, but I think it is helpful for us as a caucus to be thinking about what kind of leadership team and what kind of leader we want in this moment for the next two years — and going forward,” this senator said. “Because they may not be the same.” The question of Schumer’s future is complex: He is singularly focused on leading Democrats through the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term, but it’s also rare for Senate leaders to run again after facing dissent within their own ranks. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi took her own version of that step in 2022 by announcing she would leave leadership so incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries could rise, though she served another two-year term. Schumer won the Democratic leader job in one day after former Leader Harry Reid announced his retirement and backed Schumer in 2015. Most Democrats speculate, without direct knowledge, that Schumer is leaning against another Senate term. If Ocasio-Cortez ran for president or stayed in the House, Schumer could potentially survive a primary challenge from another opponent. The crowded bench of candidates who might jump into an open primary includes Rep. Pat Ryan, D-N.Y., whom Democrats have long considered a potential statewide candidate. Ryan doesn’t sound eager to challenge Schumer head-on yet. He told Semafor that Schumer “deserves a tremendous amount of credit for those wins, for putting us in the position we’re in, and then it’s his decision to do whatever he wants to do next.” The 44-year-old added that he didn’t want to get ahead of “what [Schumer] wants to do.” Whether Schumer should be majority leader was “up to the Senate side,” he said. ‘How to yield power’ Senators generally are not influenced by House members’ opinions on their internal matters or politics. But indicating that he’s not running could affect Schumer’s ability to lead the caucus over the next two years, some Democrats said. “That’s the kind of calculation that he has to figure out for himself,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who supports Schumer. “And also, what does that mean for actually holding power, how to yield power — does it help you use influence? So, those are the kind of decisions that he has to make.” El-Sayed, who defeated a Schumer-backed primary foe in Michigan, did not seem interested in fueling a primary challenge to the leader. In an interview, El-Sayed said he has “nothing against Senator Schumer. It’s not about him.” “The most important priority for us right now is that we have to have a plan to legislate in ways that the American public can understand, identifying their problems, identifying legislation that’s going to solve their problems, and then executing on that,” El-Sayed added. Room for Disagreement If Schumer did indicate to his caucus that he won’t seek reelection, he’d be sharing more than most Democratic senators do. None of the ambitious Democrats he leads have said explicitly yet that they are running for president, for all their visits to early states and ambitious agendas. “The more information, the better,” said Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who is neutral in the leadership race. “But I’ve not experienced colleagues ever telling us what they’re doing in a week, much less over the next few years.” Burgess’s view It’s clear that some progressives want Ocasio-Cortez to run for Senate rather than president. For all her name recognition, she would face a White House primary that promises to be as brutal as 2020’s 29-candidate field. But as she indicates she’ll decide at her own speed — she’s one of the few 2028 contenders with the luxury of doing so — we see the pragmatic side of Ocasio-Cortez. She’s tamped down progressive criticism of Jeffries. Her answer on Van Hollen was in the same vein. She’s deliberate before choosing to roil her party. Notable When Ocasio-Cortez and El-Sayed campaigned together in Michigan’s rural Upper Peninsula this fall, they were clearly test-driving a national platform for the left, as Semafor reported .

events.title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
events.summary: The incomplete AquaBounty site in Pioneer, Ohio, in 2024. The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. John D’Angelo for ProPublica When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back. JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash. AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility. The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County. But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists. Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for $1.5 million more than he’d paid. AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, as ProPublica reported last year , the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August 2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public. “Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group. While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have limited experience in production. Sherry Fleming, of the grassroots environmental group Williams County Alliance, said, “Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling.” Nick Hagen for ProPublica In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said that “there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment schedule or other accommodation.” “Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs and management distraction,” it added. Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website. JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have  long been a sore point for Ohioans.  On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is “independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment commitment, project return on investment, and project location.” The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222 million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028. Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30% built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that Pioneer had extended for its benefit. AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build. JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the community,” Fleming said. (JobsOhio is funded by profits from state-controlled liquor sales, not by taxes.) Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.   Read More The One That Got Away: This Small Town Is Left in Limbo After Betting Big on GMO Salmon If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to benefit Ohioans.” JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said, informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement. AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement. With an onerous process and uncertain outcomes, it’s “pretty rare” for JobsOhio to try to claw back money, said Kristan Wong Karinen, a research analyst with the nonprofit Good Jobs First, which tracks public subsidies in economic development. More commonly, she said, it and other agencies will renegotiate the contract — extending the time period for a company to meet commitments, perhaps, or lowering requirements. “In this case, with AquaBounty,” Wong Karinen said, “because they haven’t done anything, they haven’t fulfilled any of the requirements, I feel like JobsOhio is being forced into this.” The post Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Phoenix mayor walks fine line on AI boom
events.summary: Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego wants more tech investment in her city — but on her terms, as data centers strain resources and frustrate residents. Why it matters: Phoenix has become a bellwether for the AI industry's growing demands on electricity and water in an increasingly hot, resource-constrained world. As the mayor, Gallego is navigating an outsized dilemma facing communities nationwide: How to embrace the AI boom while protecting residents and resources. "I do want us to lead in technology, and I want us to be a tech-forward community," Gallego said at a recent event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios. But she added: "I want companies who care about our community and will give back to it, and not just a race to see who can get the deepest incentives and the cheapest" power. "We're open for business, but we're not for sale," she said. Zoom out: Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies in her efforts to strike the balance she wants. Democrats flipped both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs won reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966. Affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate, Gallego said. Catch up fast: Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity. Now the debate is expanding from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. State of play: Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, has spent recent years trying to balance that. She helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions. The state enacted a three-year pause on new applications this summer. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium, favoring more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes. Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules last year requiring special permits for new data centers. Gallego says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they're built and what residents get in return. That could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for neighbors affected by development. By the numbers: Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said. Many may never be built, but Gallego warned: "That's not a balanced economy, and that's not economically sustainable." Friction point: Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over zoning restrictions adopted last year. The city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court. "We have been open and good partners to the industry, and it's deeply disappointing that they don't want to work with us," Gallego told Axios. The other side: Developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values, entitling them to compensation under Arizona law, though industry allies have also acknowledged tensions . Reality check: It's unclear whether Gallego can have it both ways: attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority. Gallego is also navigating the tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat in the desert. Newer cooling technologies can reduce water consumption at data centers but often require more electricity, shifting some of the water footprint to power plants. "We're seeing many of these data centers get power from natural gas plants in an area of our state that is very constrained around water," Gallego said. The intrigue: Data centers are adding another source of heat to a region already struggling with dangerously high temperatures. An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit. Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she's "jealous of Midwestern mayors" who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings. What we're watching: Gallego worries Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain. She compared the risk of abandoned data centers to Phoenix's vacant Kmart stores, many of which have been difficult to redevelop. "What will I do in a community if we have these giant windowless boxes" that are no longer operating, she asked. "How will we redevelop or make them not become blight?" events.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
events.summary: María Jesús Contreras for ProPublica When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.  The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California. “I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?” Read More Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t. If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households. ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted. Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?  We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.   How does SNAP theft happen? Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby. Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.  In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case , a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits. What can I do to protect my benefits?  Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal. Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel , allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.  But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries. Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits. “I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said. Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there. An investigative analyst with the Secret Service removes an overlay from a skimming device they found on a card reader at a convenience store in California. Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica The inside of the card skimmer Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica What can I do after my benefits have been stolen? If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.  You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. ( This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).  A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”  While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. events.title: Fed’s Lisa Cook speaks ahead of hearing
events.summary: Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook is expected to address a conference in Chile this afternoon in her first public remarks since her lawyer announced she will not participate in a White House hearing on whether President Donald Trump should fire her over allegations of mortgage fraud. “Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to ​the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine [its] ​independence,” Abbe Lowell wrote to the Trump administration earlier this week, citing the involvement of Trump adviser Kevin Hassett and the demand for Cook to produce documents before the White House reveals its evidence. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on whether officials, who said last month they may “draw adverse inferences” against Cook if she did not attend, would hold the hearing without her. If they do, it will undoubtedly feature prominently in congressional Democrats’ oversight next year of Trump’s attempts to bend the central bank to his will, given many have repeatedly condemned his campaign against Cook. “Trump is convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank,” said the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, panning Trump for “playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.summary: Trump administration officials hope that a new press secretary will be named by the “end of year,” as one adviser told Semafor. events.title: Outages trigger congressional scrutiny of AI-enabled attacks
events.summary: The Trump administration says the string of recent tech outages across the country can be attributed to companies rushing to patch their networks as AI exposes vulnerabilities in old software. Cybersecurity experts say the government is largely telling the truth about the crashes’ causes, but the situation reveals a bigger problem: Much more digital instability is coming, and it will be worse. At the same time, President Donald Trump’s hands-off approach to AI signals to the private sector and Congress that the government may not be there to help as outages multiply, or when AI-enabled attacks inevitably result in even more mayhem. A tech lobbyist and a Hill source told Semafor that a letter this week from Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton urging the AI task force he leads to “launch a national effort to confront a new generation of AI-enabled cyber threats” is a bipartisan sign of things to come from Capitol Hill come January. Bolstering AI cybersecurity will emerge as a key legislative goal along with broader AI bills on catastrophic risk, the sources said. “It’s one thing that Hugging Face got attacked,” the lobbyist said. “Wait until it’s a mid-sized community bank. What’s the event that will get Congress and the White House to do something?” Meanwhile, the agency charged with protecting US infrastructure from cyber threats, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, may go even longer without a permanent director. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said they would place holds on Trump’s nominee, Palantir Chief Information Security Officer Michael LoSapio, after he denied Thursday during his confirmation hearing that there was an attack on the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021, and refused to say who won the 2020 presidential election.

events.title: Cairncross departs abruptly after widespread tech outages
events.summary: The News White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out and is being replaced by Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies, multiple officials told Semafor Thursday . The shakeup follows a series of disruptive tech outages that have raised fears about US cybersecurity — and has kicked off a heated dispute about whether Cairncross was fired or left voluntarily. One White House official and a person familiar with the White House told Semafor that Cairncross was fired on Thursday; the official said that finding a new cyber director was one of the first things Stephen Miller did in his new role as White House chief of staff, and both said Trump had supported Cairncross’ removal. But another senior White House official and a person familiar with the matter strongly disputed the idea that Cairncross had been fired, telling Semafor that he resigned — and not because he was asked to. A second source familiar with the matter, who said Cairncross had been fired, said the past week exposed the need for someone “more competent, with the expertise needed to execute this position.” Axios first reported the news of Cairncross’ departure and Davies’ new job. Ashley’s view Someone was bound to take the fall for a string of tech outages that have left the country terrified about what services might get disrupted next — even if the most basic (and likely true) explanation is that organizations are rushing to patch software bugs discovered by AI programs and are crashing their systems in the process. Cairncross told me as much this week after I interviewed him on stage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, in what would end up being his last public interview as a White House official. Director of National Intelligence Clayton echoed his words two days later, so I don’t think being off-message here was his issue. The alarming and disruptive outages over the last week, at least one of which appears to be ongoing , may have provided Cairncross’ detractors the perfect opportunity to bump him. But long before Miller took over for Susie Wiles, some in Washington said they’d seen Cairncross, whose previous experience includes being a lawyer for the Republican National Committee, as unqualified to be a cyber official. Rumors of his potential ouster go back as far as this spring, though he helped shape the administration’s June executive order on AI and cybersecurity, including its framework for voluntary pre-release testing of frontier models. He survived the “Mythos moment” — when Anthropic’s latest model made Washington freak out about AI’s cyber capabilities — but he couldn’t make it through FAA routers failing, Microsoft Outlook crashing, JP Morgan pausing services, and the NSA’s internal comms network going down. Davies does not have an easy job ahead; she will have to prove the public can trust her to help the country get through the precarious digital moment we’re in. I asked Cairncross this week if the administration would ever fully release that June executive order, much of which has not been public. “I expect that we will be making it much more clear how this is working in practice,” he said. He also told the room of CEOs that if they have questions about preparing for this cyber moment, they should reach out: “If you haven’t heard from my office, we are more than willing to engage,” he said. “We’re happy to be hyper-responsive.”

events.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
events.summary: Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures. Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks. Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying . The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes. Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended. Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser. The latest official sales figures , external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling. "Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said. "Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again." The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September. As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October. The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers. Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further". Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises. Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch Published 10 November Why should I stockpile and what will I need? Published 23 October Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October. Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn. Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago. These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel. events.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
events.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned. Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets. The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members. Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs? This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million). The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful." " Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said. At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year. How else is Lufthansa planning to save money? The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets. Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter. The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing. In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization. In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook. events.title: The US national cyber director is stepping down
events.summary: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown. Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director. We’ve reached out to the White House for comment. events.title: Why is gold price going down?
events.summary: Gold is heading for its worst weekly decline in eight months as interest-rate fears, forced liquidation and bearish bets combine to intensify bullion’s sell-off, with investors increasingly betting on further declines. Analysts warn prices could fall further before finding a floor. Spot gold dropped 2.7 per cent to $3,525.25 an ounce on Friday, after touching a 14-month low, and was down about 9.2 per cent for the week. Gold prices hit a record $5,515 an ounce in January. A stronger US dollar and mounting expectations of another Federal Reserve interest-rate increase eroded demand for the metal. “Gold is facing a perfect storm of macro headwinds and forced liquidation,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone. A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar and pushed Treasury yields higher, creating a challenging environment for gold, which pays no interest and becomes less attractive when returns on other assets rise. However, the sell-off is being amplified as investors rush to raise cash, selling assets – including gold – to meet margin calls amid a broad decline in global equities, especially technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade . Buying into IPO boom? So, are investors liquidating gold assets to buy into the initial public offering IPO boom? The surge in demand for high-profile AI listings, including Anthropic , could offer another competing destination for investor capital as gold loses momentum, according to analysts. However, there is little evidence yet of a direct rotation from gold into IPOs. “The aggressive sell-off across global equities, notably the crowded AI trade, has forced investors to reduce leverage, meet margin calls and raise cash,” Mr Weston said. “Gold has become a source of liquidity rather than a destination for safety.” Gold’s Friday slide reflects bearish forces that are now reinforcing one another, said Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “A hawkish Federal Reserve has revived the dollar, pressuring gold,” he said. "At the same time, the sell-off in AI-linked equities has prompted investors to raise cash across asset classes instead of driving them into havens." The Fed’s message that inflation remains too high has prompted markets to price in an almost certain rate increase in December, with the possibility of further tightening in January and March, Mr Weston added. Investors bet on further declines The bigger concern is that selling pressure could have further to run. Trend-following funds have already increased their short positions in gold, while exchange-traded fund investors have yet to capitulate, leaving the possibility of more selling ahead, Mr Valecha said. Despite the aggressive decline since the onset of the Iran war , gold has struggled to find a durable bottom. Options markets are also signalling a shift in sentiment. Investors typically pay a premium for call options on gold as insurance against macroeconomic and geopolitical shocks. That premium is now shrinking relative to puts, which protect investors against price declines. But a sharp correction does not necessarily mean gold’s longer-term investment thesis has collapsed, but it marks a significant cyclical repricing after investors became heavily positioned for further gains. “The options market tells the story best,” Mr Valecha said. "Investors usually pay more for gold calls than for puts because they buy them as insurance against macro and geopolitical shocks. That premium is shrinking. Why isn’t gold acting as safe haven? Gold’s traditional role as a safe haven has not been lost, but it is being overshadowed by the need for investors to raise cash during a period of market stress. “Gold’s safe-haven characteristics haven’t disappeared, but they don’t operate in isolation,” Mr Weston said. "In periods of acute market stress, investors often sell what they can rather than what they want to." Gold is being sold alongside equities and other risk assets, while the dollar is attracting defensive demand and higher Treasury yields are making bullion less attractive relative to interest-bearing investments. “For buyers to return with conviction, I’d want to see three developments: a stabilisation in US real yields, a sustained pullback in the dollar and evidence that forced selling has largely run its course,” Mr Weston said. “Until then, geopolitical uncertainty alone may not be enough to restore gold's safe-haven appeal.” How low could gold prices go? With gold trading at about $3,525 an ounce, the immediate focus is whether buyers can defend the psychologically important $3,500 level. A sustained break below that could expose the $3,400 to $3,300 region, where longer-term investors and physical buyers may begin showing greater interest, Mr Weston said. Investors should wait for selling pressure to ease, volatility to moderate and, ideally, a reversal in the dollar and US real yields before concluding that gold has established a sustainable low, he added. The shift suggests traders are increasingly positioning for further downside rather than simply unwinding bullish bets, Mr Valecha said. Gold may, therefore, continue to fall more than it recovers, with any near-term rebound potentially proving temporary rather than marking a reversal in the trend. Mr Valecha also sees stronger support potentially emerging closer to $3,500 an ounce, despite the risk that prices could fall further in the near term. On the upside, bullion would need to reclaim $3,600 before moving towards $3,700. The former support zone of $3,800 to $3,850 could now act as resistance, Mr Weston said. Gold's price action suggests it could remain under pressure in the coming days, with next week's US economic data likely to prove important. For investors and jewellery buyers in the UAE, analysts advise adopting patience and a staggered approach to buying rather than committing all their money at a single price. Gold’s immediate downside focus is around $3,500 an ounce, following the break below the previous support level, said Frank Walbaum, market analyst at Naga.com. “A sustained move below this psychological level could expose the metal to further losses towards the $3,200 level,” he said.

events.title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
events.summary: Lufthansa will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees. Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its main airline in Munich and Frankfurt to help turn around the loss-making unit. It will also cut short- and medium-haul capacity and replace some Airbus A320 planes with smaller A220s. The airline faces high fuel costs, strikes and a €180 million operating loss, while talks with unions are still unresolved. Deutsche Lufthansa will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group. The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said. The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced in September 2025 that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030. Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million (S$254.8 million) in the first nine months. “After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.” Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier in 2026 that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage. The measures revealed on Nov 20 come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement has been reached so far. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Oil prices post third weekly decline amid lingering Middle East tension
events.summary: Oil prices swung to gains on Friday but still posted a third straight weekly decline as investors continued to weigh the risk of continued Middle East tension against a rise in crude supply. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, added 0.64 per cent to settle at $90.75 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, rose 1.18 per cent to close at $83.41 a barrel. For the week, Brent and WTI, which were both down by more than 1.2 per cent earlier in the session, retreated 3.4 per cent and 5.8 per cent, respectively. Tension in the region persists. Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked a Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh’s financial centre on Thursday and ships continue to face Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for one third of the world’s crude and liquefied natural gas supplies. This week, a vessel belonging to Adnoc Logistics and Services was attacked while passing through the strait. Eleven seafarers were injured and one is missing. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump appeared to push a decision whether to renew major strikes against Iran into next year. He gave three separate interviews as he returned to Washington from a historic trip to China, where he held talks with President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin. “We’ll see what happens after January 1,” Mr Trump told Fox News in an interview broadcast on Thursday. In an interview with Axios and Israel’s News 12, he said he was "rushing to make any decisions on Iran". He made similar comments to Reuters. Rising supply from the Middle East is also affecting prices. The International Energy Agency said oil markets had returned to surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as Gulf exports recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly market report last week. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, rose to 18.4 million bpd in October but were still 26 per cent below prewar levels. The US Energy Information Administration said in a report that commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week to November 13. That points to more supply in the market.
