events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Deals and buys Intel Foundry signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P semiconductor manufacturing process, according to Intel executives. The customer has not been identified, and Intel has not disclosed a production timetable. Siemens plans to acquire Breker Verification Systems , a developer of AI-driven test suite synthesis and system-level verification technologies. The acquisition is expected to close in December. Microsoft selected Intel Foundry ‘s EMIB advanced packaging technology for custom silicon used in Azure’s infrastructure. The multiyear agreement also expands cooperation on Xeon processors, memory, and security technologies. Infineon and Megmeet are teaming up on 800V DC power architectures for AI data centers, using Infineon’s gen-2 CoolSiC MOSFETs in three-phase power shelves. GlobalFoundries and Boston Dynamics expanded their robotics collaboration to deploy autonomous Spot inspection robots across fabs in the U.S., Germany, and Singapore. GF also plans to begin evaluating Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid robots for semiconductor manufacturing tasks in early 2027. AMD completed acquisitions of AI inference chip developer Taalas and AI model research company World Labs . Funding The European Commission said more than 20 semiconductor projects have been approved under the EU Chips Act, representing over €33B in public and private investment . General Flash raised $128M to scale production of critical metals used in semiconductor and other industries. Atom Computing finalized an up to $100M CHIPS Act R&D award for neutral-atom quantum computers. Science Corporation raised $400M for its retinal implant chip that aims to restore form vision for certain types of macular degeneration. Chip trade and export controls The U.S. Department of Commerce introduced new restrictions addressing remote access to advanced U.S. AI computing through overseas data centers, along with new semiconductor licensing requirements affecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The U.S. received license requests covering 3.4 million advanced Nvidia and AMD AI chips for China and approved more than 879,000 , according to U.S. government data. It is unclear how many were actually shipped. TSMC and Samsung reportedly suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following new U.S. export restrictions, pending licensing approvals, per the Financial Times. TSMC is also reportedly halting affected Chinese customer orders at 16nm and below without U.S. approval and generally limiting those customers to 28nm and 40nm processes, provided those chips do not use HBM or advanced packaging. The U.S. government released new details of an ongoing investigation into Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor export-control violations. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025, but its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix , later received more than $800M in Nvidia AI technology , mostly through third-party manufacturers, per the NYT. Nvidia says it blocked new orders and obtained government authorization for certain repair parts shipments. An investigation is underway. The Trump administration is moving toward restrictions on Chinese optical transceiver imports , despite opposition from major U.S. cloud companies, reported Reuters. Manufacturing capacity Nvidia expanded its manufacturing agreements with Amkor , Samsung Electro-Mechanics , SPIL , TSMC , and others. The commitments cover additional substrate manufacturing, advanced packaging, and wafer capacity. As part of the expansion, ASE subsidiary SPIL signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Nvidia to triple its advanced semiconductor packaging capacity in Taiwan by mid-2029, including new production lines for wafer bumping, assembly, and testing. ASE Technology inaugurated the first phase and began construction of the second phase of its Lujhu advanced packaging facility in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Lam Research broke ground on a technology center in Zhunan , Taiwan , as part of its five-year, $3B global R&D expansion. GlobalFoundries broke ground on a new 300mm semiconductor fab in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan investment initiative providing up to $21B for two fabs. The first 300mm fab is expected to begin production in 2029. ADEKA and Entegris agreed to collaborate on advanced semiconductor materials production in Japan. Silicon Box advanced its proposed semiconductor packaging and test facility in Novara, Italy , into the basic design stage. The project is intended to establish additional European advanced packaging capacity for chiplet-based semiconductor devices. SC26 The annual supercomputing conference kicked off this week in Chicago. Nvidia announced a Rubin HPC GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores on a single GPU, along with sparse data acceleration capabilities. It also announced a 192-CPU Vera rack-scale platform for HPC with more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth. Penguin Solutions unveiled a photonics-based HBM-class memory appliance that uses Marvell technology to enable CPUs and GPUs to share memory across servers. Lambda is deploying Nvidia’s CPO switches to connect GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs. Nvidia claims up to 5× better power efficiency and 15× higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. AMD announced that its Lux supercomputer at ORNL , powered by EPYC CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs, is now open to scientific users. Fig. 1: Chicago’s SC26 event this week. Source: Liz Allan/Semiconductor Engineering Reports and analysis NAND flash contract prices are expected to decline in 2027 as Chinese cloud providers cut enterprise SSD orders amid GPU shortages and high inventories, reports TrendForce . Global NAND capital spending is projected to rise ~27% to ~US$30B. CSIS examined the risks of using Chinese memory chips , including CXMT DRAM, citing security and supply-chain concerns. The report recommends restricting their use in sensitive government systems and expanding independent chip testing. China still trails in leading-edge semiconductor fabrication, HBM, and chip manufacturing equipment , but it’s trying to work around those gaps through DUV multi-patterning, advanced packaging, 3D stacking, and photonics, said the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission in its annual report to Congress. Standards JEDEC previewed the DDR6 specification . While still subject to change, the current plan includes higher data rates and a wider bus, a pseudo-channel architecture, optimizations for die stacking and high-capacity modules, and data-center-focused low-power modes. JEDEC also started a System Level Reliability Testing subcommittee to develop qualification methodologies, reliability practices, and evaluation approaches for emerging system applications. events.title: A rare EU-UK summit as Andy Burnham seeks to mend Brexit damage
events.summary: A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences and possibly pave a way to get back together BRUSSELS -- A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union , top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together . Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners. Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week. Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining. Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.” The two sides are expected to sign a trade deal for food and drink, an agreement on emissions trading and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain’s economy. events.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
events.summary: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score. Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision. "When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says. It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud. "Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says. "Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says. Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story. "As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance. Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data. "A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa. "But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says. Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history. But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to? In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms. But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness. "Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement. Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk." If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion". But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns. "Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains. Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford. "We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past". While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation. She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past. "Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination." Upstart says it is tackling that issue. "We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement. Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score. "I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls. "When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies." That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

events.title: US chip equipment maker KLA opens expanded site in Singapore, with plans for further growth
events.summary: Semiconductor equipment maker KLA’s expanded site in Ang Mo Kio gives the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA opened its expanded Building 22B site in Ang Mo Kio, adding about 210,000 sq ft and making Singapore a major global production hub for the chip equipment maker. The firm plans a third expansion phase, pending land and approvals, and expects the site to support about 1,000 new jobs in R&D, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. Singapore leaders said KLA strengthens the country’s semiconductor ecosystem, supports local suppliers, and fits with $800 million in RIE 2030 research plans for the chip industry. SINGAPORE – US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced it has plans for a third phase of expansion, making the Republic one of its major production hubs globally. The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational – giving the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space. KLA, which makes machines and tools such as surface profilers, testers and semiconductor assembly solutions for chipmakers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing here in 2006. Theo Kneepkens, KLA Singapore country president and senior vice-president of global operations, said the company has also outlined plans for a further expansion phase here, subject to finalisation of land arrangements and relevant approvals. “I was actually hoping that this would already be a ground-breaking of our next phase. But we’re still defining a few details of our next phase of expansion before we can officially announce that,” he said. “But it’s clear that our next phase of growth will be bigger than the current expanded site .” Kneepkens said KLA’s plans for an additional phase reflect its conviction that Singapore – with its exceptional talent, supportive governance and strategic position – will remain indispensable in how the world manufactures critical semiconductor equipment powering AI and advanced computing. In the longer term, Building 22B and the planned phase are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering. KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said: “We’ve added hundreds of new roles, with over 2,200 employees working across multiple shifts, and 90% of KLA Singapore employees are locals, including both Singaporean citizens and permanent residents.” He noted that KLA’s long-term investment in Singapore has been driven by the local talent, highly collaborative partners and access to suppliers and customers. “We are experiencing unprecedented growth across the industry, and our customers show no signs of slowing. If anything, the demand environment is only accelerating,” he said. KLA’s expansion comes on the heels of several investment commitments announced in the past few years by companies that fabricate semiconductors or are part of the manufacturing value chain, such as processors of silicon substrate materials and companies that test, assemble and package chips. Chip firms that have made fresh investments include GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at KLA’s opening ceremony that Singapore has built a strong ecosystem for semiconductor equipment manufacturing, and the Republic now accounts for around one-fifth of global production. “Singapore must keep building the specialised capabilities that companies need to compete. “By working with partners like KLA, we can support their growth while creating good opportunities for our people and enterprises,” he said. Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that as chips become more powerful and specialised, manufacturing them requires greater precision. Hence, equipment made by companies like KLA, which can measure process variations and detect defects early, is increasingly important. “KLA is a key part of Singapore’s strength in this field. Its process-control tools help chipmakers bring advanced technologies into reliable, high-volume production,” he added. He said Singapore is also investing in the research capabilities needed to seize new opportunities in the chip industry, committing $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors. He lauded a three-year collaboration between KLA and A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics, saying such partnerships will help turn research into practical manufacturing solutions, so Singapore can continue to meet the semiconductor industry’s changing needs. Local suppliers are evolving alongside the multinational companies they support, Gan added.

events.title: Singapore-based DayOne to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns: Sources
events.summary: DayOne was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter. DayOne Data Centers has paused its planned US IPO, which could have raised up to US$5 billion, because investors are worried about high AI and data centre valuations. The Singapore-based firm may still list in 2027 if market sentiment improves. It has not made a final decision and declined to comment. The delay follows wider sector pressure, with other data centre IPOs also stalled. US rules on advanced chips in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia add more risk. SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering (IPO) on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom. The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.5 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously. But the company started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks. Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing. Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment. Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets. The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008. Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement, and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company. Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector. In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027. DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group. The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators that they will need a licence to purchase American tech hardware. DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

events.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
events.summary: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided- missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.” In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.” Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.” As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves. Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components. When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone. Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in. “A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says. To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch. In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US. Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.” Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.” When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said. The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.

events.title: A third of David Jones staff told employment ends days after Christmas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts David Jones staff issued with redundancy notices More than 1,600 David Jones staff will lose their jobs after Christmas. ( ABC News: Fletch Yeung ) Nearly 1,700 David Jones employees have been served their redundancy notices today. Staff were told December 30 will be their last day, as the union seeks to find them alternative employment. Those made redundant are expected to receive their entitlements, but for customers delivery options such as click and collect are unavailable. A total of 1,689 David Jones employees were served their redundancy notices on Friday. Staff were informed their employment will officially terminate on December 30. The union, the SDA, says it will be working overtime to help members find alternative employment. "We will leave no stone unturned in our efforts to find alternative employment for our members, and are grateful that already a number of companies have come forward seeking the skills and experience our DJs members have to offer," NSW secretary Bernie Smith said. The SDA says it is communicating directly with members and has established a dedicated help desk to ensure what David Jones is offering redundant employees is in line with their financial and legal entitlements. The iconic retailer went into voluntary administration earlier this month. New South Wales (7): Macquarie Centre, Macarthur Square, Parramatta, Wollongong Central, Hornsby, Green Hills and Warringah Mall Victoria (3): Malvern Central, Highpoint and Glen Waverley Western Australia (3): Hay Street Mall, Garden City and Carousel Queensland (2): Robina Town Centre and Sunshine Plaza South Australia (2): West Lakes and Marion Australian Capital Territory (1): Woden Receiver David McGrath and Joseph Hansell of FTI Consulting confirmed it would close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores across Australia and New Zealand on November 11. In a letter to suppliers, David Jones said: "We expect the affected stores to continue trading through the peak seasonal period, with closure dates anticipated to occur later in the year." Friday's news confirms staff will be asked to leave a day before New Year's Eve. "There is never a good time for a company to go under, but it is even more stressful for our affected members as it occurs in the very shadow of Christmas, normally a happy and relaxed moment in an otherwise busy year," Mr Smith said. Retail analyst Gary Mortimer described the news as "deeply disappointing". "While employees should receive their entitlements, that provides little comfort to workers and families now facing an uncertain future just weeks before Christmas," Professor Mortimer said. Earlier this week ABS data showed a broader surge in Australia's unemployment rate, and that was before the David Jones redundancies. David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. "With Australia's unemployment rate now sitting at 4.9 per cent, the loss of around 1,500 positions will place even more pressure on the labour market and add to the number of Australians seeking work," Professor Mortimer said. "My thoughts are with the affected employees, many of whom have dedicated years of service to the business and are now confronting a difficult holiday period." There has been a surge in online orders since the receivership was announced and the David Jones website warns that "deliveries may take longer than usual". Common delivery options such as express, same-day, Saturday delivery, and click and collect are unavailable. The ABC has confirmed David Jones is up to date with superannuation payments to its 6,000 employees, in line with new pay-day laws that came into effect in July. events.title: Social poker with £5 stake is booming, says dealer
events.summary: Phillip Steer says the cost-of-living crisis might have increased the appeal of the game, he says "you can have a night out for a fiver" A man who organises social poker sessions in pubs and clubs said the game's growing popularity could be down to the cost-of-living crisis. Phillip Steer, from March, Cambridgeshire, has run poker nights in Fenland for 14 years and said he has seen a 35% rise in the number of players in the area since 2022, with now about "100 players across 15 clubs and pubs". Steer added that as people can only place a maximum £5 stake, the game was often "cheaper" than other pastimes. Player Violet Cunningham said: "I have been playing poker for about 10 years; it's nice to get out of the house... it's fun and exciting." Tom Brady, the director of Live Pub Poker League (LPPL), said he had also seen an increase in the number of players joining for social tournaments in pubs and venues post-Covid, with the past 12 months being particularly busy. Steer said that poker can reduce social isolation and also improve players' numeracy On a chilly November evening about 15 people congregated in a pub in March, where they are given the use of a warm side room to set up their poker tables, cards and chips. Steer said all sorts of people get involved in the game, adding: "We have men, women, retired and working people." He said most people treat the game as a bit of fun and he did not worry that players would get into debt by taking part, due to the low-value stake. "You buy 12,000 chips at the start of the night for £5 and once those have gone it is game over," he added. Donald Rofe, 81, is dubbed "Stetson" because of his hat and says he does not mind if he wins or loses but just loves "getting out and meeting people" Donald Rofe is a widower and lives alone in March, he said his family live in Wisbech and Cambridge. "[Poker] gets me out of the house, although I have recently had my cataracts done, so I have some issues with reading the cards properly," he said. Rofe admitted that he mistook a diamond for a heart, which cost him a victory. "I put in all my chips because I thought I had a flush but I didn't, but it was still fun", he added. The cost of play is another bonus for Rofe, who added he normally has one soft drink that will "last me all night". Violet Cunningham plays poker under the name of "Ultraviolet" Violet Cunningham is a full-time carer and said she liked to relax by playing poker. "I have been playing poker for about 10 years, it's nice to get out of the house - it makes your brain tick, it's fun and exciting, but can be frustrating," she said. Cunningham said she and her family grew up playing card games on holiday and she has always enjoyed playing them. "I think women are harder to read than the men, play a bit tighter, unless they have it [a good hand] they probably won't bet on it," she added. The Gambling Commission , external said that pub poker was classed as "exempt gaming" and can be carried out without a gambling licence or permit. Players cannot place a stake more than £5 and combined stakes for the premises hosting the game cannot exceed £100 per day. Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. events.title: You tell AI everything. But who else is listening?
events.summary: The meteoric fall of Nvidia's Jensen Huang , following controversy over his personal relationships and US national security, has raised questions about judgement, trust and the people leading the world's most powerful technology companies. But it also prompts a broader question. How much do we really know about the people behind the technologies we increasingly trust with our information? And how private is that information we’re sending in confidence kept? I know I’m not alone in treating artificial intelligence as my personal doctor, giving it detailed information about my health in exchange for bespoke medical advice without needing a co-pay. It’s also my instant therapist, answering personal questions about how I should engage with problematic people in my life. Basically information I probably wouldn’t want anyone to know. We use ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and Anthropic's Claude to research, analyse documents, draft correspondence, and solve problems. In addition, people may share sensitive personal information, professional dilemmas and confidential business material. Sometimes, all we do is ask a question. And that is revealing in itself. But what actually happens to that information once we press enter? Who can see it, and where does it go? The answer may surprise people who assume their conversations with AI are entirely private. How much is out there When we enter information into a cloud-based AI platform , it travels to computing infrastructure operated by the provider or its partners. There it is processed, and depending on the service and privacy settings, it may be stored, checked by automated systems, reviewed by authorised humans or used to improve AI models. These companies are surprisingly candid about this in their posts. OpenAI says that authorised employees and contracted service providers may access consumer conversations for safety investigations, technical support, legal matters and model improvement, where permitted. Google's Gemini documentation goes further. It confirms that trained human reviewers, including external service providers, may examine information processed from connected applications. This can include excerpts and summaries of emails and documents, and sometimes the complete contents of a short email or file. Google advises users not to connect applications containing confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see. And if this is said publicly, imagine what else is happening behind closed doors that should give us pause. It's not a free-for-all, as these companies have access restrictions and operate under national and international laws. But the key message is clear: just because your entered information is not public, it doesn’t mean it's private. You might assume that, because you are using a personal AI account, it's a closed-loop conversation. But that depends on how you access it. Using office Wi-Fi alone does not ordinarily allow your employer to read encrypted AI conversations, although it may reveal which services you visit. A company laptop equipped with monitoring software, however, could expose more. Microsoft's own security tools, for example, can inspect information typed or pasted into AI prompts. The situation is different again when you use an employer-managed AI account. OpenAI confirms that authorised administrators may, depending on permissions and configuration, access or export employees' prompts, files and conversation histories. Anthropic similarly confirms that designated owners of Claude for Work accounts can request exports containing employee conversations. In other words, what feels like a private conversation may be accessible to your employer, depending on the account, device and security systems you use. Rest assured, encryption generally prevents employers from reading AI prompts over office Wi-Fi, according to the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a US-based digital rights organisation. This is true unless additional monitoring tools are in place. Nevertheless, the combination of workplace monitoring, managed accounts and third-party AI platforms creates a complicated privacy landscape that few employees fully understand. There is another side to this. What happens when executives handling sensitive information use personal AI accounts to analyse confidential acquisitions, strategic plans or financial projections? Research from Cyberhaven's 2026 AI Adoption and Risk Report found that 39.7 per cent of observed data movements into AI tools involved sensitive corporate information. Meanwhile, IBM's 2025 breach research found that one in five organisations studied had experienced breaches linked to unauthorised AI use. The risks are no longer theoretical. The recent $6.34 billion Binance hack highlights this danger. In its November investigation, the cryptocurrency exchange revealed that attackers had exploited compromised employee devices and an internal AI tool as part of the breach. Our privacy rights? Beyond corporate security lies a more fundamental question for everyday people: What rights do we have over the information we voluntarily give these systems? The UAE's Personal Data Protection Law, under Articles 13 and 15, and Europe's General Data Protection Regulation, under Articles 15 to 17, give individuals rights to access information about their personal data, correct inaccuracies and, under certain conditions, request its deletion. But these rights are not absolute. Having the legal right to request deletion does not necessarily mean every trace of an AI conversation can be erased from all systems. Google states that certain conversations reviewed by humans may remain stored for up to three years, even after the user deletes their activity. Switching off Gemini's activity history still allows temporary retention for operational and safety purposes. We can choose privacy settings, but those choices do not always amount to complete control. For the UAE, where AI is central to economic ambition and business transformation, this deserves particular attention. Companies need clear policies for AI use, while individuals need to understand the implications of using personal and corporate accounts. The issue is not whether we should abandon AI. Its benefits are enormous, world-changing even. The question is whether we can trust these technologies and the organisations behind them to keep our private information actually private, on our own terms. History clearly shows that regulation often lags behind technological innovation, leaving society exposed to risks that take years to address. We saw this with the internet and social media platforms designed to exploit reward mechanisms, particularly among young people. More than two decades later, countries such as Australia and the UAE are now introducing tougher age restrictions to protect children. Are we repeating the same mistake with AI, allowing its rapid adoption to outpace safeguards? Must we wait another two decades to act? We

events.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
events.summary: Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones "This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives. But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity. The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition. A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block. The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people. About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat. The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence. The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined. While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support . Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment. We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation. Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity. Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved". The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added. Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth" Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives. Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies. Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices. Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently. Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common. The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan. But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act. He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat. "Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building.

events.title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
events.summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses. And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation. The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one. “For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel. It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too. Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic. But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few. “For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.” In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute. “Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum. “You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.” At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it. “I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami. Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.” And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?” If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment. Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade. Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.

events.title: Former SA Health worker 'inappropriately accessed' 503 patient records
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA Health says the "vast majority" of staff members access patient information appropriately. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) SA Health has revealed that a former staff member inappropriately accessed 503 patient records. A formal investigation was launched after SA Health was notified of a privacy breach in late June. SA Health says all impacted patients have been notified in writing by the YNLHN. SA Health has revealed that a former staff member inappropriately accessed 503 patient records since September 2024. It says the Yorke and Northern Local Health Network (YNLHN) staff member was immediately put on leave when the investigation began and no longer works for SA Health. In a statement, SA Health said the incident had been reported to the relevant authorities, and the staff member will have "a note on their permanent record". SA Health says all affected patients have been notified in writing by the YNLHN. "SA Health has policies and processes in place to ensure staff only access information that is necessary and appropriate for their role," the statement read. "This includes requiring staff to verify they are authorised to access the information when they log into the electronic medical record system." SA Health says it's considering additional measures to prevent further breaches, including strengthening audits for potential inappropriate access to patient information. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) The statement noted additional measures were being explored to prevent further breaches, and that any staff member accessing information without a legitimate work-related reason may be subject to disciplinary processes, including possible employment termination. YNLHN chief executive Zoe Bishop said the Network sincerely apologises for any harm and distress caused. "Any unauthorised access of information is taken very seriously, and after a careful and comprehensive investigation process, the staff member is no longer employed by SA Health," Dr Bishop wrote in a statement. "We acted as soon as we were made aware of these potential breaches. "I want to reassure the community that this behaviour falls well below the standards we expect, and people should continue to have trust in our health services and our hardworking staff." Robyn Lindsay is the Department for Health and Wellbeing's chief executive. ( Supplied ) Department for Health and Wellbeing chief executive Robyn Lindsay said the "vast majority" of SA Health staff access patient information appropriately. "Where we find that a patient's information has been inappropriately accessed, we have a responsibility to inform the patients of the breach and take appropriate action during and after the investigation," she wrote. "While breaches such as this are rare, we must continue to remain vigilant to ensure we maintain the highest possible standards of integrity when it relates to patient information." In a separate incident in July, SA Health apologised to the family of Tony Modra amid revelations staff may have inappropriately accessed his patient records. Multiple staff members were being investigated at the time for alleged privacy breaches. events.title: Anthropic shares close 17% above IPO price after volatile Nasdaq debut
events.summary: Anthropic shares closed 17 per cent above their offer price on their first day of trading , as an early rally in the world's largest initial public offering faded amid broader caution over artificial intelligence stocks. The company behind the Claude chatbot opened on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $111.50, 34 per cent above its $83 IPO price, briefly giving it a fully diluted valuation of about $2 trillion. The stock then pared back its gains to close at $97.17. That values the company at about $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis, or about $1.27 trillion on the shares now outstanding. Anthropic, led by chief executive Dario Amodei, raised $81.3 billion by selling 980 million shares, and a further $26 billion through a private placement, bringing the total to $107.3 billion. The deal overtook SpaceX's $86 billion listing in June as the largest on record. The closing price is well above PitchBook's estimate of $79 a share, or $1.42 trillion fully diluted. Harrison Rolfes, a senior research analyst at PitchBook, said orders for the IPO reached about six times the number of shares available. "The first year will test the price," he said. PitchBook expects 2027 to be the weakest year in its forecast, with locked-up shares released in stages around Anthropic's first earnings reports. Before trading began, Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, said the listing was being watched as a "verdict on the wider AI trade", after valuation worries, rising infrastructure costs and Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia affected the sector. The debut did not lift the wider market. Major US indexes fell on Thursday and Asian chip stocks dropped on Friday.

events.title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
events.summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower... WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure , saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved.

events.title: General Pants owner warned of trouble long before collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts General Pants owner Alquemie Group warned of trouble long before collapse General Pants Co went into voluntary administration this week. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) Documents seen by the ABC show General Pants's owner Alquemie Group was told by auditors there was doubt about its operation. Financial reports show the company has lost $57 million in the 2024 and 2025 financial years. General Pants Co has been placed in the control of voluntary administrators. The owner of General Pants Co had been warned multiple times about the retailer's ability to keep operating long before the company collapsed into administration. Documents seen by the ABC show Alquemie Group, which acquired General Pants Co in 2022, was told by auditors BDO its ongoing reliance on cash injections from shareholders, combined with challenging retail conditions, cast doubt on its ability to continue operating. General Pants, which started as a jeans retailer in 1972, is the last remaining retailer of the group which once had six brands to its name, and was handed to administrators Alvarez & Marsal late on Wednesday evening. Alquemie Group reported losses after tax shot up from $2 million in 2023 to $29.6 million in 2024 and $27.2 million in 2025. General Pants was the last brand owned by Alquemie Group. ( ABC NEWS: Michael Barnett ) During that time there was a management change, with the former chief executive of the now collapsed Mosaic Brands, Scott Evans, joining the group in May 2024 "with a clear mandate to restructure the business and return it to profitability", according to its financial report. Following Mr Evans's appointment, the group sold loss-making companies SurfStitch and Ginger & Smart and shut the doors of National Geographic, which had cost it $4.4 million the year prior. Alquemie also underwrote the value of the General Pants brand by $13.2 million, leaving its worth at $38.2 million, a far cry from the $60 million it paid to acquire the company. General Pants Co in voluntary administration There are now 500 jobs in question as the administrators plan to continue trading through the busy Black Friday sales period. It received a $14 million cash injection from private equity firms and key shareholders in 2024 and a second one of $8 million in 2025. Even with the injection, the company continued to breach conditions with its main bank lender CBA, managing to carry the loans forward to avoid defaulting. But during that process, its loans ballooned from $4.6 million in 2023 to $43.8 million in 2025. Lego stores could not stem the bleeding Alquemie sold its Lego Store business earlier this year. ( AAP: Dean Lewins ) The group touted the excellent performance of its licensed Lego Stores yet sold the business for a reported $65 million to Kennedy Consolidated in May this year. Company staff numbers were also slashed from 1,246 to 929. In 2024 logistics firm Mainfreight issued the company a winding-up order, saying it was owed $125,000, and supplier UCC did the same in 2025, saying it was owed almost $70,000. Financial auditors raised concerns multiple times about Alquemie's ability to continue operating. "Ongoing challenging conditions within the retail industry, compounded by the broader economic impacts of the cost of living crisis, have contributed to the Group producing a loss before tax of $31,955,000 for the financial year, resulting in a continued breach of covenants related to the Group's loan facility with CBA," BDO audit director Josh Bresolin wrote in the financial report. It went on to say that outside factors affecting the business "were exacerbated by internal operational issues". This included decisions within General Pants that led to subsequent operating losses "which, under new leadership, have subsequently been rectified". It further pointed out that its debts, economic climate and customer sentiment indicated that "a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern". An Alquemie Group spokesperson said the retail trading environment and the growing dominance of offshore online-only retailers had seen General Pants progressively reduce its physical store footprint. "To address this, Alquemie Group actively focused on a range of options for General Pants including a sale process or significant capital injection to help it better compete against large scale competitors," they said. They said a voluntary administration process would explore restructuring scenarios which could allow General Pants the opportunity to be restructured into smaller-scale, more focused and, ultimately, viable business.

events.title: Senate passes Trump-backed permitting bill
events.summary: The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill Thursday night that's designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects. Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan, which has White House support, would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. Driving the news: The vote was 62-33. The bill would still have to pass the House before the end of the year, and any differences would have to be worked out by both chambers before President Trump could sign it into law. Catch up quick: It would make significant changes to federal permitting, including: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. Language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once they're issued, a priority for renewables groups and Democrats upset with Trump administration barriers. State of play: There are also provisions to ensure that data centers pay for needed grid upgrades, and expand federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects. Friction point: Many environmental advocates argue that the bill would dangerously erode safeguards in the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. Multiple tribal groups still oppose it despite changes aimed at easing concerns about consultation on historic preservation. Energy and business groups, ranging from renewables developers to manufacturers to the oil and gas industry, are lobbying for the measure. The AFL-CIO and many individual unions back it, too. What's next: The measure now heads to the House. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Bloomberg last week that he expects to have the votes to pass the plan. Some Democrats have called for hitting the brakes, with some arguing they can write a better package when they control Congress next year. Yet multiple backers within the wider Democratic coalition argue there isn't political space for an altered bill that President Trump would sign.

events.title: ‘IPO and beyond’: GIC to stay invested in Anthropic following Nasdaq debut
events.summary: Anthropic made the largest stock market debut on record on Nov 19, raising about US$81.3 billion (S$105 billion) through its IPO. GIC says it will stay invested in Anthropic “through the IPO and beyond”, and has become one of the AI firm’s largest backers after three funding rounds in under a year. Anthropic made a record Nasdaq debut, raising about US$81.3 billion and opening above its IPO price, even as the wider tech market fell on AI valuation worries. GIC has put in more than US$4.5 billion, with support beyond cash, including AI infrastructure, global contacts and expansion help. Anthropic’s rise has created huge gains for investors. SINGAPORE – GIC intends to remain invested in artificial intelligence company Anthropic beyond its blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), as the Singapore sovereign wealth fund looks to deepen its partnership with the Claude chatbot maker. Chris Emanuel, managing director and head of GIC’s Technology Investment Group, said in a LinkedIn post on Nov 20 that the fund was one of Anthropic’s largest investors, having participated in three funding rounds in less than a year. “An IPO is an important milestone, but it’s just one moment in a company’s journey,” he said. “We invest across multiple rounds, through the IPO and beyond. That’s life-cycle investing in practice.” His comments came after Anthropic made the largest stock market debut on record on Nov 19 , raising about US$81.3 billion (S$105 billion) through its IPO, which valued the company at around US$1.5 trillion at the offer price. The American company priced its shares at US$83 apiece, above its initial range of US$70 to US$78, after increasing the size of its offering to 980 million shares amid strong investor demand. Anthropic’s shares opened at US$111.50 on the Nasdaq, briefly lifting its valuation above US$2 trillion, before paring gains to close at US$97.17, up 17.1 % from the IPO price. Its strong debut contrasted with a broader Wall Street sell-off, as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell about 2.3% on Nov 19 amid concerns over elevated AI valuations and spending. Emanuel said GIC’s partnership with Anthropic extended beyond capital investment, with the fund drawing on its global network and investment platform to support the company’s expansion. “Three rounds, three moves forward, in under a year. Today, GIC is one of Anthropic’s largest investors, and our partnership has grown well beyond the cheque,” he wrote. The sovereign wealth fund has invested more than US$4.5 billion in Anthropic across its last three funding rounds, with its stake valued at about US$15 billion at the IPO price, Bloomberg reported. The investments included Anthropic’s US$30 billion Series G funding round in February, which GIC co-led with US investment company Coatue. The round valued the AI company at US$380 billion. Beyond financing, GIC has supported Anthropic’s AI infrastructure requirements through Theseus, connected its management with senior business leaders across the fund’s global network and assisted its international expansion, Emanuel said. The fund has also invested in Ode, which helps enterprises deploy Anthropic’s technology. Anthropic repeatedly stood out in conversations with customers, while its technical capabilities, mission and emphasis on developing AI responsibly strengthened the fund’s confidence in the company, he added. “We build conviction, back it with scale over time, and bring the broader capabilities of GIC to the founders and companies we believe in,” said Emanuel. Multibillion-dollar gains for investors Anthropic’s listing has generated substantial paper gains for its early and late-stage backers, reflecting the rapid increase in the company’s valuation. According to the Financial Times, Spark Capital, which invested in Anthropic when the company was valued at about US$4 billion in 2023, stood to hold roughly US$11 billion worth of shares at a US$1.4 trillion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested around US$3.2 billion, was estimated to hold a stake worth more than US$25 billion. Menlo Ventures’ investment of about US$1 billion was expected to be worth around US$21 billion. Strategic investors Amazon and Google’s parent Alphabet collectively held close to 30% of Anthropic following the listing. Anthropic’s rapid rise has been underpinned by strong demand for its AI models and enterprise services, although the company faces substantial computing and infrastructure costs as it expands. Its annualised revenue reached about US$81 billion last month, up from roughly US$1 billion at the start of 2025, according to Reuters. The company’s valuation has also climbed sharply, from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in its latest private-funding round in May 2026. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Alibaba defrauded shareholders by concealing ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal, lawsuit says
events.summary: Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business, the proposed class action says. Alibaba was sued by shareholders in New York for allegedly hiding ties to Megaspeed and a suspected spy, which they say inflated its share price and hid export control risks. The suit says Alibaba shares fell 14% in four days after media reports linked the company to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, and warned of tighter US rules on Chinese AI access. Alibaba denied no comment, while chief executive Eddie Wu said it still aims for $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs. NEW YORK – Alibaba was sued on Nov 19 in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week. According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business. The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14% over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer. They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of advanced processors. Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant. Nvidia faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors. Wu said on Nov 19 that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion (S$129 billion) in external cloud revenue and a 20% earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services in 2027 . The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia . In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the US Department of Defense linked to China’s military. In October , a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to firms whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies. Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat as they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government. The Nov 19 lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024, and Nov 11, 2026. REUTERS
