events.title: ‘It’s been a rough go’: Lumentum’s CEO on his $115 billion Marvell deal
events.summary: The Scene Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston knows shareholders hate his deal. “It’s been a rough go,” he told Semafor in a Thursday interview. He has a message for them: Bear with us. Lumentum was looking to buy a chip company for months. “We felt like we needed semiconductor properties, so we were actually in the market,” Hurlston said. “Marvell got word we were on a shopping spree and they said, ‘Hey, you know, rather than do that, why not combine with us?’” Lumentum and Marvell agreed to a $115 billion all-stock deal earlier this month that tacks Hurlston’s optical tech business — a key part of the data center buildout that allows high-powered GPUs to actually get their data onto users’ screens — to Marvell’s chips businesses. On paper, the deal made all the sense in the world, Hurlston said. “If you accept the premise that we needed to have a semiconductor asset, Marvell is the best semiconductor [maker] in this area,” Hurlston said. Investors howled. Shares in both Marvell and Lumentum are down roughly 40% since the deal was announced on worries over how much runway the AI trade has left. Some Lumentum shareholders also say the company sold too soon. “The deal hasn’t worked as we expected, right?” Hurlston said. “The view from investors is, you took some of your upside off the table, and you’ve now hitched your wagon to a company whose upside is a little bit less known.” Market Jitters Hurlston says he expects shares to rebound once the companies can share more information with analysts, portfolio managers, and other shareholders through regulatory filings and other meetings. And while there’s still a chance the deal falls apart — there is a material adverse change clause baked into the deal terms — “we’re going to have to see this thing through, unless shareholders vote no, or if we don’t get regulatory approval,” Hurlston said. “The set of circumstances under which we can exercise a MAC are very limited.” There is a bit of portfolio-manager-on-portfolio-manager violence going on, Hurlston noted. Despite overlap in the two company’s shareholder bases — 80%, by Hurlston’s math — portfolio managers may hold Marvell but not Lumentum, or vice versa, triggering some forced selling. “The name of the game in hyperscaling, from a supplier, is continuity of supply and time to market,” Hurlston said. “What this system-sell enables is for us to deliver to our customers massive time to market,” he continued, because Marvell and Lumentum products can be shipped out to data centers as one finished product. The companies will also face regulatory review in both the US and in China, which is likely to draw more scrutiny following the Nvidia chip scandal. Nvidia is both a shareholder and major customer of Lumentum’s. Hurlston noted that both he and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have gotten deals through China’s State Authority on Market Regulation, or SAMR, before, and that they already have a good sense of what to expect. “They really want their supply to be there, and we’re a critical supplier” of transistors into the Chinese market. Semafor has also reported that Marvell’s Murphy could be tapped to take the CEO position at Nvidia following Jensen Huang’s resignation. Hurlston said he didn’t know whether Murphy was considering the role or whether he would take it, but said, “I think he can do the job.” “The board is not going to want somebody who has any sort of besmirchment, and I think you want to have somebody who’s been a sitting CEO,” he said. “There’s no argument that this guy’s done a terrific job [at Marvell].”

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Independent examination into ElectraNet over tower fall, premier says Topic: Electricity Production and Distribution A crumpled transmission tower in a paddock. ( Supplied: Sam Telfer ) Swathes of South Australia's Eyre Peninsula were left without power after a storm knocked down major electricity transmission towers. Look back at how the situation unfolded. That's where we're leaving our live coverage of the Eyre Peninsula power outage. The situation is continuing to develop and evolve, with the state emergency centre set to host another meeting at 3pm. To stay across further developments, you can continue to follow our coverage online, and on TV and radio . For the moment, it looks like the number of properties without power is continuing to drop. At 2:45pm, the SA Power Networks website showed the number had dipped under 5,000 across SA. Potential fire risk is predicted for central and western parts of South Australia. Temperatures are set to rise to the 30s tomorrow in the state's north, the Bureau of Meteorology's Christie Johnson says. "That combination of the heat and the strong winds is going to give us elevated fire danger," she says. "There is also the risk of thunderstorms too later in the day … along the West Coast, maybe the southern and western parts of Eyre Peninsula, maybe down Kangaroo Island as well. Tomorrow's fire danger ratings will be released by Country Fire Service at 4:30-5:00pm ACST. For Karen Baines, the impacts have been manifold. Ms Baines lives about 20 kilometres from Ungarra , a small township towards the southern end of Eyre Peninsula. When power was cut to the region, her first thoughts were for her parents in Tumby Bay . "I drove up the road to be able to get some mobile signal, just so I could give them a call and just let them know everything was OK and just check on them," she said. "At the moment we're running on a generator. Without the generator running we have no mobile, no power, no landline." She said she also had a block on which she had lost canola. "A lot of farmers through the strip have lost crops through hail and wind," she said. 'Devastating' loss for crop farmers Grain Producers SA's Brad Perry says he's hearing reports of crop wipeout and significant hail damage in Arno Bay and Port Neill. "We certainly feel for those growers," he tell SA Country Hour. "It's looking like a record crop and suddenly having it on the ground is devastating." He says farmers are still assessing damage and it's too earlier to know if it will impact harvest figures this year. Janice Regan, from a Port Lincoln hearing clinic, questioned how a $300 million transmission line could fail within years of its construction. "It shouldn't be happening and it shouldn't continually be happening ," she said, in reference to the three-day outage that accompanied the statewide blackout 10 years ago. She said when the power went out, she went outside and the "street was actually deserted". "The work impact was quite severe because we lost all computer access, we lost all phones," she said. "We couldn't do any repairs to hearing aids, we couldn't make appointments, we virtually were in shutdown mode." Further accounts are emerging of the impact of the blackout on local businesses. Port Lincoln jeweller Shane Pedemonte says he was "busily working away in the workshop for Christmas trade" when the day turned dim. "Unfortunately, being a jewellery shop, security is pretty paramount. Having dark areas is not ideal so yeah, closed up," he said. "We had a couple of appointments in the late afternoon with clients that we had to cancel." Mr Pedemonte said while his power was restored pretty quickly, "whether it stays on or not is another thing". Home flooded after heavy rain yesterday Jeremy Callis also shares these photos of his mother's house at Arno Bay where water has seeped inside. Speaking to 891 ABC Adelaide, Arno Bay farmer Jeremy Callis says he was in a harvester when yesterday's storm hit. He says the rain was so intense that water found its way into sealed tractor cabs. "It was pretty eerie like those black clouds that come through and … you don't see that very often around here it was sort of more like a tropical storm that come through," he says. ElectraNet has completed its visual inspection of the old lines and is preparing to re-energise areas one by one. Earlier we heard from Sarah Prime about how crops were damaged on her family's Eyre Peninsula property when severe weather swept through yesterday. Wind gusts also ripped off metal shed doors.

events.title: Exclusive: Rep. Gregory Meeks vows to reclaim Congress' powers from Trump
events.summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said Thursday Congress is going to reclaim powers long ceded to the executive branch at the Axios Future of Defense summit. Why it matters: As the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Meeks is putting the Trump administration on notice that it's foreign policy decisions are going to be challenged through legislation and oversight hearings. What they're saying: "Whether it's a Democratic president or Republican president, we've ceded too much and we've got to stand up and take it back," Meeks told Axios' Colin Demarest. "We do, at times, have to make some difficult decisions, and not just punt them away to the executive branch, because when you do that, it's hard to get them back." Meeks also suggested that incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) may be willing to take the Trump administration to court if needed to enforce congressional oversight. "If it takes some litigation to do that, we will do that," Meeks said. "Speaker Johnson wouldn't do it. I think Speaker Jeffries will do it." Catch up quick: Meeks will likely become Foreign Affairs committee chair in January, riding the blue wave that gave Democrats the ability to control Congress' legislative agenda. Zoom in: Meeks didn't rule out calling Secretary of State Marco Rubio to testify before the committee. "The jurisdiction of the House Foreign Affairs Committee is the State Department," Meeks said. Later, he added more broadly, "[y]ou can run, but you can't hide... We're going to use the power that the committee and the Constitution gives us to make sure that we're calling in members of that administration, so they have to answer to the American people, why what has taken place has taken place." Zoom out: Meeks has already sent document-preservation letters to seven agencies, including the State Department, USAID and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, warning them to avoid destroying records that could be relevant to oversight efforts. He threatened the possibility of criminal referrals if someone is found to have done otherwise. What we're watching: Meeks said Democrats plan to address affordability concerns and introduce another War Powers Resolution aimed at the Iran war. He also floated litigation and using Congress' power of the purse, including withholding funds, as ways to force the Trump administration to comply. "The people have spoken loudly and clearly that they are against the war in Iran," Meeks said. "They see how foreign policy directly now connects to domestic policy." He added that Democrats need to investigate what's happening in the Middle East, and explain to Americans what's at stake in the war. "That is the job, a part of the job, of the Foreign Affairs Committee, and that's exactly what we're going to do on day one." events.title: The future of medicine: Could AI help predict and prevent disease?
events.summary: Can AI help build a healthier future? By Doug Burger , Technical Fellow and Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Research Ava Amini , Principal Research Manager Eric Horvitz , Chief Scientific Officer Dr. Eric Topol , Executive Vice President, Scripps Research Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse. Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come. In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI. Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend. Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab) , the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab) . So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician. Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo , a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer. So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here. It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable. And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI. I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava. I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare. Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists. In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician. You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge.

events.title: Scoop: Trump names Kirsten Davies as new national cyber director
events.summary: The White House named Kirsten A. Davies to be its new national cyber director Thursday as President Trump overhauls his AI team, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Davies, who currently serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer , has more experience in the field than the outgoing director , Sean Cairncross . Cairncross' departure was described as amicable by two sources. But two White House officials said President Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, sought the change and pushed out Cairncross because, one said, he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." Zoom out: The Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. The position requires Senate confirmation. Davies previously was cleared by the Senate as the Defense Department's chief information officer. "Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed," an administration official said. At the Pentagon, Davies has been the top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," according to her bio. Before serving in the Trump administration, Davies worked for Unilever and "led global cyber resilience for one of the world's largest consumer goods enterprises," her bio says. Davies' career also has included technology and cyber roles at Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard and Siemens. She founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit organization dedicated to citizen safety and security in the digital universe. State of play: The administration's AI team has taken shape on the fly , but Cairncross was involved in key decisions. He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet. Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee. During Trump's first term, Cairncross represented the White House chief of staff on National Security Council committees before leading the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. Cairncross' head of policy and senior adviser Thomas Lind left in June and joined OpenAI in October, further depleting the Trump administration of technical expertise. The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike. Democrats have criticized the administration's response to outages and warned that U.S. cyber defenses are falling behind AI-fueled threats. What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions. His pick for the top job at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faced a combative confirmation hearing Thursday. What they're saying: In a written statement, Cairncross said, "it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve President Donald J. Trump. I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence." This story has been updated with details on Davies' appointment and background.

events.title: Wall Street tumbles to its longest losing streak since 2024 as the Dow drops 1,100 points
events.summary: The U.S. stock market tumbled again as AI stocks kept falling on worries their boom may be over NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market tumbled again as beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence kept falling Thursday on worries their breathtaking boom may be over. The losses came even though a leading AI lab, Anthropic, found a strong welcome for the debut of its own stock on Wall Street. The S & P 500 dropped 2% for a sixth straight loss . That’s its longest losing streak in two and a half years, and the index at the heart of many 401(k) accounts is now down 8.2% from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101 points, or 2.2%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3%. The losses were widespread, and more than 90% of the stocks that make up the S & P 500 index fell. Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was a bit weaker than Wall Street expected. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting. Walmart sank 1% even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. For a while Thursday morning, gains for several AI-related stocks seemed to be enough to more than make up for such losses. The S & P 500 jumped as much as 1.3% after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold shares of its stock at $83 apiece in its initial public offering . That’s more than the $70 to $78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above $115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain and finished the day at $97.17, still up 17.1%. Even before its stock began trading, the strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remained among investors in the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost following sharp recent drops for AI-related stocks on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology. But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways in what Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, called “a very turbulent, white-knuckle period.” Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% and then swung to a loss of 2.1%. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5% leap in the morning to a drop of 6.1%. Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 3.3% amid the lengthening list of worries dogging the entire industry. Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled At first it was criticism that AI stocks had broadly gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments in data centers worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI. Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He was one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth. Other companies, meanwhile, offered more encouraging signals about AI. Palo Alto Networks climbed 6.4% after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely. The all-stock deal is valued at $4.5 billion. Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped last quarter by more than analysts expected in part because of AI-related offerings. Everpure’s stock rose 4.7%. All told, the S & P 500 fell 147.80 points to 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 to 49,097.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 550.69 to 23,879.20. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased as the drops for stock prices sent investors toward investments seen as safer. When prices for Treasury bonds go up, their yields go down, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.04% from 5.07% Wednesday. Also weighing on yields were a couple reports on the U.S. economy that came in weaker than economists expected. One said slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains low compared with history.

events.title: Firmus talks down 'modest' data centre in bid to avoid major project status
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus argues proposed AI data centre not major project amid only 'modest' economic benefits Works at Firmus Technologies' Wesley Vale site. ( Supplied: Erin Woodcock ) Firmus Technologies says one of its AI data centres should not be assessed as a major project. The company argues that unlike previously declared major projects, the data centre has only "modest" economic benefits and about 20 ongoing jobs. The State Planning Office is assessing the major project proposal made by the Latrobe Council. Firmus Technologies is fighting a local council push for one of its proposed AI data centres to be declared a major project. Latrobe Council in Tasmania's north-west has sought to defer a decision on Firmus's proposed Wesley Vale AI data centre to the state government. It has said the council's 1993 planning scheme is dated and councillors would not be able to consider all the relevant issues, such as energy, water and environmental impacts of a large AI data centre. A letter from Firmus's lawyers to Planning Minister Kerry Vincent, who is assessing the request for a major project declaration, has now been made public. "We respectfully ask that the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure not be declared a major project," the letter reads. It states that the project would have only "modest" economic benefits and ongoing job opportunities: Although the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is expected to generate some economic activity, these benefits are relatively modest and largely confined to employment opportunities, with approximately 70 jobs anticipated during the construction phase and around 20 permanent full-time positions once operational. Beyond these direct employment outcomes, the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure is not expected to materially alter the economic structure of the region, establish a significant new industry cluster, or drive broader regional economic transformation. The submission states the development cost of its facility would be $31.25 million. It compared this to major projects such as Chambroad's Kangaroo Bay Hotel proposal near Hobart , which it said would support 443 ongoing jobs and generate $42.7 million in additional annual visitor expenditure. Firmus Technologies is building AI data centres in Tasmania. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) "The economic benefits of the Wesley Vale Computing Infrastructure are considerably more limited in scale and are largely confined to construction activity and a relatively modest number of ongoing jobs," the letter reads. The process of declaring and assessing a major project in Tasmania can take years, while the council approval process is usually much quicker. A sign near Firmus' proposed AI data centre site at Wesley Vale. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Firmus told inquiry of $46b economic benefit from three projects Last week, at a Tasmanian parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres, Firmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield was asked about the benefits to Tasmania of its three projects. Tim Rosenfield appeared at a Tasmanian inquiry into data centres in Hobart. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "This is a large-scale investment we're making," he told the inquiry. "We have actually, at the request of the government some months ago, commissioned a third-party study which is close to being finalised. "It puts total state gross product contributions of up to $46 billion to the Tasmanian state economy through 2035. "We're operating these supercomputers, and that requires skills, it requires on-site presence, it requires learning pathways. "The preliminary modelled outcome shows about 8,900 ongoing FTEs [full-time equivalent jobs] through 2035 created." Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards and has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania. The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. ( Supplied: Tasmanian government ) Firmus 'deeply disappointed' by council's referral In addition to saying the economic impact of the project would not be "significant" to the region, the letter from Firmus's lawyers also said the impact on the area's environment and social fabric would be limited. It also said the project would not deliver advanced regional development objectives or significant public infrastructure to the region. events.title: China bars Bloomberg reporter from trilateral meeting after she shouted question at earlier event
events.summary: Chinese officials have blocked a Bloomberg TV journalist from a key event for shouting out a question to President Donald Trump NEW YORK -- It's a scenario seen every day: A reporter shouts a question out to a leader at an event. The leader either answers or ignores it. In China, though, Bloomberg TV journalist Annmarie Hordern was blocked from a key event by Chinese officials Thursday, apparently as retribution for having shouted a question in a way that the government considered rude. Hordern was barred from Thursday's trilateral meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, after having called out a question during an Trump meeting with Xi. She had asked Trump if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. A White House official said the Chinese insisted the reporter not be allowed in despite the White House having pushed for admission. The official insisted on speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the issue. The White House did not immediately respond to a query about what steps it took to advocate for the reporter. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, said on X that it was “commendable that the WH is advocating for press access.” A pool report from the incident said the Chinese “have passed along a message that yelling questions is considered extremely rude and we will be pulled from the room if we do so.” China’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press, and an email to Bloomberg seeking comment was not immediately returned. The incident, which reflected the way China typically seeks to tightly control news events, recalled a previous one in 2022, in which a White House pool reporter said she was knocked off balance after being yanked by her backpack when she tried to shout a question to President Joe Biden. The question was about human rights ahead of a meeting between Biden and Xi in Bali, Indonesia. Two White House staff members intervened and said the producer should be left alone. China's approach to journalists, particularly foreign media, has long been chilly and uneven. In recent decades, international reporters have been expelled both for their coverage and for perceived misbehavior during news events. Resident correspondents are occasionally detained and questioned — and in some cases in past years, compelled to sign “self-criticism” reports — for showing up where the government doesn't want them to be. Chinese journalists who stray from the party line can face even more stringent measures, including censorship, dismissal and at times even imprisonment. Associated Press reporter Michelle L. events.title: Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa in first sale of its kind
events.summary: The Trump administration has auctioned deep-sea mining leases for millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa The Trump administration on Thursday auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa , giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters. The two 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S., following President Donald Trump’s directive last year to leverage deep-ocean minerals to counter growing competition for resources from China. The leases are already the source of several legal challenges. The two lease areas each sold for the minimum bid amount of $3 million to deep-sea mining startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. While there were two bidders at the auction, only Wetstone placed bids. Wetstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press. The leases grant the company the ability to begin initial surveys of the seafloor to explore for minerals and prepare their testing or mining plans. It has the exclusive right to mine those areas commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. The auction moved forward despite passionate opposition from locals in the territory and three lawsuits seeking to halt the sales. The auction was held at the Ventura County Fire Department Headquarters in Southern California, where a few dozen protesters gathered outside. “We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, an American Samoa resident who has fought the auction for more than a year, said in a statement Thursday. Globally, deep-sea mining is still at an experimental stage. A handful of other countries have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals, but no company has started commercial operations. The U.S. has never issued a lease for deep-sea minerals beyond a short-lived mining effort in California waters more than 60 years ago. The federal interest in seafloor minerals stems from an April 2025 executive order, when the president directed his administration to search for and responsibly develop critical minerals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions of the seabed near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters. It’s unclear if the leases will withstand legal challenge. On Monday, a court ordered the National Marine Fisheries Service to more thoroughly assess the impacts the mining activities could have on endangered species, saying the agency's “cramped, expedited, informal” review violated the Endangered Species Act. The Marine Minerals Administration said in a statement that it had addressed the court's opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment. But it did not cancel or delay the auction. David Henkin, deputy managing attorney at the environmental law group Earthjustice, said the ruling made Thursday's auction unlawful. In order to issue the notice of sale, the government needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, he said. Earthjustice is representing Fa’asao Amerika Samoa, a group dedicated to safeguarding the territory’s culture, and the Conservation Council of Hawaii in the suit. Another lawsuit filed Wednesday by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Finafinau, an environmental group founded by Suluai-Mahuka, similarly argues the environmental review process was rushed and is asking the court to strike down the leases. A third lawsuit, brought by a council of local chiefs in American Samoa, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, is challenging the federal government’s authority to auction the waters near their islands. Tony Romeo, head of the deep-sea mining startup Eco Minerals, which did not participate in the auction, said any company going into deep-sea mining needs to be prepared for pushback from environmental groups. “If they can halt it through legal action, they will,” he said. “We’ll see how it ultimately plays out.” Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Association, said in a statement that he expects industry interest and investment to grow in the coming years. “Decades of environmental research and extensive assessments have helped lay the groundwork for responsible ocean mineral development," he said. events.title: Christie’s halts Frida Kahlo painting from auction at Mexico’s request
events.summary: Christie’s has withdrawn a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York after Mexican authorities requested more information about its provenance MEXICO CITY -- Christie’s withdrew a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York this week after Mexican authorities requested additional information about its provenance, the auction house confirmed Thursday. The painting, “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,” or “Congress of the Peoples for Peace,” had been scheduled for auction on Tuesday. It depicts a white dove on a tree bearing fruit alongside a smiling sun, the moon, and two slices of watermelon. Mexican authorities asked Christie’s to hold the sale until the painting's provenance could be clarified, citing a declaration that recognizes Frida Kahlo’s work as an artistic monument of Mexico . “In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” a Christie’s spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. “We look forward to selling this work at a later date." The same painting was auctioned in 2020 by Sotheby’s without any objections. Kahlo’s works in Mexico are considered artistic monuments and are protected under the country's federal law on monuments and archaeological, artistic, and historical sites. Mexican authorities said they were working with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, administered by the Bank of Mexico. The painting left Mexico more than three decades before the 1984 decree declaring Kahlo’s work an artistic monument. The decree prohibits the permanent export of her works that were in Mexico when it was published. Kahlo, whose health was seriously deteriorating, sent the painting to the congress through her husband, the painter Diego Rivera. She died in Mexico City two years after creating it. The trip to Vienna was recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s last wife, and has also been mentioned by historians such as Raquel Tibol. Last year, Kahlo’s 1940 self-portrait “El sueño (La cama)," or The Dream (The Bed), sold for $54.7 million , setting an auction record for a work by a female artist. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South Road project and Adelaide Grand Final road closures to cause traffic delays Motorists have been urged to plan ahead this weekend if they intend to use South Road for their commute. Adelaide motorists are bracing for road closures and traffic disruptions around Adelaide, as a business owner says customers are being driven away by constant roadworks. Temporary closures along South Road will be in place this weekend while road disruptions for Supercars event Adelaide Grand Final begin on Friday and would continue for two weeks. SA transport department's Matthew Bowman said Adelaide's inner west suburbs would be affected as closures start from 8pm tonight until Monday morning as part of the multi-billion-dollar Torrens to Darlington upgrade. "There'll be a full closure in place in both directions between just south of Anzac Highway to north of the South Road tramline there at Glandore," he told 891 ABC Adelaide. "There'll also be a full closure in both directions between Sir Donald Bradman Drive and James Congdon Drive at Hilton and just the northbound lane between Ashwin Parade to Gawler Ave at Torrensville." Road closures along South Rd will begin 8pm on Friday. ( ABC News ) Mr Bowman said there was no convenient time to be closing sections of South Road, but traffic volumes were lower in these areas over the weekend. Veli Uysal, who has been serving up yiros at his Brickworks shop at Torrensville for 11 years, said constant South Road disruptions have affected his business "Before Torrens to Darlington, my business was probably trading about 15 per cent more than now," he said. "All my regular customers tell me they don't want to come here anymore because they waiting at the intersection on Ashwin Parade coming to Brickworks, 15 to 20 minutes to get in and another 25 to get out. "In the long run, yes it's going to help a lot of people … but the current conditions are not helping anyone short-term — which is a lot of suffering." Veli Uysal estimates a 15 per cent downturn for his business due to South Road roadworks. ( ABC News ) The final 10.5-kilometre section of the road upgrade, which would complete 78km of North-South Corridor, is due to finish in 2031. More delays for the eastern suburbs More pain has also begun on the other side of the city for the eastern suburbs, starting from 6am on Friday with road closures for Adelaide Grand Final. Wakefield Road, Bartels Road, sections of East Terrace, Hutt Street and Dequetteville Terrace have shut with some closures staying in place until Thursday December 3. RAA's Charles Mountain said workers east of the city who have the opportunity to work from home next week should consider it. Sections around Victoria Park and east of the city will be closed for the motorsport event. ( Supplied: Daniel Kalisz ) "Traffic volumes on Friday are a little bit less than some of the other days in the week," he said. "This will be inconvenient but perhaps not so critical as come Monday morning, when we know that is usually when we see the biggest delays in commuter traffic. "Allow extra time for your commute … it's at least double if you're travelling realistically anytime after 7:30am." RAA released research on last year's Adelaide Grand Final impacts to commute times in the eastern suburbs. On the first Monday of closures last year, the median morning peak travel time on The Parade, Norwood (Portrush Road to Fullarton Road) jumped to around 29 minutes — up from the usual four. events.title: Suspects charged in brazen train heist ring that netted $22 million in cargo from major retailers
events.summary: Authorities have charged more than a dozen people for allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation LOS ANGELES -- More than a dozen people were charged Thursday with allegedly orchestrating a massive train heist operation to steal over $22 million in cargo — from popular shoes to power tools — from major retailers. A federal indictment unsealed on Thursday paints a picture of an organized group that targeted more than three dozen trains carrying Nike sneakers, Crocs footwear, power tools and other consumer goods that were imported into the United States through Los Angeles and Long Beach, which are home to the busiest ports in the country. Trains that shuttle goods to stores and customers around the country have become a prominent target for large-scale theft in recent years, especially at large ports in the U.S. that receive hundreds of millions of dollars of shipments every day. The relatively low-tech robberies have demanded attention from the world's largest retailers, including the likes of Amazon. The men would disable the trains at a planned location by busting the brakes, the indictment alleged, at which point the goods would be offloaded onto trucks. The goods were then peddled to an unnamed company that would resell the stolen merchandise for profit. “The scale of the theft is staggering,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli, promising to prosecute any future efforts to steal the merchandise. Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday JPMorganChase, Mastercard, Visa report cyberattack on third-party service providers Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled In group chats, the men shared numerous photos and videos of themselves busting into the hulking train cars, and posing with wads of cash and stolen merchandise. They also shared AI photos of themselves captioned “Los Trenes,” which means the trains in Spanish, beneath glamorized photos of men throwing boxes of shoes off trains into nearby cars while police helicopters descended overhead. The 13 men were indicted for conspiracy and theft of interstate railroad cargo. Two were also charged with violence against railroad carriers. If convicted, the men could face anywhere from five to 20 years in federal prison. Inside the brutal murder of Tom and Angela Strussion 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Exclusive: Sen. Ernst rebukes lack of "transparency" from Pentagon on Iran
events.summary: Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) said "a lot of people would be able to guess" if she regrets voting to confirm the embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, during Axios' Future of Defense Summit Thursday. Why it matters: The retiring Iowa senator, who served in the military for more than two decades, has been notably skeptical of Hegseth and hasn't always been in lockstep with the Trump administration. Catch up quick: Despite her hesitancy over his nomination, Ernst ultimately voted to confirm Hegseth . However, she's continued to question him throughout his tenure. She recently asked whether the embattled Pentagon leader has been "truthful" about the status of the Iran war, which she said Iowans rejected in the midterms. "If there is deception coming from our Pentagon and being transmitted to the president, I would want to know that," Ernst told reporters earlier this month. Driving the news: "There is very little transparency right now with what is being discussed between the White House and the Department of War," Ernst said of the Pentagon's communication about the war in Iran in a conversation with Axios' defense and space reporter Thomas Novelly. "As Congress, we would expect that we would be read into some of those conversations, and unfortunately, we have not been read into those conversations," she added. That's made it "difficult to know" the state of the war and its impact on munitions levels , she said. Friction point: House Republicans blocked an impeachment effort against Hegseth earlier this month, but the reprieve may be short-lived with a Democratic majority taking control in January. "I think we would be having a very different conversation today, if the House Democrats had actually showed up for that vote," Ernst told Axios, a nod to the 11 members who missed it, some citing traffic delays. "So, now they will face it again come January, likely, and that will be up to the House Democrats to decide how they handle that," she continued. "And then, certainly, if they decide to move forward with impeachment, then Senate Democrats will also have the majority." State of play: Ernst sits on the Senate Committee on Armed Services, where she chairs the Emerging Threats and Capabilities subcommittee. "In the past 12 years, while I have been in the Senate, the Armed Services Committee has been one of the most bipartisan committees in the Senate, and it's necessary for the safety and security of our country," she said, adding that the National Defense Authorization Act "has been a very, very bipartisan product." But Ernst predicted that given the "not even hidden animosity" between Democrats and Hegseth, "it will be very difficult" for new Senate Armed Services Committee leadership to obtain information. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

events.title: The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants
events.summary: Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang . In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went. But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero. Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World , a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China. “It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.” At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?” Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023. Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island. “When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.” At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up. “I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.” Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth. Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop. In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars. The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments. But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business. The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors. Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.” Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.

events.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
events.summary: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor. Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday . He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.” Evasive and irregular turns “FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Retailers shake up Thanksgiving meal deals amid rising food costs
events.summary: Major grocery retailers are switching up their Thanksgiving dinner deals this year, with a few lowering prices, others swapping out items and some shifting toward more flexible meal options. The big picture: Lower advertised prices from some retailers could offer relief to Americans already stretching their holiday budgets , but shifting menus mean shoppers may not be getting the same bang for their buck. State of play: Higher fuel costs, poor growing conditions and other inflationary pressures have pushed up food prices ahead of the holiday. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for ten has increased 6% since 2025, totaling an estimated $58.63. The increase is largely driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, the federation said. Driving the news: Walmart is advertising a lower price for its Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, while offering 18% more individual items. The retailer said this year's meal , which serves ten people for $35, is its "lowest priced one-click basket" ever, down from $39.93 last year. The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish. It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread. Fried onions were the only item to switch from name-brand to store-brand in 2026. The other side: Aldi is also promoting a Thanksgiving meal $1 cheaper than in 2025, though several dishes have changed . Instead of a 14-pound turkey, the 2026 dinner will have a 16-pound bird. It includes several sides, but not fan favorites such as mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese or green bean casserole. Zoom out: Costco's gourmet Thanksgiving dinner is more elaborate than its cook-at-home grocery counterparts, with a similar menu and the same advertised promotional price as last year. Both 2025 and 2026 dinners cost $199.99, serve eight people and include a five-pound turkey breast. The prepared meal includes the same traditional sides and desserts, with the addition of candied yams. This year's dinner is marketed as 30 pounds, compared with 28 pounds in some descriptions of last year's offerings. The intrigue: Kroger is shifting away from the fixed-price "Freshgiving" Thanksgiving meal bundle it offered in previous years. Instead, it is promoting individual holiday discounts and prepared foods in various portion sizes. Kroger's chief marketing officer said the approach is intended to make holiday meals more convenient and accommodate gatherings of different sizes. In 2025, Kroger advertised a Thanksgiving meal for 10 for under $4.75 a person, providing a 14- to 16-pound frozen turkey and traditional sides. The bottom line: Your food preferences, guest count and budget will help determine if a Thanksgiving meal deal is the right choice for you. Go deeper: Wholesale food prices are on the rise

events.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
events.summary: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data. Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference. Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information. NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure. To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS . Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65. Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications. Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior. Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services. EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks. The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use. Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon. Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations. Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables. Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises. Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local. On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices. For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027. Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform. BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work. An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model , developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation. Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services. Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models. Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA.

events.title: UAE highlights $1tn in US investments during Abu Dhabi Investment Forum
events.summary: The UAE on Thursday promoted its more than $1 trillion of investments in the US and its broader framework, as businesses and investors gathered in New York for the Abu Dhabi Investment Forum to expand business ties between the two countries. The Abu Dhabi Investment Forum, organised by the Abu Dhabi Investment Office , was part of broader engagements in New York this week to advance partnerships with US investors and explore commercial opportunities. “What brings us together is more than just investments. It is the strength of the relationship between the United States and the United Arab Emirates, a connection that has been built over many decades through institutions, shared objectives and, more importantly, people,” said Badr Al Olama, the director of Adio. Mr Al Olama said more than half of the 26 financial institutions that have announced plans to establish a presence in the Abu Dhabi Global Market are US companies. Health care and AI were seen as the two major sectors at Thursday's forum, which also touched on advanced manufacturing, travel and food innovation. Abu Dhabi investment firm MGX in July linked up with BlackRock on a $40 billion digital infrastructure investment. MGX also plans to invest up to 80 per cent of its total portfolio in US projects. The company said at the time that it had raised $49 billion from investors across North America, Asia, Europe and the Gulf for its AI Fund. And this month, Adnoc and AI firm G42 signed a multiyear partnership with OpenAI that would increase the company's presence in the Emirates. “We see the next chapter of Abu Dhabi-US investment extending beyond the companies we already know,” Mr Al Olama said. Among the delegates at the forum in Manhattan were representatives from a Brooklyn-based biotech venture company looking to find co-investors to launch in Abu Dhabi. Another delegate from the Colorado-Abu Dhabi Trade and Investment Council was also hoping to deepen ties between the US state and the emirate. Bilateral trade between the US and UAE totalled an estimated $55.4 billion in 2025, a 16 per cent increase from 2024, according to data from the Office of the US Trade Representative. US goods exported to the UAE totalled $31.4 billion, while it imported $7.7 billion in goods. US services trade with the UAE totalled about $16.3 billion last year. The UAE's Ministry of Investment reported in July that the Emirates had attracted $48.3 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, in a 6 per cent annual increase. Total FDI stock rose to $318.9 billion at the end of last year. The UAE aims to attract $65 billion in annual FDI and raise total FDI stock to $600 billion by 2031. No planned FDI into the UAE have been cancelled this year despite the uncertain outlook caused by the Iran war, The National previously reported. The Emirates also continues to back its $1.4 trillion investment and economic framework with the US. In a March letter to the US-UAE Business Council, Yousef Al Otaiba, UAE ambassador to the US and Minister of State, said the Emirates remains “open for business”. “The past year has reminded us that what defines us is not the challenges we face, but how we respond to them with confidence, clarity of purpose and a continued commitment to progress,” said Amna Almheiri, consul general of the UAE in New York. Despite the regional conflict, Abu Dhabi has continued to attract global capital. The Abu Dhabi Global Market said assets under management grew 54 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026 as Bain Capital, Blue Owl Capital and other major US funds have expanded into the financial centre. More than 1,500 US companies are operating in the Emirates, it said. The inaugural Abu Dhabi Investment Form in New York was held last year, when agreements were signed across digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, financial services and new energy.

events.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
events.summary: Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job. Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension , CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there. Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan County Title Extension regional specialist Member grade Senior member Alma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products. Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business. She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside. “We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.” Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in. Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and the U.N.’s International Telecommunication Union , and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC) , and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP). She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture . An early love of design and problem-solving Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors. As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs. That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings. “I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says. She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career. She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University , in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education. She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016. That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry , in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020. From outreach to extension work After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College , in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator. She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water. She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain , helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park. In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County ’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns. She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds. Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System , a nationwide network run by land-grant universities , schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states. The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture ’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture , managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties. The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program , which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship. Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person. She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says. “We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.
