events.title: "There'll be no hostage-taking": The anti-Jeffries rebellion that failed to materialize
events.summary: The left's campaign to whip up a groundswell of opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) among his members failed in stunning fashion on Wednesday. Why it matters: Fewer than a dozen members voted against Jeffries' nomination for speaker. That bodes well for Jeffries' ability to manage the House going forward, his allies say. "There'll be no hostage taking," Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) told Axios. Driving the news: Jeffries won a resounding victory Wednesday morning when House Democrats met behind closed doors to vote on their nominee for speaker of the House. Out of 264 Democratic House members and non-voting delegates, 251 voted to nominate him, 11 voted against and two did not vote. It was exactly the victory Jeffries' allies had hoped for after Tuesday's announcement that he planned to request a tallied vote rather than being nominated by acclamation. Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Chris Rabb (D-Pa.) and Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) put out a statement shortly after the vote confirming they voted against Jeffries. Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-Texas) also signed on to that statement, but a spokesperson said in a follow-up statement he "narrowly missed the vote" and that his "intended vote was no." Two other members-elect, Don Leonard (D-Ohio) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.), told Axios they also voted no. Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) missed the vote because he was in his district with family following the death of his father, but would have voted for Jeffries, a spokesperson told Axios. Zoom out: Many of the progressives who ultimately voted for Jeffries did so despite a torrent of phone calls and emails from constituents and grassroots activists urging them not to support him. Numerous high-profile progressives had said before the meeting they would vote for Jeffries, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Greg Casar (D-Texas). Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who was floated as a potential challenger to Jeffries, told the Boston Globe she voted for him. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) also voted for him, a spokesperson told Axios. What they're saying: Jayapal said after the vote that Jeffries had "a very strong meeting" with the Congressional Progressive Caucus on Tuesday. "A lot of the issues that matter to us ... on Medicare for All, on immigration, I felt very, very good both about the public direction he's moved in and his commitments to us," she said. "I voted for him, as I have said I was going to do, and I feel like we've been clear about how we're going to continue to need to push." The intrigue: Three "no" votes were still unaccounted for as of Wednesday night. Several progressives who were seen as potential defectors declined to say how they voted. Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), when asked how she voted, told Axios: "I'll say it to Hakeem, who I will talk to first before I talk to anybody in the press." Spokespeople for Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) did not respond to requests for comment. Between the lines: This isn't the posture of a left flank emboldened to take the fight to party leadership next year, as moderates and Jeffries allies gleefully pointed out. "This has been a manufactured crisis," said Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition. "A handful of folks wanted to amplify their voices and perspectives, and it's always been a handful. It was a handful today." What's next: The vote now goes to the House floor, where Jeffries needs 218 votes to secure the gavel when the 120th House convenes for the first time on Jan. 3. He can lose more than 30 votes from his current total — which is unlikely — and still come out on top. "They're not going to hold ... Hakeem hostage. It's gone. Move on from that," centrist Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told Axios.

events.title: Big Republican donor pitches Trump to save $5 billion deal
events.summary: The Scoop The scion of a prominent Republican donor family met with President Donald Trump in an effort to close a $5 billion deal facing fierce regulatory scrutiny. Cintas, an $88 billion uniform and office supply behemoth, has for months been trying to secure regulatory approval to acquire smaller rival UniFirst. Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson is inclined to block the deal , Semafor earlier reported, and the FTC is preparing a “last-rites” meeting, a precursor to suing to stop the merger. Seeking to stave off a lawsuit, Cintas Executive Chairman Scott Farmer met with Trump in recent days, according to an administration official and other people familiar with the matter. Farmer urged the president to intervene and overrule Ferguson, the people said. Cintas and the family that controls it have donated to the president’s 2016 inauguration and helped him raise hundreds of thousands of dollars. A spokesperson for Cintas declined to comment. Spokespeople for the FTC and the White House did not immediately provide comment. The president has indicated that he would defer to Ferguson’s judgment, according to one person familiar with the matter. Cintas has engaged litigation counsel and expects the FTC to sue, according to other people familiar with the situation. In an effort to appease investors souring on the deal, Cintas has indicated to some that it would seek a divestiture package to stave off a lawsuit, according to some of those people, but internally, the company has little appetite to divest, one of the people said. Rohan’s view Corporate America has gotten used to a light regulatory touch around deals, aided by a thriving scene of lobbyists and fixers in Trump’s orbit. Then came the midterms, which delivered a repudiation of both AI and the perceived corporate capture of the White House and regulatory bodies. Those in and around the administration, aware of these shifting tides, have begun to take small, cautious steps to tamp down that perception. The family that controls Cintas has long supported Trump, but their currency in this administration is significantly less valuable than it was a few weeks ago. Administration officials, chastened by the public rebuke, are no longer willing to play ball.

events.title: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
events.summary: Alderperson Pat Dowell, center, chair of the Finance Committee, speaks to reporters following a Chicago City Council meeting on Wednesday. Dowell called for an outside review of the city’s finances. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny. The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances. It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days. The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.  Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on. Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.  But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.) The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.” The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.  “We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.” Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance. Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson presides over a special City Council meeting on Wednesday. Victor Hilitski/WTTW News Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.  “The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.” In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.” Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies. Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors .  Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit. The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”). Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit. “If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.” Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation. S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.” That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.  Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed. events.summary: Anthropic on Wednesday priced its initial public offering at $83 a share , above the price range the startup initially set, as the company’s highly anticipated debut tests the appetite for the AI trade. The debut could draw about $250 million in net retail buying — potentially twice as much as SpaceX’s record of $118 ​million in retail buying . — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
events.summary: Anthropic on Wednesday raised over $81 billion in a long-awaited IPO that valued the Claude maker at over $1 trillion. Why it matters: Wall Street expects the AI boom to continue, despite some recent tumult. Zoom in: Anthropic priced at $83 per share, well above its planned range of $70 to $78 per share. It imputes an initial market cap of $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value of around $1.5 trillion. Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares, but increased it to 980 million shares. The company also could raise significantly more money if underwriters exercise their so-called "greenshoe" option, while Anthropic also will receive $26 billion via a concurrent private placement from tech giants like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft. Allocation decisions were expected to last several hours on Wednesday evening. Context: Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its most recent private round. The apples-to-apples comparison would be with the fully diluted value. SpaceX is the current IPO record-holder having raised $86.25 billion, although that included the greenshoe. What we're watching: Shares are expected to begin trading Thursday, Nov. 19, on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT."

events.title: Republicans warily eye Trump’s meeting with Putin, Xi
events.summary: The News Republican senators are casting a wary eye on President Donald Trump’s high-stakes Thursday summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, where Xi greeted him warmly on the tarmac. The three leaders are expected to hold a trilateral summit on Thursday. “I’d rather see a summit with our NATO members talking about how we’re going to beat Russia,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Semafor when asked about the meeting. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost his primary to Trump-backed challenger Ken Paxton, struck a more measured tone — but added a warning. “It’s important that the president engage with our principal adversaries around the world. I just hope he doesn’t give away too much,” the Texas Republican said. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., similarly expressed support for the diplomatic effort, though he acknowledged it is unlikely to produce results. “I’m glad he’s meeting with them. I know that’s what he does,” Scott said. “But, I don’t expect anything to happen, because these are two thugs that hate our way of life.” Nvidia scandal clouds meeting Others implored Trump to confront Xi over Chinese espionage. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., praised the president for being “the toughest negotiator we’ve ever had,” but said he hoped Trump would raise concerns about Chinese intelligence operations. He pointed to the recent controversy swirling around Nvidia, the chipmaker that saw its CEO Jensen Huang step down last week amid revelations of his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “I hope he pushes President Xi on these Chinese espionage issues. They’re obviously targeted at America,” Banks said. “This is a very serious issue. Why is President Xi allowing for Chinese spies to perform operations against our top American CEOs? Those are big questions.” Tillis also questioned whether the circumstances surrounding the Nvidia scandal made for a productive diplomatic atmosphere. “We’ve sent people on Air Force One to Beijing, only to find out that one of them may have been a Chinese asset spying against us,” Tillis said. “How does that serve as a basis for a good, you know, happy meeting? Let’s be realistic.” Room for Disagreement Still, not all Republicans were skeptical of the summit: Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., praised the “historic meeting,” describing the relationship between the US and China as “too big to fail.” The two countries represent “42% of the world economy” and are “both now nuclear superpowers,” Daines said. “I’m glad he’s doing it.”

events.title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
events.summary: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.” By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it: “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.” “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.” Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again: Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?) Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment. Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post. And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot. Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this. Paresh Dave contributed to this article. events.title: Mississippi senator-elect turns historic win into nationwide Nike offer
events.summary: High school students across the U.S. have a new reason to vie for the top spot in their class: a custom pair of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers, thanks to a request from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom . Why it matters: Colom is putting a fresh spin on academic achievement, turning his historic election into a nationwide incentive for students to hit the books — with a little help from Nike and no taxpayer dollars. What they're saying: Colom initially asked if Nike would celebrate the historic milestone by giving a custom-made version of his favorite sneakers to every Mississippi valedictorian for the 2026-2027 school year. "It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit," he wrote on X . Nike then upped the ante, extending the offer to valedictorians nationwide. "The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea," Nike said. Colom praised Nike for "stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment," and suggested the design honor Hiram Revels, the first Black member of Congress who represented Mississippi. Context: There were more than 23,000 public high schools in the U.S. during the 2020-2021 school year and more than 3,600 private high schools during the 2019-2020 school year, according to the National Center for Education Statistics . A classic pair of Nike Air Force 1s retails for about $115 on Nike's website . Zoom in: In January, Colom will become Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in almost 150 years. The senator-elect pulled off a stunning upset of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the ruby-red state, which hadn't elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. His victory was fueled in part by voters in the Mississippi Delta, where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. What we're watching: What Nike cooks up for the nation's brightest students.

events.title: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways
events.summary: This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China . This is known as remote access. But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place. These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life. As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling. The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”) It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips. It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations. The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead. Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week. The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China. At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter. According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.) Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips. But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them.

events.title: Why Microsoft is investing in recycling the rare earth metals behind modern tech
events.summary: How investment in rare earth recycling is helping advance circular supply chains—and creating opportunities for local communities Nov 17, 2026 | James Lockyer - Director, Climate Innovation Fund, Microsoft The technologies powering our economy depend on materials that are too valuable to use only once. Rare earth elements are key ingredients for the permanent magnets found in electric vehicles, wind turbines, electronics, and datacenter equipment. Yet recovering these materials when products reach the end of their useful lives remains a challenge. At Microsoft, we see an opportunity to help change that. Through our Climate Innovation Fund, we invest in companies developing solutions that can advance sustainability while addressing the practical needs of businesses and communities. One of those companies is https://www.cyclicmaterials.com/ , which is building technology and infrastructure to recover rare earths and other critical materials from end-of-life products. Our new video highlights Cyclic’s work and the opportunity to build more circular supply chains. It also comes at an important moment for the company: the opening of its first commercial-scale rare earth magnet recycling facility in Mesa, Arizona. A milestone in bringing circular innovation to scale Moving from a promising technology to a commercial facility is a significant step for any emerging company. It requires engineering, capital, reliable sources of material, and customers for the recovered products. Cyclic’s new Mesa facility, which opened in September, marks that transition. The facility has the capacity to process up to 25,000 metric tons of magnet-bearing end-of-life products each year, creating a domestic destination for materials that might otherwise leave the country as waste. Using Cyclic’s proprietary MagCycle technology, the facility mechanically separates magnet material from end-of-life products. It also recovers metals including copper, aluminum, and steel for reuse in manufacturing. The recovered magnet material is the starting point for a further processing step. Cyclic’s REEPure technology then recovers rare earth oxides that can re-enter the supply chain for new permanent magnets. Together, these technologies offer a way to keep valuable materials in circulation and diversify the sources available to manufacturers, creating a source of rare earth elements that reduces the world’s reliance on traditional mining. By mining “above ground”, Cyclic Materials is building a circular supply with lower carbon footprint and reducing waste. Investing in the technologies circularity requires Microsoft’s investment in Cyclic through the Climate Innovation Fund reflects our interest in advancing a circular economy, including new approaches to recovering rare earths from end-of-life hard drives. Hard drives illustrate why this work matters. Traditional disposal processes prioritize secure data destruction and the recovery of certain metals, but rare earth magnets can be lost along the way. Cyclic has developed technology specifically designed to separate magnet-containing components for recovery while allowing the rest of the drive to follow established disposal processes. For Microsoft, supporting innovation like this is part of a broader effort to help promising climate technologies move toward commercial scale. Investment alone is not enough. New solutions also need opportunities to demonstrate performance, develop commercial relationships, and become part of established supply chains. Mesa is an encouraging example of that progress. Building opportunity alongside infrastructure The value of this infrastructure extends beyond the materials it recovers. Operating advanced recycling facilities also requires skilled people and creates opportunities for the communities around them. Cyclic’s next planned US campus, in McBee, South Carolina, will bring magnet recovery and rare earth processing together on one site. Operations are expected to begin in 2028, creating more than 90 highly skilled jobs. For a small community, an investment like this can have significance beyond the facility itself. It can create opportunities for local suppliers and businesses, support workforce development, and provide a foundation for further industrial investment. Realizing those benefits takes sustained engagement with local partners as projects develop. Progress worth celebrating—and building on Recycling may not meet every critical-material need. But it can become an increasingly important part of a more resilient supply chain—one that recognizes end-of-life products as a resource, rather than simply a disposal challenge. We congratulate the Cyclic Materials team on the opening of Mesa. It is a milestone worth celebrating: technology moving into commercial deployment, valuable materials finding a path back into use, and new opportunities taking shape for workers and communities. Watch the video above to learn more about Cyclic Materials and its approach to building circular supply chains. events.title: Microsoft unveils 7 AI models for coding, image editing, voice and more
events.summary: Models Transcribe Turn audio into precise transcripts Voice Generate custom voice from text Realtime Natural speech-to-speech conversations Image Generate images from text Code Fast, lightweight agentic coding Cyber Agentic defense at codebase scale Thinking Expert reasoning for complex problems Custom Models Models tuned for your needs Seven new world-class models at scalable price-performance Nov 17, 2026 · Announcements · Ignite At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability. But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work. That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance. MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. MAI Code 2 Flash shows comparable performance GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. MAI Image 2.7 is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Maia 200 , Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt. Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7 Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost. Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools. MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price. Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price. We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work. MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here . MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . The best image and transcription models in the world MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here . MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here . Dragon Copilot Transcribe , built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians. The leading Decision model in the market Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model. And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data? We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives. Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights : models under your control. Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment. You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.

events.title: Hakeem Jeffries wins big in speaker nomination vote
events.summary: House Democrats resoundingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning in a 251-11 vote. The large Democratic majority gives him plenty of wiggle room as he faces the next hurdle to becoming the first Black speaker on Jan. 3, when the full House votes. The few votes against Jeffries largely came from the progressive left of the caucus, and he’s projecting unity. “We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters. Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., won the day’s only contested election for vice chair in a 143-118 vote over Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif. The caucus will continue elections tomorrow, with Reps. Maxwell Frost of Florida, Eric Sorensen of Illinois, Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California, and Sarah McBride of Delaware competing for three DPCC co-chair spots. Jeffries has plenty of big decisions to make now that the top leadership slate has been assembled. He’ll have to select a DCCC chair, with Reps. Steven Horsford of Nevada, Lizzie Fletcher of Texas, Brad Schneider of Illinois, and Greg Stanton of Arizona all in the mix. The caucus is also weighing whether to implement committee leadership term limits and what to do about the select committee on China and calls for a special panel on AI. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Cyberattacks are getting faster. Here’s how Microsoft is fighting back
events.summary: Security for the agentic era, powered by Microsoft Perception A new cyber stack, built to fight AI with AI Delivering agentic security at Microsoft Ignite Changing how security work gets done A year ago, finding a serious, exploitable vulnerability was slow and expensive work done by elite security researchers. That’s no longer true. Over the past 12 months, frontier AI models have become remarkably good at discovering and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and similar levels of capability are quickly becoming available in open weights models with limited cyber guardrails. Attacks that once required specialized resources are now within reach of almost anyone. We saw what that looks like in a single week this fall when PHP disclosed two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, flaws that let an attacker take control of a server with a single request over the internet. 1 At the time of disclosure, tens of millions of internet-facing PHP services were running affected versions. Nearly two weeks later, about 29 million services remained vulnerable. Behind those servers are banks, healthcare providers, energy companies, and much of the infrastructure the internet runs on. And that same day brought five other major disclosures across the industry. Turning a flaw like the PHP one into a working attack once took a specialist team months. Within roughly a day of PHP2Shell’s disclosure, security researchers had developed a working, weaponized exploit. By the following week, that research had expanded to cover additional PHP versions and configurations. The time from discovery to exploit is shrinking from months to minutes. The physics of cybersecurity are changing, and fast. AI is amplifying risk. Attackers can now find and exploit gaps faster than defenders can close them. Attacks are becoming fully automated. AI has moved from assisting attackers, to executing their tasks, to planning and running entire campaigns on its own. Agents are the new insiders. While not inherently malicious, they perform tasks and business workflows at machine speed, around the clock, and have broad access to data, apps, tools, and other agents. Like any insider, they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. What we built for humans does not scale for AI. Frontier Transformation starts with business outcomes and a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. To help organizations bring their ideas to life and innovate safely in the agentic era, we need a new cyber stack, built for agentic security. The Microsoft cyber stack has three layers: Signals, sensors, and actuators . This foundational layer is powered by sensors and actuators in Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Sentinel, the network, the operating system, the browser, and our hyperscale cloud. Sensors tell you something is wrong. Actuators let you do something about it: contain a device on the network, revoke an identity’s access, or block an agent at the authorization layer. And because we know we’re not the only security solution provider in your environment, we connect to the wider ecosystem through more than 500 connectors. Together, Microsoft and partner sources produce more than 165 trillion signals a day, 2 which, enriched by Microsoft and customer threat intelligence, fuel the context layer. Context . This layer organizes those signals, together with each customer’s own environment, into agent-ready, real-time understanding of the digital estate that is optimized for precision, recall, and token efficiency. Agents, harness, and models . On top are specialized security agents that work together as teams through playbooks, directed by a harness, and a multi-model approach that uses the right model for each task, designed to ensure effective and efficient security outcomes, at scale. At Microsoft Ignite 2026 , we’re delivering innovation across every layer of the stack. It starts with Microsoft Perception , now generally available . Perception brings the top of the stack together. It orchestrates red, blue, and green team agents through playbooks, working together in a closed loop to deliver security outcomes. Red team agents simulate attacks from an attacker’s perspective before a breach occurs. Blue team agents detect, triage alerts, and investigate attacks, freeing analysts to focus on the critical decisions that matter most. Green team agents fix and remediate. Perception is built to help security teams move at machine speed, drive outcomes rather than tasks, and automate while staying in control. Your team sets the guardrails and signs off on high-impact actions, and automated triggers launch playbooks when an incident meets the criteria you set. New cost management dashboards and a cost estimator help you track AI usage, forecast spending, and connect costs to measurable security outcomes. Agents are only as good as what they can see and what they can do. That’s why we are investing as much in the foundation as in the layers above it. Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , generally available for core capabilities , is part of that foundation. ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) capabilities, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), threat intelligence, and threat protection and disruption together so you can start your journey to the agentic security operations center (SOC). Eligible Defender Suite, Microsoft 365 E5, and Microsoft 365 E7 customers receive all Microsoft Sentinel SIEM features, 90-day default data retention for Defender data, more than 500 connectors, reduced ingestion rates, and a built-in data lake. The complete breadth of SIEM capabilities is now in preview. Read on to learn how Microsoft Perception, ISOC in Defender, and new capabilities across the stack work together to help customers secure their foundations, secure agentic insiders, and defend with agents. Defending against AI-speed attacks starts with closing the doors attackers walk through first, and the scale of that work is increasing. In 2026, more than 96,000 vulnerabilities 3 have been published to the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) Program, more than double 2024’s roughly 40,000 and more than 20 times the level of 2010, 4 driven in part by AI-assisted vulnerability discovery tools. Yet only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were remediated in 2025, as remediation typically extends into weeks and months. AI finds those gaps faster than teams can close them. Today we’re announcing new capabilities to help. Strengthen your security foundation with Perception .

events.title: Islam will overtake Christianity as world's largest religion by 2035: Pew
events.summary: Data: Pew Research ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035, according to Pew Research Center projections released Wednesday. Why it matters: The shift has less to do with people converting to Islam and more to do with who's having more kiddos , a demographic trend poised to reshape the world's religious makeup as Christianity's center of gravity moves to Africa. By the numbers: Muslims are projected to gain 1.6 billion people through births exceeding deaths from 2020 to 2070, according to new Pew data released Wednesday. Christians are expected to gain 792 million people through natural population change. From 2020 to 2025, Muslim women had an average fertility rate of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women. For all other women, the average was 1.6. What they're saying: "These religious figures are driven by demographic change," David Voas, a University College London professor who researches secularization, tells Axios. He says the countries growing the fastest — in North Africa, the Middle East, Near East and South Asia — have a relatively high Muslim population, so naturally Islam would eventually be the most populous religion. Zoom in: The U.S. is expected to lose more Christians than any other country by 2070, even as Christianity grows globally. The U.S. had the world's largest Christian population in 2020, at 217 million. By 2070, that number is expected to drop to 174 million. Meanwhile, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is expected to have nearly 300 million Christians by 2070, far surpassing the U.S. By then, 54% of the world's Christians are projected to live in sub-Saharan Africa. "The center of gravity of Christianity has been shifting towards the global south," Voas says. "Traditionally, we tended to think of Christianity as being a kind of Western religion … but of course Christianity was taken to Africa and around the world, and Africa is now growing faster than anywhere else." Between the lines: Both Christianity and Islam are expected to lose more followers than they gain through religious switching, including people leaving religion entirely. But Christianity's losses will be far larger. Zoom out: Islam becoming the world's largest religion doesn't necessarily mean a dramatic shift in global political or cultural power, Voas says. "I would not see any major change in the balance of either political or cultural power, at least in the medium term," he said, adding that it's possible some will assimilate to the local culture and expectations. "There's some wild talk about Europe being taken over by Muslims and so on. That is not going to happen in any foreseeable future." The bottom line: Islam may soon claim the top spot, but the numbers don't necessarily translate into a seismic shift in global influence.
